MitCad document API

MitCad document API

The application and mitcad-cli drive a document only through JSON: Document::command, query, preview, run_script and report (core/model-api/src/lib.rs, exposed to C++ by core/ffi/src/lib.rs). Geometry comes back as Shape handles (body_shape, profile_shape, preview_body_shape, preview_tool_shape), so a new command needs no change to the C++ bridge. A rejected command or query raises an error (rust::Error in C++) with a message for the user and leaves the document unchanged. The model’s design (recompute, caches, file format, threads) is in docs/architecture.md.

Identities and names

WhatFormNotes
feature"F7"assigned when created and saved in the design file; its timeline position is separate
body"F7.b0"the creating feature and a number; its display name (Body1) is separate and can be renamed
component, occurrence"C2", "O3"C0 is the root component; names Plate and Plate:2 are separate (see Components and occurrences)
sketch point, curve"p4", "c3"one id space per sketch; sketch.add_rectangle makes lines c<k>..c<k+3> (line i from corner i to i + 1, corners counter-clockwise from the anchor) and then their corner points, a circle a curve and its centre
sketch constraint, dimension"k2"one id space per sketch
sketch text"t5"numbered with the points and curves
glyph contour of a text"t5.g2.c1"contour 1 of character 2 (spaces and line breaks counted) of text t5; usable wherever a curve id can stand in a name (r{t5.g2.c0}, F3:side(t5.g2.c0)#1, #k numbering the contour’s pieces)
profile region"r{c1[c4,c2],c2[c1,c3],c3[c2,c4],c4[c3,c1]}"the sorted segments of its outer boundary; a circle alone is "r{c5}"; an end where several curves meet is c2+c5, a free end -
face"F3:side(c1[c4,c2])", "F3:end(r{…})#1"named by the feature that made it; each feature type lists its face names below; #k numbers the pieces of a split face
edge"E{<face>|<face>}"the two faces that meet there, sorted by text; #k when several edges lie between the same faces
vertex"V{<face>|<face>|…}"the faces that meet there, sorted

The grammar is in core/model-base/src/topo.rs. A reference without #k means every piece: "E{F2:end(…)|F2:side(c1[c4,c2])}" rounds both halves of an edge a cut divided. A segment c3[c2,c4] is the piece of curve c3 between the curves c2 and c4, in the curve’s own direction.

Faces, edges and vertices a sketch change renamed

A side face is named by its segment, so a sketch edit that gives the segment another neighbour renames the face although it is the same face: deleting the arc c72 at a corner and adding the circle c103 there turns F31:side(c71[c104,c72]) into F31:side(c71[c104,c103]). Features find such faces, edges and vertices again (mitcad#272, core/model/src/features/renamed.rs), wherever they resolve a name on a body: fillet and chamfer edges, faces and reference faces, the faces of shell, draft, offset, delete, replace and split face, tools and targets on faces, extents to faces, sketch planes and projections, hole placements, threads, loft sections, sweep guide surfaces and paths of edges, patterns of faces, construction geometry, alignments, joints and assembly constraints:

  1. A name that finds what it names is used as it is.
  2. A face name that finds no face finds the faces of the same feature and role whose key has the most curves in common with it: a side face’s segment must have the same own curve (then the most end curves, those at the same end first), a region key the most shared curves; names in keys (a fillet’s edge, a shell’s face) compare the same way. A reference takes the best match only when it is the only one (the pieces #k of one face count once); a tie fails with the candidates: F31:side(c71[c104,c72]) is ambiguous after a sketch change: F31:side(c71[c103,c72]), F31:side(c71[c104,c103]).
  3. An edge name E{A|B} that finds no edge finds A and B each by rule 2 and takes the edges between the faces found: one with #k, all without. Of tied faces only those that meet the other face count; several edges so found fail as a tie does.
  4. A vertex finds each of its faces by rule 2.
  5. A name with nothing like it fails as before (the body has no face …).

A modelled thread’s pieces are renumbered when the thread gets more or fewer turns (A modelled thread’s end pieces, mitcad#1231). For their names:

  • An edge name between a piece of a thread (<f>:thread(<face>)#n, <f>:low_thread(<face>)#k, <f>:high_thread(<face>)#k) and another face that finds no edge, also where the piece still exists elsewhere on the thread, finds the edge with the same #k between a piece of the same thread and that face (the other face by rules 1 and 2). Where both ends of the thread meet that face, the end the name means counts: a name from an end means that end; a number along the thread the end whose end piece’s number now lies nearer to it (the count changes by less than the thread is long); a number below half the pieces’ count, of the order before mitcad#490, tells no end. Of several pieces at that end, the one nearest the end. A name counted from one end never finds the other end; when nothing tells the end, or the edges found are several, the name is not found (with suggestions, below).
  • A face name in a key (a chamfer’s or a fillet’s face of such an edge, F4:chamfer(E{…|F3:thread(…)#22}#0)) takes another piece of the same thread as like it (rule 2), least alike, and a key’s edge #0 as like the same edge without a number (one edge where there were two), less alike than the same number.
  • A face name of a piece that is gone finds the thread’s piece only when the thread has one: a face alone says nothing of its neighbours.

The feature warns as for a sketch change (edge E{…#22…} found as E{…high_thread(…)#0…} after a change in Thread1), and Auto Fix writes the new name into the definition.

The feature keeps the name it was given (undo and the comparison of versions see no change) and succeeds with a warning (timeline status warning, the feature’s warnings), shown in the timeline and the browser as other warnings: edge E{…c72…} found as E{…c103…} after a change in Sketch10 (the sketch of the profiles of the feature that made the face). Its notice says it in plain words, “an edge found again after a change in Sketch10” (one notice for several edges: “2 edges found again …”), the names its places (Notices, mitcad#1334). Profile regions and face appearances follow the same rule (Profile references after a sketch change, Appearances of faces).

Suggestions for an edge that is not found

An edge name that finds no edge by these rules still fails (mitcad#1187). Its error (the body has no edge E{…}, edge E{…} no longer exists after Chamfer1, edge E{…} does not exist because Fillet1 failed) is followed by at most five existing edges of the body that share one of the name’s faces as rules 1 and 2 find them, each with the face it has in place of the name’s other face, and how many more there are:

edge E{F2:end(r{…})|F2:side(c1[c4,c2])} no longer exists after Chamfer1;
existing edges of body F2.b0 that share a face with it (suggestions only,
not applied): E{F2:end(r{…})|F3:chamfer(E{…})} (F3:chamfer(E{…}) instead
of F2:side(c1[c4,c2])), E{F2:side(c1[c4,c2])|F3:chamfer(E{…})}
(F3:chamfer(E{…}) instead of F2:end(r{…})), … and 3 more
  • They are suggestions only: the feature fails, its stored reference is not changed and no feature takes a suggested edge. Pick one and edit the feature. A name found again by rule 3 (one edge) is used with its warning, and a tie fails with its candidates, as above.
  • Best first: edges between the same two faces (another #k), then, for a missing piece of a modelled thread, the edges between another piece of that thread and the name’s other face (mitcad#1231: the thread’s pieces renumbered, before the edges that keep the piece number), then edges whose other face was made on the name’s other face (a chamfer or fillet of the edge, an offset of the face), then edges whose other face is like it by rule 2, then the rest; each group in text order.
  • None when neither face of the name is found (a face found only as a tie counts as not found), when the faces found have no edges, or when the geometry kernel cannot list edges.
  • The lookup reads the body’s edge list once, reads only the names that hold a found face, and keeps only the best five: a large body’s edges never fill the message.
  • The tangent_chains query’s error for an edge the body lacks lists them the same way.

Values

Every length or angle of a definition is a parameter. In commands a value is a parameter name ("d3"), a number in millimetres or radians, or an expression ("d1 / 2 + 5 mm", "30 deg"; syntax and unit rules in core/expr/src/lib.rs).

  • A number or an expression creates a dimension parameter owned by the feature (the next free d<n>, with a comment like Extrude1 distance). Editing a feature with a number or an expression in a slot whose parameter the feature owns changes that parameter instead.

  • An expression in a length slot reads its bare numbers in the document’s length unit, as evaluate reads them (mitcad#1452): in a design in inches "0.875" is 22.225 mm, for a new parameter and for the slot’s own one alike. A slot’s own length parameter made in another length unit (before set_units changed the document’s) takes the document’s unit with a new expression, so "0.25 * 2" typed into a dimension made in millimetres is 12.7 mm, not 0.5 mm; a number keeps its unit, and a parameter a slot names by name is never changed. JSON numbers stay millimetres in every design: a client that takes lengths in the design’s unit converts them, or writes them as texts ("0.875", "0.875 in"); positions (corner, center, at) take numbers only. Tests: inch_entry_tests (core/model-tests/api).

  • New dimension parameters show lengths in the document’s length unit (set_units) and angles in degrees. A slot whose name ends in angle (size.angle, extent.angle, dimensions[k3].angle) is an angle, every other slot a length unless it is one of the unitless slots below. A slot refuses a parameter of another kind; a unitless parameter’s number is used as it is.

  • Unitless slots (counts, factors, fractions; mitcad#662): a number or an expression there makes a unitless parameter (3, never 3 mm), in every document unit:

    • counts: a pattern’s quantity (rectangular direction1.quantity, direction2.quantity and direction3.quantity, circular (and its axis2.quantity), path and scale patterns), a pattern’s or mirror’s scale_groups and scale_copies and scales[i].groups and scales[i].copies, a gear’s teeth and mate_teeth, a pulley’s teeth and set_screws.count, a printable bearing’s element_count, a boss’s ribs;
    • factors: a pattern’s or mirror’s scale and scales[i].scale, a scale’s scale.factor, scale.x, scale.y and scale.z, a sweep’s end_scale, a motion link’s coupling.ratio, a gear’s profile_shift, a sheet’s allowance.k;
    • fractions, ratios and weights: a construction plane’s or point’s position along a path without physical (definition.fraction; with physical it is the length definition.distance), extent.fraction and every other slot whose name starts with fraction, a helix’s revolutions, slots ending in weight (tangency_weight).

    An expression there that gives a length or an angle is refused with what to write instead: d1 / 3 gives “the result is a length (5 mm); for a count write d1 / 3 mm”. A count that is not a whole number is an error, never rounded, and says to use floor(…) or round(…). Designs saved before keep these parameters in a length unit, whose value in millimetres the slot read as its number. On load, a slot’s own parameter that only unitless slots of its feature use, that no other parameter refers to and that no configuration sets becomes unitless with that number (its expression stays when it gives the same number without a unit, else the number replaces it, with a load warning when the expression named parameters). Any other parameter there (a user parameter in a length unit) keeps its unit with a load warning; the slot reads its number as before and keeps it on edits until it is changed.

  • Parameters a feature owns are deleted with it, unless another feature or parameter still uses them (they then become user parameters).

  • Decimal point or comma: "1,5 mm" is "1.5 mm". A comma directly between two digits is a decimal comma (also ,5 and 5,); any other comma separates function arguments (max(a, b), max(1, 5)), and ; always does. max(1,5) is therefore max(1.5), and its error says to write max(1; 5). No thousands separators: 1,000 is 1 and 1 000 an error. Parameters keep their expressions with decimal points, in the design file and in the parameters query.

  • Inch and foot marks (mitcad#1531): a " (or '') right after a number, spaces allowed between, is in, and a ' is ft: ".875\"" is 22.225 mm in any design, "3' 6\"" is 42 in (feet and inches add up). Only a number takes a mark; elsewhere a quote starts a text. Expressions are kept as typed.

  • name = expression in a slot ("width = 40", "width = d1 * 2") names the slot’s parameter as it sets it, in the same command and undo step (mitcad#231): the parameter the feature owns there (or the one the slot uses, when it already has that name) is renamed and takes the expression; without one, a new dimension parameter of that name is made. A name another parameter has, or an invalid name, rejects the command. A single = after a word is this form; expressions compare with ==. Renames by any command keep configurations, bindings and the comments on a parameter in step.

  • Removing a name (mitcad#1577): remove_parameter_name gives a parameter a dimension or a feature owns (or a driven dimension’s reference) its automatic name back, the next free d<n> as a new dimension parameter would get (d1 again when nothing took it meanwhile). It is a rename: the expressions and limits that use the name are rewritten (the result’s rewritten lists them), configurations, bindings and comments follow, features keep the parameter (they refer to it by id), all in one undo step (Remove Name width), and it is refused for what a rename refuses. A name that is automatic already (d3) stays, with no undo step; a user parameter has no automatic name and is refused (gap is a user parameter: …). The sketch’s dimension editor runs it when the name = before the value is deleted (app/COMMANDS.md). Tests: remove_name_tests (core/model-tests/sketch-refs).

  • A sketch dimension’s value that uses the dimension’s own parameter (mitcad#1535), by its name or through other parameters (BuckleDiameter * 2 in the dimension of BuckleDiameter), keeps that parameter, with its name, expression and value, as a user parameter, and the dimension takes the value as a new parameter of its own (the next free d<n>; Slot = BuckleDiameter * 2 names it Slot), in the same sketch.set_dimension and undo step. Every expression, configuration and comment that names the parameter keeps it. The bare name (BuckleDiameter) only moves the parameter to the user parameters and makes the dimension use it, at the same value. The result’s user_parameters lists what moved (name, dimension, and the parameter the dimension uses now) and its notes say it (BuckleDiameter is now a user parameter (5 mm); dimension k3 is d7 = BuckleDiameter * 2), and its note_messages in plain words for a person (…; the dimension is d7 = BuckleDiameter * 2, mitcad#1612: a sketch command’s warnings and notes are the agents’, with ids, and warning_messages and note_messages beside them what the application shows). A parameter that another dimension of the sketch uses as well stays the sketch’s: the dimension only gets a parameter of its own. BuckleDiameter = BuckleDiameter * 2 (the own name on the left) names and sets the own parameter as before, so it is refused as a circular reference, as any parameter’s own name in its own expression is (set_parameter). A 3D sketch’s dimensions follow the same rule in sketch3d.set_dimension, with the same result fields (mitcad#1550).

  • A feature value that uses the slot’s own parameter (mitcad#1536) follows the same rule in edit_feature: depth * 2 in the distance of an extrusion whose distance is depth (its own parameter) keeps depth, with its name, expression and value, as a user parameter, and the distance takes the value as a new parameter of the extrusion (the next free d<n>; height = depth * 2 names it height), in the same command and undo step. Unlike a sketch dimension’s, the bare own name (depth) leaves the slot as it is: definitions read back from the model (the feature query’s def) name their own parameters so. A parameter another slot of the feature or another feature uses as well stays the feature’s: the slot only gets a parameter of its own. The result’s user_parameters lists what moved (name, slot such as extent.distance, and the parameter the slot uses now) and its notes say it (depth is now a user parameter (10 mm); Extrude1 distance is d3 = depth * 2); a preview of the edit says it in its infos and moves nothing. depth = depth * 2 is a circular reference, as above.

  • A driven sketch dimension has a read-only reference parameter (mitcad#231): the next free d<n>, commented Sketch1 length (driven), kind reference in the parameters query, owned by the sketch. Its value is what the dimension measures, set each time the sketch solves; its expression is that value as a number. It can be renamed and used in expressions; set_parameter with a value, an expression or a unit is refused. sketch.set_dimension on the dimension makes it driving, and the reference becomes its model parameter under the same name; sketch.set_driven makes a driving dimension’s own parameter its reference, keeping the name.

  • A reference’s value is known only after its sketch: only features after the sketch in the timeline may use it, directly or through other parameters’ expressions, and the sketch’s own driving dimensions and pattern spacings and angles (next items). A use by a feature before the sketch, by a parameter such a feature uses, or by another value of the sketch itself (an offset’s distance, a text, its placement; a 3D sketch’s patterns too) rejects the command with an error naming the reference, its dimension, the sketch and, for a value of the sketch, that value in words (d3 is what the driven dimension k7 of Sketch1 measures: Sketch1's offset distance cannot use it (through parameter d8); only its dimensions, pattern spacings and angles, and the features after Sketch1 can, mitcad#2057); so does a reorder_feature that would make one (can_reorder tells). A parameter no feature uses may use it.

  • A driving dimension may use a driven dimension of its own sketch (mitcad#1116), directly or through parameters ((d1 - d2) / 2), when it cannot move what that driven dimension measures. The sketch then solves in stages: without the dimensions that use references first, where the driven dimensions they cannot move measure; then with those users at the measured values, and so on until the whole sketch solves. A recompute takes changed measurements through all stages, and the reference stays read-only. A dimension can move what a driven one measures when their geometry is connected through constraints, dimensions, patterns or offsets by entities that are not already fully constrained (or fixed) without the dimensions that use references. A command that makes such a dependency, directly or through other driven dimensions, is refused with the dimensions and parameters named (Sketch1: k6 (d2) uses d3 and can move what the driven dimension k7 (d3) measures, so d3 would depend on itself. …); so is an edit that later connects them (removing the constraint that fixed the measured geometry). A value whose measurement the whole solve still moves fails the sketch with what moved it.

  • A sketch pattern’s spacing (either direction) or circular angle may use a driven dimension of its own sketch (mitcad#2057), directly (sketch.edit_pattern with "spacing": ["d5", 10]) or through parameters (its own d6 set to d5), as a driving dimension does: the pattern is solved in the stages above, left out of the first ones (its copies stay where they are) and put back once the driven dimensions it uses are measured, so the copies are placed by the measured value and follow it in the same recompute. A pattern that uses a reference moves only its copies: the originals need not be fully constrained. A pattern whose copies can move what a driven dimension it uses measures (a driven dimension that measures a copy, a copy constrained or dimensioned to the measured geometry) is a circular dependency, refused the same way with the pattern named (Sketch1: the pattern k8 (d3, d4) uses d3 and can move what the driven dimension k7 (d3) measures, so d3 would depend on itself. A pattern's spacing or angle can use …), at the command and in a recompute. Pattern counts are plain numbers, not values. A 3D sketch’s planar patterns keep the rule above.

  • Deleting a driven dimension deletes its reference unless a parameter or a feature still uses it; deleting its sketch likewise. A reference still used becomes a user parameter with its last value as a fixed number.

  • A driven dimension’s reference in a sketch definition (add_feature, edit_feature: {"type": "length", "line": "c1", "driven": true, "reference": "height"}) names its reference parameter (mitcad#250): the sketch’s own reference keeps it; a user parameter becomes the sketch’s reference (its expression its value until the sketch measures it, the reference’s comment when it had none), and the ordering rule above applies to its uses; anything else is left alone and the dimension gets the next free d<n>. The .f3d, .ipt and FreeCAD imports give a driven dimension the source file’s parameter of it this way (a named FreeCAD reference constraint’s, where the dimension measures the constraint’s value), and add the sketch without these references when the model refuses one.

  • An angle of more than one turn where one turn is the most (mitcad#714) warns: a move’s or move face’s rotation (transform.angle), a revolve’s angles, a draft’s, a chamfer’s angle, an extrusion’s tapers, a hole’s taper, countersink and tip angles and a construction plane’s angle. A JSON number there is radians, so "angle": 90 meant as degrees turns by 5156.6°; the feature succeeds with the warning Move1 angle: 90 is read as radians (5156.6°); write "90 deg" for degrees (in its warnings, the timeline’s error, and the add_feature or edit_feature result’s warnings), or a failed feature’s error ends with it. A value that is not a short number in radians ("720 deg") says Revolve1 angle: 720° is more than one turn. Only a number as typed warns, with or without a sign and a unit (90, -7, "450 deg", mitcad#1092): an angle computed from parameters or functions ("d1", "d660 + step", "d1 + 30 deg"), such as construction planes stepping round an axis, may pass a turn without a warning. Helices, coils, a sweep’s twist and other slots that take several turns never warn (parameters::one_turn_slot, recompute::turn_warnings).

  • Parameters are evaluated in dependency order. Cycles, unknown names, syntax errors and unit mismatches reject the command. Renaming a parameter rewrites the expressions that use it (features refer to parameters by id).

  • A parameter change recomputes only the features whose inputs changed value; a parameter command that changes no value (a rename, a comment, an equivalent expression) recomputes nothing.

Defaults are metric (docs/architecture.md): leaving out a unit means millimetres (degrees for angles). A new document and a design file without units are in mm and degrees, and bare numbers in expressions take the document’s unit. export writes STEP and IGES in mm (unit), import_file reads STL and OBJ in mm (unit_mm 1), sketch.import_dxf reads a drawing that names no unit in mm; a file’s own units (STEP, IGES, a DXF’s $INSUNITS, an .f3d design’s) are kept. A thread or tapped hole without a standard is ISO metric. Densities are g/cm³ (a body without a material has none, and no mass, mitcad#1817), masses kg, moments of inertia kg mm². Tests: api::metric_defaults_tests, tools/ui-units-test.sh.

Formulas in the style of spreadsheets

Expressions also take the syntax and functions of spreadsheet formulas (mitcad#663), as a superset: every expression that parsed before parses and evaluates the same. The full rules are in core/expr/src/lib.rs (grammar, rules 13 to 22); tests core/expr/src/tests.rs.

  • Function names and PI are case-insensitive (FLOOR, Floor, floor; pi); parameter names, units and E are not. A parameter name that is a function or PI in any case (Max, pi, Sum) is reserved: add_parameter and rename_parameter refuse it, and a design file or an import with such a parameter renames it (Max_1, a load warning or an import report row) and rewrites the expressions, configuration rows and features that use it.
  • Inside parentheses a single = compares (if(GridX = 6; a; b)), the same as ==. At the top level of a slot, name = expression still names the slot’s parameter.
  • Rounding: round(x; [digits]), roundup, rounddown, trunc(x; [digits]), int(x); to a step floor(x; [step]), ceiling(x; [step]) (and ceil), mround(x; step): floor(d1; 0.5 mm). Digits count in the default unit of the value’s dimension; a step has the value’s dimension and the result keeps it. round, floor and ceil with one argument are unchanged.
  • Integers: mod(a; b) (sign of b; % stays the remainder with the sign of a), quotient(a; b), even(x), odd(x). Aggregates: sum, average, median (one dimension), product (dimensions multiply). clamp(x; low; high).
  • Choice: ifs(c1; v1; ...), switch(x; k1; v1; ...; [default]), choose(i; v1; ...), iferror(x; fallback) (division by zero, a value out of range, no match; not unknown names or unit errors).
  • let(name1; value1; ...; result): names local to the formula, not parameter references (a parameter’s dependencies do not list them); a name may not be a parameter’s.
  • value(x; "mm"): the number of x in the unit, unitless (15 for d1 = 15 mm). Quoted text is accepted only there.
  • radians(x), degrees(x): an angle from a plain number in degrees or radians, so sin(radians(30)) is 0.5. PI() is PI.
  • Texts in quotes, &, concat, text, left, right and len (mitcad#664): see Text parameters. A text is never a number: a slot that takes a number refuses one.

References to geometry

Every feature or query that takes a plane, an axis, a point, a face, a body or sketch curves takes it in one form (GeomRef, core/model/src/features/geom_ref.rs):

JSONMeaning
"xy", "xz", "yz"origin planes; frames XY: x = +X, y = +Y; XZ: x = +X, y = -Z (normal +Y); YZ: x = -Z, y = +Y (normal +X)
"x", "y", "z", "origin"origin axes and point
"F5"the datum (plane, axis or point) of construction feature F5
{"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:end(r{c5})"}a face; a plane when planar (outward normal), an axis when a cylinder, cone or torus
{"body": "F2.b0", "edge": "E{…|…}"}an edge; an axis (straight: along the edge’s curve; circular: through the centre) or a point (a circle’s centre, a line’s middle)
{"body": "F2.b0", "vertex": "V{…|…|…}"}a vertex; a point
{"body": "F2.b0"}a body (a face feature’s tool)
{"sketch": "F1", "curve": "c4"}a sketch curve; a line is an axis from its start to its end, a circle or an arc (where an axis is wanted: pattern, align, move) the axis through its centre normal to the sketch. "curves": ["c1", "c3"] several, neither all (a face feature’s tool)
{"sketch": "F1", "point": "p3"}a sketch point
{"origin": [x, y, z], "normal": [x, y, z], "x_axis": [x, y, z]}a fixed plane (x_axis optional)
{"origin": [x, y, z], "direction": [x, y, z]}a fixed axis
{"point": [x, y, z]}a fixed point
  • Frames: an origin plane has the frame above. A planar face and a fixed plane without x_axis have the model origin projected onto the plane as origin and the model X axis projected as x axis (Y when the plane faces ±X), with the face’s outward normal; sketches on faces, mirror planes, primitives and extents to faces all use it.
  • The axes of cylinders, cones, tori and circular edges point along their largest component (+Z for a hole along Z).
  • A face name may name the pieces of a split face when they lie on one surface; an edge or vertex name must name one (#k).
  • Older files’ forms with a "type" ({"type": "origin_plane", "plane": "yz", "offset": d}, {"type": "origin", …}, {"type": "plane" | "face" | "edge" | "vertex" | "construction" | "fixed" | "sketch_curve" | "line" | "body" | "sketch", …}; a face without body means the feature’s own body) are read and saved in the forms above.

Paths

A path (of a sweep, a pipe or a path pattern, a sweep’s guide rail, a loft’s centre line or rails, a rib’s or web’s curves, a construction plane or point along a path) is a PathRef:

JSONMeaning
{"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1", "c4"]}curves of a sketch (any order), joined end to end
{"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1"], "chain": true}also every curve joined to them end to end (construction curves only when listed)
{"sketch": "F1", "curve": "c1"}one curve; a circle starts at its start_angle (the sketch x axis by default) and runs counter-clockwise
"reversed": true (with curves or curve)the same curves, the other way (mitcad#1550: a 3D sketch turned back into 2D keeps its paths’ direction this way)
{"body": "F2.b0", "edges": ["E{…}", …]}connected edges of a body, in order; each name must name one edge
{"start": [x, y, z], "end": [x, y, z]}a fixed line
{"helix": {"center": [x, y, z], "axis": [x, y, z], "x_axis": [x, y, z], "radius": r, "pitch": p, "start_angle": a, "end_angle": b}}a fixed helix (mitcad#385): the points center + r (cos t x + sin t (axis × x)) + p t / 2π axis (x is x_axis made square to the axis) for t from start_angle to end_angle (radians, either way round: the path runs from the first to the second); p, the rise per turn counter-clockwise about the axis, is negative for a left-handed helix
{"fixed_curves": [{"type": "line", "start": [x, y, z], "end": [x, y, z]}, {"type": "conic", "center", "normal", "x_axis", "major", "minor", "start", "end", "closed"}, {"type": "spline", "degree": d, "poles": [[x, y, z], …], "weights": [w, …], "knots": [k, …]}]}fixed curves in model space, joined end to end (mitcad#548): lines, circle or ellipse arcs (center + major cos t x_axis + minor sin t (normal × x_axis) for t from start to end), B-splines (weights left out: not rational; the full knot vector, poles + degree + 1 knots, never decreasing); the FreeCAD import’s edges that lie in no plane, a conical helix as its file stores it. Not a construction plane’s or point’s path, nor a path pattern’s
{"feature": "F5"}the curve of an Intersection Curve before the feature, in its component, or with a construction feature’s datum_links in another (mitcad#1417) (Intersection Curve); every path takes it, and ribs’ and webs’ curves when it lies in one plane

A Pipe’s or Sweep’s path (and a sweep’s guide rails and auxiliary curve) may also be curves of a 3D sketch: {"spatial_sketch": "F3", "curves": ["c3", "c6"], "reversed": false}, with "chain": true for chain selection (Pipe and Sweep along 3D sketch curves); a loft’s centre line and rails and the other paths do not take it yet.

A path runs from the free end of the first listed curve or edge when it ends the chain, else along the first listed curve’s own direction (a closed chain from that curve’s start); "reversed": true runs it the other way. A path may not branch or have gaps; a closed curve is a path by itself. A path pattern’s path is a sketch line, arc or circle, a chain of sketch lines and arcs ({"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1", "c2"]}, mitcad#464), connected edges of a body (mitcad#2105, with the pattern’s tangent_chain), or a fixed line.

Feature definitions

The def of add_feature, edit_feature and preview, and the def the feature query returns. Design files store the same fields with parameter names. Each type is a module core/model/src/features/<type>.rs. Lengths in millimetres, angles in radians; every length, angle, quantity, fraction and factor is a value (Values).

Shared rules:

  • operation: new_body, join, cut, intersect, or new_component (new bodies in a new component placed in the feature’s component, see Components and occurrences); participants: the bodies a join, cut or intersection works on (all bodies when empty or left out). Their results are described under extrude; “as for extrude” elsewhere means the same.
  • A feature that asks for something the geometry kernel cannot do fails with a message starting unsupported: (mitcad_model::features::UNSUPPORTED); the .f3d importer then falls back to the body the file stores.
  • A face or edge that a later edit removed is explained (face X no longer exists after Fillet2, ... does not exist because Fillet1 is suppressed).
  • A feature an importer left a note on (a fallback, a partial item) is warning too, and a placeholder of an item the file had suppressed or failed is suppressed with that note (The import’s outcomes on the timeline).
  • A feature that succeeds with a caveat has warnings (timeline status warning): a fillet or chamfer whose made faces reach out of the body (a folded or spiked corner, fillet), a fillet built as rings about its circles that leaves an edge on a face it runs onto, a sketch text whose font is not installed. A warning reports a fault in the result, never the method that built it (mitcad#1327): a dressup built as rings, over cut-outs or with the kernel’s own tangent chains warns only where its result is faulty. Evaluators call EvalContext::warn (warn_at with the warning’s places); Kernel::notes gives what is wrong with a shape the geometry kept (geometry::Shape::notes), Kernel::note_places their places (Notices).
  • What is worth knowing of how a feature was built but needs no action is information (mitcad#1106): its status stays ok, its level is info, each an info notice after the warnings, listed in the feature query’s infos and a preview’s infos (beside its warnings). A fillet or chamfer built 0.1 % smaller than asked says so: where OCCT fails at the exact size because the dressup takes a face away and builds 0.1 % smaller, which leaves a strip of 1e-3 of the size where the face was, the strip is removed (its neighbours extended to meet, the dressup’s face taking its names) and the info stays. A strip with more than 16 faces beside it stays (mitcad#1337: OCCT’s defeaturing grows every one of them by the strip’s whole extent and intersects each with each; a strip along a rounding of 44 edges round a circle took minutes and gigabytes). Where a strip stays (it has that many faces beside it, or its neighbours cannot be extended to meet, as the disc a boss’s top edge rounded with the boss’s radius leaves), the feature has a warning instead of the info, its places the strips (mitcad#1783): “the fillet is built 0.1 % smaller than asked and leaves a sliver of a face it should take away: at its exact size the geometry kernel cannot build it”. A dressup that takes a face away and that OCCT builds at its size (the port’s patch 1100: a pocket’s walls as high as the bevel of their top edges) has no note. Evaluators call EvalContext::inform; Kernel::infos gives the geometry’s (geometry::Shape::infos).
  • What a feature’s panel points out while it is open, but the user accepts with the result, is a remark (mitcad#1914): a fillet’s or a chamfer’s tangent chain that stops where other sharp edges meet, the edges that continue it left sharp (fillet, tangent_chain). A remark is no warning and does not count in the feature’s level or status: once the feature is accepted nothing in the application marks it. Agents keep the fact: each remark is an info notice with its places, after the feature’s other notices, in the timeline and feature queries, a preview’s notices (without target) and the results of add_feature and edit_feature, and its message is listed in their remarks (the plain words). design_review does not count it. The command panel shows a preview’s remarks in its message line as information, after its infos; the pointer over the message paints their places. Evaluators call EvalContext::remark (warn_notes takes the geometry’s); Kernel::remarks gives the geometry’s with their places (geometry::Shape::remarks, kept with the feature’s result in the result store, not in a stored shape).

sketch 

{"type": "sketch", "plane": "xy",
 "entities": [
   {"id": "c1", "type": "line", "start": "p2", "end": "p3"},
   {"id": "p2", "type": "point", "at": [0, 0], "fixed": true},
   {"id": "p3", "type": "point", "at": [60, 0]},
   {"id": "c4", "type": "circle", "center": "p5", "radius": 5},
   {"id": "p5", "type": "point", "at": [45, 20]}],
 "constraints": [{"id": "k1", "type": "horizontal", "line": "c1"}],
 "dimensions": [{"id": "k2", "type": "length", "line": "c1", "value": 60},
                {"id": "k3", "type": "diameter", "curve": "c4", "driven": true}]}

Code in core/sketch/. Coordinates are sketch plane millimetres, angles radians. Build sketches with the sketch commands, which pick the ids.

  • plane: "xy" (default), "xz", "yz" (the origin datums’ frames), a construction plane feature before the sketch ("F5"), or a planar face {"face": "<face name>", "body": "F2.b0"} (body optional) of the bodies before the sketch (frame as in References to geometry). A cylindrical or conical face with "developed": {"angle": …}: the sketch in the face’s developed coordinates (Sketches on cylindrical and conical faces).
  • plane_link (optional): {"source": "O1", "target": "O2"} when the plane is another component’s (Geometry of other components); projections may have a link of the same form.
  • frame (optional): the sketch’s own frame in the plane’s frame, {"origin": [x, y, z], "x_axis": [..], "y_axis": [..]} in the plane frame’s (x, y, normal) coordinates; imports keep a file’s exact sketch transform this way, and Create Sketch stores an upright frame this way (sketch.create with upright, below).
  • placement (optional): where the sketch lies on its plane after the own frame, {"offset": .., "x": .., "y": .., "angle": .., "flip": true}, each value optional (see Redefine Sketch Plane).
  • entities: points p<n> and curves c<n> in one id space. Curves refer to points, and curves that share a point are joined there: line (start, end, centerline), circle (center, radius, and start_angle, in radians, where the circle starts: the seam of a cylinder made from it; default 0, the sketch x axis; an import sets it), arc (center, start, end, counter-clockwise), ellipse (center, major: the end point of the major axis, minor_radius), elliptical_arc (also start, end), spline (degree, control points, optional weights and knots; default clamped uniform on [0, 1]) and fitted_spline (points: a cubic through them; closed: it runs on from the last point back to the first, listed once, and is smooth (C2) through it: one closed curve without ends, at least three points; mitcad#783). Flags: construction (not in profiles), fixed, reference (projected), axis ("x" or "y": the line that stands for a sketch axis and its far end, see The sketch’s axes and origin as entities). Positions and radii are the last solved ones and the start of the next solve; a new definition may give any reasonable positions.
  • constraints (k<n>, shared with dimensions): coincident (point, entity: a point or a curve; sketch.add_constraint merges two curve ends instead, see Points that become one), horizontal/vertical (line), horizontal_points/vertical_points (a, b points), parallel, perpendicular, collinear, tangent, smooth (G2), equal (lines; circles and arcs; ellipses by their minor radius); tangent and smooth take an optional at (a point, mitcad#783): the end of each curve at that point (joined to it, else the nearer end), so that a curve can be tangent at both ends, to different curves or to the same one; with a and b the same open spline whose ends are both at, the spline is smooth where it closes; an elliptical arc takes a tangent or smooth only with a spline that ends at one of its ends (mitcad#2107). Without at (older designs), at the point the curves share or their nearest ends, concentric (a, b curves), midpoint (point, curve), symmetric (a, b: points or curves, axis: a line; radii, two circles or arcs only, default true: their radii are made equal too, see Symmetry of circles with fixed radii), equal_spacing (anchors, mode, direction; see Equal spacing in sketches). perpendicular (a, b, mitcad#2114) takes two lines, a line and a circle or arc in either order, or two circles or arcs. With a line, the center of the circle or arc lies on the infinite line: the line need not reach the arc, only its extension passes through the center, as with two perpendicular lines. Two circles or arcs: the circles they lie on cross at right angles, |c1 c2|^2 = r1^2 + r2^2 (one degree of freedom, as for two lines); for arcs the crossing may lie on an arc’s extension. Circles with a common center (coincident centers or a concentric) conflict with it; ellipses, splines and points are refused.
  • dimensions: distance, horizontal_distance, vertical_distance (a, b points, and optional signed; see Signed point dimensions), point_line_distance (point, line), line_distance (a, b parallel lines), tangent_distance (circle or arc, line: the gap between them, the centre’s distance from the line minus the radius), tangent_circle_distance (a, b circles or arcs) and tangent_point_distance (circle or arc, point): gaps from a circle’s tangent side, with an optional side (see Tangent dimensions between circles), concentric_distance (a, b circles or arcs about one centre: the gap between them, the difference of their radii; mitcad#445), length (line), angle (a, b lines, and optional reverse_a, reverse_b; see Angle dimensions), radius, diameter (curve), arc_length (arc), major_radius, minor_radius (ellipse), linear_diameter (axis, entity), spacing (constraint: an equal spacing’s common spacing). A driving dimension has a value (slot dimensions[k3].<type>, so angle is an angle and the others lengths); a driven one has "driven": true and only measures, with its reference parameter’s name in reference (see Values); a file without it gets one when it is read. text: where the value is shown.
  • Constraints and dimensions alike may be inactive: "active": false, with an optional inactive_reason text; the solve leaves them out (see Inactive constraints and dimensions). Written only when false.
  • projections: linked projections, {"source": "<edge, face or vertex>", "body": "F2.b0", "entities": ["p7", "p8", "c9", …]}; the entities follow the source when the model changes (sketch.project). The stored positions are those of the last edit of the sketch; the evaluation moves them (a large move in steps), the sketch query shows them moved and the next edit stores them. Geometry constrained to them keeps the side it has in the stored sketch, whatever the size of the move (mitcad#1047): the solve takes every orientation choice where the stored positions have the geometry (the side of a point_line_distance, line_distance or tangent_distance, of an offset’s distances and of a tangency, an angle’s quadrant) and starts from the moved projection, so that a point 0.5 mm from a projected edge that moved 0.5 mm toward it follows the edge instead of ending up on its other side. The entities are listed as sketch.project makes them, each curve after its points (a line’s start and end in the source’s direction, an arc’s centre, start and end); a circle keeps its start_angle (an import’s seam) when it follows. Each entity follows the source’s current curve of its kind most like it (its points and sizes; in the order the kernel lists them when that is as good), so a projection may hold only some of its source’s curves (mitcad#232); an entity that finds none keeps its last geometry and the sketch has a warning (as does a projection whose source is gone). An entity the same as another of its projection follows the same curve. "section": true marks section curves: where the sketch’s plane cuts the source face, or the points where it crosses the source edge or another sketch’s curve (mitcad#736, mitcad#998; Section curves in sketches). "outline": true marks a face’s outline: its entities follow the face as the sketch’s normal sees it, its silhouettes included (mitcad#1265; Projecting a curved face). "chain": ["E{…}", …] (an import’s, mitcad#389): the edges the source edge continues into, in order; the entities are one curve, the projection of the edges joined end to end into one B-spline (exactly, a line raised to the splines' degree; a curve the model splits into pieces, such as a thread’s helix of an edge per turn). A piece gone, or pieces that no longer meet within 1e-4 mm, lose the source. "after": "F7" (an import’s, mitcad#998; with body and a face, edge or vertex as source): the source as the earlier feature F7 left the body (the shape the last feature up to and including F7 set), not as the features after it changed it before the sketch, as FreeCAD’s external geometry names an element of a feature’s own shape; a body no feature up to F7 set loses the source, and F7 must come before the sketch.
  • texts: {"id": "t9", "text": "…", "at": [x, y], "height": h, "angle": a, "font": "…", "bold": false, "italic": false}, optional align (left, center, right), valign (baseline, bottom, middle, top), spacing (extra character spacing, % of the height), frame (three point ids: a corner and its neighbours along the text’s x and y, the corners of a construction rectangle the text fills; at and angle follow it), path ({"curve": "c4", "above": true, "fit": false}: the text runs along the curve, fitted to its length when fit; above puts its baseline on the curve, on the curve’s left, false hangs it on the right from its top, the capitals’ top with cap_height, else the ascender, mitcad#1177; align places it from the curve’s start, a circle’s start_angle; on a path the flips act in the curve’s own frame, mitcad#1946: flip_y mirrors the text across the curve, so its baseline, or a hanging text’s top, stays on the curve and the text moves to the curve’s other side, flip_x mirrors it along the curve about the middle of the text block, and both turn it half round about that middle point, reading from the curve’s other end, with fit, align and closed curves alike), no_kerning (the characters advance by their own widths, without the font’s kerning of pairs; the .f3d import sets it for a text on a path, mitcad#1177), flip_x, flip_y, cap_height (height is the capital letters’ height, measured at the top of an A; a frame aligns the first line’s capitals to its top and the last baseline to its bottom, a line aligns by its outlines, and lines are one ascender plus descender apart) and wrap (a text in a frame breaks its lines at spaces to the frame’s width); the .f3d import sets both. line_spacing (mm from one baseline to the next; 0, the default, for the font’s), pen_align (lines align by their pens, from the first pen to the end of the last advance, also with cap_height) and ink_top (the top of the lines, a frame’s top or valign top or middle, is the first line’s highest outline point instead of the capitals’ top or the ascender); the .ipt import sets all three (mitcad#414). Multi-line text breaks at \n. Each glyph contour (t9.g<k>.c<j>, from the font’s outlines through the kernel’s font_glyphs; the bundled Droid Sans when the font is missing) bounds profile regions like a closed curve: a letter is a region with its counters as holes, a counter a region of its own. A contour whose pieces do not join end to end bounds no profile; the sketch warns “an outline of the letter … of a text is not closed, so it bounds no profile”, a box about the letter its place (mitcad#1993). glyphs (mitcad#416): the outlines a file stores for the text’s characters, {"text": "…", "font": "…", "bold": false, "italic": false, "glyphs": [{"advance": a, "contours": [[piece, …], …]}, …]}, one per character of text (newlines included), each piece the control points of a line or a quadratic or cubic Bézier curve ([[x, y], …], two to four), each piece starting where the one before it ends; lengths in units of the text’s height, from the character’s pen on the baseline, y up; advance to the next character’s pen. While the text’s font is not installed and its text, font, bold and italic are still those of its glyphs, these outlines and advances take the place of the substitute font’s: the text is laid out from them with all its options (height, frame, alignment, spacing, flips, path), so moving or resizing its frame, a new height or alignment keep the file’s shapes, and the sketch has no font warning. The vertical metrics a file does not store (the ascender and descender, the font’s line spacing) stay the substitute font’s, relative to its capitals with cap_height. On a computer with the font the font is used. A new string, font or style (sketch.edit_text) drops glyphs: the text is laid out in its font, or in Droid Sans with the warning. The .ipt import sets it from the glyph contours the file keeps; .f3d files keep none. glyphs may also hold the font’s vertical metrics in the same units, ascender, descender and line_spacing; then they are used instead of the substitute font’s. font_file (mitcad#473, sketch/fonts.rs): {"path": "…/Font.ttf", "index": 0, "licence": "…"}, the font file the text’s font comes from instead of an installed font (.ttf, .otf, a collection .ttc with the face index, .woff or .woff2), and what the file’s name table says of its copyright and licence. font is then the file’s family, and the text’s glyphs (with the metrics) are the file’s outlines of the text, stored when the file is chosen and whenever the string or the style changes: while they fit the text, the text is laid out from them and the file is not read, so the design is the same on every computer (stored_outlines is true). Outlines that do not fit are read from the file again only when the file was chosen in this session (font_file of sketch.add_text or sketch.edit_text); a file that is not there then fails the sketch with “choose the font file again”. A path that came with a design file (opened, or a definition given as JSON) is never read (mitcad#929): without fitting outlines the sketch fails with “the text has no outlines stored for its font file …; choose the font file again”, and a new string or style of sketch.edit_text without font_file is refused the same way, so a design cannot make the application read a file it names. The model reads the file itself (skrifa; wuff decodes WOFF and WOFF2), not through the kernel. A font file is one face: bold does not change it, italic slants an upright face by 0.2 of the height. Shaping and both directions (mitcad#473): a text in a font file, and a text in an installed font with characters of right-to-left or joining scripts, combining marks or bidirectional controls (Hebrew, Arabic, Syriac, the Indic scripts, Thai, …; sketch::fonts::needs_shaping), is shaped by the model (harfrust: joined forms, ligatures, marks, kerning) from the font’s file (an installed font’s through the kernel’s font_source), in runs of one direction by the Unicode bidirectional algorithm (unicode-bidi), each line on its own. Characters that shape together (a ligature, a letter and its marks) are one glyph g<k>, k the first character’s index, with all their contours; the others of the cluster have none. Every line’s characters are laid out in their visual order (text::visual_lines): a right-to-left run reads from right to left, numbers in it from left to right, and alignment, frames, paths and flips work on the visual line. Other installed-font text keeps the kernel’s glyphs. Glyphs of joined letters overlap a little, as fonts draw them, so a letter’s contour can cut its neighbour’s region in two: extrude the whole word. code (mitcad#473, sketch/code.rs): {"kind": "qr", "ecc": "M"}, the text is a QR code of its text (the qrcode crate; error correction L, M the default, Q or H) instead of characters: height is a module’s size (mm), at the lower left corner of the modules, turned by angle; fonts, alignment, frames and paths do not apply (a frame or a path is refused). The dark modules that share sides are one area, bounded by one contour along their outside and one round each light island in it, glyph contours t9.g0.c<j> numbered from the lowest leftmost one up; modules that touch only at a corner are apart there (their contours meet at that point). A region bounded by several such contours (a light island that meets another at a corner) still has the region’s text, and letter true when a point inside it lies within an odd number of the text’s contours (the material).
  • text_values (mitcad#664): [{"text": "t9", "value": "Label"}], texts whose text is a text parameter’s value (slot texts[t9].text): a parameter’s name, or in a command a text expression, which becomes the sketch’s own text parameter of the text. The text is laid out with the parameter’s text and follows it; its text keeps the string it had when it was last set.
  • steps (mitcad#1750): the work steps that made its items, [{"id": 2, "kind": "rectangle", "entities": ["c1", "p5"], "constraints": ["k1"]}], recorded by the sketch.* commands, with texts and a trim’s or an extension’s changed curves where there are any; left out when there are none (The work steps of a sketch).
  • patterns: copy groups, {"id": "k5", "type": "circular", "center": "p3", "count": 6, "angle": "d4", "entities": ["c2", "p7"], "copies": [{"index": [1, 0], "entities": {"c2": "c9", "p7": "p10"}}, …]} or {"type": "rectangular", "direction": [1, 0], "count": [3, 2], "symmetric": [true, false], "spacing": ["d5", "d6"], …}, with "direction2": [0.5, 0.866] when its second direction is not a quarter turn counter-clockwise from the first (mitcad#1969; left out otherwise, and in older files). Each solve binds every copy to its original with the pattern’s transform (solver constraints Translated, Rotated, TurnedDirection, EqualSize; not stored as constraints), so the copies follow the originals and add no degrees of freedom. Each copy is bound through its neighbour instance one step toward the originals (mitcad#677), so the solve’s cost grows about linearly with the copies. Slots patterns[k5].angle, .spacing1, .spacing2. A new count regenerates the copies, keeping those that stay. A symmetric direction (an odd count) has the originals at its middle instance: the copies’ indices count from the end against the direction, and the originals are the instance [count / 2, 0]. Copies cannot be patterned again or moved on their own.
    • Copies deleted, patterns freed (mitcad#2007, GitHub mitcad/Mitcad#432). sketch.remove of a copy (a curve or a point of one instance, while its original stays) leaves that instance out: its index goes into the record’s skipped ("skipped": [[2, 0]], sorted; left out when none, and in older files; no new file version, and an older MitCad refuses a design with one, as an unknown field), the pattern makes it no more, and the copies of that instance not deleted stay where they are as plain sketch geometry. The pattern stays editable: sketch.edit_pattern keeps each skip while its index is still an instance (a smaller count drops the skips past it; a larger one again makes that instance anew). Deleting the last copy, every instance left out while an original stays (one sketch.remove or several), removes the pattern as Free Pattern does, in the same command and undo step (mitcad#2058, GitHub mitcad/Mitcad#471): the originals stay as plain sketch geometry, the edit releases the pattern’s spacing or angle parameters that nothing else uses, and the notes say the pattern was removed with its last copy (the agents’ text: pattern k5 was removed with its last copy). Every sketch edit does this (SketchEdit::sync_patterns), so a design saved with such a record (0.66.0) loses it, with the same note, on the next edit of that sketch; opening it changes nothing. Deleting an original still takes all its copies. sketch.trim, sketch.extend, sketch.fillet and sketch.chamfer on a pattern’s curve (an original or a copy) first free that pattern, as sketch.remove of the pattern (k5) does, in the same undo step (SketchEdit::free_patterns_of): the record goes, and since the solve bound the copies to their originals without stored constraints, every curve keeps its id, shape, shared points and the user’s constraints; nothing makes the copies again afterwards. The command’s notes say the pattern's copies are now plain sketch geometry (one for each pattern freed; the agents’ text names it, pattern k5's copies are now plain sketch geometry). Before, a deleted or trimmed copy was made again after the edit (a trim left a stray piece beside it). Tests: core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_pattern_free_2007_tests.rs, core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_pattern_last_copy_2058_tests.rs, core/model-tests/files/src/sketch_pattern_last_copy_reported_2058_tests.rs (a reported design, from MITCAD_MITCAD_REPORTED), tools/ui-sketch-pattern-free-test.sh, app.ui-windows-sketch-pattern-free and app.ui-macos-sketch-pattern-free.
  • offsets: {"id": "k8", "curves": ["c1", "c4"], "distance": "d6", "left": false, "results": ["c10", "c11"], "corners": [{"join": 0, "arc": "c12"}], "derived": true}: the source chain, the distance (slot offsets[k8].distance, not negative; left is the side) and the curves made.
    • A chain of lines and arcs, or a circle, is offset exactly by constraints: the results are ordinary curves, and dragging one drags the source along (the distance dimension drives). The construction lines across the gap of its arcs and circles are listed as helpers (mitcad#358) and go with the results when sketch.edit_offset flips the side and makes them again. Each solve starts its results where the offset of the source is (mitcad#641), so that a source moved before the solve (a linked projection that followed its face farther than the distance) keeps them on their side; a shared corner starts where the two offset curves cross, an arc’s free ends at the source’s angles, and each helper across an arc’s gap where the solve holds it (mitcad#890, mitcad#1171: across the arc’s middle, a circle’s level with its centre).
    • Where the source curves touch at a corner by their definition (fixed curves, a linked projection’s, that touch at their shared point; curves tangent by a constraint; results of an offset whose corner is held so), the solve also holds the results’ shared corner where the result line touches the result arc, or where the two result arcs touch (mitcad#890, offset::tangent_corners). The corner was fixed only to the second order before: it slid along the line by the square root of the solve’s rounding (2e-5 mm), the arc ended past the touching point and the profile turned there by about 1e-6 rad, so that a grid design’s offset outlines lost the edges its chamfers name and a sweep along them cut its chute into rings after a width change. The sketch’s dof and fully_constrained count such a corner as fixed. Free curves that only happen to touch are not held. A sketch that cannot be solved says what contradicts as it would without the corners held: the held tangencies restate what the offsets’ own constraints imply, and counted in the failed solve’s explanation they named every constraint of the offsets.
    • An independent set (mitcad#1171, offset::independent): with its corners held, an offset’s stored constraints held each tangent corner three times (the line at its distance, the arc’s radius by its helper’s length, the tangency), so half of its dimensions were listed in redundant, and each helper slid along its arc (a degree of freedom per arc). The solve now leaves out what the held corners imply: the distance dimension of a result line that touches a result arc at a held corner (that arc’s circle places it), also its parallel when it touches one at both ends, and the helper length of a result arc that touches the previous result arc at a held corner (along the chain from an arc whose own length holds its radius; a closed chain of arcs alone keeps its first arc’s length only, and its arcs and held corners, which close the loop by themselves, are the offset’s own and not listed). Each helper’s end on an arc source is held at the arc’s middle, on a circle level with the centre (a helper something else constrains too is left as it is). An exact offset of a tangent chain, and an offset of that offset, then has nothing in redundant and adds no degrees of freedom. Nothing is stored: the definition keeps all of the offset’s constraints and dimensions (the dimensions show the distance as before), an older design solves the same way when it is opened, and where a source corner no longer touches by its definition the line keeps its own constraints. Tests: core/sketch/src/offset_tests.rs, core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_offset_tangent_corners_890_tests.rs, redundant_constraints_are_grouped_by_their_origin (core/model-api/src/sketch.rs).
    • round (mitcad#1774, "round": true; left out: false) is Corners: Round of an offset made by constraints: at each corner where two of its curves meet at an angle (two lines, a line and an arc or two arcs, mitcad#1786) and the chain turns away from the offset, an arc in corners about the source’s corner point (that point is its centre) joins the two results, tangent to both; see Rounded corners of offsets.
    • A chain with an ellipse, an elliptical arc or a spline is derived: its curves are computed from the solved source after every solve (lines and arcs exactly, an ellipse or spline as a C1 cubic B-spline within 1e-4 mm of the exact offset), with round arcs at outer corners and trimmed inner corners. Constraints cannot refer to them; sketch.drag or sketch.move of them moves the whole source chain by the same motion. A chain is closed by a shared point only, not by ends that lie at the same place (mitcad#360), when it is made and at every later solve; a curve of it is not removed alone (mitcad#361): removing the offset leaves its curves as plain geometry (below).
    • The distance changes only in sketch.edit_offset. The source’s constraints apply (a fixed source holds its offset). A copy (sketch.move with copy) is an ordinary curve that no longer follows the source. Each corner’s kind is fixed when the offset is made: an edit that would change it is refused (as .f3d offsets fail likewise), but for the curves that vanish (below).
    • Freed from the source (mitcad#1755, GitHub mitcad/Mitcad#314): sketch.trim, sketch.extend, sketch.fillet and sketch.chamfer on a curve an offset made (a result or a corner arc, of either kind), sketch.convert_projected with one of them, and sketch.remove of the offset (k8) first turn all of that offset’s curves into plain sketch geometry, in the same undo step (SketchEdit::free_offset): the record goes, with what tied the curves to the source (each line’s parallel and line_distance, the helper lines with their points, constraints and length dimensions); a result arc or circle about its source’s centre gets a centre point of its own at the same place (an offset of these curves goes round the new one too); the curves keep their ids, shapes, shared points and the user’s constraints, and a tangent corner the solve held (offset::tangent_corners, above) becomes a tangent constraint between them. The source is not changed. Nothing makes the curves again afterwards: a trimmed curve stays cut when the source changes, the distance’s parameter is set elsewhere or the design is recomputed. The command’s notes say the offset is no longer linked to its source (one for each offset freed; the agents' text names it, offset k8 is no longer linked to its source). Before, Trim on an exact offset’s arc was cut at its helper line too, a trimmed result could be made again whole from the record when the curves that vanish changed, a derived offset’s curve was refused, and deleting the offset left its curves tied to the source. Tests: core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_offset_free_1755_tests.rs, tools/ui-sketch-offset-trim-test.sh and app.ui-windows-sketch-offset-trim.
    • What vanishes is left out (mitcad#1234, both kinds, offset::trim): an arc whose offset radius is not above zero (1e-7 of the chain’s size), a curve of another kind whose offset folds over (the distance passes its radius of curvature), and then, again until none is left, a curve whose offset turns inside out because its neighbors’ offsets cross beyond it (a loop on the source’s side). The offsets of the curves on either side are cut or run on (lines along themselves, arcs round their circles) to where they cross, so the overlap on the source’s side is trimmed away and the outer outline is kept: a hexagon with 2 mm corner arcs offset 2 mm or more inward is a sharp hexagon. The record lists those source curves in dropped ("dropped": ["c4", "c7"], left out when empty); results are those of the others in chain order, and the corners of a derived offset count their join between the results. An offset made by constraints joins the two results across a curve that vanished at a shared point (a coincidence) where their offset curves cross, which the results’ own constraints place, so it stays fully constrained when its source is. An open chain keeps its free ends. It fails, naming the curve, where the curves on either side do not meet (c2 vanishes at this distance, and the offsets of c1 and c3 on either side do not meet: a slot offset inward past its arcs’ radius, whose sides are parallel), where every curve (of a closed chain, all but one) vanishes, and where the point they meet at lies nearer than the distance to a curve that folds over (only part of it would vanish: the offset is larger than c2's radius of curvature on that side). The command’s result has notes (not warnings): corner arcs c4 and c7 vanish at this distance, which the panel’s preview shows as information.
    • Curves that fold over in places (mitcad#1938, derived offsets, offset::split_folds): a spline, ellipse or elliptical arc whose radius of curvature on the offset’s side is smaller than the distance only in places (a tight bend of a short imported piece, an ellipse’s ends) is cut there: the stretches whose offset folds over vanish, and the parts on either side meet where their offsets cross, or vanish in turn when their offsets lie in the overlap, as whole curves do. What is left of the curve is still its one result, a spline with a corner (a triple knot) where its parts meet; a single closed curve so cut is trimmed as a closed chain of its parts (an ellipse offset inward past the radius at its ends is a lens). The offset fails only when nothing is left, or where the parts of one curve fall into different outlines (the offset of a curve whose radius of curvature is smaller than the distance falls apart where it folds over), or a fold ends an open chain, where nothing trims it.
    • What vanishes changes: when an edit leaves other curves vanishing at the distance (sketch.edit_offset with a distance, or any edit that moves or resizes the source), the offset is made again with the curves it needs (SketchEdit::settle_offsets; an offset made by constraints at once from the source’s stored places on a distance edit, so that it never solves in a shape that no longer fits). The result of a source curve that has one before and after keeps its id, so constraints, dimensions and profile regions that name it keep working; a curve that comes back gets a new id. The user’s constraints and dimensions on the results move onto the points made again in the same place of their curves; one on a result that vanishes is removed (removed) with a warning, k12 is removed: it was on c30, which vanishes at this distance. This replaces “an offset fails when its topology would change” for this case.
    • Outside the sketch: when a parameter set elsewhere (the parameters table, an expression) or a linked projection that follows its source at a recompute changes what vanishes, the sketch’s evaluation makes the offsets again the same way (offset::retrim_for_evaluation, from the evaluation’s solve, or a solve of the sources without the offsets’ curves when the stale offsets do not solve): kept results keep their ids, so the profile regions and the features made from them follow. The evaluation’s output carries that definition with the stored one it was made from (SketchOutput::retrimmed); the sketch query shows it and the next edit of the sketch starts from it and stores it. The notes become the feature’s information (infos) and the warnings its warnings. While the stored definition is the one it was made from, an evaluation makes it again the same way, with the same ids.
    • Loops away from the joins: where two neighbors’ offsets do not meet, and after the joins are trimmed, a curve whose offset lies wholly nearer the source than the distance (sampled inside its range: the overlap on the source’s side) is left out too, and the curves on either side meet instead; for example the walls of a neck narrower than twice the distance, whose offsets pass each other, so that the sides on either side of the neck meet at a sharp corner. When nothing would be left (a slot’s two sides) the offset fails as above. Tests: core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_offset_vanishing_1234_tests.rs, tools/ui-sketch-offset-vanishing-test.sh and app.ui-windows-sketch-offset-vanishing.
    • Lines on one line (mitcad#1244, both kinds): two lines whose offsets lie on one line, running the same way, across what vanished (a narrow notch in a straight side that the offset closes) are one result, that of the first along the chain: the later line is listed in dropped and in merged with the line it runs on along ("merged": [{"curve": "c13", "into": "c1"}], left out when empty), and the result runs on to where the curve after the later line meets it (at an open chain’s end, to the later line’s end). The result is held by the first line’s constraints, so the sketch stays fully constrained. The note says c13's offset runs on along c1's at this distance.
    • Several outlines (mitcad#1244, closed chains, both kinds): across a waist narrower than twice the distance between two wider parts, the offsets of the curves on either side of the waist do not meet; where each meets the offset of a curve on the other side of the waist instead (on one line, or crossing no nearer any curve than the distance), the outline falls into two there, and so on for each such waist. The one record keeps all of them: results stay in the source’s chain order (with the ids of their source curves as above), and outlines lists the results of each closed outline in order ("outlines": [["c20", "c21", "c24", "c25"], ["c22", "c23", "c26", "c27"]], left out for one outline or an open chain, whose results follow each other in results’ order). Each outline is joined at shared points like a single one, so each is fully constrained when its source is; a derived offset’s corner arcs count their join by the result before them in results. The note says the offset falls into 2 outlines at this distance. A dog-bone offset inward past its waist is two outlines, each wall on either side of the waist running on along the one across it. Where no such pairing is found the offset fails as before, or, made by constraints where no arc collapses, is made as before with its curves crossing. An open chain falls into parts since mitcad#1246 (below).
    • Offsets of offsets (mitcad#1244): when an offset made by constraints is made again (its distance edited, its source changed, or at an evaluation), the offsets of its results, and theirs, are made again after it from its new results, with their ids, distances and sides and the user’s constraints as above: an offset of all of its results takes all of the new ones (those that come back too), an offset of some keeps those that are kept (a result whose source now runs on along another’s becomes that one’s) and notes the others (offset k9 is made again without c31, which vanishes at this distance); one whose curves all vanish is removed with a warning. An offset of an offset whose middle arc vanishes is no longer refused by the definition check.
    • The record’s merged and outlines are new in mitcad#1244 and left out when empty: designs saved before read and solve as before, and a design with them is saved and read back the same (a_dog_bone_offset_inward_past_its_waist_falls_into_two_outlines). Tests: core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_offset_outlines_1244_tests.rs.
    • Open parts, arcs on one circle, crossing walls, parts too small (mitcad#1246, both kinds, offset::trim):
      • An open chain falls into parts as a closed one does (a waist whose sides meet across it), and where the offsets on either side of what vanished do not meet at all and no such pairing is found, it ends on both sides, each part keeping its own end there, when those ends lie no nearer any curve than the distance (else it fails as before). The record lists every part in outlines and the last result of each open one in ends ("ends": ["c24", "c29"], left out when empty); an outline whose last result is not in ends closes on its first. An open dog-bone (a dog-bone outline without one wall of its waist) offset inward past its waist is two open parts. As for any open chain, each part’s two free ends slide along their curves (two degrees of freedom per part); the rest is held as above.
      • Two arcs whose offsets lie on one circle, running the same way, across what vanished (a notch in a circle that the offset closes) are one result, as two lines on one line are (merged): the result runs on round the circle to where the curve after the later arc meets it. An arc left alone in its outline whose offset circle lies no nearer any curve than the distance runs round its whole circle: its result is a circle about the arc’s centre, held by the helper across the arc’s middle, so a circle drawn as two arcs with a narrow notch, offset outward past it, is one circle, fully constrained.
      • Where the offsets of two curves that do not follow each other cross at a point no nearer any curve than the distance, and what runs on past the crossing lies nearer the source than the distance (the walls of a tapered waist, whose offsets cross on the source’s side; an outline that merely crosses itself is left as it is), the outline is split there as across a waist: the first runs into the crossing and on along the second, and the curve before the second goes on to the one after the first; the loop between is then trimmed as above. A dog-bone whose waist is a trapezoid, offset inward past its narrow end, is two outlines with no crossing curves.
      • An outline left with one curve that cannot close, or what is left of a part between two neighbours whose offsets do not meet, which cannot close on its own while the curves on either side of it meet (a lobe narrower than twice the distance beyond a waist that vanished), is left out when anything else is left; it is listed in dropped, and the note says the offset leaves out c5, a part too small for this distance.
      • The record’s ends is new and left out when empty: designs saved before read and solve as before. Tests: core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_offset_open_parts_1246_tests.rs.

Evaluation solves the sketch (an over- or inconsistently constrained sketch fails with the conflicting constraint ids; a solve that does not converge is tried again at a tolerance of 1e-7 of the sketch’s size, so that fixed geometry that misses itself by rounding still solves) and cuts the non-construction curves into profile regions: the faces of the planar arrangement, with islands as holes; overlapping shapes split into separate regions, and curves on each other (a circle drawn twice) bound them once, the one with the lower id (a spline that follows a curve within a micron, a projected edge, replaces it: they are one edge). A region reference whose key no longer exists means the regions inside the outline its key traces on the changed curves (all pieces of a region the change split), else the region with the most curves in common, with a warning (see Profile references after a sketch change). A region whose hole is a circle that touches its outer boundary at a point (tangent circles) is one face (the hole shares the boundary’s vertex there); regions beside such a region are united as faces before a feature extrudes, revolves or sweeps them. Older files’ shapes (rectangles and circles) are read as entities, constraints and dimensions with the same curve ids and parameters.

extrude 

{"type": "extrude",
 "profiles": [{"sketch": "F1", "region": "r{c1[c4,c2],c2[c1,c3],c3[c2,c4],c4[c3,c1]}"}],
 "extent": {"type": "distance", "distance": 20},
 "flip": false,
 "operation": "join",
 "participants": ["F2.b0"]}
  • surface, curves: a surface extrusion, walls without caps, of the profiles and of sketch curves (Surface modelling, mitcad#455).
  • profiles: regions of one sketch, a set (see Profile selections); touching regions fuse into one body (and taper as one region).
  • start (optional): {"type": "profile_plane"} (default), {"type": "offset", "offset": s} (the profile moved s along the sketch normal, whatever flip says) or {"type": "object", "object": <object>, "offset": s} (the profile projected along the sketch normal onto a plane or planar face, or the plane through a point or a line parallel to the sketch, moved s along its normal; the distance is then measured from there, and a start plane not parallel to the sketch takes no taper). The object may also be a curved face, {"type": "face", "body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:side(c1)"} (mitcad#1848: a cylinder, cone, sphere, torus or any other surface, continued past its edges unless chained): each profile curve is projected onto it along the extrusion’s direction, where the projection first reaches it from the profile’s side, moved s along the sketch normal, and each side runs its distance from that outline (or up to its object), every line along the direction through the profile the same length in the solid: a cut of 0.1 leaves its floor 0.1 below the face under every letter of a text. The profile’s side is told by where the face’s middle lies from the sketch plane, measured along the sketch normal: a face the projection crosses twice (a whole cylinder) starts the extrusion where it faces the sketch, whichever way the extrusion runs, also along a direction off the normal (mitcad#1852). Join, Cut and New Body as from a plane; no taper (a tapered extrusion cannot start from a curved face), and a side up to an object only away from the profile’s side. A face that does not lie under the whole profile fails the feature (the start face does not lie under the whole profile along the extrusion direction, the face in its places).
  • extent, each with an optional "taper" (radians; positive widens the profile away from the start: the outside grows and holes shrink):
    • {"type": "distance", "distance": d}: one side; negative goes the other way;
    • {"type": "to_object", "object": <object>, "offset": o}: one side up to an object; a positive offset makes the extrusion longer. It goes toward the object (mitcad#2118): an object that lies wholly behind the start along the direction (after flip), and ahead of it the other way, is reached the other way, as a cut sketched on a plate’s face (its normal out of the material) up to the plate’s far face; the geometry’s extrude_feature turns it (turns_to_target, geometry/src/extrude.cpp). A start on a plane not parallel to the sketch or on a curved face keeps its direction.
