The sketch’s other geometry follows as its constraints and dimensions say: a wall dimensioned 3 mm from the bore’s line moves out with it.
  • No source: a face of an imported body, one a fillet or a boolean made, a face whose diameter comes from several dimensions or from none, or one moved after it was made: the warning ends ; the hole has to be changed by hand (<why>) (the shaft on a shaft), and Auto Fix is not offered for it. A face of a projected curve (a reference curve of the sketch, which follows the model geometry it was projected from) says so (mitcad#1780): the face follows an edge projected into Sketch50: draw and dimension the curve instead, or change the geometry it was projected from.
  • The expression keeps its form: one number of the dimension’s expression is solved for, the one that carries most of its value, in its own unit and with as few decimals as give the value within half a micrometre (M76x2’s minor diameter 73.8349 mm: 72/2 becomes 73.835/2; 1 in becomes 1.25 in); an expression no number of which can give it becomes the plain value. The value is worked out from the face’s diameter as the geometry measured it and the dimension’s slope (a diameter 1, a radius or a distance from the axis 2), so that the sketch solver’s last digits do not reach it.
  • A named parameter: a dimension whose value is a parameter’s name (bore) or whose expression uses one (bore/2, the parameter that carries most of it): when nothing else uses the parameter it is changed, its own expression keeping its form. When other places use it (other slots of the definitions, other parameters’ expressions), the fit is not silent: shared parameter changes the parameter (the result says in how many other places it is used), shared own gives the dimension a value of its own in its place (a new dimension parameter where the slot named the parameter); without shared the fit is left, and auto_fix’s choices names the parameter.
  • Checked before it is taken, as Auto Fix’s reference fixes: a fit that would make a feature that built fail, or after which the face still does not fit, is not taken, with the reason.
  • add_feature of a thread with "fit_faces": true (and shared) adds the thread and fits its faces in one undo step (Add Thread1); its result has fitted (as auto_fix’s) and fit_left (face and its reason or choice). The same in a preview (fit_faces, shared): it shows what moves with the face. A preview of a thread whose faces do not fit has thread_fits: each face (its name, for agents), body, diameter, needed (mm), internal, fixable, and reason (why not), source (the feature that sets it) or choice (parameter, others).

Tests: core/model-tests/features-profile/src/thread_autofix_tests.rs (a Hole, an extruded circle, a revolved line and its wall, a Cylinder; a named parameter used elsewhere, both choices, and one used only there; a face no dimension sets; fit_faces and its undo; the previews), features::thread::fit::tests, document::thread_fit::tests (the expressions), and cli.thread_fit_reported on a reported design (tools/cli/thread-fit-reported-test.cmake, under MITCAD_MITCAD_REPORTED: a revolved bore of 72/2 under an M76x2 thread; as saved the fit is refused because a chamfer on the step between the bore and the thread’s crest would fail; without that chamfer the bore becomes 73.835/2, nothing newly fails, the 3 mm wall stays).

fillet 

{"type": "fillet", "body": "F2.b0", "edges": ["E{F2:side(c1[c4,c2])|F2:side(c2[c1,c3])}"], "radius": 2}

The short form is one set of edges with a constant radius. The general form lists edge sets:

{"type": "fillet", "body": "F2.b0", "sets": [
  {"edges": ["E{…}"], "size": {"type": "constant", "radius": 5}, "tangent_chain": false},
  {"faces": ["F2:end(r{…})"], "size": {"type": "chord_length", "length": 3}},
  {"edges": ["E{…}"], "size": {"type": "variable", "start": 2, "end": 4, "start_vertex": "V{…}",
   "mid": [{"position": 0.25, "radius": 3}]}, "continuity": "tangent"},
  {"edges": ["E{…}"], "size": {"type": "constant", "radius": 2}, "continuity": "curvature",
   "tangency_weight": 1.5},
  {"edges": ["E{…}"], "size": {"type": "asymmetric", "distance1": 2, "distance2": 4, "flip": false},
   "reference_face": "F2:side(c1[c4,c2])"}],
 "rolling_ball_corners": true}
  • A set rounds its edges and every edge of its faces; an edge may be in one set only. Any number of fillets per body.
  • all_edges (default false, mitcad#793): the set rounds every edge of the body as it is when the fillet is computed (the FreeCAD import’s “use all edges”), so that the edges an edit upstream adds are rounded too and those it takes away are no error. Such a set lists no edges or faces, has no start_vertex and is the fillet’s only set: {"type": "fillet", "body": "F2.b0", "sets": [{"all_edges": true, "size": {"type": "constant", "radius": 1}}]}. Patterns that copy fillets onto their copies leave such a set out.
  • size: constant (radius), chord_length (length, the width across the rounding; the faces must meet at a constant angle along the chain), variable, asymmetric or spline.
  • variable: start at start_vertex (an end of the chain, or the kernel’s start when left out) to end at the chain’s other end, through the mid radii at their positions along the chain (0 to 1 from the start, increasing). The radius follows OCCT’s smooth interpolation of all the radii, level at both ends, along the whole tangent chain (not confirmed to be the law of .f3d variable fillets). Mid radii around a closed chain are unsupported.
  • spline (mitcad#464): {"type": "spline", "knots": [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1], "radii": [2, 6, 3, 4], "start_vertex": "V{…}"}, the radius a clamped B-spline of the position along the chain (0 at start_vertex, an end of the chain or the kernel’s start when left out, 1 at the other end; by arc length): radii its control radii (2 to 100, each greater than zero) and knots its full knot vector, as many as the radii and the degree and one more (degree 1 to 3), from 0 to 1, each end repeated degree + 1 times and an inner knot at most degree times. The radius keeps within its control radii, passes through the first and the last, and runs exactly as the spline does (the law goes to OCCT’s fillet as it is, port patch 0920; geometry/tests/test_dressup.cpp, test_fillet_spline_radius). Slots radii[k]. Not around a closed chain and not with curvature continuity (unsupported); the kernel’s chain, as for variable.
  • asymmetric: distance1 from the edge along the set’s reference_face (or along the first face of each edge’s name), and distance2 along the other face; flip swaps the faces. The cross-section is a conic, the affine image of the circular arc, tangent to both faces (MitCad’s own convention).
  • tangent_chain (default true): the edges that continue an edge smoothly are rounded too: every edge that meets an edge of the set end to end in the same direction (within 0.01 rad) and lies between two faces at an angle, convex where the edge is convex and concave where it is concave (a rounding vanishes where a concave edge runs on into a convex one, mitcad#439), and so on from those (MitCad’s own chain, mitcad#224; constant and chord length sets and chamfers; variable, asymmetric and G2 sets keep the kernel’s chain), besides the edges the kernel follows itself where the faces at a vertex go on tangentially. The kernel stops where a third sharp edge meets the vertex (a ring that two chamfers split into two arcs); MitCad’s chain does not. Where the kernel cannot build MitCad’s chain, the set takes the kernel’s chain alone, with a warning only where the result leaves edges of MitCad’s chain sharp, a remark, not a warning (mitcad#1914: The fillet's tangent chain stops where other sharp edges meet: 2 edges that continue it are left sharp., the edges its places; mitcad#1327): the panel points it out as information while it is open, and nothing marks the feature once it is accepted (the chamfer’s The chamfer's … the same). The kernel chain of a fillet or a chamfer also stops where its edges turn (by 0.01 rad or more) although the faces go on tangentially across a shallow crease there (a wall drafted by a few degrees above a vertical one), unless the next edge is bevelled too (OCCT port patches 0180, mitcad#241, and 0531, mitcad#263): a rounding ends at that vertex, cut by the face beyond the crease, where the crease is concave (at a convex crease that end is not built and the fillet fails); a chamfer’s analytic blend (a cone along an arc) runs on past the vertex, cut by the face beyond the crease, up to where its other contact reaches that face. Elsewhere the kernel follows its own chains, and edges the kernel chains beyond MitCad’s chain stay bevelled.
  • Without tangent_chain, only the selected edges are rounded or bevelled, also where the kernel’s chain runs on into an edge no set selects (a straight edge into a rounded corner; mitcad#2037): the dressup is built over the kernel’s whole chain and kept over the selected edges. Where a selected edge meets the next edge, the rounding or bevel runs out over that edge: in each section its profile (the bevel’s line, the rounding’s arc) lies closer to the edge by a depth that grows linearly with the length along it, from the full section at the vertex to nothing just before the edge’s far vertex (2 % of its length). The edges beyond stay sharp. Where the next edge is shorter than the dressup is wide, or the run-out does not build, the dressup ends flat at the vertex, in the plane normal to the edge there. The run-out’s face is <feature>:runout(<edge>) (the edge it runs over), the flat end’s <feature>:runout_end(<vertex>); the other faces keep the dressup’s names. Constant and chord length fillets and every chamfer do this; variable, asymmetric, spline and curvature continuous (G2) fillets are refused there, in words ("… need Tangent Chain on where a selected edge continues smoothly into an edge not selected"), as is a set where neither the run-out nor the flat end builds.
  • A rolling ball rounding of constant radius whose chain ends at a small notch in the rim it rounds (edges not rounded, each within the rounding’s contact on the face the notch breaks and within the ball’s diameter of the chain’s end) carries on across the notch onto the next edge of the rim, when that edge lies on the same line or circle between faces of the same two surfaces, whether or not the set selects it or follows tangent chains (OCCT port patch 0260, mitcad#307): the rounding is one surface over both edges, cut by the notch’s faces, as in the .f3d files' roundings. A wider notch ends the rounding.
  • continuity: tangent (G1, default) or curvature (G2). A G2 set touches the faces where the G1 rounding of its radius would (the asymmetric one at its distances) and its quintic cross-section follows the faces’ curvature there; tangency_weight (0.1 to 2, default 1) pulls it closer to the edge’s corner (larger) or to the chord (smaller). MitCad’s own shape; variable radius G2 sets are unsupported.
  • Asymmetric and G2 sets are built from a chamfer at their contact distances whose bevels are replaced by blend surfaces (along circles between faces of revolution about their axis the cross-section turned about it, elsewhere Gordon surfaces through cross-sections and the chamfer’s contact lines; the faces a chain ends on take the end cross-sections). Their chains must end on planar faces or close on themselves; a chain that meets another rounded edge at a vertex, or a non-planar end face, is unsupported. Rolling ball sets of the same fillet are built first.
  • rolling_ball_corners (default true): false asks for setback corners where three or more rounded edges meet: the roundings stop 1.5 times the largest radius there from the vertex and an N-sided patch tangent to them and to the faces (OCCT’s plate surface) closes the corner, named corner(<vertex>) (MitCad’s own convention). An edge shorter than the setback is unsupported.
  • Slots: radius, chord_length, start_radius, end_radius, mid[k].radius, distance1, distance2, tangency_weight (unitless), radii[k] for the first set, sets[i].radius, … for the others.
  • New faces: <fillet>:fillet(<edge>) along every rounded edge (also the ones a tangent chain adds) and <fillet>:corner(<vertex>) where rounded edges meet.
  • Rings: OCCT’s roundings and bevels stop where they would run over the edge of a neighbouring face (the rim of a hole closer to a side than its radius). When OCCT fails and every selected edge is a whole circle between two faces of revolution about its axis with straight sections (planes square to the axis, cylinders, cones), the cross-section turned about the axis is cut from the body (convex edges) or joined to it (concave), running over what it meets; constant radius and chord length sets, and chamfers of every size (geometry/src/ring_dressup.cpp). How it was built is no warning (mitcad#1327; until then every ring warned “the fillet is built as a ring about its circle …”): the ring’s result is checked, and a rounding that meets a face it runs onto (not one of its edge’s two) at more than 30°, leaving an edge there, or a ring that cuts such a face down to a sliver (under a hundredth of the size across) warns, its places the made face, that face and the edge or the sliver (Notices). A rim’s rounding that runs 0.65 mm onto the rounded face beside the flat face it rounds, smooth there, has no warning.
  • Second tries of OCCT’s own rounding, before any of the above (mitcad#107): when it fails at the size asked, it is built again on the body with the pieces of its edges merged (a whole circle in two arcs, a line in pieces between the same two faces; the new faces carry the names of every piece), then with tighter tolerances of OCCT’s fillet (knife edges, where the faces’ normals are opposite), then with the faces of one surface that meet along an edge at the selected edges’ vertices joined as well (a rounding’s end cut by one face, not by the two halves of a pillar’s full-rounded end, mitcad#343). A result OCCT’s checker rejects only where the input body already was invalid, on faces the rounding neither changed nor touches, is taken as it is (stored bodies of imported designs are at times invalid in places); other invalid results are healed as before, never those of a second try.
  • Edges in groups that round apart (mitcad#2161): the kernel’s contours (the edges’ tangent chains) joined where they share a vertex, or a face on which they come within twice the rounding’s reach of each other (its size or the farthest its contact lies from its edge); the copies of a pattern’s rounding standing far apart on one floor face are groups of their own. Where there are several such groups and they do not build at their exact size together, each group is built on its own, one after another, with all the ways round a failure below (the narrow faces continued, the 0.1 % smaller retry, the cut-outs cleared); only where a group fails are all the edges built together with those ways, as before. Those ways on all the groups at once (a narrow face continued at one copy) took 90 s on a pattern’s seven copies, where the copies one by one took 5 s; and the smaller retry no longer takes groups that build at their exact size 0.1 % smaller with the one that does not.
  • Edge overflow (mitcad#121, OCCT’s fillet as patched in the port): a rounding wider than a face next to its edge along the whole edge runs onto the face beyond that face’s far edge, or, where it cannot touch that face, rolls on the far edge; the narrow face vanishes (also all round a closed edge). It runs over several narrow faces in a row (a strip and a sliver beyond it) and over narrow faces on both sides of the edge, as long as the ball touching the faces it reaches clears those it passes; otherwise it rolls on the last edge before a face it cannot touch. Two roundings of the edges of a face narrower than both (their contacts on it cross) are one rounding over that face, from the face beyond one edge to the face beyond the other. Where a rounding is wider only along part of the edge, OCCT’s rounding rolls on the far edge where its contact reaches it, and near an end of the edge it is cut by the face beyond, as before. Chamfers overflow too (mitcad#1232, see chamfer).
  • A rounding that takes a narrow face away where OCCT’s fillet fails at the exact size or leaves the body open (mitcad#1819): where a face beside the edges is narrower than the rounding reaches along it (its contact, r tan(a / 2) from the edge), it is built by the chamfer’s one path past narrow faces (see chamfer, edge overflow): at its full size on the picked edges, measured from them, on the body with the narrow faces continued along their own surfaces past their far edges; the faces beyond grow out (or are cut back) along their own surfaces to meet the rounding’s boundary, and the narrow face is gone, for convex and concave edges, planar and curved narrow faces. A strip narrower than 0.1 % of the rounding left of the narrow face is taken away with it. A face exactly as wide as the rounding reaches (or up to 0.1 % wider), where OCCT’s fillet fails at that size, takes this path too (GitHub #353): a rounding as large as the side face below its edge is high ends on the face’s far edge and takes the face away at its size, with no information, rather than 0.1 % smaller with a sliver of the face left (geometry.suite.dressup_takes_face’s stepped block, cli.fillet_exact_reported). Where two chains along one narrow face end on one plane from opposite sides (the front’s and the step’s upright edges of a stepped block), the material past the face’s far edge is looked for near each chain on its own ends’ side of that plane. Where a chain ends on the far edge of the face it takes away (the face at its end being the face beyond: a rounding of every edge round a side face but its bottom and back edges, the front’s upright edge ending on the bottom’s edge), the space past that far edge is filled too, on the face’s side of the ending edge’s other face, so that the rounding runs on past the end there and is cut by the face beyond (GitHub #353’s second design). A narrow face beside a concave edge whose far edges all go on tangentially into convex faces beyond (a step’s riser running into a round face, GitHub #560, mitcad#2208) is not continued along its own surface: the ball takes it away and rolls on over the faces beyond, touching them and the edge’s other face. It is built on the body with the narrow face replaced by the faces beyond continued along their own surfaces up to the other face, the rounding of that new edge at the full size named after the picked edge; it is taken where the whole input lies within it (the narrow face consumed all along). Before, the ball kept to the narrow face’s surface continued, and the rounding hung beside the round face as a sheet. Where that build fails, the path above follows. A chain that ends against a plane that does not reach across the rounding there (a shelf standing out from a bore’s wall, flush with the top, the rim’s rounding ending against the shelf’s end wall, which lies on the bore’s side of the wall), where the kernel fails at every size, is ended on that plane as on a chamfer (see chamfer, chain ends). Where the rounded corners at both ends of a selected straight edge meet in its middle (three selected edges of one constant radius square to each other at each end, the edge 2r long within 2e-4 r: a cube of 10 rounded by 5 on all its edges, every face taken away; GitHub #353’s third design), OCCT’s fillet never returned and a cancel did not reach it; such a fillet is never given to the kernel (mitcad#1954). It is built exactly as the body’s core swept by the ball where the body is a prism of planar faces (two parallel ends at least 2r apart, every other face a plane along the prism from end to end), every selected edge has one constant radius r, every outer edge between two faces that have a selected edge is selected, and the faces with no selected edge are sides on the body’s outside: the core is the section with every rounded side moved inward by r (its corners mitred, as the kernel’s roundings meet at an inner corner of a face), between the ends moved inward by r, and the result every point within r of it, cut by the sides left alone. A cube of 10 rounded by 5 is the ball of 5 (one face holding the names of all its roundings and corners), a block of 10 x 10 x 20 the capsule, GitHub #403’s stepped block rounded by 5 on its sides’ and steps’ edges a quarter ball at each end of a bent half cylinder, (625 pi - 500) / 3. Where an inner edge between two rounded sides is selected too (GitHub #403’s fifth and #375’s second design, mitcad#2068), the ball rolls between those sides’ roundings: the core’s inner corner is closed by a disc of 2r touching both core edges beside it or their far ends, and the inner edge’s rounding is the ball swept along that arc (the stepped block so: (625 pi - 500) / 3 + 21.2368). Elsewhere (no such disc, curved faces, several radii) it is refused in words, with no 0.1 % smaller retry: the roundings of the corners at both ends of an edge meet, leaving none of the edge to round between them, and an inner corner's edge is rounded with them, which cannot be built there: a radius of 4.999 mm or less leaves some of the edge to round (or ..., which is built exactly only on a block of flat faces whose outer edges between the faces it rounds are all rounded by one radius: ...), the edge and the inner edges as its places; the radius said is the edge’s length less corners_meet’s margin, halved, in thousandths of a mm. This comes before the 0.1 % smaller retry. Where it cannot be built so (the faces beyond do not meet it, or grown out they would cover all of the rounding: it reaches past them too), the error says so in words after the kernel’s own, never that the result is not a closed solid: …; the fillet is wider than the face beside its edge and would take that face away, but cannot meet the face beyond it, the edge, the narrow face and the faces beyond as its places, their names in the detail (the fillet of edge E{…} is wider than face F…, which it would take away, and cannot meet face F… beyond it). A result OCCT’s fillet leaves open is a failure of its try in every case (the other tries follow); geometry.dressup_consumes_face. A narrow face that is a B-spline surface exactly a plane, cylinder, cone, sphere or torus (a body converted to B-splines) is continued as that surface. Where the kernel’s own error already says what failed in words of its own (no ball of the radius touches both faces), the person reads the words above after its opening clause (fillet failed; the fillet is wider …) and the kernel’s message moves to the detail; chamfers likewise.
  • The end of a groove (mitcad#2154): an edge that is an arc of a tube’s circle between a flat end cap across the tube and its floor (a cylinder whose axis runs through the circle’s centre, or a torus with the circle’s centre on its spine: a circle swept along a line or an arc), the body’s material outside the tube, the end cap all inside the circle and cut across by planar faces beyond it, the circle’s centre outside the body (a shallow groove; not a pocket floor’s concave corner arc, whose floor reaches outside the circle, nor a blind hole’s bottom, a whole disc: those stay the kernel’s). A rounding of radius r wider than the end cap is high (a shallow groove) takes the end cap away by the rule above, built on the body with the end cap continued to the whole disc and the floor to the whole tube, so that the rounding closes round the circle (OCCT’s fillet there, below the circle’s radius Rc: a torus piece for a straight groove); what it adds is cut by the planar faces beyond the end cap and joined to the body (where OCCT’s rounding of the edge itself fails: its corners at the edge’s ends meet the same edge twice). At r = Rc (within 1e-6 mm) the ball does not move along the edge, which no rolling ball builds: the end is the sphere of radius Rc centred on the tube’s axis (spine) Rc from the end cap’s plane, the tube’s piece up to its centre less the sphere, cut by the faces beyond; the sets’ other edges are rounded on that body. Its faces are named <feature>:fillet(<edge>). Above Rc it is refused before the kernel is asked, no 0.1 % smaller retry: fillet failed; the fillet is wider than the groove it ends: no ball of that radius fits in the groove, the edge as its place, the radii and the floor’s name in the detail. geometry.dressup_groove_end.
  • Narrow faces across the face, and chains that overlap (mitcad#1926): a face beside the edges counts as narrow (for the path past narrow faces and its failure in words, chamfers too) only where the dressup reaches its far edge across the face, the middle of the way from the edge to the far edge inside the face, not through the body or across a hole of the face (a plate’s edge with a 2 mm wall’s other side lies 2 from the wall’s foot, across the wall: the plate is no narrow face for a rounding of 3 at the foot); in the failure’s words a far edge that meets the edge where the face ends in a point there counts as in the path, not one with the chain’s next face. A fin’s top edges rounded with 0.5 along its outer and inner sides, two chains running round the top, are built together by the kernel (OCCT port patch 1710: it judged them overlapping on the top by the wrong edges; cli.f3d_edit_reported). Two chains of a rounding that OCCT’s fillet still finds overlapping on a face between them, sharing no vertex, are built one after the other, the later one’s ball rolling on the first one’s faces where they meet. The fin’s foot rounded with 3, higher than the arms’ flat outer sides, is the kernel’s own: it runs the rounding on over those sides’ planes and the fin’s top cuts it and grows out to meet it (OCCT port patch 1700).
  • Pieces left of a face the dressup takes away (mitcad#1821; chamfers too): a face of the result that is a new piece of one of the input’s faces (its name the input face’s with a piece’s #k), between two or more faces the dressup made, smaller than the dressup’s reach squared and wholly within that reach of the chain’s edges (a triangle of the old end face left at each corner of a chain over rounded corners, between the neighbouring bevels) is removed: where the faces round it are planes, cylinders, cones, spheres or tori, they are extended to meet; elsewhere (beside a rounding’s faces, mitcad#1858), or where that fails, the dressup’s faces beside the piece are cut back a little past it and the piece with their near parts is replaced by one smooth patch, tangent to the dressup’s faces round it and, for a fillet, to the faces it rounds (a face <feature>:corner(<vertex>), named after the input’s vertex where the dressed edges beside it meet, the nearest such; the other faces keep their names). Where neither gives one valid solid of nearly the same volume the result keeps the pieces with a warning, the chamfer leaves 8 small pieces of a face it takes away, which could not be removed: check the result, the pieces as its places; geometry.dressup_blend_remnants.
  • Overlapping roundings of opposite kinds (mitcad#235): where the roundings of a convex and a concave edge overlap on the face between them (a step narrower than the two are wide) and OCCT’s fillet fails on that, the convex roundings are built first and the concave ones on that result (found by their edges’ names): the concave ball rolls on the convex rounding, an S-shaped section without the step’s face, as the .ipt files keep such steps rounded.
  • Groups of edges whose roundings cannot meet (mitcad#2165, GitHub mitcad/Mitcad#536): where neither the build of all the edges at once nor the path past narrow faces builds the fillet at its exact size, the selected edges are parted into groups: edges that share a vertex, or that run side by side (a point inside one with its foot inside the other) within twice the rounding’s contact of each other, so that their roundings meet on the face between them or take it away together, are one group. These groups are finer than those of mitcad#2161 above, which join edges on a shared face within that reach anywhere: edges that come that near only end to end (the vertical edges of a step’s upper and lower face on the end face they share) are apart. Two to six groups are built one after the other at the exact size (each as the fillet builds its edges alone, the path past narrow faces included), each on the result of the ones before, in the order the sets list their edges: as a feature for each group builds them. The result stands only where it is the body the build of all at once would be: the volume the body loses in all equals the sum of what each group alone takes from the body (within 1e-6 of the body’s volume); else the 0.1 % smaller retry follows as before. The vertical edges of a step’s upper and lower face rounded with 5 as one feature, each pair taking its 10 wide face away and the upper pair the end faces’ upper parts too, the ledge between narrowing to a point at each end of the upper rounding: the pairs one after the other, no warning, as the same edges in two features (geometry.fillet_stacked_step).
  • A face the roundings of two of its edges reach across (mitcad#1482): where the fillet fails and a planar face lies between two selected straight edges parallel to each other whose roundings’ contacts on it (r tan(a / 2) from each edge, a the angle between the edge’s faces' normals, r the set’s largest radius; asymmetric sets left out) add up to more than the face’s width there, the error names the face where they overlap most for its width, ahead of the geometry kernel’s words, which follow in brackets after the error’s first clause: fillet failed; the roundings of the edges E{…} and E{…} reach 1.73 and 0.577 mm into face F… between them, which is only 1.51 mm wide there: the face would vanish under them (and 3 more faces like it) (the geometry kernel …), likewise after the fillet would leave the body open: . Its notice shows the edges and the face as places. A roof slab’s eave 1.506 wide between an acute edge at its tip and the underside’s obtuse one, all edges rounded with 1 (geometry.fillet_roof_slab). Likewise a planar, conical or cylindrical face between two selected straight edges that close in on each other without meeting, its width the straight distance across at the narrowest of nine points along them (mitcad#2038): the side of a rib 4 degrees wide about a bend’s axis, rounded with 0.5 on both edges, is 0.91 mm wide at its foot on a bend of 15 mm (cli.fcstd_bend_limit_reported).
  • A suspect result is a warning, never a refusal (mitcad#1253): where the geometry kernel builds a corner that folds back on itself or ends in a spike and its checker accepts it, the faces the fillet made (<fillet>:…) are looked at, at a bounded number of points each (geometry/src/dressup_check.hpp). Where every selected edge is convex (concave), a made face that reaches out of (into) the input body farther than 3 % of the largest size and its tolerances (those counted up to 5 % of the size; a corner patch beside three or more dressup faces, up to 25 %) gives the feature the warning The corner of the fillet reaches 0.035 mm out of the body, where a fillet of convex edges only takes material away: it folds back on itself or ends in a spike there (and on 1 more face). Check the result. (The fillet for a rounding’s face), its places the face and the deepest point (Notices); mixed selections are not looked at. The same holds for chamfers (The corner of the chamfer, The chamfer). The allowance was 1 % before mitcad#1327: a three-fillet corner whose patch differs from the faces beside it by 0.057 mm on a radius of 3 (1.9 %), which no one can see, warned; the smallest folded corner of mitcad#1253 was 4.7 %. Of concave edges also (mitcad#1260): a made face of an edge hanging out past the body’s original extent (a point of it over neither of the edge’s faces nor a face that continues one of them smoothly, the rounding of its far edge where a tangent chain runs on: no input face on a short ray to its foot on such a face’s surface), The chamfer hangs 1.8 mm past the edge of the face beside it, where a chamfer of concave edges only fills the corner between its faces., its places the made face, the face beside it and the farthest point, and a face of the result on the surface of the input’s face it is named after but facing the other way, A face beside the chamfer is turned over on its surface (it faces into the body), where the chamfer hangs out past it.; several findings are joined in one warning. Not past a convex edge of such a face where the rounding meets the rounding of another of the edges in a mitre (mitcad#1458, GitHub mitcad/Mitcad#177): three foot edges of a block on a plate rounded, two meeting the block’s vertical corners, each end’s rounding runs on past the corner to the mitre that continues the corner’s edge down to the plate, filling the corner outside it; a point whose foot on the face lies no farther from such an edge (from a vertex of the rounded edge, its other face holding another rounded edge from that vertex) than from the face is not counted. That had warned The fillet hangs 0.72 mm past the edge of the face beside it of a sound result (geometry.fillet_foot_mitre). A fillet or chamfer of whole circles built as rings (where the kernel’s own stops at a neighbouring face) gets no warning for that: only a rounding that meets a face it runs onto at more than 30° (The fillet runs onto a face beside it and leaves an edge there, 53 degrees between the faces.) or that cuts such a face down to a sliver warns, with its places. A dressup whose result is not a valid solid fails as before, its error naming where the fault lies: fillet produced an invalid shape (wire: BRepCheck_SelfIntersectingWire); the fault lies in the corner of the fillet at V{…} (the first made face the checker rejects, with how many more; nothing added where none is; the corner without the word “vertex”, which the .f3d import reads as a failure more edges may mend). Its error notice says it without the name (… the fault lies in the corner of the fillet at a vertex), the vertex its place (Notices).

chamfer 

{"type": "chamfer", "body": "F2.b0", "edges": ["E{…|…}"],
 "size": {"type": "equal_distance", "distance": 2}, "flip": false}

size is {"type": "equal_distance", "distance": d}, {"type": "two_distances", "distance1": d1, "distance2": d2} or {"type": "distance_angle", "distance": d, "angle": a} (0 < a < π/2). The first distance and the angle (from that face) are measured on the first face of the name (E{<first>|<second>}) of the first edge the set lists in a tangent chain, or on its second face with flip; the chain’s other edges measure on the same side (the geometry kernel carries it along the chain), whatever order their own names list their faces in. The general form has edge sets with a reference face:

{"type": "chamfer", "body": "F2.b0", "sets": [
  {"edges": ["E{…}"], "faces": ["F2:end(…)"],
   "size": {"type": "two_distances", "distance1": 5, "distance2": 3},
   "reference_face": "F2:side(c4[c3,c1])", "flip": false, "tangent_chain": true}],
 "corner": "chamfer"}
  • reference_face: the face the first distance and the angle are measured on; every edge of the set must border it, and flip takes the edge’s other face. Tangent chains as for fillets.
  • all_edges (default false, mitcad#793): every edge of the body as it is when the chamfer is computed, as for fillets (no edges or faces, the only set).
  • Slots: size.distance, size.distance1, … for the first set, sets[i].size.distance, … for the others.
  • corner shapes the vertices where three or more bevelled edges meet: chamfer (default) is OCCT’s corner face; miter runs the bevels on until they meet, with no face of its own (a corner of convex and concave edges is unsupported); blend stops the bevels 1.5 times their largest distance from the vertex and closes the corner with a patch tangent to them and through the faces’ edges, named corner(<vertex>). Where no three bevelled edges meet, miter and blend make the plain chamfer with the warning the miter corner type shapes nothing here (whether .f3d corner types change two-edge vertices is unknown).
  • New faces: <chamfer>:chamfer(<edge>), <chamfer>:corner(<vertex>).
  • Bevels of whole circles that run over a neighbouring face are built as rings, as for fillets.
  • A failed bevel is built again on the body with merged edge pieces, and an input’s own faults away from it are taken over, as for fillets.
  • Edge overflow (mitcad#1232): a bevel wider than a face next to its edge (its contact on that face running past the face’s far edge) goes on past that edge at its full size and is cut by the faces beyond: the face beyond cuts it where the bevel meets it (a face falling away from the narrow face, or a slope it runs into); where it cannot meet that face (a wall rising past the narrow face’s far edge, on any of the narrow face types below, mitcad#1238), the bevel is cut at the far edge, the wall’s faces continued down to it along their own surfaces (a plane or cylinder as itself, a B-spline flank to its bounds and extrapolated past them), and where the bevel comes out of a thin wall again near the far edge it cuts through the wall. The narrow face vanishes where the bevel is wider than it and stays, narrower, where it is not: along part of an edge or all of it, on one or both sides, round a closed edge, over several narrow faces in a row, any surface beyond (a thread’s B-spline flanks); the narrow face itself a plane, cylinder, cone, sphere or torus. All sizes, flip and reference_face as elsewhere, and the corner types: the bevel is built on the body with the narrow faces continued past their far edges (the space beyond filled, a wall there taken away), and that space is cut out again and the walls are put back (geometry/src/cutouts.hpp). The bevel’s faces are <chamfer>:chamfer(<edge>), the pieces of the narrow face left keep its name, a wall’s face continued down the wall’s. It is never built smaller than asked (no 0.1 % smaller retry where a face beside the edges is narrower than the bevel): where it cannot be built so, the error says so in words with the edge and faces as its places (mitcad#1612): the message reads …; the chamfer is wider than the face beside its edge and would take that face away, but cannot meet the face beyond it, the detail (MCP) …; the chamfer of edge E{…} is wider than face F…, which it would take away, and cannot meet face F… beyond it. This one path (mitcad#1819) is taken also where the geometry kernel’s bevel leaves the body open (its band ending on the narrow face’s continuation where the face beyond does not reach): an open result is a failure of the kernel’s try, and where nothing builds and a face beside the edges is narrower than the bevel the error is the words above alone, never that the result is not a closed solid. A result where the faces beyond, grown out, would cover all of the bevel (it reaches past them too) is not taken; it fails so. Roundings take the same path (see fillet). A narrow face that is a B-spline surface (an imported body’s, or a sweep’s) is continued as the plane, cylinder, cone, sphere or torus it is within 1e-4; round a closed chain each narrow face then looks for the material past it only within its own part of the chain (between the planes that part it from the next faces at the chain’s corners), and that material is put back whole, the faces beyond grown out to meet the bevel (mitcad#1849). A narrow face of free form cannot be continued: the error then adds : the face beside its edge is a free-form surface, which cannot be continued past its far edge. Where an overflowing bevel meets other bevels at a vertex (mitcad#1238), the corner is built as without the overflow on the body continued past each edge’s narrow faces on its own; where the corner type cannot build it there, the error adds the corner’s failure and the other corner types that build it, …; past the narrow face the corner fails: …; the corner type chamfer or miter builds it.
  • Chain ends against a plane (mitcad#1819, the owner’s rebuilt case of GitHub #353): where the kernel cannot end a bevel at a chain’s end because the one face there beside the edge’s own two is a plane that does not reach across the bevel (a band standing out from a bore’s wall, flush with the collar’s end face, the bore’s rim bevelled from one end wall of the band to the other; at any size), the bevel ends on that plane, the end wall grown out along it to meet the bevel, as on a plane that does reach across: the material past the plane near the end (within a box of 1.5, 2.2 or 3 times the bevel’s reach) is taken off, the bevel built on that body (the narrow-face path included) and the material put back, the faces of one surface joined, the bevel’s faces named after the input’s edges. The same holds on the body with the narrow faces continued, and for roundings. A bevel of convex edges that the kernel builds larger than its body (folded out) gives way to these tries first, and stands with its warning (mitcad#1253) only where none builds. geometry.suite.dressup_takes_face (a tube with a shelf in its bore), cli.chamfer_end_wall_reported. A bevel of concave edges (mitcad#1260, an octagon’s foot on a disc) adds material: past the narrow face’s far edge, where the face beyond falls away (a convex far edge), it is cut by that face’s surface continued (the disc’s rim cylinder grows up to the bevel), never left hanging out past it, so nothing lies outside the body’s original extent. Where the bevel’s contact touches a far edge exactly (the bevel as wide as the narrow face at a point, which ends the face in a point there, or covers it with the face gone: an octagon’s foot chamfered as wide as the ring of the disc at its flats), it is built the same way where the result is one valid closed solid and the dressup check (mitcad#1253) finds nothing of the bevel hanging out or turned over (mitcad#1613); pieces of one surface that cannot be joined into a valid face there stay apart. Otherwise it fails in plain words, the chamfer reaches exactly to the far edge of the narrow face beside its edge: its contact touches that edge in a point, and the chamfer cannot be built there as a sound solid at this size.
  • A bevel the geometry kernel cannot build fails with what was asked in its error, the kernel’s own message kept at its end (mitcad#1185): the selected edges and the faces their chains end against, chamfer: the geometry kernel could not build the bevel of edge E{…}, its chain ending against face F3:chamfer(…) (kernel error: …), or after the kernel’s explanation, chamfer failed; the distance may be too large for the edges (edge E{…}, …). Those are the agents’ texts: the error’s detail, which the timeline’s and MCP’s error carry; a person reads the message without the names, the edges and faces painted from its places (mitcad#1612, “Errors: message, places and detail”).

Face features: shell, draft, offset_face, delete_face, replace_face, split_body, split_face

These work on named faces of one body (body, faces). The plane, face, body or sketch curves a feature works against (plane, target, tool) is a reference: a plane ("yz", "F5", a fixed plane), a face {"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:end(…)"}, a body {"body": "F4.b0"} or sketch curves {"sketch": "F6", "curves": ["c1", "c3"]}. Two fields go with it: offset (optional, a slot) moves a plane, not a face, along its normal; direction (split body and split face, optional) is the direction sketch curves are swept along, the sketch normal by default.

{"type": "shell", "body": "F2.b0", "faces": ["F2:end(…)"], "inside": 2, "outside": 0,
 "tangent_chain": true, "rounded": false}

Shell: the faces are removed (none: a closed void); the wall runs inside into and outside out of the surface (at least one, not negative). tangent_chain (default true) also removes faces tangent to a removed one; rounded rounds the outer corners. The outside of the wall keeps the face names; the inside is <shell>:offset(<face>) and the end of the wall where a removed face was <shell>:offset_cap(<face>). A face whose surface is only C0 continuous (a B-spline with a crease in its parametrisation, as imported bodies have them) is split at the creases first, so its wall comes in pieces (#k) under the face’s name. A face that vanishes at the wall’s thickness (a strip narrower, or a convex rounding tighter, than the wall) has no inside face: the insides of the faces beside it meet (mitcad#172, the OCCT port’s patch 0100). A wall the kernel cannot close (an open face ending smoothly in a kept one, without the tangent chain), which before came back as the body itself, makes the shell fail.

Parts no thicker than the wall stay solid (mitcad#1233). Where the kernel’s thick solid (or closed offset) fails, the inside of the wall is the body less a cavity: the body’s inward offset with the removed faces moved out past the body, so that it opens through them. Left out of the cavity, and solid with their own faces: the part under a face no further from a removed face than the wall (a 2 mm flange shelled 2 or 3 mm from its removed bottom; the exact coincident case is no special one), a plate between two opposite planar faces no further apart than twice the wall (cut off the body before the offset), and a curved or tapered part (a conical skirt, a cylindrical sleeve, a wedge-shaped fin, mitcad#1237): a kept face no further than twice the wall from another kept face across the body under at least half of it, together with the faces it turns away from convexly (up to the concave edges where the part stands on the rest of the body), taken away before the offset with the faces round it extended over its root. Where no face round such a part can be extended over its root (a fin whose ends continue the body’s sides, mitcad#1240) and the offset fails, the part is cut off at its root instead: the body is split by the surfaces the faces its thin faces stand on concavely lie on (each reaching past the body; several where it stands in a corner, a whole cylinder where its root is curved, mitcad#1241), and the pieces the thin faces bound are cut off before the offset, unless they hold more volume than the wall times their area, are the whole body or hold all of a removed face. Where the offset still fails, convex roundings tighter than the wall (and the curved faces round them, such as a chamfer’s cone round a rounded corner) are taken away before it: the inside of the wall runs past them. Where the cavity then comes nearer than the wall to a face it runs past or leaves out, the faces the nearest part of it is offset from go deeper by the difference, so that the wall keeps its thickness; where that does not help, the feature warns “the wall is thinner than mm beside face(s) …: down to mm (<t - d> mm less)”. A cavity that would cut into a kept face is refused. The outside keeps every face’s name; the inside is <shell>:offset(<face>) and what is left of a removed face <shell>:offset_cap(<face>), as above. The feature warns, naming the named faces without an inside of the wall (the first four, then “and N more”), whichever way the shell was built: “the wall does not fit under face(s) …; it is (the body is) left solid there” where some of the face is further than twice the wall from the inside of the wall, else “the inside of the wall runs past face(s) …, which is (are) too small or too tightly curved for it to follow”. Where the wall fits under no face, the shell fails: “shell failed; the wall does not fit under faces …: nothing can be hollowed”. A loft from a polygon to a circle, whose corners' creases flatten to tangency at the circle, shells and offsets where the walls lean out towards the circle (the OCCT port’s patch 1130, mitcad#1184) and where they lean in (patch 1190, mitcad#1193). Leaning in, a removed end’s walls are extended to it along the corners’ creases; the slivers, hundredths of a millimetre wide, by which the exact extended walls cross beside a corner are left out. With the circle’s seam on a side of the polygon (the loft splits that side into two faces tangent along the edge between them), its closed inward offsets are valid too (patch 1160, mitcad#1199). For a crease that flattens to tangency where its faces go on smoothly into a further face (a Y tube’s crotch, where the arms leave the common straight part), the offset keeps the branch along the crease alone, cut where the crease fades, each of the crease’s edges with its own piece, and a mirrored body’s reversed faces meet their seams on the right side of the period (patch 2140, mitcad#2140): such a tube shells inside with its ends open, Sharp. After the crease is rounded, the rounding’s pointed ends (degenerated edges where its section vanishes) are no apex for the offset (patch 2143), and the shell is built too. Where the kernel’s offset fails without saying why and the cavity cannot be built either, the shell fails in words instead of “the geometry kernel’s offset raised an error” (which stays in the error’s detail): “shell failed; the geometry kernel cannot offset the faces along an edge (edges) where their angle fades out to a smooth join at an end of it”, the edges as the error’s places, where the body has such creases between kept faces, else “shell failed; the geometry kernel cannot join the offsets of the faces into the inside of the wall at this thickness”. Tests make both refuse with the environment variable MITCAD_TEST_OCCT_REFUSES=shell.

{"type": "draft", "body": "F2.b0", "faces": ["F2:side(c1[c4,c2])"],
 "plane": {"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:start(…)"}, "angle": 0.0873,
 "symmetric": false, "angle2": null, "flip": false, "tangent_chain": true}

Draft with a fixed plane (a plane or a planar face): the faces turn about their intersection with it by angle (|a| < π/2, not zero). The pull direction is the plane’s normal, or from a face into its material; flip reverses it. A positive angle removes material on the pull side, so a side face drafted about the bottom face leans in towards the top. symmetric drafts both sides of the plane by angle, angle2 sets the other side’s angle: the faces are split at the plane (pieces #k) and each side narrows away from it. Without tangent_chain, a face tangent to a drafted one is unsupported. Parting line drafts are not modelled.

{"type": "offset_face", "body": "F2.b0", "faces": ["F2:end(…)"], "distance": 5}
{"type": "delete_face", "body": "F2.b0", "faces": ["F3:fillet(E{…})"]}
{"type": "replace_face", "body": "F2.b0", "faces": ["F2:end(…)"],
 "target": {"origin": [0, 0, 25], "normal": [0, 0, 1]}, "tangent_chain": true}
{"type": "replace_face", "body": "F2.b0", "faces": ["F2:end(…)"], "target": {"body": "F4.b0"}}

Offset face (also Press Pull on a face): the faces move along their normals, positive out of the material; the neighbouring faces extend or shorten along their own surfaces; the faces keep their names. A face that continues smoothly into a face that stays, such as one piece of a face split by split_face (mitcad#1928, mitcad#1947), moves alone, flat or curved: the chosen faces that share edges are thickened together by the distance along their normals, and that cell is cut from the body (inward) or added to it (outward). So only the chosen pieces move, never the rest of the faces they were cut from:

  • the seam becomes a step along the moved face’s normal, named <feature>:step(<moved face>) (#k for several; steps in one plane are one face), and the other piece stays where it is;
  • where two moved pieces meet, their new positions are extended or trimmed to each other, so convex and concave corners at any angle close (two pieces at a corner by d in: the body loses d·(A1 + A2) less d²·L·tan(θ/2), L the corner’s length and θ the angle between the pieces’ normals);
  • a face that stays and meets a moved piece at a sharp edge, at any angle, flat or curved, extends or trims along its own surface to the piece’s new position, as for whole faces (mitcad#1973): the cell’s wall there is removed and the faces around it close the gap. So a pocket, hole or boss inside a moved piece keeps its walls on their surfaces and gets shallower or deeper by the distance. The walls are removed one group (walls that share edges) at a time;
  • where the two faces turn tangent somewhere along their edge (an end of a mitre between roundings, mitcad#1974), the face that stays can be trimmed but not extended: past the tangent point it turns tangent to the faces it blends and has no surface to extend along. Where the face that stays curves towards the piece’s new position (a convex rounding beside a rounding piece moved in, a concave one beside one moved out), it is trimmed back along its surface to that position, up to the tangent point, where the step along the piece’s tangent edge closes against it, and no wall remains. Where it would have to extend (a convex rounding beside a piece moved out, a concave one beside one moved in), that side is a step along the piece’s normal over the whole edge: a ruled face from the edge to the piece’s new position, named as a step. test_offset_split_mitre (geometry tests) and cli.offset_split_reported state both results.

Where it cannot be built, the feature fails with the cause in words and the faces as its places: “a curved face would shrink to nothing: the distance is as large as its radius or larger”, “the faces cannot be moved by this distance: …” (the reason: a face narrower than the distance that would vanish, new positions that cannot be extended or trimmed to meet each other, …), “the moved faces’ new positions could not be cut into the body” (joined to outward), or “the faces around the moved faces cannot be extended or trimmed along their surfaces to meet their new positions”.

Delete face removes the faces and extends the neighbours until they close the gap, failing when they cannot.

Replace face replaces faces of any surface type with a target: a plane, a face of a body (any surface type; a face of the body itself works too) or a body (all its faces, such as a surface body; not the body itself).

  • The neighbours extend or shorten along their own surfaces to it; the new face is <feature>:replace(<face>) (pieces #k) and the neighbours keep their names.
  • Planar faces onto a plane or a planar face move there. Otherwise the region between the faces and the target, closed by the neighbours continued along their surfaces and by the target (when it is one face) continued along its own, is added to or removed from the body; B-splines continue by extrapolation, so their results are close, not exact.
  • MitCad’s own rules: the target need not cover the faces’ neighbourhood (it is continued); a face with the target on both sides goes to the nearer side (the smaller region); a region that would reach past the body’s other faces does not count (the target passes beyond the other faces of the body).
  • The tangent chain also replaces faces tangent to the replaced ones, such as the straight sides of a slot with its round end; replacing only the round end needs "tangent_chain": false.
  • Other failures: the target does not meet the body where the faces are, the target splits the body, face … could not be replaced (the target does not reach all of it) and, for planar faces onto a plane, the target is perpendicular to face ….
{"type": "split_body", "bodies": ["F2.b0"], "tool": "yz", "offset": 20, "extend": true}
{"type": "split_face", "body": "F2.b0", "faces": ["F2:end(…)"], "tool": {"sketch": "F6"},
 "direction": [0, 0, 1], "extend": true}

Split body cuts each body with a plane, a face (with extend, the default, grown along its surface: planes, cylinders, cones and spheres), a body or sketch curves; a body the tool does not divide fails it. The pieces come in order along a planar tool’s normal (else in geometric order): the first keeps the body (uid and name), the others are new bodies of the split (<split>.b0, …, named Body<n>); later evaluations keep the pieces’ ids (Body ids of a split’s pieces). The cut faces are <split>:split (<split>:split(<tool face>) for a face or body tool) and faces cut in two get #k. Split Face makes one face of a region that crosses a cylinder’s or a cone’s seam (mitcad#1853): the pieces the split leaves on either side of the seam are joined, every other edge kept.

more_tools (a list of tools like tool) divides the bodies by further tools as well, one after another: each divides the pieces it reaches and leaves the others, and one that reaches none fails. The cells are those of all the tools at once; offset and direction belong to tool.

A body tool, or the body of a face tool, may be a body of another component when tool_links names where it is seen, as a combine’s tools do (combine); it is read there, moved into the split’s coordinates and left as it is:

{"type": "split_body", "bodies": ["F7.b0"], "tool": {"body": "F2.b0"},
 "tool_links": {"F2.b0": {"source": "O1", "target": "O2"}}}

Split face splits the faces along the tool (the same kinds; sketch curves swept along direction); the shape does not change and the pieces keep the face’s name with #k. Every face must be split.

remove_body 

{"type": "remove_body", "bodies": ["F4.b1"]}

Takes the bodies out of the design (RemoveBody<n>): the features before it keep their results, and a later feature that refers to a removed body fails. A body is listed once. A listed piece of a split that the split no longer makes after an upstream edit is passed by with a warning (Body ids of a split’s pieces).

sweep 

{"type": "sweep", "profiles": [{"sketch": "F2", "region": "r{c1}"}],
 "path": {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1"], "chain": true},
 "orientation": "perpendicular", "twist_angle": 0, "taper_angle": 0,
 "guide_rail": {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c9"]}, "profile_scaling": "scale",
 "extent": {"type": "partial", "fraction": 0.5, "fraction2": 1}, "flip": false,
 "operation": "new_body"}
{"type": "sweep", "profiles": [{"sketch": "F2", "region": "r{c1}"}],
 "path": {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1"]}, "end_scale": 0.5, "operation": "new_body"}
{"type": "sweep", "profiles": [{"sketch": "F2", "region": "r{c1}"}],
 "path": {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1"]}, "guide_rail": {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c2"]},
 "guide_rail2": {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c3"]}, "operation": "new_body"}
{"type": "sweep", "profiles": [{"sketch": "F2", "region": "r{c1}"}],
 "path": {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1"]}, "guide_rail": {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c2"]},
 "rail_point": "plane", "operation": "new_body"}

A surface sweep ("surface": true, with curves): Surface modelling (mitcad#455).

Sweeps, lofts, pipes, coils, ribs and webs: kernel inputs in core/model-base/src/sweeps.rs, geometry in geometry/src/{path_sweep,loft,rib,spine}.cpp. Fractions of a path, revolutions and loft weights are unitless values. Examples: tools/cli/tests/f3_*.json.

  • profiles: regions of one sketch (touching regions sweep together, holes stay holes). The sweep starts where the path crosses the profile’s plane (the crossing nearest to the profile), or at the path’s point nearest to the profile; a profile beside the path is swept as it is placed against it.
  • path: a path. Along a fixed helix (a spiral stair’s rail, mitcad#385) a perpendicular profile keeps its angle to the helix’s axis as it turns about it (tools/cli/tests/f3_sweep.json, Sweep6); the helix and coil features instead keep their section in a plane through the axis.
  • Where a path turns at a corner, the sides of the swept profile run on until they meet (a mitre); a profile of one closed edge whose mitres do not build from its seam is swept as its two halves (mitcad#385: an ellipse whose seam lies along the normal of the path’s plane), and a swept solid must enclose a positive volume (a mitre whose sides fold through each other can pass the shape check).
  • orientation: perpendicular (default; the profile keeps its angle to the path, without twisting about it) or parallel (it keeps its direction and only moves; where the path turns back through the profile’s plane, the copies passing over each other are fused into one body).
  • twist_angle: the profile’s turn about the path over the swept length (right hand about the path’s direction). taper_angle: positive widens; every side of the profile leans out by the angle as an extrusion’s taper does, the outline offset by s tan(taper) at distance s (a circle on the path becomes a cone, a square stays a square: 5 degrees over 50 mm turn a 10 mm square into one of 18.75 mm; checked against the stored body of a reference model, 10650.14 mm3). A taper alone whose walls meet or vanish on the way (a slot it closes, a narrow part it eats away), where the copies cannot be lofted, is an extrusion’s taper from the profile with its topology events resolved (mitcad#1851): along a line as it is, along a smooth curved path (mitcad#1854) bent along it, each place of the straight taper going to the profile’s frame as far along the path, the copy there. Its caps are planes, its walls B-splines within 1e-7 of their size of the bend; a path of several curves is bent curve by curve, the walls split where the curves meet (#k). Not where the profile reaches as far from the path as its centres of curvature. A taper that closes the whole profile before the end fails as before (the taper closes the profile before the end of the sweep).
  • guide_rail: turns the profile towards the rail and with profile_scaling scale (default) sizes it by the rail’s distance from the path, stretch only towards the rail, none not at all. The rail point is chosen by rail_point. Twist and taper are ignored with a rail.
  • rail_point (mitcad#469, with guide_rail): where the rail’s point is for each place along the path. plane: where the rail crosses the plane square to the path there. At the profile that is the crossing nearest to the path; from there the sweep follows the rail place by place, each time to the next crossing onwards along the rail in the way it runs with the path (back along it before the profile), so a rail that crosses a plane more than once is taken in order, and the rail’s direction does not matter. An end of the rail within 1e-3 mm (or a millionth of the path’s length) of a plane counts as crossing it; a rail that does not reach the plane of every place of the swept part fails the sweep (the guide rail does not reach the plane square to the path …% of the way along the swept part). fraction (left out, as designs saved before the option have it): the point at the same fraction of the rail’s length as the place is of the path’s, taken into the plane square to the path. The two agree for a rail that runs evenly beside the path (a straight rail beside a straight path) and differ where the rail’s speed along the path varies: an arc that bulges away from a straight path (geometry/tests/test_sweeps.cpp, test_rail_plane; the .solidcraft test design sweep-rail-plane). The .f3d and .solidcraft imports and the Sweep command take plane.
  • guide_rail2 (mitcad#464, with guide_rail): a second rail. The profile moves with its point where the first rail starts (the first rail’s point in the plane square to the path), turns with the line across to the second rail and is sized by that line’s length against its length at the profile: scale evenly about the first rail’s point, stretch only along the line, none not at all. Each rail’s point is chosen by rail_point (each rail followed on its own), in the plane square to the path (geometry/tests/test_sweeps.cpp, test_two_rails_and_end_scale, test_rail_plane). Rails that meet are an error.
  • end_scale (mitcad#464, unitless, 0.01 to 100): the profile’s size at the ends of the swept part, from 1 at the profile in proportion to the length run along the path, about the path (a circle on a straight path becomes a cone frustum; with extent the scale is reached at each end of the swept part). With twist and taper; refused with a guide rail, guide surfaces or a fixed binormal (they decide the profile’s size).
  • guide_surfaces (mitcad#157): faces the path lies on, [{"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:side(c1)"}, …] (every piece of a split face), instead of a rail. The profile keeps its place in the frame of the path’s tangent and the surface’s normal where the path runs, so it turns with the surface (a thread’s profile swept along a helical edge of the thread’s flank keeps its angle to the flank). A path on the faces (within 1e-4 mm) takes their normal where it runs; a path beside them (mitcad#161: a thread’s crest guided by its flank) takes their normal at their points nearest to it. The orientation must be perpendicular; twist and taper are ignored. The path is usually an edge of the faces, or sketch curves on them. A sweep that passes over itself (a profile taller than a helix’s pitch) is swept in pieces that do not, each from the profile placed in the frame where it starts, and the pieces are fused.
  • body_links (mitcad#161): bodies of other components the path’s edges and the guide surfaces are on, each with where it is seen, {"F2.b0": {"source": "O1", "target": "O2"}} (an OccurrenceLink, as a combine’s tool_links, Geometry of other components): the body is read in its component and moved into the sweep’s coordinates by the occurrences' placements at the sweep’s point of the timeline. A link for a body neither the path nor a guide surface is on is refused; another component’s body without a link fails the sweep (body F2.b0 (from Extrude1) belongs to A; …).
  • extent: {"type": "full"} (default: the whole path both ways from the profile, once round a closed path) or {"type": "partial", "fraction": f1, "fraction2": f2}: f1 of the path’s part beyond the profile, f2 of the part before it (distanceOne and distanceTwo in .f3d designs; left out, the whole part before it, none on a closed path, where f1 + f2 <= 1). The Sweep panel shows them as Distance 1 and Distance 2 (mitcad#795, app/COMMANDS.md), and writes 1 / 1 as full.
  • A sweep’s preview adds sweep_path (mitcad#795): {"closed": false, "profile_at": "start"}: whether the path is closed and where the profile lies on it as it is swept (after flip): start or end when that end of an open path lies in the profile’s plane (the end nearer to the middle of the profile’s bounds when both do), else inside (always on a closed path). Reported also when the sweep then fails (an extent the path cannot take); not for a body face as the profile, fixed curves or a surface sweep of curves only. Test: f3_tests::sweep_previews_tell_where_the_profile_lies_on_the_path.
  • flip: runs the path the other way (isDirectionFlipped in .f3d designs).

Twists, tapers, end scales and rails sweep copies of the profile placed along the path through a smooth loft: the path must be smooth, the orientation perpendicular and the sweep not round a whole closed path (otherwise unsupported: …). Sharp corners of a plain sweep are mitred; a corner whose mitre does not build (a slight kink between path curves) is rounded, or else the profile turns through it. A profile within the modelling tolerance (1e-7 mm) of an end of the path is at that end: fraction 0 with the whole fraction2 sweeps only backwards from it, and an extent that covers none of the path is an error.

Faces: side(<segment>) from each profile segment, #k pieces where the path has several curves; start(<region>) and end(<region>): with the profile at an end of the swept part start is at the profile, otherwise start ends side one (beyond the profile) and end side two, as for extrusions. A sweep round a whole closed path has no caps. With the parallel orientation, where the path turns back through the profile’s plane the copy there is a face of its own, turn(<region>) (#k when it turns back several times).

A fixed binormal (mitcad#397)

"binormal": [x, y, z] (any length but zero; left out by default) keeps a perpendicular sweep’s profile at its angles to that direction instead of to the path: its frame along the path is the tangent, binormal × tangent and the binormal made square to the tangent. With the binormal up, a profile whose x is level where the sweep starts stays level and square to the path all along a sloped path (the .rvt import’s sloped elliptical rail pieces), where without it the profile keeps its angle to a planar path’s plane. It is refused with the parallel orientation, a guide rail, guide surfaces, a twist or a taper, and fails where the path runs along the binormal or turns at a corner (unsupported: …: the frames either side of a corner do not meet in a mitre). The geometry sweeps the profile with the path’s curves on the surfaces they sweep along the binormal, whose normals give the frames (geometry/src/path_sweep.cpp; test_fixed_binormal in geometry/tests/test_sweeps.cpp).

A Frenet or auxiliary frame (mitcad#539)

"frame" (left out by default) sets how a perpendicular sweep’s profile turns along the path instead of keeping its angle to it:

  • {"type": "frenet"}: the path’s Frenet frame (its tangent, its principal normal towards the centre of its curvature, their binormal); the profile turns with the path’s curvature. Along a planar path it is the default frame, except where the path’s bend changes side.
  • {"type": "auxiliary", "curve": <path>, "curvilinear": false}: the frame’s normal points from the path to a curve beside it (an auxiliary spine, a path), so the profile turns about the path as that direction does; the curve’s point is where it crosses the plane square to the path there, or with curvilinear the point at the same fraction of its length as the path’s (the frame’s normal then the direction to it, its tangent square to that normal). The curve runs the way the path runs (flip reverses both) and must stay apart from the path. Unlike a guide rail it never sizes the profile.
  • {"type": "constant_binormal", "binormal": [x, y, z]} (any length but zero): the frame keeps that binormal exactly, its normal binormal × tangent and its tangent the path’s made square to the binormal, so the profile turns only about the binormal. Unlike the fixed binormal above (which keeps the path’s tangent and makes the binormal square to it), the profile leans with the path where the path leaves the plane square to the binormal; where the path runs at right angles to it the two agree.

The geometry sweeps them as OCCT’s pipe shell’s Frenet, auxiliary and constant binormal modes, approximated within 1e-7 mm (geometry/src/spine.cpp, geometry/src/path_sweep.cpp; test_sweep_frames in geometry/tests/test_sweeps.cpp: along a straight path a curve crossing from one side above it to the other turns a bar a quarter turn, by either rule; the OCCT port’s patch 1030 corrects the second derivative of the curvilinear rule’s frame, which bent the pipe between its sections). A frame is refused with the parallel orientation, a guide rail, guide surfaces, a fixed binormal, curves, a twist, a taper or an end scale. The FreeCAD import’s pipes in the Frenet, Auxiliary and Binormal modes are sweeps with these frames (the Binormal mode’s binormal turned by the pipe’s own placement, in which FreeCAD sweeps it).

A body face as the profile (mitcad#543)

"profile_face": {"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:end(r{…})"} instead of profiles sweeps a planar face of a body (as an extrusion’s and a revolution’s profile_face): its bounded area with its holes, found by its topological name on every recompute, its plane the profile’s (Kernel::face_sweep); the body is left as it is. Faces: side(<edge>) by the edges’ names in the body (an edge without a name by its index among the face’s edges), the caps start(<face>) and end(<face>) keyed by the stored reference. Perpendicular or parallel, with a frame or a fixed binormal; refused with profiles, curves, surface, a twist, a taper, an end scale, guide rails or guide surfaces. A face that is gone, not planar or of a mesh body fails the sweep (geometry/tests/test_sweeps.cpp, test_face_sweep). The Sweep command does not open such a sweep (its profiles are a sketch’s); the FreeCAD import’s pipes of a face are these.

A profile that passes through itself (mitcad#1697)

A perpendicular sweep of sketch profiles without a twist, a taper, an end scale, guide rails, guide surfaces or a frame of its own (the default, and a constant binormal) whose profile passes through itself along the path (it reaches past the centre of a circular arc of the path, a straight piece is too short for the miters at its ends, or the path comes back near itself and the sweep’s faces cross) is built in pieces fused into one solid, as a pipe is (pipe, “Passing through itself”): the profile’s reach is that of its farthest point from the path, and its own extent in each direction decides the arcs and the miters. The sweep then shows the information the swept profile passes through itself along the path; it was built in pieces joined into one solid as a note. A circle about a path in one plane along a tight bend of an ellipse or a spline, and about a path in no plane along a tight bend of a helix between straight legs, is built from its tube as a pipe is (mitcad#1709). Where it is not built in pieces (a tight bend of another curve, or of such a curve under another profile; a path in no plane with other curves than lines and arcs, for a profile that is not a circle about the path) it is swept as before; where that fails, it is refused with the sweep passes through itself along its path and could not be built in pieces there, or the sweep's path turns right back at a corner, where no mitered corner can be built. Test: geometry.pipe_folds, f3_tests (mock kernel).

Fixed curves of a surface sweep (mitcad#548)

"fixed_curves": [...] (the curves of a path’s fixed_curves) with "surface": true sweeps curves that no sketch can hold, lying in no plane, into walls without caps, as a surface sweep’s curves: their chains (open or closed) along the path, faces side(fixed<n>) by the curves’ places in the list. The sweep starts where the path meets the plane through the first curve’s start square to the path at its start. Refused with profiles, curves, profile_face, a solid sweep, a join or cut, a twist, a taper, guide rails, guide surfaces or a frame. The FreeCAD import’s Part sweeps of a section in no plane are these.

loft 

{"type": "loft", "sections": [
   {"type": "profile", "sketch": "F1", "region": "r{…}"},
   {"type": "face", "body": "F4.b0", "face": "F4:end(r{c1})"},
   {"type": "point", "point": "F7"},
   {"type": "point", "point": {"sketch": "F3", "point": "p5"}}],
 "start_condition": {"type": "free"}, "end_condition": {"type": "point_sharp"},
 "centerline": {"sketch": "F9", "curves": ["c1"]}, "rails": [],
 "closed": false, "ruled": false, "surface": false, "operation": "new_body"}

  • sections: two or more, in order: sketch regions without holes, faces of bodies (their outer boundary), and points (a point reference) only first or last. Sections of different numbers of edges are matched by the kernel. A face with holes lofts its outer boundary too: the loft is solid across its holes, and its tangent and smooth conditions follow the faces next to that boundary; the body keeps its face as it was (mitcad#1183). A sketch region with holes is refused (unsupported: a loft section with holes).

  • ruled: straight between neighbouring sections; smooth otherwise (two sections are straight either way; three circles give the parabola through their radii). A smooth loft through three or more sections, without end conditions or rails, is a piecewise cubic Hermite surface (the form of the stored lofts, checked against the bodies of the reference models diff_loft_closed_*: 9503.318 mm3 open and 12880.53 closed for four circles of 10 mm 30 mm from the axis at quarter turns): every point of a section follows the curve through its matching points of the sections, a cubic piece between two sections whose tangent at a section is the derivative of the parabola through its neighbours (by the chord lengths between the sections’ centres), the curve continuous in its tangent but not its curvature; at an end the first piece is the parabola that arrives with the inner tangent. The sections’ edges are matched corner for corner (each section turned and reversed to lie as near as possible to the one before it).

  • Two sections, free, smooth or ruled (mitcad#2141, mitcad#2143; ruled ones too since mitcad#2191, as the .solidcraft import makes every loft): a face runs straight across each pair of matched edges. Where both sections run on smoothly through a pair of matched vertices (a circle cut where a slot’s arcs meet its straight sides; a rounded rectangle), the two faces beside the line between them are tangent all along it: each face’s edges are eased (followed faster or slower towards an end, the edges themselves unchanged) so that on both sides of the line the two sections advance alike, and the faces joined so are pieces of one B-spline surface (periodic when they run round the whole section), within 1e-7 mm of the edges. Without it the faces met at a crease that grows from nothing at the sections to some ten degrees between them, which a Shell or a Thicken of the loft could not offset; faces only tangent on surfaces of their own were offset into edges of an invalid range by the geometry kernel. Where a section has a corner the faces meet at an angle as before, and lofts with no such line (a square to a circle, a circle to a circle) are the kernel’s ruled lofts as before. The eased faces still run straight between the two sections, so a ruled loft gets the same faces as a smooth one. Test: geometry.loft_circle_slot, cli.loft_circle_slot_reported.

  • closed: from the last section back to the first, without caps and without point sections; three or more sections. A smooth closed loft is tangent where it closes: the same curves, periodic, which needs sections of as many edges, starting at corresponding points.

  • surface: the loft as a surface, a sheet body of the side faces only (no caps; isSolid false in .f3d designs). A new body or a new component, never joined or cut; a sheet has no volume. Sections of sketch curves ({"type": "curves", "sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1", "c2"]}, one chain each) loft a surface only (Surface modelling, mitcad#455).

  • centerline: a path; keeps the sections at right angles to it on the way (the part of it between the first and the last section).

  • frame (mitcad#543, only with a centerline): how the sections turn along it instead, as a sweep’s frame: {"type": "frenet"}, {"type": "auxiliary", "curve": <path>, "curvilinear": false} or {"type": "constant_binormal", "binormal": [x, y, z]}; the pipe shell through the sections then follows that frame, approximated within 1e-7 mm (the FreeCAD import’s pipes through several sections in the Frenet, Auxiliary and Binormal modes).

  • orientation (mitcad#547, only with a centerline and without a frame): perpendicular (default, left out) keeps the sections’ angle to the centre line; parallel keeps their direction, as a sweep’s parallel orientation: they only move along it (a pipe shell of a fixed frame, approximated within 1e-7 mm; the FreeCAD import’s pipes through several sections in the Fixed mode).

  • tangent_edges (mitcad#2162): what the loft does with a section’s edges that meet tangentially (within the model’s angular tolerance, 1e-6 rad): merge joins each run of them into one smooth edge before the loft, so that the side between such runs is one face, keep (left out, also when saved) keeps every edge its own face, as a design saved before the choice built.
