The parts list (parts_list) has supplier, part_number and supplier_url in every row: a BUILD part’s from its source (the row’s own part_number first) and its designation with its values; an inserted library part’s as the library gave them when it was inserted (a component’s library record keeps them). A configuration row may have its own part_number and supplier_url.

A row’s part_number (mitcad#2138) is the component’s own stored Part number (of any set, Identity/Part number as Property Sets’ standing row stores it) first; without one, its BUILD or options entry’s, then its library’s. An empty number counts as none at every step. The drawing Bill of Materials table, the Build tab’s Bill of Materials window and bom_rows’ grouping read this row. The read-only Library/Part number of property_sets keeps the entry’s own number (none when that is empty), also when the component’s own wins here.

derived_part 

{"type": "derived_part", "source": "S1", "config": "M6",
 "parameters": {"L": "d12"},
 "ends": {"a": {"angle": "45 deg", "tilt": "x"}, "b": {"angle": 0}},
 "operation": "new_body"}

The first body of a placed part’s component (named Part<n>). To make it, the model:

  1. evaluates the source’s design with the configuration row config (the source’s default when left out) and parameters set ({the source’s user parameter: a value}; a cut-to-length part always lists its length parameter);
  2. copies its visible bodies in;
  3. cuts its ends.
  • Ends (cut-to-length parts only):
    • angle is the cut’s angle from square, from 0 up to (not including) 90°.
    • tilt is the section axis the cut turns about: x or y of the source’s section, the cut leaning towards +y or +x; -x and -y lean the other way.
    • The length is the part’s outer length, its long point (mitcad#443). End A is cut at z = 0 and end B at z = L, each by the plane through the section’s outermost edge on the long side (the side the cut leans away from, measured from the section’s bounds, so an asymmetric section works too). The body never reaches past 0 and L; the short point is the section’s width across the tilt × tan(angle) shorter (a 20 mm profile of 500 mm cut at 45°: 500 on the long side, 480 on the short one). The cuts only take material away; the frames stay those of the length itself.
    • The cut is made inside the feature, not as a cut feature of its own, so the cut list reads it from the definition.
  • Names.
    • The bodies are <feature>.b<i>, in the source’s order.
    • A face of the source is <feature>:part(<the source's face name>).
    • The end faces are always <feature>:end_a and <feature>:end_b, cut or not, so a sketch or hole on an end stays on it when its mitre changes.
    • The source’s names do not change with its parameters (a profile’s side faces are named after its section’s curves). So sketches, holes and cuts on the part keep their place when the length or a mitre changes.
    • The face in part(...) is named in the source’s own ids: they are no features of the design (references to F7:part(F2:side(c1)) depend on F7 only, and copies leave the inner name as it is).
    • A square end’s faces are the source’s planar faces at z = 0 facing −z (z = L facing +z); the faces of the kernel’s other names are kept.
  • Frames.
    • Every mount:<name> joint origin of the source becomes a frame of the feature, <feature>:mount(<name>), moved with the part’s parameters (end_b follows the length).
    • A joint origin’s geometry may name one: {"mount": "F7:mount(slot_x+_1)"} (Kinds and frames). Its origin and axes are then the frame’s, not a face’s middle.
  • Editing.
    • The component can be activated and given features like any other component: a sketch on F7:part(...) and a hole, a cut.
    • Paste New copies the derived part with its own parameters. Move to Component, of its bodies and of its occurrence (another parent), keeps it.
    • Convert to Features (convert_derived_part, mitcad#1815) replaces it with its source’s own features, every reference to it rewritten (Convert to Features).
    • Results are cached by the source’s digest, the row, the parameters' values and the ends; they are not kept in the result store (the source is evaluated again when the design opens).
    • parameters take lengths (a number is millimetres). A length outside the build block’s limits is a warning of the feature (the commands refuse it).
  • Look and material (mitcad#478, #1817). A part whose library’s build block names a material takes, on its bodies, the appearance its source’s bodies all show (the end grain on its ends) and its library’s material: the one the source’s bodies all name, else the block’s species or product with its density for the part’s row (planed spruce 28 x 45 x 1800 mm is Spruce, 0.45 g/cm³, 1.02 kg). See Materials, “A part placed from a library”. A part of a design saved without it gets it when the design opens.

bound_length 

{"type": "bound_length", "parameter": "d12",
 "from": {"occurrence": "O3", "geometry": {"mount": "F5:mount(slot_y+_1)"},
          "shift": {"x": "d9", "y": 0, "z": 0}},
 "direction": "z",
 "to": {"occurrence": "O4", "geometry": {"body": "F8.b0", "face": "F8:part(...)"}},
 "mode": "face", "add": 0}

BoundLength<n> is a feature of the component that places both parts: the BUILD commands make it in the parent of the two occurrences. It owns parameter, a reference parameter (kind reference, like a driven dimension’s, Values). Its value is a length measured at the feature’s point of the timeline:

  • The ray starts at from’s frame, an origin as for a joint, taken in the feature’s component through the occurrences’ placements there.

  • The start is shifted along that frame’s axes by shift, a set of values. BUILD writes there the parameters of the joint that slides the new part along a slot, so the ray follows the part when it is moved along the slot.

  • The ray runs along the frame’s direction (z, the default, -z, x, …), or a vector [x, y, z] in the frame’s coordinates (a part turned at an end).

  • It ends on to, a planar face or a frame (the plane through its origin across its z axis). mode decides where:

    • face: the distance to the face;
    • centre: to the middle of the profile the face belongs to, half its section further;
    • through: to its far side;
    • to_face (mitcad#1630): to the plane of a face picked anywhere, not only one in the ray’s way (Length to a face below); to may then also be an origin or construction plane.

    (The part is the body of the face, or of the derived part the frame is of; its far side is the farthest corner of its box along the ray.)

  • add is added to the result: an overlap or a gap, and may be negative.

Timeline order. BUILD always puts the three features in this order:

  1. the bound_length;
  2. the derived part whose length the parameter sets;
  3. the joint that places that part.

The ray never depends on the part it sizes. So moving the target (dragging its joint), or moving the part along its slot, recomputes the length.

Failures and detaching.

  • A ray that meets nothing (its target behind the start or along the ray), a length of zero or less, or a target that is gone, fails the feature with the reason, and the reference keeps its last value.
  • Two lengths bound to each other (each part’s ray ends on the other) make a cycle, and the second one is refused when it is made. A length is bound only to a part placed before it in the timeline (its joint before the part’s derived part): one placed later is refused too.
  • Detaching (build_edit with a length value) replaces the reference with a dimension parameter of the same name, keeps its last value, and deletes the feature; the value given is then the length.
  • A new bound length’s parameter is given as a number, its first value: it becomes the feature’s own reference parameter.

Placement

Where parts go (mitcad#394). BUILD needs no component to be activated first. Its commands place parts in the BUILD host: the active component when its policy takes components, else the nearest component up from it (along its first path from the root) that takes components and can be edited, as the design policy puts a new component beside a part (Design policy, mitcad#292). In a new design Component1 takes components (the general defaults, mitcad#421), so the host is Component1, the active component, and nothing is redirected; a component set to part still sends its parts up. When no component up takes components, the active one (and the policy’s refusal). The build_host query names it. Every path (at.occurrence, length.bind.occurrence) is from the host and every point and direction (at.point, at.direction) in its coordinates; the joints and bound lengths go into it. Bound lengths are assembly features, as joints are: a component with the Assembly policy takes them. So no policy refusal comes from where BUILD puts things.

A placed part is one component with one occurrence in the BUILD host. With it come:

  • its derived_part;
  • the joint that places it;
  • its bound_length features, when its length or size is bound.

The component records what BUILD made, in the design file too:

"build": {"role": "profile", "source": "S1", "part": "F7", "joint": "F9",
          "bound": ["F6"], "added_by": null, "adds": [], "from": "b"}
  • added_by is the connector component that added this one (a nut, a screw).
  • adds lists the components and features a connector added ("C5", "F12"): its fasteners, and the holes it machined into the profiles; a panel’s clamps; a part’s own end machining (build_edit’s machining).
  • junction (a connector’s only) is the build_junctions id it was placed at.
  • bound lists the part’s bound lengths (a panel has one per size).
  • from (a part on a side or a rail, mitcad#417) is the reference its joint’s slide is bound to: a, b or middle (Side placements).
  • tilt (a part on a side tilted along its target, mitcad#444) is its tilt in radians, positive towards the target’s end B (Tilt).
  • named_after (mitcad#2030) is the designation the component’s name came from, while that name is automatic (BUILD: a part’s automatic name).
  • BUILD reads these records. Other commands treat the component as any other, and a component without build is not a BUILD part.

Joints BUILD makes. Two frames that mate face each other: their z axes are opposite, so every joint BUILD makes between two frames is flipped (flip: true, docs/libraries.md, Which way a frame’s z points). Each is named <part> on <target> after the components it joins (mitcad#2088, BUILD: drags and travel limits).

  • A profile on another profile’s side gets a slider joint along the slot (slide_axis x, the slot’s direction). The joint is between the new profile’s end_a frame (end_b with flip) and the slot frame, flipped:
    • its position.tx is the distance of the new part’s frame (its centre line, for a profile standing on the slot) from the target’s end A along the slot, bound to the placement’s reference from (mitcad#417; kept in the component’s record, Side placements below), so that the part keeps its place from it when the target’s length changes:
      • from end A the offset is to the new part’s near face (mitcad#394): tx is the offset plus the part’s reach behind its frame (half the section for a profile: offset 0 is flush with end A), a number (or the typed expression, shifted);
      • from end B the offset is to its far face (far from end A: its face nearer end B): tx is L - offset - reach, an expression of the target’s length parameter (d12 - 65 for offset 50 of a 30 profile);
      • from the middle the offset is of the new part’s middle from the target’s, positive towards end B: tx is L / 2 + offset - middle (d12 / 2 + 15 for offset 30 of a 30 profile, middle the part’s middle from its frame);
    • without an offset the click places it, and its reference and offset are stored as if typed (see Side placements below);
    • its angle is the rotation about the axis: 0, 90, 180 or 270°;
    • a drag does not move it: its slide changes only through Placement (build_edit), so a frame stays put (BUILD: drags and travel limits below).
    • A part that is not a profile (a rail, a plate) mounts with its first frame of kind slot, face or hole the same way.
  • A profile on an end gets a rigid joint between its end_a (or end_b) and the target’s end frame, flipped. Its angle is the rotation. Straight, the new profile continues the target on its axis. Turned (a corner, End placements below), the target’s frame has a frame_override whose z is the new direction (in the target’s coordinates), whose x is the end frame’s first axis not along it, and whose shift (along the turned frame’s axes) aligns the corner; the shift moves with the end frame, so the corner follows the target’s length. A bound length’s ray starts at the shifted frame (its shift in the end frame’s axes).
  • The first part, on a plane, a point or a face, gets a rigid joint to that geometry, flipped, with a frame_override origin at point (anywhere on the plane, far from its origin too; without point at the geometry’s own origin: the app’s Enter on a chosen plane before the click that says where, mitcad#1196); without at.geometry it has no joint and is grounded at at.point (the origin when left out; the app’s Enter without a pick), along the host’s +Z. at.direction (mitcad#394; the app’s X, Y and Z buttons) turns it: grounded, its axis runs along it; on a plane or face the joint’s frame_override turns the frame’s z to it (its first axis that is not along it keeps the roll), so the part lies on an XY pick along X or Y from the click. The picked geometry may be the host’s own (its origin planes, construction planes and faces) or any occurrence’s under it, resolved through the occurrence path as joints resolve it.
  • A part that moves on another (linear.mate: a carriage on its rail) gets the mate’s joint (joint, axis; slider by default) between its mate.frame and the target’s first frame of kind mate.on, flipped, its slide at at.offset along x from at.from (end A, end B or the middle, as on a side but to the part’s frame). Its slide gets travel limits, by default flush with the target’s end A to flush with its end B, and it drags within them (BUILD: drags and travel limits below). One whose mate.on is slot (a slider) placed on a profile’s side (a side face or a slot frame as at.geometry) goes on that side as a profile does (mitcad#448): place is side, the slot is the one of the face picked nearest at.point, its mate.frame slides on it at the click’s snaps or at.offset from at.from. A cap gets a rigid joint between its first end (or face) frame and the picked end, flipped.
  • A connector gets a slider joint between its first mate’s frame and profile a’s frame of the mate’s kind (to) that faces the inner corner (the one turned most towards b), at the distance from a’s meeting end that the second mate’s frame lies from the first one’s plane, turned about z so that its second arm lies towards b. Its fasteners (nut, screw, washer) get rigid joints, flipped, between their first slot, hole or face frame (their design’s XY when they have none) and the connector’s fastener frame.
  • A panel gets a rigid joint (not flipped) between its design’s XY frame and the picked profile’s slot frame with a frame_override that puts the middle of the design’s box at the panel’s middle: its x along that profile, its z across the frame’s plane. A panel design has its width along X, its height along Y and its thickness along Z (centred on its XY origin, or drawn from its corner and extruded from XY: its box says where it is).

Commands

CommandFieldsResult
build_placepart ({"library", "url", "rev", "component", "config"}, or {"source": "S1", "config"} to reuse a source), at (below), rotate (an angle: 0, 90, 180 or 270 deg on a part’s side or end, any angle on a plane or a face, mitcad#2046; a number is radians), flip (true: the other end first), length (a value, or {"bind": {"occurrence", "geometry"}, "mode": "face"/"centre"/"through", "add"}, or to a picked face {"mode": "to_face", "face": {"occurrence", "geometry"}, "offset"}, Length to a face; left out: the source’s default), mitre ({"angle", "cut": "new"/"existing"/"shared"/"none"}; left out: none, also on a square corner; shared on a corner at another angle at offset 0, mitcad#427; every cut keeps the lengths as long points and a shared one makes the outer corners meet, mitcad#443), tilt (on a side, mitcad#444: an angle from -80 to 80 deg, positive towards the target’s end B; Tilt), parameters (other source parameters), name, limits (a part that slides on another, a carriage on its rail, mitcad#2088: {"min", "max"}, lengths from the target’s end A to the part’s frame, each left out or null for its default; refused for another part; BUILD: drags and travel limits)component, occurrence, name, features (everything it added), joint, bound, adds, warnings, place (side, end, frame, geometry or grounded); undo step Place <designation>

The application and mitcad-cli run it when they open a design; a refusal leaves the design as loaded, with a warning (mitcad#1151)

at says where the part goes: {"occurrence", "geometry", "point", "place", "offset", "from", "direction", "snap"}.

  • occurrence is a path from the BUILD host (uids or names).

  • geometry is what was picked: a face or a frame of a placed part, or, for the first part, a plane, a point or a face. Without it the part is grounded at point.

  • point is where it was picked, in the host’s coordinates.

  • place is auto (the default), side or end. With auto, the click decides:

    • a pick on a profile’s end face (<F>:end_a, <F>:end_b) or end frame is end;
    • a pick on a side face is side: at the slot of that side nearest to point (of the slots on the face’s plane when the kernel tells the face’s plane; none there is a closed side), where point is along the profile (Side placements);
    • a slot frame is side at that slot; another frame (a rail’s) is a mate.

  • from (mitcad#417) is what offset is measured from on a side or a rail: a (the default), b or middle; on a side also gap (Middle of Gap below, mitcad#1401). It is accepted on an end and not used there.

  • offset (a length: a number in mm or an expression) replaces the click on a side:

    • from a: the new part’s near face from end A (0: flush with A);
    • from b: its far face (its face nearer end B) from end B (0: flush with B), positive towards A;
    • from middle: the new part’s middle from the target’s, positive towards end B (0: centred).

    On a turned end (a corner) it is the new part’s end from the target’s outer side (End placements); on a straight end it is not used. On a plane or a face (mitcad#2046) it moves the first part off it along its normal, positive to the normal’s side (out of a face), negative into it, whatever the direction: a standing part starts that far from it, a lying part is lifted off it. It is kept as the shift of the joint’s origin b frame override, in that frame’s axes, so it follows the face; the face’s centre snap and its edge alignment stay. Grounded at a point it is not used.

  • direction: on an end, the new part’s axis in the host’s coordinates (along the target: straight; or one of the four square to it, or any other); left out, a click on the end face decides (End placements). For the first part, the axis it runs along: grounded at point, +Z when left out; on a plane or a face, the frame’s z when left out (a plane’s normal, a planar face’s outward normal: down from a face that faces down, mitcad#2000). A planar face of another body (not a BUILD part’s) lines the part’s sides up with the face’s longest straight edge (its frame’s x along that edge, unless the part runs along it; rotate turns it further), and without point the part starts at the face’s centre of area (the app’s Face normal sends neither direction nor point, so the part snaps there).

  • snap (mm, optional, mitcad#417): the app’s least snap distance, about 12 pixels at the click’s depth. The model uses the larger of it and its own for the side snaps and the end face’s zones, so that snapping works when the view is zoomed out and is never a one-pixel target.

Side placements (mitcad#394, mitcad#417). On a side the new part never overhangs the target, a click snaps, and the placement is bound to the reference the click resolved to:

  • The part’s reach along the slot is that of its box, turned as the joint turns it: a profile standing on the slot reaches half its section to either side of its centre line; its width along the slot is the whole section.

  • A click centres the part on point’s distance along the profile, then (each distance at least at.snap):

    • within one section width of end A (its near face less than a width from the end, or past it) it goes flush with end A: from a, offset 0;
    • likewise flush with end B: from b, offset 0;
    • within a quarter width of the middle it is centred on the middle: from middle, offset 0;
    • within a quarter width of a place where it lines up with another profile of the frame it goes there (In line with other profiles below, mitcad#1886);
    • within a quarter width (at most a quarter of the grid, at most half of it with at.snap) of a grid point of the target’s system (system.grid: its near face a whole number of grids from end A) it goes there;
    • at a grid point or between the snaps it is from the nearer end, its offset the distance of the new part’s face from that end (to a thousandth of a millimetre).

    With at.from and no at.offset, the click’s place is measured from that reference instead.

  • The click’s reference and offset are stored as a typed one would be: the joint’s position.tx follows the target’s length from end B and from the middle, and the component’s record keeps from. So a part flush with end B stays flush with it, and one on the middle stays on it, when the target gets longer or shorter.

  • Every placement on a side, a click’s or a typed offset’s, is kept within the target’s length; one that would overhang goes flush with that end (from it, offset 0), a typed offset with a warning (... flush with end B instead). A part longer than the target stays flush with end A.

  • build_edit’s at.offset and at.from are measured the same way: an offset alone is from the part’s reference; a from alone keeps the part where it is and recomputes the offset from the new reference (its changed has offset and from).

  • build_preview’s side gives from and offset as at.from and at.offset take them.

Middle of Gap (mitcad#1401). The profiles standing on a side’s slot (BUILD profiles whose slider joint is on that slot frame of that target) split it into free stretches, each from the far face of the profile towards end A (or end A) to the near face of the one towards end B (or end B). A part on the side can be centred in one and stay centred there:

  • A click within a quarter width (at least at.snap) of the middle of a free stretch that a profile bounds and the new part fits in centres it there: side.kind gap, from gap, offset 0. The side’s middle comes first where the two are the same place (a stretch without a profile is the whole side: its middle is the side’s).
  • at.from gap: offset is the new part’s middle from the middle of the free stretch the click (at.point, needed) is in, positive towards end B; a click in no free stretch (on a profile) is refused (there is no free stretch between profiles where the side was clicked).
  • The joint’s position.tx is the middle of the bounding faces, an expression of the two profiles’ slides: for 30 profiles (d14, d20 their slides, each face 15 from its slide) (d14 + d20) / 2 between two, d20 / 2 - 7.5 from end A, (d14 + d12) / 2 + 7.5 to end B (d12 the target’s length), less the new part’s middle from its frame, plus the offset. So the part stays centred when either profile moves or the target’s length changes. The component’s record keeps from gap and gap, the two profiles ([a, b], null for an end).
  • When one of the two goes (build_remove, a delete, its joint deleted), the part keeps its place and is bound to the end of the side nearer its frame: from end A its slide as a number, from end B the target’s length less its distance from there (d12 - 242.5); its record’s from is then a or b and its gap goes. Nothing is refused and the gone profile’s slide parameter goes with it.
  • build_edit’s at.from gap keeps the part in place, centred in the free stretch it stands in between the other profiles on its slot (its offset the distance from that stretch’s middle); a profile whose slide uses the part’s (one centred against it) is left out, so no cycle is made. An offset alone on a part from gap is from the middle of the stretch it stands in. A wall’s from (timber frames) is never gap (refused).
  • build_preview’s snaps have a gap at the middle of each free stretch a profile bounds and the part fits in (where no end or middle snap is); its side has gap: {start, end, a, b}, the free stretch the part stands in (from end A; null on a profile), whatever its reference, so that a change of From to Middle of Gap can keep it in place. build_parts gives gap (the record’s, else null).

In line with other profiles (mitcad#1886). A part placed on a side by a click also snaps where it lines up with the frame’s other profiles: a post a little beside the member crossing below goes in line with it without measuring.

  • The profiles are the BUILD host’s profiles cut to length, but the target and those standing on the side’s slot (Middle of Gap), whose axis is square to the slot and whose box has faces across it: a profile beside the target, above or below it, crossing it, or standing on another member (a brace at an angle has none).

  • Each gives the places where the new part’s near face is (from end A):

    • inline: its centre plane across the slot on that profile’s;
    • flush_face: its face towards end A flush with that profile’s face towards end A, or its face towards end B with that profile’s face towards end B.

    Only places where the part stays on the side and fits in a free stretch (it stands on no profile of the slot) count; at one place inline comes first, then the profile made first.

  • A click within a quarter width (at least at.snap) of one, after the ends, the middle and the middle of a gap and before a grid point, takes the nearest: side.kind inline or flush_face, side.with the profile. A grid point at the same place stays a grid snap. It is bound as a click between snaps is: from the nearer end, its offset the distance from it, so a typed at.offset overrides it.

  • build_preview’s snaps have them, with with, where no end, middle, gap or grid snap is. A placing without at.point, a tilted part and a part on a side with no length have none.

Across a side with several slots (mitcad#2002). A side with two or more slots (the long sides of a 30x60) has a frame of its own that no library lists: its middle, side_<side> (side_x+), the side’s first slot frame (slot_<side>_1) with its origin halfway between the first and the last slot frames’ (by number; all of them in one plane, facing one way). A profile standing on it is centred across the side: matching sections have flush side faces and one centre plane.

  • A click on a side (at.geometry a face, at.point) of a profile placed standing on its end (a part with build.length, role profile) takes the side’s middle where the click is nearer its centre line than any slot’s, else the nearest slot as before; with no at.point, or as near a slot as the middle, the slot. Other parts (a slider, a nut, a bracket) take the nearest slot.
  • at.geometry may name it ({"mount": "F7:mount(side_x+)"}), as a slot frame. A part that does not stand on it with its end is refused (... goes in a slot: only a profile stands centered between the slots of a side).
  • How it stands across is apart from the snaps along the side: the ends, the middle, a gap, a line-up and the grid snap as on a slot, and at.offset and at.from are measured the same way.
  • The joint is a slider on that frame (F7:mount(side_x+)), resolved from the slot frames on every recompute, so the part stays centred when the host’s section changes (another row or version) and keeps its place along the side when its length changes. A file saved with it opens with it.
  • The profiles on a side’s middle and those on its slots are in each other’s way: each counts the others in its free stretches (Middle of Gap) and leaves them out of its line-ups.
  • tilt and build_edit’s at.offset, at.from and tilt work on it as on a slot.
  • build_preview’s side.across says how the part stands: middle (on the side’s middle), slot (on a slot of a side that has a middle), null on a side with one slot. build_parts and the queries that list a part’s frames do not list the middles; a placed part’s joint names one.

Tilt (mitcad#444). A profile on a side can lean along its host: a brace. tilt (an angle, build_place, build_preview, build_edit; 0 or left out: square) leans it in the plane of the host’s axis and the side’s normal, positive towards the host’s end B, negative towards end A, never across the slot. It is from -80° up to 80°; more is refused (the tilt is 85 degrees; it is from -80 up to 80). Only a part on a side tilts (a profile standing on the slot with an end); on an end its direction turns it, and a tilted part takes no mitre.

  • The foot (the end on the slot) is cut by the tilt’s angle about the section axis across the slot, so it lies flat on the side; the cut keeps the length as its long point (Ends of the derived part), and the foot’s long point stands on the slot’s centre line.
  • at.offset and at.from refer to the foot’s long point on the slot: from a its distance from end A, from b from end B, from middle from the host’s middle. A click and the snaps place the foot (its reach along the slot is the foot’s, the section’s width / cos(tilt)), and the foot stays within the host’s length.
  • The far end: with a bound length (face, centre, through) it is cut flush with the plane the length ends on (parallel to the face it meets), and the length is measured along the axis to that end’s long point; with a typed length it stays square.
  • The cuts are ordinary end cuts (ends): the cut list shows them and build_edit’s ends changes them. build_edit’s tilt sets the tilt again and cuts both ends anew (0: square, square ends); a turn, a flip or a new length of a tilted part keeps its tilt and recuts its ends.
  • How it is made: the joint’s side a (the part’s end frame) has a frame_override that turns it and moves it to the foot’s long point; the slot’s frame and the slide (position.tx, the long point’s place) stay as they are. A bound length’s ray starts at the far end’s long side in the foot’s plane (from.shift.x the slide plus that shift) and runs along the part’s axis (direction). The component’s record keeps tilt (radians).

End placements (mitcad#417). On a profile’s end the new part continues it straight or turns 90° at a corner:

  • Without at.direction, a click on the end face (at.point) decides, in the target’s own axes (those of its end frame, so a tilted profile turns as well):

    • in the inner half of the face both ways (at least at.snap across, as far as the face allows) the part continues straight;
    • in the band along an edge it turns 90° towards that edge (in a corner of the face, towards the nearer edge).

    A pick of an end frame, or without a point, continues straight.

  • A corner is aligned: the new part lies in the target’s plane (the plane of the two axes), centred on the target’s section across the turn, and:

    • without a shared mitre it lies on the target’s end face, its end flush with the target’s outer side (the side away from the turn);
    • with a shared mitre the outer corners meet (mitcad#443): the two overlap fully, the new part’s outer side (away from the corner’s inside) through the target’s outer edge at its end and its end on that edge, and both are cut on the bisector of their axes through that shared outer corner, each at its long point. Both lengths are outer lengths: two 500 mm parts make a corner 500 × 500 mm outside, at 90° or any other angle;
    • at.offset moves the new part’s end from the target’s outer side along its axis, positive towards the turn (0: flush; negative: past the outer side).

  • A corner’s mitre left out (mitcad#427): a square corner (90°, as the four turns are) has none, lying on the target’s end face flush with its outer side; a corner at another angle is shared at offset 0 (by half the angle the corner has), none at another offset. cut: "none" places it without one, cut: "shared" mitres a square corner at 45°. A shared mitre at another offset is refused (a shared mitre needs offset 0).

  • A direction back along the target is refused.

Mitres.

  • On an end placement, cut decides which ends are cut:
    • existing cuts the target’s end by angle and leaves the new part square;
    • shared cuts both on the bisector, each by half the angle between their axes (45° each for two profiles at 90°; angle is not needed);
    • new cuts only the new part (the default cut);
    • none cuts nothing (a corner’s default is shared, End placements).
  • On a side placement only new is accepted.
  • The cut’s tilt comes from the two axes at the moment of placing and is stored in each part’s ends: the target’s end leans towards the new part’s axis, the new part’s end towards the target’s. On a side the new part’s end leans along the slot. Later rotations do not change it; build_edit does.
  • Only cut-to-length parts have mitres.
  • Every cut (new, existing, shared, the Ends command’s and build_edit’s ends) keeps the part’s length as its long point (Ends of the derived part): a mitred part never reaches past its length, and build_cut_list’s length is the length the body has on its long side. Designs made before simply rebuild with this rule.

Ends that meet (mitcad#1940). Two profiles placed apart (one on the other’s side near its end, a square corner on an end face, two parts placed on planes) meet in a corner when an end of each touches, overlaps or comes within 5 mm (near) of the other’s section, their axes at an angle and less than 0.5 mm apart across the corner’s plane (build_end_meets). build_edit’s shared_mitre (a or b) makes there the shared miter a corner placement makes: both ends cut on the bisector, each by half the angle between the axes and leaning towards the other part, and each end moved to the outer corner, its length the long point:

  • a part’s free end moves by its length;
  • the end it is placed by moves by its joint’s frame on the other side (frame_override.shift, along that frame’s axes) and its length, so that its other end stays: a part on a side runs through to the other part’s outer side;
  • a grounded part’s end A moves its occurrence and its length;
  • a member along an edge or a sketch line (Members along an edge, Along sketch lines, mitcad#1965) moves its end by its edge frame’s start (end A) or end (end B) offset, so that it still follows the edge or the line (changed lists along); two members along sketch lines of one component get the condition mitre kept with their joint instead (Joint conditions, mitcad#2200), their ends following the lines.

It is refused, in words, for a part tilted on a side, a part whose length is bound or that is placed by two points or by a frame of its own, when an end would move, and for a length outside the part’s limits. One undo step. A bound length refers only to parts placed before it, by design; its refusal says so and how to miter the corner instead.

Refusals. The command changes nothing when:

  • the part has no build;
  • the role cannot go there (a panel, a connector or a fastener through build_place: they have build_panel, build_connect and their connector);
  • the side has no slot frame (a closed side);
  • the systems do not fit (a B-type slot 8 connector on an I-type slot 5 profile), or the frame does not take the role (its accepts);
  • the placement does not allow the mitre’s cut (a shared mitre on a corner with an offset);
  • an offset from end B or the middle on a part without a length;
  • a direction on an end runs back along the target;
  • a bound length would make a cycle, or ends on a part placed later;
  • the length is outside the part’s limits;
  • the rotation is not a quarter turn.

Queries

Frames in answers are {"origin", "x_axis", "y_axis", "z_axis"} in the design’s coordinates; lengths are numbers in mm and angles numbers in radians, as joints have them.

A placing: frame (the new part’s own axes at its end A, z running from A to B), place (side, end, frame, geometry or grounded, as auto decided), length (value: the length given, else what the part’s ray gives in mode, else the source’s default; default; target: what the ray meets first, {occurrence, geometry} with a frame of another BUILD part facing it, or the bind given, null when nothing; and mode), ends (a, b: {angle, tilt} or null; target: the target’s end cut), tilt (radians, mitcad#444), snaps (on a side, mitcad#394: {kind, offset, point} for each place a click snaps to: kind end_a, end_b, middle, gap (mitcad#1401), grid, inline or flush_face (mitcad#1886, with with: {component, occurrence, name}, the profile it lines up with), offset the new part’s near face from end A, point where its middle then stands on the slot, in the design), side (on a side: {kind, from, offset, point, width, gap, with, across}: the snap the click took (end_a, end_b, middle, gap, grid, inline, flush_face; A panel: frame, fits, reason, width, height, bound. A connector: frame, junction, fasteners ({frame, at}), fastener_parts, machining ({component, at, point, diameter, depth, thread}). build_partsparts: for each BUILD component, component, name, role, source, part, joint, designation, supplier, part_number, config, length, ends, bound ({feature, parameter, to: {occurrence, geometry}, mode, add}, add the value in mm, a length to a face’s offset, mitcad#1630; or null), flip, rotate, tilt (radians, 0 square, mitcad#444), machining (its own, as build_edit takes it), added_by, adds, junction, from (a part on a side or a rail: a, b, middle or gap, else null), gap (from gap, mitcad#1401: the two profiles it is centred between, [a, b], null for an end; else null), offset (a part on a side or a rail: its offset from from in mm, as build_edit’s at.offset takes it, mitcad#1885; a part on a plane or a face: its offset along the normal, mitcad#2046; else null), ground (true for a part on a plane or a face, mitcad#2046), slides (true for a part that slides on another by its joint, a carriage on its rail, mitcad#2088), limits (such a part on a part cut to length: {min, max, default_min, default_max} in mm from the target’s end A to the part’s frame, min and max the joint’s, null in a design saved without them; else null)
build_junctionscomponents (optional: only the junctions of these)junctions: id (<a's component>:<a's at>|<b's component>:<b's at>, stable while the two parts and their meeting stay), kind (L, T, cross, inline), a and b (component, occurrence, at (end_a, end_b, the slot frame, or side on a closed side), frame (the part’s own axes at its end A), at_frame (the at frame)), angle (between the axes), systems (B8/30), space (the free room in the inner corner: {"x", "y", "z"}: along a, along b to its farther end, across), connectors (components already there)
build_end_meetscomponent (optional: the ends it meets of this part only), meets (false: where the ends are only, none met; default true)ends: each end of a profile cut to length: component, occurrence, end (a, b), point (where its axis ends), out (its axis out of the part), leans (x, -x, y, -y: where each tilt leans the cut’s outward normal), meets (null, or the end it meets in a corner: component, occurrence, end, angle (each end’s cut, half the corner), lengthen and other_lengthen (how far each end moves out for the outer corners to meet, negative in), tilt and other_tilt (the shared miter’s, each leaning towards the other part), away, across (this end’s other tilts: away from the other part, across the corner one way and the other), problem (why shared_mitre would be refused, in words, else null)), why (why it meets none, in words), joint (null, or the joint it is in, mitcad#2200: kind (L or T), component (the other profile), end (an L’s other end, a T’s null), condition (mitre, butt, square, near_side, far_side), through (a butt’s profile that runs through, else null), problem (why the condition cannot be kept and changed, in words, else null); Joint conditions); near (the gap still taken, mm). Ends that meet (mitcad#1940)
build_cut_listkerf (optional, default 3 mm)rows, one per group of identical results (source, row, length, ends, machining and own features the same): source, designation, supplier, part_number, config, length (the part’s length, its long point: the body’s length on the long side of its angled ends, mitcad#443), ends (a, b: {angle, tilt} or null), machining ({at, diameter, depth, thread, connector}: holes from connectors, and the part’s own, connector null), features (how many own features the part has: holes, cuts), quantity, mass (each, kg; a section of a typed size, mitcad#1328: the value of its build block’s area_parameter, the source’s parameter of its area in the part’s combination, times the density and the length), components, and for a section of a typed size size (its options’ values but the length, B 76.2, T 4.8: its rows and stock apart from its source’s other sizes). stock: per source and row (and typed size, whose designation is the source’s name with its size in parentheses), cut from its longest stock length, {"source", "designation", "stock_length", "pieces": [lengths in cutting order], "bars" (where each stock piece's cuts end in pieces), "needed", "offcut", "too_long"}, longest pieces first into the first stock piece they fit (a kerf after each). kerf. other: the parts list’s rows for everything else
build_hostthe BUILD host (mitcad#394, Where parts go): component (its uid), name, path (its first occurrence path from the root, uids joined by /, "" for the root) and active (the active component); the app gives paths from it and points in its coordinates

analysis_shape with {"shape": "build_preview", ...} and the same fields gives the new part’s bodies (a connector’s, a panel’s) in the design’s coordinates, as other analysis shapes, for the view to show while a command is open. A profile’s bodies are at the length the query says (length.value): a bound length or none given is what the ray meets, not the source’s default. With spacing (a set, Spacing sets) it gives every member’s bodies, the last one ripped when the set rips it (mitcad#487).

How junctions are found. From the derived parts’ frames and boxes at the marker: two profiles meet when their boxes touch or overlap within the model’s tolerance (0.001 mm). Then:

  • an end on a side face (on a slot frame’s plane, facing it, or on a closed side of the box) is T, or L when it is within the section’s size of that side’s end;
  • two ends at one point are L (axes at an angle) or inline (on one axis);
  • two sides crossing are cross.

a is the part whose end meets; of two ends, and of two sides, the newer part.

Cut ends (mitcad#521). A part whose metadata gives its section (a timber member) has its material as its box on the inner side of its end cuts, the planes its derived part cuts them by: an end on a side is in the other part’s material, not only its box; a cut end whose frame (on its axis at the end, beyond the cut) is on no side meets a side with its cut face’s middle, the junction’s frame there with z out of the cut (a rafter’s plumb cut on a ridge board: a T, L near the board’s end); two cut ends are a shared mitre only when their cut planes are one plane; and two sides cross only where their materials meet: touching or overlapping square to both axes and with an area in common across that direction. So the two rafters of a pair, whose plumb cut ends stand on the two sides of a ridge board and whose boxes overlap above it, are no junction. A part of no such section is found by its box, as before.

A connector fits a junction when its junctions, systems and space match the junction. The list of fitting library parts comes from the library side (library_build_candidates in Library commands, given the junction), since the model knows no library. build_connect refuses a connector whose junctions or systems do not fit, or whose envelope is larger than the junction’s space.

Where a connector goes (mitcad#1115). Its first mate’s frame slides on profile a’s frame of the mate’s kind that faces most into b (a slider joint, flipped): at an L on b’s side, towards b’s farther end, so that at every corner of a frame, the opposite and mirrored ones too, the connector lies inside the frame. Along a slot its corner seats where b’s face towards a crosses that slot (a’s end on b’s side; at a shared mitre b’s inner face, half b’s section further in), and its first mate lies its distance from the second mate’s face beyond that (tx an expression of a’s length when the end is a’s end B). Its fasteners get rigid joints on their frames: a nut by its slot frame, not flipped (the nut’s frame and the connector’s both point into the profile, so the nut lies in the slot), a screw or a washer with its shank into the profile and a frame_override shift that moves its seat (a screw’s head underside, a washer’s face) back by the connector’s wall: the head bears on the wall’s outer face, on a washer when there is one (mitcad#2001). Held by its mount frame (an ISO screw’s shaft frame seat, z along the shank; a washer’s hole frame, z out of its bearing face; any mount frame’s z points towards what the part goes on), it is not flipped and the shift is along the frame’s +z; a fastener without mount frames is held by its design’s origin (z out of the head), flipped, and the shift is along its -z. The wall is measured on the connector’s own shape (Kernel::segment_crossings): segments along the frame’s -z, from half a millimetre in front of it, at eight points nine tenths of the head’s radius around the frame’s origin (beside the hole), the nearest exit of those that enter the material at the frame. A fastener whose library row the design already holds as a source is taken from it without reading the library. The records of such connectors and fasteners have rule: 2; those without it were placed by the first rule (on a’s side facing b’s own axis, a nut flipped, a screw’s head on the profile’s face), and build_upgrade places them again: a connector only while it is where the first rule put it (one moved along its slot since stays), a fastener only while its joint is as the first rule made it. It also sets right a fastener of rule: 2 held by a mount frame whose joint is flipped, as the rule placed it before mitcad#2001 (its shank out of the profile, its seat on the wall’s far side): not flipped, its shift’s z negated, so that its seat lies on the wall’s outer face.

Panels. A panel in slots is placed from a picked inner face (or slot frame) of a frame’s profile: the slot there, the profile across the frame whose slot faces it in the same plane, and those beside to the left and right along the picked profile. Its height is the room across plus twice the slot’s depth less the clearance, its width the room between the profiles beside likewise; bound lengths keep both so (from the picked slot to the one across, from the left slot to the right). A size that is no parameter of the panel (a sheet sold in widths) keeps its value: it fits when it reaches into both slots and is no wider than their depth less the clearance. A face with no profile across is refused (not inside a frame). A surface panel (mount: "surface") lies on the picked outer face, its back on it. Where its width and height are parameters it covers the frame around the face: across from the outer side of the picked profile to that of the profile whose slot faces the picked one’s inner side, along between the outer sides of the profiles beside (without them, the picked profile’s length, with a warning); bound lengths in through mode keep both so. Without a profile across it keeps its size (a warning). Its clamps slide in the picked slot at the panel’s two ends, kept on the profile and inset by their own reach along the slot (one in the middle when there is no room for two); they are its adds, and build_remove takes them with it.

Classes

  • build_place, build_connect and build_panel read a new source from a library, so they are class remote (as update_library_parts). With part.source (a source already in the design) they need no library, and the MCP server allows them (classes::command_class_with, which looks at the fields).
  • build_edit, build_remove and the queries are class model.

Length to a face

A length may end at a face the part does not run into (mitcad#1630): the uprights of a split-level frame standing on bases at different heights, each ending level with the first one’s top.

{"cmd": "build_place", "part": {"source": "S1"}, "at": {"point": [200, 0, 100]},
 "length": {"mode": "to_face",
            "face": {"occurrence": "O1", "geometry": {"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:end_b"}},
            "offset": 10}}
  • face is what the length ends at, as bind names it: a planar face (a profile’s end face too), a frame of a placed part, or an origin or construction plane of the BUILD host or of an occurrence under it.
  • The part ends where its axis, from its start, meets that plane, wherever the face is: beside the part, above or below it. offset (a length, default 0) is added along the part, so 10 ends 10 mm past the plane and -10 short of it.
  • It is a bound_length with mode to_face, its to the face and its add the offset: {"bind": ..., "mode": "to_face", "add": ...} says the same. The length stays bound: moving the part the face is of, or changing its length, moves this part’s end with it.
  • Refused, with the reason, when the plane runs along the part’s axis (they never meet), when it is behind the part’s start, or when the offset would end the part at or before its start. A face that is not planar is refused too; its place is painted.
  • build_edit takes the same length (an offset left out is 0); the build_parts query names the mode to_face with the offset as add, and build_preview’s length.target is the face given.

Along sketch lines

A frame from a sketch (mitcad#1965): draw the lines, pick a profile, get one member per straight line, the corners mitered and butted.

{"cmd": "build_place", "part": {"source": "S1"},
 "lines": {"occurrence": "",
           "curves": [{"sketch": "F1", "curve": "c5"}, {"sketch": "F1", "curve": "c6"}],
           "chain": false, "align": "center", "corners": "mitre"},
 "rotate": "90 deg", "flip": false}
  • curves are sketch lines ({"sketch", "curve"}), curves of one sketch ({"sketch", "curves"}) or whole sketches ({"sketch"}: its lines that are no construction, no reference geometry and no axis), of a planar sketch or a 3D sketch; occurrence the path from the BUILD host to the component they are in (empty: the host’s own). chain adds the straight lines of the same sketches joined end to end to the picked ones, over and over. Each line is taken once.
  • Each straight line gets one member of the part, cut to the line’s length, placed along the line as a member along an edge whose edge is the line (Members along an edge, below; along with a sketch line and no face places one member so): an edge_frame on the line holds it, so moving or resizing the line moves and resizes its member on recompute.
  • align is how each section sits on its line: center (the default), above or below (centred across the line, resting on the sketch’s plane or hanging under it), or a corner: left_above, right_above, left_below, right_below (left and right looking along the line with the sketch’s normal up; a 3D sketch’s line has the host’s Z square to it as up, its Y for a line along Z). rotate turns each member about its line in quarter turns; flip runs each one from its line’s end to its start (the edge frame’s reversed).
  • Corners (corners: mitre, the default, butt or none; true and false read as mitre and none, mitcad#2200), in the same undo step, each joint’s condition kept with it (Joint conditions, below): where two ends meet alone at a point, not in line (an L), mitre gives both the shared miter (Ends that meet: cut on the bisector, to the outer corner) and butt runs the member of the line picked first on to the outer corner and stops the other at its side (lines chain adds come after the picked ones, in the chain’s order); where an end lies on another member’s line between its ends (a T), it stops at that member’s near side. Where three or more ends meet at one point, the member of the line picked first runs on to the outer corner (unless another end there continues its line) and the others stop at its side (one in line with it stays square); two of them that would still overlap are left square, named in warnings. none leaves every end square. Each joint changes afterwards with build_edit’s joint; an end to a face is Length’s to_face (Length to a face). A corner that cannot be treated is left as it is, said in warnings.
  • Refused, in words and before anything is placed: an arc, a circle, an ellipse, a spline or a point among the curves (members go along straight lines only), a pick that is no sketch, a line with no length, and at, to, length, spacing, mitre, tilt, along and lie with lines.
  • The answer is the first member’s, with members (every member’s component, in the lines’ order) and count; place is lines. One undo step, Place <part> along sketch lines: <n>.
  • build_preview with lines answers the first member’s preview with lines: {"count", "frames", "lengths", "joints"} (each member’s end A frame and length, the corners square; joints each joint as corners treats it: at, kind (L, T or three), condition, members and through, the member that runs through, each an index in the lines’ order, or null); its shape (analysis_shape) is every member’s.
  • build_parts gives a member along a sketch line along.line: {"align", "rotate", "flip"}. build_edit takes along.align, rotate and flip for it (with along’s offsets and config), the joint’s turn and shift worked out again; lie is refused for it. The joints it is in keep its section anew in the same undo step.

Joint conditions

How profiles along sketch lines meet (mitcad#2200; code core/model-build/src/conditions.rs), kept with each joint and changed afterwards in one undo step for both members:

{"cmd": "build_edit", "component": "C3", "joint": {"end": "b", "condition": "butt", "through": "C4"}}
  • An L (two ends that meet, as Ends that meet finds them: touching, overlapping or within 5 mm): mitre (the shared miter: both cut on the bisector, each to the outer corner), butt (the member through runs on to the outer corner, square, the other stops square at its side; through is either member, left out the one that runs through now, else the one placed first) or square (both ends where their lines end, no cut).
  • A T (an end whose axis crosses another member’s axis between its ends, the end touching its side, into it or up to 5 mm short of it): near_side (to the side facing it), far_side (through to its other side) or square (where its line ends). Only this end changes.
  • A condition that does not fit the joint’s kind is refused in words, as is an end that meets nothing within 5 mm, and a joint of profiles that are not both along sketch lines of one component (use the shared miter or Length’s to_face for them). joint goes on its own: ends, length, at, rotate, flip, tilt and along with it are refused. changed is joint, along and, for a miter, ends; undo step Joint of <name> and <name>: <condition>. A condition that would leave a member no length is refused.
  • Kept: each end’s condition is its edge frame’s start_meets or end_meets (edge_frame, below): the other member’s sketch line and both sections across their lines. The edge frame works the end out from the lines at every recompute, so an end follows when the member it meets moves with its line, and each member keeps following its own line (its edge frame’s offset, not a detached length). A member edited with build_edit (along, rotate, flip, config) gets its sections kept anew in the joints it is in. A miter’s cuts are the derived parts’ ends, set when the condition is set.
  • The joint refers to the other member’s line, not to the member: no length binds to a part placed later, so neither the placing order nor the timeline’s order of the members matters and nothing is reordered.
  • shared_mitre on a member along a sketch line whose end meets another one’s in an L sets the condition mitre (as joint).
  • build_end_meets reports each end’s joint: its kind, the other member, the condition (mitre for an end cut before the conditions were kept, square for none) and the member that runs through.

BUILD: timber construction

Timber members, wood fasteners, brackets and hangers, joinery and sheets (mitcad#478) use the commands of BUILD: profile assemblies above, extended here. Everything said there holds; the slot path (profiles with slot frames, their connectors, nuts and panels) is unchanged: no field below is needed for it and none changes what it does. The app’s Timber tool (app/COMMANDS.md, Timber) and its Profile tool drive the same commands; the Profile picker lists no timber. Code: core/model/src/build/meta.rs, core/model-build/src/ (place.rs, timber.rs, spacing.rs, wood.rs, joinery.rs, cut_list.rs, edge.rs); tests core/model-tests/build-timber/src/timber_tests.rs, edge_tests.rs.

Library metadata the model reads

The library’s format is in docs/libraries.md (Timber). The model reads these fields of a source’s build block, leniently (unknown fields are ignored, a value is a number in mm, kg, kg/m³ or % or a text with its unit):

  • Rows. build.rows is {"<configuration row>": {a partial build block}}. For a part made in a row, the row’s block is deep-merged over the component’s: objects merge key by key, other values (numbers, texts, arrays) replace. The component’s own fields are the default row’s. Every read below is of the merged block of the part’s row (config, or the source’s default row when left out).
  • A timber member: role: "profile", kind: "timber". section {width, height} is the actual size: the section lies on XY centred at the origin, width (W) along X and height (T, the thickness) along Y; L runs along +Z. nominal {width, height} is the nominal size (at 20 % moisture). material {species, finish, grade, density, moisture, product}: species spruce, pine, …; finish sawn, planed or dimensioned; grade ("" or C24, …) the default grade; density kg/m³; moisture %. availability standard or less common. tolerance is carried, not used. length as a profile’s (parameter L, min, max, stock the stock lengths, default). frames: end_a, end_b (kind end) and four face frames face_xp, face_xn, face_yp, face_yn at z = 0 on the side’s centre line, z out of the side, x along +Z (as slot frames). No system, no slot frames, no mass_per_metre: the mass is the density times the volume (W × T × the length).
  • A wood fastener: role: "fastener", wood {kind: "screw" | "nail", diameter, length, head} (the row’s sizes, through rows), and an axis frame (kind shaft): on the axis at the head’s bearing surface, z along the shank towards the tip (the tip at z = length).
  • A bracket, joist hanger or post base: role: "connector", connector.placement: "outer", connector.fit {kind: "angle" | "hanger" | "post_base", section: [a, b], width: [min, max]}, connector.mates whose first frame ({"frame": "mount", "to": "face"}) places it (Brackets, hangers and post bases below), and connector.fasteners: [{"frames": [hole frames], "count": n, "on": "a" | "b", "screw" | "nail": {library reference, with its row}}]. A hole frame (kind hole) lies on the connector’s surface the head bears on, z out of it towards the head (facing the screw’s axis frame). on is the member the fasteners are driven into (a the one whose end meets).
  • A sheet: role: "panel", panel.mount: "face", panel.thickness (a value or its parameter), panel.width and panel.height (the parameters that size it), panel.stock ([[w, h], ...], the sheet sizes sold, mm), material {product, density}; thicknesses as rows. The design’s width runs along X, its height along Y and its thickness along +Z, as other panels.

A part is timber when its merged block’s kind is timber; a design has timber when one of its BUILD parts is. A placed part whose block names a material (timber, sheets, their brackets and screws) takes its source’s body appearance and material, when the source’s bodies that set one set the same (a document appearance of the source is copied in); slot profiles keep their look. A cut-to-length part whose source gives the caps of its extrusion (<F>:start(...), <F>:end(...), its faces at z = 0 and L) one face appearance (set_face_appearance; the timber’s end grain, mitcad#484) shows it on its end faces, <F>:end_a and <F>:end_b, square or cut at an angle.

Face sides

A face frame of a member (role: "profile") is a side as a slot frame is: build_place (and build_preview, build_edit, build_junctions, bound lengths) treat it as one, with these differences:

  • at.geometry may be a face frame ({"mount": "F7:mount(face_yp)"}) or a side face of the member with at.point: the face frame of that side (the one on the face’s plane when the kernel tells it, else the nearest to at.point). A side with a slot frame takes the slot as before; a face frame is taken only where a side has no slot frame.
  • The new part sits anywhere along the side: no grid snaps (a member has no system); the end and middle snaps, at.offset and at.from (a, b, middle), keeping within the length, rotate, flip, tilt, mitre (new), bound lengths (face, centre, through), corners and shared mitres on an end work as for profiles.
  • Across the side the new part stands centred on the side’s centre line.
  • No systems are checked between members (a part without systems fits any); a slot connector or nut is refused on a member (a member has no slots).
  • A bound length’s ray meets a member’s face frames as it meets a profile’s slot frames.

Members by two points

build_place takes to and lie:

{"cmd": "build_place", "part": {"source": "S1", "config": "48x148"},
 "at": {"occurrence": "", "geometry": "xy", "point": [0, 0, 0]},
 "to": {"point": [3000, 0, 0]}, "lie": "edge"}
  • at.point is the start and to.point the end, both in the BUILD host’s coordinates. The member runs from start to end (end A at the start, unless flip). Without length its length is the distance; a length (a value or a bind) replaces it.
  • at.geometry (optional) is what the member lies on: a plane ("xy"), a planar face, or a face frame or side face of a member (with at.occurrence). The member lies on that plane: its axis is lifted off it by half the section across it, and it is held to it by a rigid joint whose frame_override gives the start and the axes (so it follows a member it lies on). Without at.geometry it is grounded, its axis through the two points.
  • lie turns it about its axis: flat (the default), the section’s smaller dimension across the plane it lies on (without a plane: along the host’s +Z, its “up”); edge, the larger one. On a plane the side that faces it lies on it. A member standing square to the plane (a post) stands centred on the start, its X along the host’s X. rotate (quarter turns) turns it further.
  • A point and a direction (the app’s Timber tool: a click, then a typed or auto length, mitcad#478): with length, to.point gives only the direction. A value runs the member that long from the start; a bind (mode face, centre, through, add) binds it to what the ray from its start along the direction meets, as on a side: its bound_length starts at the plane it lies on (the host’s origin when grounded), shifted to the start, so the length follows the target.
  • The answer’s place is points. build_preview answers as for any placing (frame, length, box). Without length its length.value is the points’ distance (as placed), and length.target names what the ray from the start towards to.point meets first, the target an auto length binds to (null when nothing is in the way).
  • build_edit of a member by two points takes to ({"point"}), at ({"point"}) and lie again: it is placed anew from them (the same component, derived part and junctions).
  • Between members (mitcad#509): without length (and without spacing), an end whose point is inside another member cut to length (a timber member or a profile; its box), while the other point is not on that member, is cut back to where the member’s axis meets that member’s face: a square butt there, so that a member clicked between two studs (on their centre lines, as the app’s snaps give them) fits between them, not into them. A free member (no at.geometry: its axis through the points) is cut so too where its point is on a member’s face and its axis runs through that member (a click on its far side); on the near face it ends there already. A member lying on a plane has its axis off the points: only a point inside a member counts (members lapped on a plane stay so). The far end so cut that meets a member end to end closes the corner (Frames of members: a square butt, closing). Ends that would meet leave nothing between them: refused (nothing is left between them). The member keeps the points given (build_edit places it anew from them, cut again). build_preview answers points: {"start": {"on", "name", "cut"}, "end": {...}, "lies": "plane" | "free"}, the member each point is on or in (its component and name, or null), whether that end was cut back, and whether the member lies on at.geometry or is free; its length.value is the length after the cuts.

Members along an edge (mitcad#1814)

build_place takes along: a member laid along a straight edge, lying on a face beside it (a batten along a plate’s edge, flush with it):

{"cmd": "build_place", "part": {"source": "S1", "config": "28x45"},
 "along": {"occurrence": "",
           "edge": {"body": "F1.b0", "edge": "E{F1:side0|F1:top}"},
           "face": {"body": "F1.b0", "face": "F1:top"},
           "inset": 10, "start": 50, "end": 20, "lift": 5},
 "lie": "flat"}
  • occurrence is the path from the BUILD host to the component the edge and the face are in (empty: the host’s own bodies); edge a straight edge and face the planar face the member lies on, which decides the side of the edge it is on. The edge is taken onto the face’s plane.
  • The member runs the edge from end to end, its side flush with the edge and its underside on the face. The offsets are values (numbers in mm or expressions), 0 when left out: inset across the face away from the edge (negative out over it), start and end along the edge at each end (positive shortens, negative runs past the end), lift off the face along its normal.
  • The edge’s start is the end from which, looking along the edge with the face’s normal up, the face lies on the left (the edge frame’s start, below); start is measured from it.
  • lie turns it about its axis as for a member by two points: flat (the default) puts the section’s smaller dimension up, edge the larger one. rotate, to, length, spacing, mitre, tilt and at.geometry are refused with it: the edge and its offsets give the member’s place and length.
  • It is placed associatively: an edge_frame feature (below) keeps the edge, the face and the offsets, before the member’s derived part; the member’s bound_length runs from the frame start along z to the plane of the frame end (its length is the edge’s less start and end), and its rigid joint (flipped) is between its end_a frame and start, shifted by half its section so that it lies flush. So a change of the body the edge is on (its length, width or thickness) moves and resizes the member on recompute, the offsets kept. The edge frame is in the component record’s adds, so build_remove takes it with the member.
  • A curved edge is refused (the edge is curved: a member along an edge needs a straight edge), as are a face that is not flat, an edge that does not run along the face and offsets that leave nothing of the edge; the messages name no edge or face (the place is painted). After it is placed, a lost edge or face fails the edge frame in words, as other features’ lost references do, and the member keeps its last length.
  • The answer’s place is edge. build_preview with along answers as for any placing (frame, length.value the run’s length, box).
  • build_parts gives such a member along: {"feature", "joint", "lie"}, its edge frame (whose definition has the edge, the face and the offsets), its joint and how it lies (flat or edge); null for other parts.
  • Along a sketch line (mitcad#1965, Along sketch lines): edge may be a sketch line ({"sketch", "curve"}) with no face; the member follows the line, sits on it as align says (center by default) and is turned by rotate (quarter turns) and run the other way by flip; lie is refused with it, and align along a body’s edge.
  • Editing (build_edit): along ({"occurrence", "edge", "face", "inset", "start", "end", "lift"}, each left out kept) changes the edge frame; lie turns the member; config changes its row. With any of them the joint’s turn and the shift that keeps the member flush and on the face are worked out again for the lie and the row’s section, and parameters and ends may come along; one undo step (Edit <name>), changed lists along, lie, config, parameters, ends. The edge, the face and the offsets are checked as when placing. length, rotate, flip, at, tilt, machining, cuts, to and grade are refused with them (edit them apart); along on a member not placed along an edge is refused.

edge_frame 

{"type": "edge_frame", "occurrence": "O3",
 "edge": {"body": "F2.b0", "edge": "E{F2:side0|F2:top}"},
 "face": {"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:top"},
 "inset": 10, "start": 50, "end": 20, "lift": 5}

EdgeFrame<n> (mitcad#1814; core/model/src/features/edge_frame.rs) is a feature of the component that places the member (the BUILD host): two frames along a straight edge on a planar face, <feature>:mount(start) and <feature>:mount(end), which joints and bound lengths name as a derived part’s frames ({"mount": "F9:mount(start)"}). occurrence, edge, face and the offsets inset, start, end and lift (lengths, 0 when left out) are as along’s above. The edge and the face are geometry of the component the path ends in, taken into the feature’s component through the occurrences’ placements at its point of the timeline, as a bound length’s are.

  • Both frames have z along the edge from its start to its end, x across the face away from the edge and y the face’s outward normal. start is at the edge’s start moved start along it, end at its end moved end back along it; both are moved inset along x and lift along y. The distance between them along z is the edge’s length less start and end.
  • It fails in words for a curved edge, a face that is not planar, an edge not parallel to the face, offsets that leave no length, and a lost edge or face. Its frames are not stored with the results (evaluated again when a design opens), as a derived part’s are not.
  • Along a sketch line (mitcad#1965): edge is one line of a planar or a 3D sketch and face is left out. Both frames have z along the line from its start to its end ("reversed": true: from its end to its start), y the sketch’s normal square to the line (a 3D sketch’s line: the component’s Z square to it, its Y for a line along Z) and x y × z; inset and lift move them along x and y. An arc, a circle, an ellipse or a spline fails it in words: members go along straight lines only.
  • Along a sketch line, start_meets and end_meets (mitcad#2200, Joint conditions) keep the joint the member’s end A (at start) or end B (at end) is in: {"to", "edge", "section", "own"}. to is near_side (the end’s section middle on the side of the other member facing it), far_side (on its far side) or corner (a shared miter’s long point: the end square to its line through the point where the outer sides of both members cross; the other member’s end there is its line’s end nearer this one); edge the other member’s sketch line, in the same component; section and own the other member’s and this one’s section across their lines, [x min, x max, y min, y max] in mm in the frame of each line as it runs from its start to its end (x and y as above, reversed left out). The end is worked out from both lines at every evaluation and start or end adds to it; a line along the other one fails the feature in words.

Spacing sets

build_place with spacing places a member and repeats it: studs, joists, rafters (a centre distance), deck boards, fence boards and cladding (a board row: a gap).

{"cmd": "build_place", "part": {"source": "S1", "config": "48x198"},
 "at": {"occurrence": "O3", "geometry": {"mount": "F9:mount(face_yn)"}},
 "length": {"bind": {"occurrence": "O4", "geometry": {"mount": "F12:mount(face_yp)"}}},
 "spacing": {"mode": "centre", "distance": 400}}

spacing is {"mode", "distance", "count", "from", "to", "along", "length", "fit"}:

  • mode: centre (the default: distance is the centre distance) or gap (a board row: distance is the gap between boards).
  • On a side (at on a member’s side or slot, the base placement a side placement): the members stand along the host member, the first flush with from (an offset of its near face from end A, default 0) and the last flush with to (its far face’s offset from end A; default end B, and then the last is bound from end B, so it stays flush when the host’s length changes). A set between two members is this with length bound to the second member (as above): the members stand on the first and reach the second, each with its own bound length.
  • Otherwise (members by two points, or one at a point): along (a direction in the host’s coordinates, required) and length (the span along it, required): the first member is the one at and to give, the others moved along along.
  • The span is from the first member’s near face to the last one’s far face. With w the member’s width along the set (its box along it):
    • centre: the members at 0, d, 2d, … and the last at span - w; the count is ceil((span - w) / d) + 1 (the last space is at most d);
    • gap: the step is w + gap; with fit cut (the default) the count is ceil(span / (w + gap)) and the last board is ripped to what is left (a rip cut, Joinery, when less than w); with fit spread the count is floor((span + gap) / (w + gap)) and the gaps are widened so that the last board ends at the span. Profiled boards that join are laid edge to edge instead (Profiled boards below).
    • count (optional) fixes the count instead: centre spreads the members evenly over the span, gap spreads the gaps; 0 (in build_edit) goes back to the count from the span.
  • build_preview with spacing answers the first member as a placing does and adds spacing: {count, frames, rip} (each member’s own axes at its end A, and whether the last is ripped); analysis_shape with the same fields gives every member’s bodies (mitcad#487).
  • One member is placed when the span holds only one. A refusal of any member refuses the whole set.
  • The answer’s component is the first member (the set’s lead), set lists every member’s component, count their number; undo step Place <designation> x<count>.
  • The lead’s record keeps the set (spacing: the definition and the base placement, the part as {"source", "config"}); every member’s record has set, the lead’s component. build_parts gives both.
  • Editing the set: build_edit with spacing (any of its fields; {} lays the set out again from the members’ places now, after the host or the span changed) and optionally config acts on the whole set, through any of its members: the members are laid out anew in one undo step. The first min(old, new) members keep their components (their joints, bound lengths and lengths are made anew; connectors and junctions on them stay), new ones are added after them, extra ones removed as by build_remove. changed has spacing (and config); the answer adds set and count.
  • build_remove with "set": true removes every member of the set; without it one member goes and the set keeps the others (laying it out again counts what is left as its members).

Wood fasteners

build_connect at a junction of two members with a wood fastener as part drives screws or nails through one member into the other:

{"cmd": "build_connect", "junction": "C5:end_a|C3:face_xp",
 "part": {"library": "mitcad-parts", "url": "...", "rev": "...", "component": "wood-screw"},
 "count": 2}
  • Which way. An end on a side (T, and an L whose end meets the other’s side or end face): through the member whose side it is (b) into the end of a, along a’s axis, from b’s far face; at a cut end met by its cut face (mitcad#521) square to the cut face, the contact the cut face within b (a rafter nailed through the ridge board into its plumb cut end, horizontally). Two members crossing or lying on each other (cross): through the newer (a) into b, square to both axes, from a’s far side. Ends meeting on one axis (inline) are refused (an inline joint takes a plate).
  • Where. count (default 2) fasteners in a row along the longer side of the contact (the end’s section on the side face, or the members' overlap), centred across it, at (i + 0.5) / count of its length.
  • The size. part.config names the row. Left out, for a source with rows: the diameter is the largest row’s wood.diameter not over the thinner member’s smaller section dimension / 7 (else the smallest diameter); the length the shortest of that diameter at least the thickness gone through + 8 × the diameter (else the longest). build_junctions gives the numbers for a picker (wood below).
  • Seating (mitcad#512). A wood screw or nail is driven until its head top lies on the unchanged entry face. build.wood.seat can name a mount frame or use head_top / head_underside. A named frame has z along the shaft. Without one, head_top is the least body coordinate along the source’s axis-aligned shaft; oblique library parts must supply a frame. Pan, hex, washer, button and socket heads default to head_underside (the existing axis bearing frame); other wood screws and nails default to head_top. A non-wood bolt keeps its existing bearing placement. Nominal wood.length and row selection are unchanged: a head K mm behind the axis is driven K mm deeper, with tip and embedment increased by K. A countersunk source already starting at its axis needs no shift, and keeps its tip at L. No head holes are cut; intentional head/shank overlap with wood is not an error of the frame’s fastening checks. Fasteners on a metal connector keep their hole’s bearing placement. Swap Fastener recomputes seating from the new source and selected row while keeping the member’s entry frame, component and joint. build_parts.parts[].seating gives the measured head_top_distance from the entry face (negative stands proud, positive is sunk) and tip_distance, in millimetres; both come from the placed body’s bounds for an axis-aligned source (otherwise seating is null), whatever way the fastener is driven (a sloped roof’s too). With them members and of (mitcad#521): how many of its junction’s members its shaft passes through (its points from the entry face to the tip, every half millimetre, in a member’s material) and how many the junction has.
