  • Warnings, not refusals (in warnings, d the diameter):
    • the embedment (the length less the thickness gone through) under 6 × d: screw 1 embeds 22 mm in Beam1: at least 30 mm (the members by their component names);
    • a fastener nearer than 3 × d to an edge of the contact: screw 2 is 10 mm from an edge: at least 15 mm;
    • nearer than 10 × d to an end of the member it goes through, along that member’s axis: screw 1 is 37 mm from the end of C3: at least 50 mm;
    • longer than both members together: screw 1 goes through C5.
  • What is made. One component per fastener (role fastener, its source the wood fastener’s), each with a rigid joint, flipped, between its axis frame and the member it is driven from, at its entry point (that member’s end_a frame with a frame_override: the entry point, z out of the member towards the head). The first is the answer’s component; its record’s adds lists the others, and build_remove of it takes them all. Every one’s record has junction. No holes are cut.
  • build_preview with the same fields answers fasteners ({frame, at} per fastener, at the joint’s frame in the design), fastener_parts, size ({config, diameter, length}) and warnings.

Brackets, hangers and post bases

build_connect with a connector whose placement is outer fits it by the members’ sections and places it on their outer faces:

  • fit.kind hanger and angle go on a junction with an end on a side (T, L); post_base on a member’s free end, named instead of a junction: "end": {"component": "C3", "end": "a"}.
  • fit.section [a, b]: the member that is carried (a; the post) has that section, either way round, within 1 mm; fit.width [min, max]: its smaller section dimension is within it. Otherwise refused (the hanger fits 48 × 148, C5 is 48 × 123). A slot connector at a junction of members, or an outer one at a junction of slot profiles, is refused.
  • The connector’s first mate’s frame (mount; its to, face or end, is not read) is placed by a rigid joint, flipped, on b’s (the post’s) end_a frame with a frame_override whose z points out of b towards the connector; so in the connector’s design the mount frame’s z points into the carrier or the post. Where the mount frame goes, its axes in the connector’s design:
    • hanger: at the middle of a’s end on b’s face, z into b, x the direction of a’s section most up (the host’s +Z; of a vertical a, its +X);
    • angle: on b’s face at the middle of the edge where a’s chosen side meets it, z into b, x that side’s outward normal; side (x+, x-, y+, y- of a’s section; default the larger side, y+ when W ≥ T, else x+) chooses it;
    • post_base: at the middle of the end, z into the member along its axis, x its +X.
  • Its fasteners: one per hole frame of each fasteners entry, a rigid joint, flipped, between the fastener’s axis frame and the hole frame; the warnings above (embedment into on, edges) apply to each.
  • The answer and the record as a slot connector’s (adds, junction).

Joinery

build_connect with joint instead of part cuts the members:

{"cmd": "build_connect", "junction": "C7:end_b|C6:side", "joint": {"kind": "half_lap"}}

joint is {"kind", "depth", "on"}:

  • housing (an end on a side): a pocket in b the size of a’s section where it meets, depth deep (default a third of b’s thickness there, at most 15 mm);
  • notch (members crossing or lying on each other): a cut in on (default a) the size of the other’s section across it, depth deep (default their overlap, or a third of on’s thickness when they only touch);
  • half_lap (members crossing in one plane, overlapping): both are cut over their overlap, a from below and b from above (along a’s axis × b’s, turned towards the host’s +Z), a by depth (default half the overlap’s thickness) and b by the rest. Members that do not overlap are refused (a half-lap needs the members overlapping).

The cuts are kept in the members’ derived parts, in cuts (beside ends):

{"type": "derived_part", "source": "S1", "config": "48x148", "parameters": {"L": "d12"},
 "cuts": [{"kind": "half_lap", "with": "C7", "junction": "C7:end_b|C6:side",
           "origin": [-74, 0, "d12 - 148"], "x": [1, 0, 0], "y": [0, 1, 0],
           "size": [148, 24, 148], "depth": 24}]}
  • Each is a box in the part’s coordinates: from origin along x, y and their cross product by size; origin and size are values; depth (a number) is the depth the joint was asked for, kept to cut it anew. kind is housing, notch, half_lap or rip (a board ripped to the width left, Spacing sets), or birdsmouth (a rafter notched over a wall’s top plate, BUILD: timber frames). with and junction name the other member and the junction.
  • Bound to the members. The coordinate along the member is an expression: of the other member’s slide when it slides on this one (d20 + 24), else of this member’s length when the cut is nearer end B (d12 - 148), else a number. So a cut follows a joist moved along its beam and a member’s end when its length changes. build_edit with "cuts": "refit" cuts the member’s joinery anew from where the members are now.
  • The cuts are made inside the derived part after the end cuts; the cut list reads them from the definition. build_remove of a member takes the cuts with it out of the others.
  • The answer: component null, features (the derived parts cut), cuts ({component, kind, size}), warnings; undo step Connect half_lap. build_preview with joint answers cuts likewise.

Sheets on a face

build_panel with a sheet (panel.mount: "face") picks a member’s face (a face frame, or a side face with at.point) and lays the sheet on it:

  • faces (optional): more picks ([{"occurrence", "geometry"}]). The sheet covers the rectangle of the picked faces in the picked face’s plane (x along the first member, y across); without faces, of every member face on that plane facing the same way.
  • Its width and height, where they are parameters, are that rectangle’s (numbers, not bound: placing it again sizes it again); a fixed size keeps its value and fits is false with reason when it does not cover the rectangle. thickness and part.config as for other panels.
  • It is held by a rigid joint (not flipped) on the first member’s face frame with a frame_override. The middle of the design’s box at its sizes goes to the middle of the rectangle and the box’s back (its least z) lies on the face, so the design may be drawn from a corner (a box from (0, 0, 0) to (W, H, T)) or centred; no frame of the sheet is read. The answer as for panels (fits, bound empty).

Lists

build_cut_list (a design without timber answers exactly as before):

  • With timber the answer adds timber: true and totals ({running_metres, volume, mass} over the timber rows), and every row adds kind (timber or null), material ({species, finish, grade, density}, the grade the part’s own), nominal and section ({width, height}, mm), availability, running_metres (length × quantity / 1000) and volume (m³, the section’s area × length × quantity; the area W × T, a profiled board’s board.area). A timber row’s mass (each) is the density × the area × length.
  • With profiled boards (Profiled boards below) the answer adds profiled: true and totals.area, and every row profile, cover and area (null for other rows).
  • Rows are grouped by the grade too, and machining lists the joinery cuts after the holes: {at: null, kind, size, with, diameter: null}.
  • stock is per source and configuration row (config in the entry when the source has rows). A timber entry adds stock_lengths: each stock piece’s length, the shortest of the source’s stock lengths that holds its cuts (first fit of the longest pieces into the longest stock, then each piece shortened).
  • build_parts adds to each part kind (timber or null), grade, set (the lead’s component or null), spacing (the lead’s: the definition and count), cuts ({kind, with, junction, size}), and board (a profiled board’s {profile, cover, joined}, else null).
  • build_junctions adds wood to a junction whose members are both timber: {through, into, thickness, max_diameter, sections} (the member a fastener goes through and the one it goes into, the thickness gone through, the largest diameter by the sizing rule, and sections {"a": [W, T], "b": [W, T]} for the pickers).
  • build_place, build_edit take grade (text; null clears): the part’s own grade, else its row’s material.grade.

Profiled boards

Tongue and groove boards, shiplap and feather-edge cladding and deck boards (mitcad#477; build/profiled.rs, tests build/profiled_tests.rs) are timber members with a board block (docs/libraries.md, Timber parts):

"board": {"profile": "tongue_and_groove", "cover": "112 mm", "area": 3123.5,
          "tongue": {"length": "8 mm", "thickness": "8 mm"}}
  • profile: tongue_and_groove, shiplap, feather_edge or deck; cover the width a board covers in a row (a deck board’s: its width, when left out); area the section’s area in mm²; tongue, overlap, edge_radius and grooves the sizes of its joint or edges (a row’s own through build.rows). The section’s box lies as any member’s (centred, section.width its full width along X, the thickness along Y), its visible face towards +Y.
  • Boards that join (tongue and groove, shiplap, feather-edge) have two more frames: groove (kind groove) on the box’s −X side, z −X, and tongue (kind tongue) the cover width on from it, z +X, both at y = 0 and z = 0, x along +Z. The tongue’s edge goes under the next board (a shiplap’s lip, a feather-edge board’s thin edge).
  • Against another board. build_place with at.geometry a board’s tongue frame mates the new board’s groove there (its tongue in a groove frame): a rigid joint, flipped, so the new board lies beside it the cover width on, tongue into groove, its ends level (its length as length gives). The profiles must match: both boards of one profile and thickness, with the same tongue (length and thickness) or overlap within 0.01 mm; otherwise refused (the profiles do not match: the tongues of <new> and <target> differ). The answer’s place is frame.
  • Rows. A spacing set in gap mode (Spacing sets) of boards that join, laid across their width (the set’s direction along the board’s X), is laid edge to edge: the step is the cover width c, no gap (a gap asked for is not kept, and warnings says so: <part> joins edge to edge: laid without the gap of 5 mm), the count ceil((span - (w - c)) / c) with w the full width, and the last board ripped to what is left (span - (n - 1) × c) when that is less than w. fit spread lays them as cut; a count lays that many edge to edge (refused when they do not fit the span). Deck boards, and boards laid another way, keep the gap and the rules above.
  • Lists. A profiled board’s mass and volume come from its board.area. With profiled boards the cut list adds profiled: true, each row profile, cover (mm) and area (m², the area covered: the cover width × length × quantity; a ripped board covers what is left of it up to its cover width), and totals.area. build_parts gives each part’s board.

Pickers

library_search and library_build_candidates (Library commands):

  • role: "profile" with kind: "timber" lists timber only; role: "profile" without kind lists no timber (the Profile picker).
  • role: "panel" with mount: "face" lists sheets; without mount, no sheets.
  • A junction with wood (from build_junctions) is offered wood fasteners and outer connectors whose fit fits its members, and no slot connectors; a junction without wood, as before.

Frames of members (mitcad#485)

Three rules for frames of members (code build/place.rs; tests build/close_tests.rs):

  • A member on the ground lies flat or on edge. build_place’s lie (Members by two points) also turns a member placed on the ground along at.direction: on a plane or a face (the plane’s normal is “up”) or grounded (the host’s +Z): flat puts the section’s smaller dimension across the plane, edge the larger one. A member standing square to the plane keeps its X along the host’s X. Without lie (Profile) the placement is as before.

  • A member on a member’s end lies as that member does. A timber member placed on a timber member’s end, straight on or turned at a corner, has its thickness axis (its section’s smaller side) parallel to the target’s where the direction allows it: the end frame’s x is turned a quarter about the new axis when only that does (straight on, a frame_override with x_axis only). Two boards of one size meet with ends of the same width and flush faces. rotate and flip turn it further; a square section, or a slot profile, is placed as before.

  • Closing a frame. A part placed on an end (place end) whose length is bound (length.bind) to a member its far end meets end to end, as a corner, gets that end made as its start: the ray from its start along its axis meets the member, not along the member’s axis, within the member’s section size of one of its ends (as build_junctions finds an L), and the member is not the one the start is on. Then:

    • with the start mitred (a cut at the end that meets, a corner’s shared mitre), both ends at the corner get a shared mitre, each by half the angle between the axes (45° in a square frame), leaning towards the other’s axis away from the corner, and the bound length’s mode is through: the length runs to the member’s outer side, the long point, so the outer corners meet;
    • with the start square, the bound length’s mode is face: a square butt on the member’s face, never into it.

    The bound length stays: moving either member (a length changed, a joint dragged) keeps the corner. build_preview answers it as closing: {component, end ("a" or "b": the member's end at the corner), mitre ("shared" or "none"), angle}, null when the placing closes no corner; its length.mode is the mode the length gets.

Resting, lying as the host, typed corners (mitcad#492)

Four more rules (code build/place.rs, build/spacing.rs; tests build/close_tests.rs, build/timber_tests.rs):

  • A member lying on a plane rests on it. A part placed on the ground (place grounded: on the host’s XY plane; geometry: on a picked plane or planar face) with at.direction along the plane is lifted along the plane’s normal until its box’s lowest point is on the plane: it lies on the normal’s side (+Z on XY, +Y on XZ, +X on YZ, a face’s outward side), not centred on the plane, timber and slot profiles alike, as lie, rotate and flip turn it. On a picked plane or face the lift is in the joint’s frame_override.origin (and a bound length’s ray starts from the lifted axis); build_edit’s rotate and flip lift it anew, so it keeps resting. A part standing along the normal (or without at.direction) stands on its end as before. An at.offset (mitcad#2046) lifts it further, as the override’s shift apart from the rest.
  • A member on a member’s side lies as that member does. A timber member placed standing on a timber member’s side (place side, not tilted) is turned a quarter about its axis when only that puts its section’s thickness axis parallel to the target’s or, where its axis takes the target’s thickness axis (on the target’s wide face), its width axis parallel to the target’s width axis: same-size members have flush sides. The turn is the joint’s own frame override (a.frame_override with x_axis), so the slide along the side and its offsets are as before; rotate turns it further, and a flip edit sets the turn anew for the end that then meets. A square section, or a slot profile, is placed as before.
  • A typed length closes a corner too. A part placed on an end whose typed length (length a value) ends on the face or the outer side of a member it meets as a corner (as Closing a frame finds it, the far end within 0.05 mm of that face or side) closes the corner as a bound length does: ending on the outer side after a mitred start, both ends get the shared mitre; on the face, a square butt. A typed length that ends inside the member gets a warning naming the two lengths that would meet it. build_preview answers it as closing. Its axis must run through the member, not along one of its faces. A member by two points (place points, whose start is square) with the points’ distance or a typed length gets the same: a square butt where it ends on the member’s face, else the warning; a bound length keeps the mode given. With the points’ distance, an end in the member (or, free, on its outer side) is cut back to its face first (mitcad#509, Members by two points): the square butt, no warning.
  • A set on a side starts at the typed offset. In a spacing set on a side whose base placement has at.offset (the app’s Offset and From) and no spacing.from or spacing.to: from end A (or the middle) the first member’s near face is where that offset puts it; from end B the last member’s far face.

Classes

build_connect with joint (no part) is class model; with a part, as before.

Section curves in sketches

sketch.project with "section": true (mitcad#389) adds the curves where the sketch’s plane cuts a face (source, a face name; every face of a name without #k) instead of the face’s projected boundary:

{"cmd": "sketch.project", "sketch": "F5", "source": "F2:side(c3)", "body": "F2.b0",
 "linked": true, "section": true}
  • The fields are sketch.project’s: body, linked, and occurrence and context for a face of another component (Geometry of other components); the sketch’s plane is moved into that component’s coordinates, cut there, and the curves moved back.
  • The kernel cuts each face by itself (Kernel::section_curves, geometry/include/mitcad/geometry/sketch_ref.hpp): a line, circle or ellipse per piece; B-spline pieces that meet end to end where no other piece ends (a thread’s faces cut along its axis) become one B-spline, exactly. The curves come in as sketch.project makes entities: fixed reference geometry, ends that meet sharing a point.
  • A linked section is recorded as a projection with "section": true in the sketch’s projections; it is recomputed from the body at every evaluation and its entities follow it as a linked projection’s do (each the fresh curve of its kind most like it; one that finds none keeps its last geometry and the sketch warns). A face the plane no longer cuts is a lost source.
  • An edge (Intersect, mitcad#736): source an edge name; the entities are points where the plane crosses the edge (every edge of a name without #k; Kernel::section_points, OCCT’s section of the edge by the plane): a point where it passes through or touches the plane, the ends of an edge or a piece of it lying in the plane. Linked, the record is a projection with "section": true whose source is the edge, and its points follow the fresh crossings.
  • Another sketch’s curve or point (mitcad#998): source as in Projecting another sketch’s curves and points, without body; the entities are the points where the plane crosses the curve where its sketch solved it (sketch::project::plane_crossings: lines and conics exactly, splines and helices by sign changes refined by bisection; a curve lying in the plane gives its ends, a point on the plane itself), in the curve’s order. A single curve the plane does not cross is refused (the sketch's plane does not cross c4 of Sketch1); of a whole sketch, the curves it does not cross are left out. Linked, each is a projection with "section": true whose source is the curve, and its points follow the fresh crossings when the source sketch changes. One edit, one undo step (Section Curves to Sketch2). The app’s Intersect sends it for another sketch’s curves and points, or a whole sketch picked in the browser (mitcad#1031).
  • A whole body (Intersect, mitcad#736): no source, body given. The kernel cuts all of the body’s faces (section_curves without a face) and the pieces come in grouped by the face they lie on: each face’s pieces are a section of that face of their own (linked: one projection record per face, as a face’s section would be), a B-spline joined across faces one of its first face with the others as its chain, and pieces on faces without names unlinked. One edit, one undo step (Section Curves to Sketch1). Each record follows its face; a face the body gains later in the plane adds nothing.
  • Refused: a vertex (a section's source is a face, an edge or a body); a face or edge that is not before the sketch or that the plane does not cut (the sketch's plane does not cut it (or nothing named so is before the sketch)); a body the plane does not cut (the sketch's plane does not cut the body); sketch.project without source and without section (needs a source).

Tests: core/model-tests/sketch-refs/src/sketch_projection_tests.rs (a_section_of_another_sketchs_curves_gives_where_its_plane_crosses_them), core/sketch/src/tests.rs (plane_crossings_of_lines_conics_splines_and_points), core/model-tests/sketch-refs/src/section_curve_tests.rs (mock kernel: the section of a face is where the plane cuts the body’s bounds; a whole body’s section puts side k of it on the body’s face k; an edge’s crossing is where the plane crosses its line in named_curves); geometry/tests/test_section_curves.cpp (an edge through the plane and one lying in it).

Projecting another sketch’s curves and points

sketch.project takes a curve or a point of an earlier sketch as its source (mitcad#904), in the form the references to geometry give sketch entities:

{"cmd": "sketch.project", "sketch": "F4", "source": {"sketch": "F1", "curve": "c3"}, "linked": true}
{"cmd": "sketch.project", "sketch": "F4", "source": {"sketch": "F1", "point": "p7"}}
{"cmd": "sketch.project", "sketch": "F4", "source": {"sketch": "F1"}, "linked": true}
  • Any entity of the source sketch: lines, arcs, circles, ellipses and elliptical arcs, splines (by control points and through fit points) and points, construction and projected ones too. {"sketch": "F1"} without curve or point (a whole sketch picked in the browser) takes every curve of it, each as a projection of its own; its loose points are not curves and are left out.
  • The geometry is where the source sketch’s last evaluation solved it, in model space, projected along the sketch’s normal onto its plane as body edges are: on the same plane an exact copy, on a parallel plane the same shapes, on an oblique plane lines shorter, circles and arcs ellipses and elliptical arcs, splines with their poles projected; a curve seen edge on is a line, a point stays a point. The entities are fixed reference geometry, joined to the projected geometry already there as projections of model geometry are, but only to that of the same source sketch.
  • Linked ("linked": true), each entity’s projection is recorded in the sketch’s projections with the entity as its source: {"source": {"sketch": "F1", "curve": "c3"}, "entities": [...], "by_geometry": true}. Entity ids stay with a sketch’s entities across its edits, so the record follows the same curve when the source sketch is edited, solved again or its parameters change: at every evaluation its entities take the fresh geometry, each the fresh curve of its kind most like it. A source entity removed from its sketch makes the projection lost, as a body edge that is gone: its entities keep their last geometry, the sketch query marks the record "lost": true, and the sketch warns the projection of F1/c3 does not follow it: it is gone, ... (messages name the entity F1/c3). Unlinked, the entities are fixed copies with no record.
  • Order: only a sketch before the edited one in the timeline. A later sketch is refused (Sketch3 (F3) comes after Sketch2 (F2) in the timeline; only the curves and points of a sketch before it can be projected), so no sketch follows one that follows it; a linked projection whose source the timeline later puts after it fails the sketch’s check, as a reference to a later feature does. The sketch’s own geometry is refused (a sketch does not project its own geometry), as is an entity the sketch does not have (Sketch1 has no c99) and a body with a sketch’s geometry. With "section": true (mitcad#998) the entities are where the sketch’s plane crosses the curves (Section curves in sketches).
  • Another component’s sketch, and a sketch of a component placed more than once, come through occurrence and context as its bodies’ edges do (Geometry of other components): the record keeps the link and the geometry is moved by the occurrence’s placement. Without the occurrence such a sketch is refused (Sketch1 is a sketch of A, not of …; pick it where an occurrence of A shows it).
  • In the design file the source of a projection of model geometry is the name’s text, as in every earlier version, so earlier files open unchanged; a sketch entity’s source is the object above. A copied sketch’s projection of a copied sketch names the copy.

Tests: core/model-tests/sketch-refs/src/sketch_projection_tests.rs (the same, a parallel and an oblique plane; a dimension change followed; an unlinked copy; a removed source curve; a later sketch and the sketch itself refused; a whole sketch; save and reopen; another component’s sketch through its occurrence).

Failed features in command results

A feature that fails does not reject a command (mitcad#401): the command is applied and the feature is skipped. So that a client can tell “the feature this command made fails” from “a feature elsewhere fails”, a command’s result has, when any feature is in error after it, "failed_features": every failed feature in timeline order, each

  • uid, name, error (the feature’s error for agents: with its topological names, ids and coordinates, mitcad#1612);
  • message: what a person reads of it, without those, when it differs from error; places: the faces, edges, vertices and points it is about, when it has any (Errors: message, places and detail);
  • edited: the command added the feature or edited it: its definition, suppression or component changed, or it is the uid of edit_feature, suppress_feature or reorder_feature or the sketch of a sketch command (an edit of a dimension’s value changes no definition);
  • new: it did not fail before the command (also a later feature this command broke, for example through a parameter, with edited false).
{"changed": ["d4"], "recomputed": 1, "error": "Fillet1: fillet failed",
 "failed_features": [{"uid": "F3", "name": "Fillet1", "error": "fillet failed",
                      "edited": false, "new": true}]}

Without failed features the field is left out. error stays the first failed feature, as before; error_notice beside it is that failure as a person reads it (level, message “Fillet1: …” without names, ids or coordinates, target, places), which the application’s status line shows. The MCP server’s model_command is an error only when one of these is edited and lists them at the top level (docs/mcp.md). Its error text then says that the feature stays in the timeline and how to remove it (mitcad#1481): F57 (Fillet3) was added but failed: fillet failed. It stays in the timeline; edit it, or remove it with undo or delete_feature (“was changed” for an edit; an array’s entry is named, commands[1]: …).

Tests: core/model-tests/api/src/failed_features_tests.rs (mock kernel), core/mcp/src/tests.rs, tools/cli/mcp-results-test.cmake.

Errors: message, places and detail

What a person reads never names topological names (E{…}, V{…}, F3:side(…), a bare F1:top), sketch region keys (r{…}), internal ids (k5, p15, c14, F57, a body’s F2.b0) or coordinates (mitcad#1612, docs/ui-conventions.md “What a message says”). So a failure is structured (notice::FeatureError): its message in plain words, its places (faces, edges and vertices of a body, a sketch’s regions, points in the model’s space), and its detail, the same with the names, ids and points, for agents and the log.

Where a result gives text, that text is the agents’: a command’s error, failed_features[].error, the timeline and feature queries’ error, MCP’s results. The person’s side is beside it: error_notice of a command’s result and message and places of each failed feature, an error notice in the feature’s notices, and a preview’s error notice. A refusal of a command (the Err of command, query or preview through the application’s bridge) is its message, then a last line [placed: {"message": …, "detail": …, "places": […]}]; the application shows only the text before that line, and a sketch refusal’s [conflicts: …] line stays last. The geometry kernel throws the same form (placed_error, geometry/include/mitcad/geometry/user_error.hpp), which the bridge reads into the feature’s error.

An example, a chamfer wider than the face beside its edge:

{"error": "Chamfer4: the chamfer of edge E{F2:end(…)|F2:side(c1[c4,c2])} is wider than face F2:side(c1[c4,c2]), which it would take away, and cannot meet face F2:start(…) beyond it",
 "error_notice": {"level": "error", "target": "F4",
                  "message": "Chamfer4: the chamfer is wider than the face beside its edge and would take that face away, but cannot meet the face beyond it",
                  "places": [{"kind": "edge", "body": "F2.b0", "name": "E{…}"},
                             {"kind": "face", "body": "F2.b0", "name": "F2:side(c1[c4,c2])"},
                             {"kind": "face", "body": "F2.b0", "name": "F2:start(…)"}]}}

A point is a place too, {"kind": "point", "at": [28.28, -28.28, 202]}, where an error says where in the model’s space; its coordinates are in the detail, never in the message. So is an occurrence, {"kind": "occurrence", "path": "O1/O4"} (its path of uids from the root, mitcad#1745: what holds a joint’s side), painted as every body it places, and a joint or constraint set, {"kind": "joint", "feature": "F7"} (mitcad#1753: the joints of a loop that cannot all hold), painted as the pointer over its Browser row draws it.

An older text, or an imported one, that still names them is cleaned on the way: the names become their kind in words (“an edge”, “a face”, “a body”) and their places, a coordinate tuple “a point” and a point place, and the text as it was the detail. Tests: core/model-base/src/notice.rs, core/model-tests/api/src/user_text_guard_tests.rs, geometry/tests/test_user_text_scan.cpp.

Errors

What an agent tells the user of an error in an MCP result, and what it keeps (mitcad#1897). An error there has up to three parts, the same as a feature’s failure (Errors: message, places and detail):

FieldWhat it isUse
errorthe short cause in the design’s words: the feature’s name and what is wrong, without topological names, region keys or coordinates (an MCP text still names an array’s entry, commands[2], and a failed feature’s uid, F57)summarize this to the user
error_detailthe same text with the exact names, ids and coordinates the short one leaves out, word for word as the model gave it; only where it differs from errorkeep it whole for diagnosis and bug reports; do not shorten or paraphrase it
placesthe faces, edges, vertices, sketch regions, points, occurrences and joints the error is about, each with its exact persistent reference (name, body, sketch, at, path, feature)select or query that geometry with them (model_query, ui_select); a place is never replaced by a shorter label

An error with nothing to place has error only. A result’s keys are in alphabetical order, so its text shows error before error_detail. Where they are:

  • A refused model_command (isError, applied: false; in an array also entry and undone): nothing of the call stayed. Its error, error_detail and places as above.
  • An applied model_command whose added or edited feature fails (isError, applied: true; in an array stopped_at): the feature stays in the timeline. error is F57 (Chamfer3) was added but failed: <the short cause>. It stays in the timeline; …, error_detail the same with the exact cause, places those of the failed features. Each entry of failed_features keeps the model’s form (Failed features in command results): error exact, message the short cause where it differs, places.
  • Other tools’ errors (model_query, model_export, model_render, model_reference): the same, where the model’s text carries places.
  • The timeline and feature queries: a failed feature’s error is the exact text; its short cause and its places are its error notice in notices (level error, message, places).
{"applied": false, "entry": 1, "undone": 1,
 "error": "commands[1]: an edge is listed more than once; the 1 step(s) of the entries before it were undone",
 "error_detail": "commands[1]: edge E{F2:end(r{…})|F2:side(r{…})} is listed more than once; the 1 step(s) of the entries before it were undone",
 "places": [{"kind": "edge", "body": "F2.b0", "name": "E{F2:end(r{…})|F2:side(r{…})}"}]}

For a bug report keep the whole result as it came: isError, applied, entry or stopped_at, error, error_detail, places, failed_features, warnings and notices. Tell the user the error; quote error_detail and places only where the exact reference matters.

Compatibility. Before mitcad#1897 the error of these MCP results was the exact text; it is now in error_detail, and error is the short cause. A client that reads names from error reads error_detail where there is one, else error: that gives the earlier text word for word (the model’s FeatureError::agent_text). The model’s own results are unchanged: a command’s error and error_notice, failed_features, and the queries. Tests: core/mcp/src/tests.rs (a_refusal_with_long_names_leads_with_its_short_cause, a_failed_feature_with_long_names_leads_with_its_short_cause).

Slicer keys in print values

A plate’s values (edit_print_plate’s values), a profile’s and a print setting’s take Mitcad’s keys of the print settings (mitcad#1897). A slicer’s own key for the same setting is refused with the key to write instead, from the key map’s dialect keys (core/print-keys): with values: {"wall_generator": "arachne"} the refusal says that wall_generator is the Bambu Studio, OrcaSlicer and QIDI Studio key of perimeter_generator (Wall generator), with the value in Mitcad’s form where it converts ("arachne"). A slicer key that means different settings in different slicers (support_angle: the support pattern’s angle in the Bambu Studio family, the support threshold in UltiMaker Cura) names every candidate and picks none. A key of another set names that set. A key that is no slicer’s either is refused as before. Nothing is stored under a slicer’s key and no key is guessed: the value is written again with the Mitcad key. The print_keys query (set: process, filament or printer) lists every key with its name, kind, unit, choices, range and each slicer’s key.

Adding a feature in the middle of the timeline

add_feature with "after": "F12" (a feature’s uid) or "index": 3 (the number of features before the new one) inserts the feature there instead of at the marker (mitcad#403):

{"cmd": "add_feature", "after": "F1", "def": {"type": "extrude",
 "profiles": [{"sketch": "F1", "region": "r{c1}"}],
 "extent": {"type": "distance", "distance": 5}, "operation": "new_body"}}
  • One undo step (Add Extrude2) and one recompute: the features before the place come from the cache, the new one and those after it are evaluated.
  • The marker stays after the feature it was after (it counts one more); features after it stay rolled back. The place must be at or before the marker: index past it, after a rolled-back feature are refused.
  • The new feature may refer only to features before it, as reorder_feature requires; a refused insert (that, an unknown after, both after and index) leaves the document as it was. A feature that is added but fails is in the result’s failed_features with edited.
  • Not with a Face’s inline rules (sheet_face with a rules definition); the preview takes neither field.

Tests: core/model-tests/api/src/insert_feature_tests.rs (mock kernel), tools/cli/mcp-results-test.cmake (through MCP).

Signed point dimensions

A horizontal_distance or vertical_distance with "signed": true (mitcad#404) is the coordinate offset b.x - a.x (b.y - a.y) in sketch axes, which may be negative, instead of its size. Its sign says on which side of a the point b lies, so a point p3 dimensioned from a centre p1 with

{"cmd": "sketch.add_dimension", "sketch": "F1", "value": "r * cos(angle)",
 "dimension": {"type": "horizontal_distance", "a": "p1", "b": "p3", "signed": true}}
{"cmd": "sketch.add_dimension", "sketch": "F1", "value": "r * sin(angle)",
 "dimension": {"type": "vertical_distance", "a": "p1", "b": "p3", "signed": true}}

follows the parameter angle through all four quadrants: a value that changes sign moves p3 to the other side of p1, where an unsigned dimension would refuse it. To dimension a point from the sketch origin, use a fixed point at [0, 0] (sketch.add_point with "fixed": true) as a.

  • Without signed (default false; sketches stored before, every import), the dimensions are as before: the size |b.x - a.x|, never negative (a negative value is an error of the sketch, d4 must not be negative), on the side where b is when the sketch is solved.
  • Its value may be any finite number; a driven one measures the signed offset (its reference parameter and the measured field in the sketch query), as does a driving one added without a value.
  • The sketch query and saved files give "signed": true only on a signed dimension, so files without signed dimensions are unchanged.
  • Solver: HorizontalDistance { signed: true } keeps side 1 and holds dx - d (core/solver/README.md).

sketch.set_signed switches an existing horizontal or vertical distance between signed and unsigned (mitcad#409), one undo step Change Dimension in Sketch1, keeping the point where it is:

{"cmd": "sketch.set_signed", "sketch": "F1", "dimension": "k4", "signed": true}
  • Where b lies on the positive side of a (or level with it), the value stays as it is. Where it lies on the negative side, a driving value is negated: a value without parameters as a number (30 becomes -30), an expression as -(…) (r * 0.6 becomes -(r * 0.6); one that is -(…) already loses it instead, so switching back and forth does not nest), and a dimension that uses another parameter by name gets an expression of its own (w becomes -w).
  • A driven dimension only measures the other way.
  • Other dimension types are refused (dimension k3 is a length, not a horizontal or vertical distance); switching to what it is already changes nothing.

Tests: core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_tests.rs (a_signed_point_dimension_*, an_unsigned_point_dimension_*, signed_point_dimensions_round_trip_*, switching_a_distance_signed_*, unsigned_point_dimensions_switched_*), core/solver/tests/constraints.rs (signed_distances_follow_through_all_quadrants).

The library parts a design uses

The part picker’s In this design group (mitcad#418, app/COMMANDS.md) lists the library parts the open design already uses, with how many times each is placed:

QueryResult
library_usageparts: one per library component, {"library", "url", "component", "count", "rows"}
  • library is the library’s id and component the component’s id in it, as library_search gives them; url is where the library was fetched from, without credentials.
  • Both kinds of library parts count: BUILD’s derived parts by their source and components inserted from a library (Library parts), linked or copied.
  • A component’s versions and configuration rows are one entry: an M4x16 and an M4x20 of the same screw count together in count.
  • rows (mitcad#518) gives the same count per configuration row, so the part picker can show each size’s own use count: [{"config": "M4x16", "count": 35}, {"config": "M4x20", "count": 2}], in the order the rows first appear in the parts list; a row the design does not use is not listed. It is each use’s row as the part was placed (a BUILD part’s config, an insert’s config). A use placed without a row is in count only (it is the component’s default row), so count is at least the sum of the rows’ counts; rows is empty for a part without rows.
  • count is the parts list’s quantity summed: how many times the design places the part, through every occurrence of the components it is in. A part placed nowhere (its last occurrence deleted) is left out.
  • The entries come in the order of the parts list (the order the components were made).

Tests: core/model-tests/links/src/library_tests.rs (the_library_usage_counts_each_library_component_once, the_library_usage_counts_each_configuration_row_of_a_component), core/model-tests/build-timber/src/source_tests.rs (the_library_usage_counts_build_parts_by_their_source), core/model-tests/build-timber/src/timber_tests.rs (the_library_usage_counts_build_parts_per_row).

Motion studies and contact sets

Assemblies’ motion studies and contact sets (mitcad#454; core/model/src/motion.rs the data, contact.rs the contact checks, document/motion.rs and api/motion.rs the commands). Both are definition state, not timeline features: saved in the design file (motion_studies, contact_sets, left out when there are none), changed by undoable commands that recompute nothing, deleted with what they name (a study’s keys of a joint that is deleted or no longer has the motion; a set’s occurrences that are gone), and moved with an occurrence that moves to another parent. Tests: core/model-tests/joints/src/motion_tests.rs, tools/cli/tests/motion_contact.json, tools/ui-motion-study-test.sh, tools/ui-contact-test.sh.

{"motion_studies": [{"name": "Open", "steps": 40, "keys": [
   {"joint": "F7", "motion": "tz", "points": [[0, 0], [40, 12.5]]},
   {"joint": "F8", "motion": "rz", "points": [[10, 0], [40, 1.5708]]}]}],
 "contact_sets": [{"name": "Contact1", "occurrences": ["O2", "O3/O5"]},
                  {"name": "Stops", "occurrences": ["O1", "O2"], "suppressed": true}]}
  • Motion study: a name, steps (1 to 100 000) and keys: per joint (or as-built joint) and one of its free motions (a cylindrical joint’s tz and rz each), points [step, value] sorted by step, values in millimetres or radians. A motion’s value at a step is linear between the points around it, the first point’s before the first, the last’s after the last. Steps outside 0..steps are allowed.
  • Contact set: a name, two or more occurrence paths from the root, suppressed. Its bodies are the visible bodies placed in the design whose instance paths start with one of the paths (a body belongs to the innermost one); the pairs checked are bodies of different occurrences of one set, once each however many sets hold them.
  • Contact: two bodies pass through each other when the kernel finds more than 0.001 mm³ in common (Kernel::overlap_volumes, OCCT’s boolean common with a fuzzy value of 0.01 mm, so that faces within 0.01 mm of each other only touch); pairs whose boxes, moved by their placements, are more than 0.01 mm apart cost no boolean. Pairs that already pass through each other where a motion starts are left out (parts can move apart). Shapes are those at the marker: a feature whose body depends on placements is not built again while the joints move.
  • Motions that stop at contact: drive_joint, drag_occurrence and the joint_drag query, play_study, and the previews below. A motion is sampled from where it starts (Drive Joint and a study’s straight path: every 5° of a turn and 1 mm of a slide, at most 64 samples; a drag: every 2 mm of the grabbed point, at most 16; a study’s playback: every step), each sample the document’s state with the joints driven there and recomputed (the joints solved as Drive Joint solves them, so constraints and other joints follow), and at the first sample with a contact the step before it is bisected 14 times: the motion stops at the last state without one. Values are held within the joints’ limits. Without contact sets nothing is sampled.
  • A stopped motion’s answer has contact: set, bodies (each body, name, occurrence (path name), path), fraction (how far it went, 0 to 1; not for drags) and message (stopped at contact: Body2 (Pin:1) and Body3 (Wall:1) in Contact1). drive_joint also gives the message in warnings (a panel shows it) and keeps the value where it stopped as the joint’s position (a number, not the expression given).
CommandFieldsResult
add_motion_studyname (Study<n> when left out), steps (default 100), keys (each joint (uid or name), motion, points [[step, value], …], a value a number in mm or radians or an expression in the motion’s unit, "90 deg")name; undo step Add Study1
edit_motion_studyname, new_name, steps, keys (all of them)name
delete_motion_studyname
set_study_keystudy, joint, motion, step, value (where the joint is at the marker when left out: Add Key)joint, motion, step, value; a point at the same step is replaced; undo step Key Joint1 in Study1
remove_study_keystudy, joint, motion, step (without it the whole key)
play_studystudy, stepvalues (per joint uid, per motion), fraction, contact; the keyed joints driven from where they are straight to their values at the step, stopping at the first contact, and kept: one undo step Play Study1
add_contact_setname (Contact<n>), occurrences (paths from the root by uids or names, or one occurrence placed once), suppressedname
edit_contact_setname, new_name, occurrences, suppressedname; undo steps Suppress Contact1, Unsuppress Contact1, Edit Contact1
delete_contact_setname
QueryFieldsResult
motion_studieseach study’s name, steps, keys (joint, joint_name, motion, points)
study_valuesstudy, stepvalues per joint uid and motion at the step
contact_setseach set’s name, occurrences (path, name), suppressed
contact_checkoverlaps: the pairs of the active sets that pass through each other at the marker (set, volume, bodies)

Previews (preview, changing nothing but the preview; the report has the preview’s placements and values, fraction, contact):

  • {"cmd": "play_study", "study", "step", "from"}: the study at step, along the study from step from (the application’s playback, frame by frame), else from where the joints are.
  • {"cmd": "drive_joint", "joint", "values": {"tx": 12}, "from": {"tx": 8}}: the joint driven to the values from from (Animate Joint’s frames while a contact set applies; without one they come from the joint_poses query, Animate Joint’s frames), else from where it is.

The .solidcraft import maps the file’s contact sets and motion studies onto these (.solidcraft import, core/import-solidcraft/docs/solidcraft.md).

Contour Flange, Convert to Sheet Metal and Perforate

Three sheet features of mitcad#461, with add_feature and edit_feature, ordinary parameters, preview, Undo and persistence. Contour Flange and Convert to Sheet Metal take their rules as a Face does: a sheet_rules uid, or the rules’ definition inline (a sheet_rules feature is added just before them in the same undo step). The geometry and its conventions are in docs/sheet-metal.md.

Contour Flange 

{"type":"sheet_contour","rules":"F1","sketch":"F2","curves":["c1","c4","c6"],
 "width":50,"side":"right","reverse":false,"radius":3}

curves are sketch lines joined end to end, in the order the chain runs (the first line runs away from the second; one line runs from its start). The chain is the sheet’s surface on the rules’ reference side, the material on side of it (right, the default, or left of travel, seen from the sketch’s front), width along the sketch’s normal (against it with reverse). Every corner is the virtual sharp of a bend of radius (default: the rules’). The new body is <feature>.b0; panel i is the straight part of line i (slot i, its curves g<50+100i> to g<53+100i>, 51 at its far end), bend i (slot i) joins panels i and i+1. Refused: curves that are not lines or do not join, lines in one line, and a line not longer than the setbacks of its bends.

Convert to Sheet Metal 

{"type":"sheet_convert","rules":"F1","body":"F5.b0","face":"F5:side(c1[c12,c4])",
 "bends":["E{F5:side(c1[c12,c4])|F5:side(c12[c10,c1])}"],"radius":3}

The body becomes a sheet of the rules, keeping its uid. face (planar) is the first panel’s front, the material behind it. Without bends the body must be a plate of the rules’ thickness behind the face: the sheet built from the face must have the body’s volume and centre of mass. With bends (edges between two planar faces), the faces reached from face across them are panels with the rules’ thickness behind them, each bend edge the virtual sharp of a bend of radius (default: the rules’). Panel k is the k-th face reached (slot 0 the picked face), bend k the bend that reached panel k+1.

Every other edge between two panels is a rip (mitcad#1949; a tray from a solid: the base picked, its four edges the bends, the four corners ripped). rips may name such edges too; each must lie between two panels and not be a bend. At a rip the panels are cut apart as the walls of a flange on several edges are at a corner (A flange on several edges): miter (bisect, the default, earlier_runs_past or later_runs_past, earlier and later in the order the faces are reached) and corner_gap (default: the rules’ thickness) say how. A panel is cut normal to its surfaces where the cutting plane meets the surface that reaches further. The bends at a rip’s ends end square where all their material clears that plane, the panel before them cut back to the tangent line beside them (a corner relief). A bend runs only as far as both its faces reach its tangent lines: a wall whose ends are not square to its bend (a vertical side wall on an inclined base) converts, running past the bend at one end and ending short of the edge’s end at the other.

{"type":"sheet_convert","rules":"F1","body":"F2.b0","face":"F2:bottom",
 "bends":["E{F2:bottom|F2:side0}","E{F2:bottom|F2:side1}",
          "E{F2:bottom|F2:side2}","E{F2:bottom|F2:side3}"],
 "corner_gap":1,"miter":"bisect"}

Refused: a face that is not planar, a bend edge that is not straight, does not join the picked face through the others or closes a loop (leave it out of the bends to rip it open), a picked rip that is no edge between two panels or is a bend, a rip whose cut takes a face away whole, faces at a bend that leave no room for it along the edge.

Perforate 

{"type":"sheet_perforate","body":"F3.b0","diameter":5,"pitch":10,"margin":5,
 "pattern":"square","stationary":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},
 "outline":{"profiles":[{"sketch":"F4","region":"r{c1[c4,c2],c2[c1,c3],c3[c2,c4],c4[c3,c1]}"}]}}

Round holes of diameter, pitch apart on a staggered (default) or square grid, cut through the sheet as a developed cut with every bend open. The grid lies in the chart of stationary (default: the sheet’s lowest panel) developed with all bends, from the developed material’s lower left corner; a hole is kept where it lies on a panel, on no bend, and margin (default: the diameter) or more from every edge, cut-out and bend. Optional outline.profiles selects closed regions of one sketch on a flat face of the sheet. The sketch profiles are clipped to the panels they lie on and follow those panels into the development. The grid starts at the clipped outline’s lower left, with the same margin from its outer and inner loops. An open profile or outline outside the sheet’s flat faces is refused. Without an outline the field covers the whole sheet.

The holes are generated curves g<k> of the feature. The operation also refuses a pitch at most the diameter, a negative margin, a sheet with overlays that block development and more than 100000 holes.

Tests: core/model-tests/sheet/src/sheet_more_tests.rs, core/model/src/sheet/folded/perforate.rs (the grid), the CLI fixtures sheet_contour, sheet_convert, sheet_perforate with their reopen passes, sheet_perforate_outline with a DXF check, sheet_convert_tray (mitcad#1949), and the .solidcraft test designs sheet-contour-perforate and sheet-convert (cli.import_solidcraft).

Motion links

A motion_link feature (mitcad#466; features/motion_link.rs the definition, core/model/src/motion_links.rs what recompute does with it, document/motion_links.rs and api/joints.rs the commands; the cam’s geometry adapted from SolidCraft in third_party/solidcraft/cam.rs) makes one joint’s free motion (b, the follower) follow another’s (a, the driver) in the link’s component. Tests: core/model-tests/joints/src/motion_link_tests.rs, core/solver/tests/rigid_couplings.rs, tools/cli/tests/motion_links.json, tools/ui-motion-link-test.sh.

{"type": "motion_link", "a": {"joint": "F7", "motion": "rz"}, "b": {"joint": "F8", "motion": "tx"},
 "coupling": {"type": "rack_pinion",
              "radius": {"occurrence": "O2", "geometry": {"body": "F4.b0", "face": "F4:side(c1)"}}},
 "offset": "d12"}
couplingFieldsb follows a
ratioratio (unitless, not zero)b = ratio · a + offset (mm or radians each)
gearra, rb (sizes), internaltwo turns: b = −(ra / rb) · a + offset (+ for an internal, ring gear)
rack_pinionradius (a size)a turn and a slide, either way round: the slide travels radius per radian
screwlead (a size)a turn and a slide (a cylindrical joint’s own two, or a revolute joint and a slider): lead per turn
camprofile, follower, tipthe follower rides the cam’s profile (below)
  • Sizes (ra, rb, radius, lead, a roller’s radius) are a value (a parameter, an expression or a number, mm; tooth counts work as sizes in proportion) or round geometry picked on an occurrence, a joint origin (occurrence, geometry): the radius of a cylindrical, conical or spherical face, a circular edge or a sketch circle or arc, found again on every recompute.
  • reverse turns the follower the other way (a cam’s follower rides it from the other side). offset (mm or an angle, as b’s motion) is added to the follower’s value.
  • Joints: a and b name joints (or as-built joints) of the link’s component, or with occurrence of a flexible occurrence’s component (Flexible subassemblies), and one of their free motions each; the two must differ (a screw may name one cylindrical joint’s rz and tz). Gears couple two turns; a rack and pinion and a screw a turn and a slide.
  • Solving: at its point of the timeline the link works out its relation and solves its two joints together with every joint, constraint and link sharing moving occurrences with them (mitcad_solver::RigidCoupling: one row b − relation(a)). A follower whose driver is driven (a position or a rest value, or followed from a driven motion) lets go of its own position; a driven follower whose driver is free drives the driver. drive_joint (and a study’s keys) take away the positions of the motions linked to the ones they drive (through links), so the last driven motion drives; a cam’s follower is not driven (refused: drive the cam). Drags move linked joints together; the degrees of freedom count the link (two gears on revolute joints: one). A contact of a contact set stops the whole linked motion (the linked joints move in each sample of Drive Joint, a drag, Animate Joint or a study). A free driving turn is known from the placements only within a turn: the solve takes the turn its follower says (a gear past half a turn keeps its mate).
  • Cam: a is a revolute joint (the cam), b a slider (a translating follower) or a revolute joint (an oscillating one). profile is a joint origin on the side of a that turns: a planar face (its outer boundary) or curves of a sketch ({"sketch": "F3", "curves": [...]}: the profile they bound, the one sharing most of them, the largest with none). In the cam’s fixed frame (the other side’s frame) the profile lies square to the axis and turns by a’s value. The follower’s guide is the side of b on the part the cam turns against (else b’s own side b); a translating follower comes along its slide axis through its tip, from the side of the cam’s axis its tip is on now; an oscillating one swings about its axis (along the cam’s) from its arm pointing away from the cam’s axis, toward the cam the way its arm is turned now. follower: {"type": "knife"} (default), {"type": "roller", "radius": <size>} or {"type": "flat"} (a sliding follower only). tip: the knife’s point or the roller’s centre on the follower (a joint origin; a roller picked by its round face is its own tip); without it a sliding follower’s tip is its joint frame’s origin; a swinging one needs it. Over one turn of the cam the follower stands where it first touches the profile (360 samples, followed sample by sample for a swinging one; a jump off the profile is refused), its value there with its tip where it is now along its line (or arm): it touches the cam, offset added. Between samples a monotone cubic.
  • Failures name the link and the cause: a joint not in effect, a coupling that does not fit its motions, a size that is not positive, a profile not on the turning part, not flat or square to the axis, a follower that misses the cam.
CommandFieldsResult
add_motion_linka, b (joint by uid or name, motion), coupling (occurrences of picked geometry by uids or names), reverse, offset, as_built (default: true but for a cam), name, componentuid, name, parameters, state, solved; without offset and with as_built, the offset that keeps the joints where they are at the marker (b’s value less what the relation gives for a’s); undo step Add MotionLink1

add_feature and edit_feature take the definition as it is (its offset as given, zero without one).

QueryFieldsResult
jointsalso links: per link uid, name, component, coupling, a and b (joint, name, motion), reverse, status, error, state (placed, satisfied, failed, suppressed), solved (b follows a at the marker), ratio (a linear coupling’s b per a), offset, values (a, b at the marker), moved
motion_link_offseta, b, coupling, reverse, component (as add_motion_link)offset: what as_built would give (Motion Link’s panel)

The .solidcraft import maps the file’s motion links onto these (.solidcraft import, core/import-solidcraft/docs/solidcraft.md).

Boundary Fill

A boundary_fill feature (mitcad#457; features/boundary_fill.rs, Kernel::boundary_cells, geometry/src/boundary_fill.cpp) makes solids of the cells that tool bodies enclose, with add_feature and edit_feature, preview, Undo and persistence; the application’s Boundary Fill command makes and edits it (mitcad#2149, app/COMMANDS.md, “Boundary Fill”):

{"type": "boundary_fill", "tools": ["F2.b0", "F4.b0"], "cells": [[15, 15, 15], [5, 5, 5]],
 "operation": "new_body", "remove_tools": false}
{"type": "boundary_fill", "tools": ["F2.b0", "F4.b0", "F6.b0", "F8.b0"], "planes": ["F9", "xy"],
 "cells": [[10, 10, 15]], "operation": "new_body"}
  • With solid tools only, the tools’ faces divide space into cells; a cell is all of the space inside every tool that holds its point and outside every other tool (several solids where that space falls apart). cells gives a point inside each cell to fill, in the coordinates of the feature’s component. Two points in one cell fill it once, with a warning. Such definitions mean what they meant before mitcad#2149: saved designs and .solidcraft imports do not change.
  • Surface bodies and planes as tools (mitcad#2149): tools may hold surface bodies besides solids, untrimmed and overlapping, and planes plane references written as Split Body’s plane tool is (origin planes "xy", construction planes "F9", planar faces {"body", "face"} as their whole plane, fixed planes {"origin", "normal"}; with planes tools may be left out, planes alone need four or more). With a plane or a surface body among the tools, a cell is the closed region around its point that the faces of all the tools and the planes bound together (Kernel::boundary_regions: the faces divided once by OCCT’s BOPAlgo_MakerVolume, every part of space they close off all round a region, faces that close nothing off left out). A plane is cut to a square reaching past the box of the tools and the points (with planes alone, of the points where three planes cross); the pieces of the i-th plane are named <feature>:plane<i>. A point in a region the tools leave open fails in words, the tools do not close off the region of a cell: it is open where the surfaces end; …, its places the point and points along the tools’ free edges where the region leaks out (found by dividing the faces again inside a box that closes the region off); a point on a face fails too. The preview’s tool (Evaluate::preview_tool) is every closed region, which the panel draws see-through.
  • operation: new_body (a body per cell, in the order of the points, <feature>.b<i>), new_component (the same in a new component), or join, cut and intersect: the cells together are one tool that works on participants as an extrusion’s tool does (none: all bodies of the component, the tools that stay among them; a cut that splits a body makes bodies of the pieces, Body ids of a split’s pieces).
  • remove_tools takes the tools out of the design before the operation; a removed tool cannot be a participant. Without it the tools stay as they are.
  • Names: a cell’s faces are pieces of the tools’ faces and keep their names (F2:top, pieces of one face side by side merged again, others numbered #k), as a boolean keeps them; the fill gives no names of its own.
  • Refused: no tools and no planes, a tool or a plane listed twice, a plane reference that is not a plane, fewer than four planes alone, no points, participants of a new body. Failures: a point inside no tool (the point (50, 50, 50) is inside no tool body: no enclosed cell there) or on a tool’s boundary, a point in an open region, a mesh body as a tool, a join, cut or intersection that reaches no participant.

The boundary_regions query (mitcad#2149, model-api/src/boundary_regions.rs) lists the closed regions of tools and planes for the panel, at the timeline marker, and places points among them:

{"query": "boundary_regions", "tools": ["F2.b0", "F4.b0"], "planes": ["F9"], "points": [[10, 10, 15]]}
→ {"regions": [{"point": [10, 10, 15], "min": [0, 0, 5], "max": [20, 20, 25]}],
   "places": [{"region": 0}]}

Each region has a point inside it (its centre of mass where that is inside), in the order of the points (x, then y, then z); a place is {"region": i}, {"on_face": true} or {"open": true, "gap": [...]}. The regions are those of the faces (as with a surface or a plane among the tools) also for solids alone, whose cell holding such a point may be larger.

Tests: core/model/src/boundary_fill_tests.rs (mock kernel: surfaces and planes as tools, the open region with its gap, the refusals, solid tools alone unchanged), geometry.boundary_fill (geometry/tests/test_boundary_fill.cpp, OCCT: four untrimmed, overlapping surfaces and two planes enclose one box; a surface across a solid, the chosen cell cut out; a region open on one side; planes alone), cli.boundary_fill (tools/cli/tests/boundary_fill.json, a plane across a body too, saved and opened again by cli.boundary_fill_info), the .solidcraft test design boundary-fill (cli.import_solidcraft), and the panel’s UI test tools/ui-boundary-fill-test.sh (app.ui-windows-boundary-fill, app.ui-macos-boundary-fill).

Convert Mesh

A mesh_convert feature (mitcad#462; features/mesh_convert.rs, the conversion adapted from SolidCraft in third_party/solidcraft/mesh_convert.rs; the application’s Convert Mesh panel, and Insert Mesh’s Convert to solid, mitcad#1082; its Faceted solid mode below takes any closed mesh) rebuilds a mesh body of one profile extruded straight (a constant-section part from an STL or OBJ file) as a solid of planar and cylindrical faces, with add_feature and edit_feature, ordinary parameters, preview, Undo and persistence.

{"type": "mesh_convert", "body": "F3.b0", "tolerance": 0.05}

body is a mesh body (Mesh bodies in surface operations); tolerance (mm, 0.000001 to 1; slot tolerance) is how far the rebuilt faces may lie from the triangles. The body keeps its uid, name and appearance; the mesh it was stays as the features before this one left it (suppressed or deleted, the mesh body is back). Default name ConvertMesh<n>.

  • The mesh: its vertices within a ten-millionth of its size (at most a hundredth of the tolerance) are one; it must be closed and consistently oriented (two triangles at every edge), enclose a volume, and have at most 50000 triangles.
  • The direction: the triangles’ normals, those covering most area first (at most 16 are tried). Along a direction the triangles at the lowest and the highest level are the caps; every other triangle must stand upright, the two caps’ boundaries projected across the direction must be the same loops (at most 50, 8192 corners), and every vertex between the caps must lie on them. So a twisted, tapered or stepped mesh is no prism.
  • The section: a loop of 12 or more corners on one circle, each chord at most 30 degrees and within the tolerance of its arc, is that circle (a cylindrical face); other loops are polygons without their corners in a line (planar faces). A fitted circle may not reach across another loop, and the section’s volume must agree with the mesh’s within the tolerance times the boundary’s length and the height.
  • The solid is the kernel’s extrusion of the section, so its faces are named as an extrusion’s after the feature: <feature>:side(<segment>), start(<region>) at the low cap and end(<region>) at the high one. The section’s edges are curves c1, c2, … loop by loop: an outer loop counter-clockwise from its lowest corner (smallest x, then y, in a frame whose x axis is the model axis least along the direction), its holes clockwise, a circle one curve (F4:side(c1[c4,c2]), F4:side(c5)).
  • Refused, with nothing converted: a body that is no mesh body (body F2.b0 (from Extrude1) is not a mesh body; …), a tolerance out of range (also when adding or editing the feature), an open or inside-out mesh, a mesh over the budgets, and a mesh that is no prism (the mesh is not a supported constant-section prism (one profile extruded straight); no geometry was converted).

The .solidcraft import maps the file’s mesh conversions onto it (.solidcraft import). Tests: core/model/src/features/mesh_convert/tests.rs (core.model: the conversion on meshes built there, the feature on the mock kernel), cli.mesh_convert and cli.mesh_convert_reopen (tools/cli/tests/mesh_convert.json: an STL file’s plate through the OCCT kernel), the .solidcraft test design mesh-convert (cli.import_solidcraft) and solidcraft::tests (core.import).

Faceted solid (mitcad#1082)

With "mode": "faceted" the feature takes any closed mesh (a printed part’s STL file, not only a straight-extruded profile) and makes a new solid body of planar faces (features/mesh_convert/faceted.rs):

{"type": "mesh_convert", "body": "F3.b0", "mode": "faceted", "tolerance": 0.01, "angle": "0.5 deg"}
  • mode: analytic (the default, written only when faceted: designs saved before keep their meaning) or faceted. tolerance (mm, 0.000001 to 1; slot tolerance) is then the weld tolerance; angle (radians, more than 0 and at most 30 degrees; slot angle, 0.5 degrees when left out) is Faceted solid’s only: an analytic definition with one is refused. The application’s panel starts with 0.01 mm and 0.5 degrees.
  • Weld: vertices within tolerance of a vertex kept before them are that vertex (the nearest; the first stays where it is). Triangles that welding made degenerate are left out.
  • Closed and manifold: every edge must then be on exactly two triangles. Otherwise the feature fails with the counts, e.g. the mesh has 3 open edges (edges of one triangle only) after welding within 0.01 mm; Faceted solid needs a closed mesh in which every edge is on two triangles (and … non-manifold edges (edges of more than two triangles)).
  • Orientation: the triangles are turned to agree with their neighbours across every edge, each connected shell outwards; a mesh that cannot be oriented (a one-sided surface), a shell that encloses no volume and a shell inside another (a hollow part: 1 of the mesh's 2 shells lie inside other shells …) are refused. Shells apart become one solid each in the one body.
  • Faces: neighbouring triangles merge into one planar face while their normals lie within angle of the first one’s (the largest triangle first) and their corners within tolerance of its plane. A face’s loops follow its triangles’ edges, the outer loop first; a run of edges between the same two faces whose inner corners lie within tolerance of a straight line is one edge.
  • Limit: at most 500000 triangles (MAX_TRIANGLES): the mesh has 812345 triangles; Faceted solid takes at most 500000.
  • The body: the faces go to Kernel::boundary_body (the IFC import’s builder: one solid per closed shell), adopted under the feature’s face names <feature>:import(<n>) in the face order; the new body is <feature>.b0 (Body<n>). The feature fails, converting nothing, when a face is left out or a shell is not closed, the kernel finds the solid invalid, or its volume differs from the mesh’s by more than tolerance times the mesh’s area.
  • The mesh body stays as it was. add_feature (also at a timeline position) hides it in the same undo step (document/mesh_convert.rs), and refuses a faceted conversion that fails with ConvertMesh1: <the reason>, so that nothing changes and the mesh body stays shown. Editing, suppressing or deleting the feature later leaves the mesh body’s visibility as it is. A Show When condition on the mesh body (visible_when, mitcad#809) stays (mitcad#1157), but while a faceted conversion of the body is in the timeline (suppressed or not) it does not show the body, and the body’s warnings (query bodies) say show when: not followed while ConvertMesh1 replaces this mesh body; once the feature is deleted, or edited to the analytic mode, the body follows the condition again.

Tests: core/model/src/features/mesh_convert/faceted_tests.rs (core.model: a cube of 12 triangles is 6 faces, a block with a through hole one solid of the expected volume, a mesh with one triangle removed refused with its 3 open edges, vertices 0.005 mm apart welded at 0.01 mm, the feature on the mock kernel with the mesh body hidden and Undo, a mesh body’s Show When condition kept, not followed while converted and followed again after the delete) and cli.mesh_convert_faceted (tools/cli/tests/mesh_convert_faceted.json: an STL file’s plate and a torus’s mesh through the OCCT kernel).

Patch, Stitch and Thicken

Three features of surface (sheet) bodies (mitcad#456), with add_feature and edit_feature, ordinary parameters, preview, Undo and persistence: a patch fills sketch regions or a closed loop of a body’s edges with new surface bodies, a stitch sews bodies’ faces into one body, a thicken makes surface bodies solid. Their inputs are any surface bodies: patches, a loft’s surface, a delete_face that leaves the gap open, imported surfaces; mesh bodies are refused (Mesh bodies in surface operations). None changes the bodies it reads but those a stitch sews or a thicken joins, cuts or intersects. The definitions are features/patch.rs, stitch.rs and thicken.rs, the kernel’s inputs crate::surfaces, the OCCT side geometry/src/surfaces.cpp.

patch 

{"type": "patch", "profiles": [{"sketch": "F1", "region": "r{c1[c4,c2],c2[c1,c3],c3[c2,c4],c4[c3,c1]}"}]}
{"type": "patch", "boundary": {"body": "F5.b0", "edges": ["E{F5:end(r{c1})|F5:side(c1)}", "..."],
 "continuity": "g1", "edge_continuity": [{"edge": "E{…}", "continuity": "g0"}],
 "points": [[10, 10, 24]]}}
{"type": "patch", "boundary": {"body": "F5.b0", "opening": {"faces": ["F3:patch(r{c1})", "F4:side(c2)"], "index": 0}}}
{"type": "patch", "boundary": {"body": "F2.b0", "opening": {"faces": ["F2:side(c1)", "F2:side(c2)", "F2:side(c3)", "F2:side(c4)"]}, "stitch": true}}
{"type": "patch", "boundary": {"body": "F2.b0", "edges": ["E{F2:side(c4)|F2:side(c1)}", "E{F2:side(c1)|F2:side(c2)}"],
 "openings": [{"opening": {"faces": ["F2:side(c1)", "F2:side(c2)", "F2:side(c3)", "F2:side(c4)"]}, "at": [[10, 0, 5]]},
              {"opening": {"faces": ["F2:side(c1)", "F2:side(c2)", "F2:side(c3)", "F2:side(c4)"], "index": 1}, "at": [[10, 0, 0]]}]}}
{"type": "patch", "boundary": {"body": "F2.b0",
 "openings": [{"opening": {"faces": ["F2:side(c1)", "F2:side(c2)", "F2:side(c3)", "F2:side(c4)"]}, "at": [[10, 0, 5], [20, 5, 5]]}],
 "sketch_curves": [{"sketch": "F3", "curves": ["c1"]}]}}
  • profiles: regions of one sketch, as an extrusion’s (a set); each is a new surface body of one planar face <feature>:patch(<region>), its normal the sketch’s.
  • boundary: a closed loop of a body’s edges, one new surface body of one face <feature>:patch. The loop is edges (named edges; every edge a name without #k resolves to) or opening: a loop of the body’s free edges (edges of one face only, the open boundary of a surface body, which have no names of their own), the index-th (default 0) in the kernel’s geometric order of those whose edges bound exactly the faces named in faces. The open_boundaries of a body are the kernel’s (Kernel::open_boundaries: each loop’s faces and points along it). Beside edges (or alone), openings (mitcad#1955) adds free edges as the surface features take them (Free edges: an opening and the edge nearest each point of at, or the edges of faces): named and single free edges in one loop, so that a patch can close part of an opening (the second example: a wall of an open tube, its top and bottom free edges and its two corners). The kernel gets them as PatchLoopSpec::openings beside PatchBoundary::Edges.
  • sketch_curves (mitcad#1972): sketch curves in the loop beside edges and openings, each entry {"sketch", "curves"} (curves of a planar or a 3D sketch, projected ones too, as a boundary surface takes them; not chain or reversed), so that a line across an opening closes part of it with free edges (the third example: two top free edges of an open tube 20 x 10 and a sketch line from corner to corner across its top, a triangle). Their order does not matter; each curve’s ends must meet the ends of the loop’s edges or of another curve within 0.01 mm (the kernel joins them there). The patch only passes through them (G0, as edge_continuity cannot name them); continuity is for the edges. The kernel gets them in model space as PatchLoopSpec::curves; the patch depends on their sketches.
  • How the patch meets the face beside each edge: continuity g0 (the default: through the edge), g1 (tangent to the face) or g2 (tangent and of the same curvature); edge_continuity sets single named edges of the loop otherwise. g1 and g2 need the one face beside the edge: an edge between two faces is refused with them (unsupported: …). points (mm, the component’s coordinates) are points the patch passes through.
  • A loop in a plane that the patch only passes through (g0 everywhere, no points) is filled by the plane; otherwise by a surface fitted to the edges (OCCT’s BRepFill_Filling).
  • Both may be given: the regions’ bodies first (<feature>.b0, …), then the loop’s. The body of the loop is not changed.
  • stitch (default false, mitcad#1927): the loop’s patch is sewn onto the body of the loop, as a stitch of the two within 0.01 mm, instead of a new body: the body keeps its uid and becomes a solid where the patch closes it (a solid’s face taken out by unstitch and its body removed, then patched with stitch, is a solid again), else a surface body. The patch’s face keeps its name <feature>:patch.
  • Refused: neither regions nor a loop; opening with edges or openings; points at without an opening; a continuity of an edge not in edges; an opening that is not there (body F5.b0 (from Stitch1) has no opening along the faces …, or fewer of them than index); edges that do not close up into one loop; sketch_curves without edges or openings (no edges or opening to fill selected) or with opening (a whole opening is a loop by itself; …), reversed curves, curves their sketch does not have; when it is computed, a closed curve (a loop by itself), a curve that meets the loop at one point only, and edges and curves that do not close up into one loop (the edges and sketch curves of the patch do not close up into one loop).

stitch 

{"type": "stitch", "bodies": ["F2.b0", "F4.b0", "F6.b0"], "tolerance": 0.01}

The bodies’ faces sewn together where their edges meet within tolerance (mm; 0 for the kernel’s own precision, 1e-6 mm). The first body keeps its uid and becomes the sewn body: a solid where the faces close up (a closed shell), else a surface body; the others are consumed. The faces keep their names. Faces that meet nothing stay as they are, in the same body. Refused: no bodies, a body twice, a negative tolerance.

thicken 

{"type": "thicken", "bodies": ["F3.b0"], "thickness": 2, "symmetric": false,
 "operation": "new_body", "participants": []}

Each surface body (a solid is refused: body F2.b0 (from Extrude1) is a solid; Thicken makes surface bodies solid) becomes solids by a wall thickness thick along its faces’ normals (their orientations applied), against them when negative, or half of it to each side with symmetric. The surface bodies stay. operation and participants are an extrusion’s; a join, cut or intersection without participants works on every body but the thickened ones (and mesh bodies). New faces: <feature>:front(<face>) on the side the face’s normal points to, <feature>:back(<face>) on the other, <feature>:wall(<face>) along the face’s free edges (#k several). Refused: a thickness of 0, a body twice, a thickened body among the participants; the kernel fails where the wall does not close up into a solid (a face curved more tightly than the thickness, faces meeting at an inside corner the wall crosses). Symmetric offsets the faces by half the thickness first and thickens that; a face of the half-way offset whose surface is only C0 as a whole (the offset of a surface continuous in its first derivative only where faces meet, as a loft through two smooth sections makes it, mitcad#2143) is thickened on the part of its surface over the face itself, which the kernel’s offset takes.

Tests: core/model/src/surface_tests.rs (mock kernel: bodies, names, refusals; a loop of named and single free edges of an open tube, mitcad#1955), geometry/tests/test_surface_modelling.cpp (test_a_patch_closes_a_loop_of_free_and_named_edges), geometry/tests/test_surfaces.cpp (geometry.surfaces: an open box of five patches stitched, its opening patched and closed into a solid, a fill through a point, the stitch tolerance, thickening to either side and both, the input check on), the .solidcraft test design patch-stitch-thicken (cli.import_solidcraft) and core/import-solidcraft/src/tests.rs. The .solidcraft import maps SolidCraft’s patches, stitches and thickens onto these (.solidcraft import, core/import-solidcraft/docs/solidcraft.md).

Surface modelling

Features that make and change surface (sheet) bodies (mitcad#455), beside Patch, Stitch and Thicken, with add_feature and edit_feature, ordinary parameters, preview, Undo and persistence. Their inputs are any surface bodies (and the faces of solids where a family says so); mesh bodies are refused (Mesh bodies in surface operations). The kernel’s methods are grouped under “Surface modelling” in Kernel (core/model-base/src/kernel.rs), the OCCT side is geometry/src/surface_*.cpp. The application has them in the SURFACE tab (app/COMMANDS.md, “Surface modeling”).

Surface extrude, revolve, sweep and loft

The solid features with "surface": true (features/surface_sweeps.rs): walls without caps, new surface bodies, never joined or cut (the operation is new_body or new_component, without participants).

{"type": "extrude", "surface": true, "operation": "new_body",
 "profiles": [{"sketch": "F1", "region": "r{…}"}],
 "curves": {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c5", "c6"]},
 "extent": {"type": "distance", "distance": 15}}
{"type": "revolve", "surface": true, "operation": "new_body",
 "curves": {"sketch": "F3", "curves": ["c1"]}, "axis": "z", "extent": {"type": "full"}}
{"type": "sweep", "surface": true, "operation": "new_body",
 "curves": {"sketch": "F5", "curves": ["c1"]}, "path": {"sketch": "F6", "curves": ["c1"]}}
{"type": "loft", "surface": true, "operation": "new_body", "ruled": true, "sections": [
   {"type": "curves", "sketch": "F8", "curves": ["c1"]},
