   {"type": "curves", "sketch": "F9", "curves": ["c1"]}]}
  • profiles: the walls the regions’ boundaries sweep: the solid feature’s faces without its caps (Kernel::open_faces drops the faces <feature>:start, end and mid), so every option of the solid feature applies (two sides, tapers, up to an object, partial paths, guide rails and surfaces) and the walls keep its names, <feature>:side(<segment>). A full revolution is a closed surface without caps.
  • curves: sketch curves (of the profiles’ sketch; chain adds the curves joined to them) in chains of curves that meet end to end, open or closed; each curve’s wall is <feature>:side(<curve>) (#k pieces, e.g. along the curves of a sweep’s path). An extrusion of curves takes distances (one side, two sides, symmetric, through all) and a start offset, not a taper, a start object or an end at an object; a revolution of curves angles, not an object; a sweep of curves its path, extent, orientation and flip, not a twist, taper, end scale, guide rail or guide surfaces (Kernel::extrude_sheet, revolve_sheet, sweep_sheet).
  • With both, the profiles’ walls are the first new body (<feature>.b0), the curves’ walls the second.
  • A loft’s curves sections (Kernel::loft_sheet): every section a chain of one sketch’s curves, all open or all closed, through which the surface runs in order, ruled or smooth, closed back to the first; no end conditions, centre line or rails. Its faces are <feature>:side(<curve>) after the first section’s curves. A surface loft of profiles and faces is the loft’s own surface, with its rails or centre line. A 3D sketch’s curves are curve sections anywhere in space (the sketch-curves form), its closed loops in its sketch plane profile sections, and its curves in any plane rails or a centre line in the typed path form (mitcad#1550, “Pipe and Sweep along 3D sketch curves”).
  • Refused: a join, cut or intersect; curves without surface (only a surface extrusion sweeps sketch curves); neither profiles nor curves; a thin surface extrusion; curves of another sketch than the profiles’; a curve section beside sections of another kind.

The .f3d import brings surface extrusions, revolutions and sweeps (isSolid false) in as these; the .solidcraft import SolidCraft’s SurfaceExtrude, SurfaceRevolve, SurfaceSweep and SurfaceLoft.

Free edges

A surface body’s open boundary is made of free edges (edges of one face only), which have no names of their own (E{a|b} needs two faces). The features that take free edges take them as openings (features/sheet_edges.rs):

"openings": [{"opening": {"faces": ["F3:side(c1)", "F3:side(c2)"], "index": 1},
              "faces": ["F3:side(c1)"], "at": [[10, 0, 5]]}]
  • opening: a loop of free edges as patch’s opening names it: the index-th, in the kernel’s geometric order (Kernel::open_boundaries), of those whose edges bound exactly faces. Left out: every opening of the body.
  • faces: only the free edges that bound these faces; left out: all of the opening’s.
  • at: of those, only the edge nearest each point (mm, the component’s coordinates; with an opening only); left out: all. A surface of one face has one loop of free edges, all bounding that face: the points pick some of them, as an import’s picks do.

offset_surface 

{"type": "offset_surface", "body": "F2.b0", "faces": ["F2:end(r{…})"], "distance": 2, "chain": false}

A new surface body of the faces (every face of the body when faces is left out; with chain also the faces joined to them through smooth edges) moved distance along their normals (the faces’ orientations applied; against them when negative; 0 copies them). Faces <feature>:offset(<face>). The body is not changed. OCCT offsets the faces as one sheet (BRepOffset_MakeOffset, intersecting where neighbours meet); a face curved more tightly than the distance fails.

ruled_surface 

{"type": "ruled_surface", "body": "F2.b0", "edges": ["E{…|…}"], "openings": [],
 "face": "F2:end(r{…})", "distance": 3, "mode": "tangent", "angle": 0.5,
 "direction": [0, 0, 1], "flip": false, "corners": "mitre"}

A new surface body: strips distance wide (more than 0) off chains of the body’s edges (edges and the free edges of openings together, each run of them joined end to end a chain, open or closed; none branches). Each edge leaves the face beside it (face where an edge lies between two faces), and the strip goes

  • normal (the default): along that face’s normal;
  • tangent: continuing the face, square to the edge, away from it;
  • angle: at angle (radians) from the face’s normal (or from direction when given), turned towards the tangent mode’s direction;
  • direction: along the fixed direction;

and the other way with flip. At a sharp corner of the chain the neighbouring strips are mitred (their ends lean to meet along the corner’s bisector) or joined by a round sector turned about the corner. Faces <feature>:ruled(<edge>), for a free edge <feature>:ruled(<face>) after the face it leaves (#k pieces), and <feature>:corner(<vertex>); the strips are sewn into one body. Refused: no edges, a distance of 0 or less, the direction mode without direction, the angle mode without angle, a direction of no length; the kernel fails edges that branch (three at a vertex) and an edge between two faces without face.

extend_surface 

{"type": "extend_surface", "body": "F3.b0", "openings": [{"faces": ["F3:side(c1)"]}],
 "distance": 2, "mode": "natural"}

The surface body’s faces extended distance (more than 0, along the surface) past free edges (edges by name, or openings): natural continues the surface (an analytic surface its parameter range, a B-spline its polynomials), tangent leaves the edge tangent to it (G1), curvature also with its curvature (G2; both by OCCT’s GeomLib::ExtendSurfByLength). The body keeps its id and its faces their names: each extended face stays one face; the faces are sewn again where they meet. A face is extended where it is bounded by its surface’s parameter range only (four sides, no holes), and each edge must run along a side of that range (unsupported: … otherwise); a solid is refused. Extending a whole periodic surface onto itself fails. A planar face trimmed inside its plane (any outline, e.g. a wall cut at a slant, mitcad#1955) is extended past straight edges of any direction instead: the plane continued away from the face up to the line distance from each edge and parallel to it, joined to the face as one face (every mode alike); a curved edge of such a face is unsupported. The extension’s sides continue the face’s neighbouring edges (their tangents at the shared vertices, as straight lines), so a face cut at a slant keeps its outline; where the neighbour is picked too, the two end lines meet in a mitre and the corner is filled (mitcad#2056, GitHub mitcad/Mitcad#462). A side is square to its edge where the neighbour cannot be continued: it turns back into the face (a reflex corner) or meets the end line at less than 15 degrees, or the strip’s two sides would cross before the end line. Tests: geometry/tests/test_surface_modelling.cpp (test_a_trimmed_plane_is_extended_past_one_edge: a trapezoid extended past its bottom and its slanted edge, picked by a point each, the long edges continued; test_a_trimmed_plane_is_extended_round_a_corner: two adjacent edges of a rectangle, one larger rectangle; test_a_trimmed_plane_falls_back_to_square_sides: a reflex corner and a neighbour under the angle limit) and the ctest cli.extend_slanted_plane_reported (the reported design under MITCAD_MITCAD_REPORTED: its slanted edge extended by 26, four edges, the long edges one straight edge each).

trim_surface 

{"type": "trim_surface", "body": "F3.b0", "tool": "F4", "offset": 2, "extend": true,
 "keep": [[50, -1, 4]]}
{"type": "trim_surface", "body": "F3.b0", "tool": {"sketch": "F5", "curves": ["c1", "c4"]},
 "direction": [0, 0, 1], "keep": [[10, 5, 0]]}

A surface body cut by tool and only the pieces kept that the keep points (mm, the component’s coordinates; at least one) pick, the piece nearest each. The tool is split_face’s (Face features): a plane (moved offset along its normal), a face of any body (continued along its surface with extend, the default), a body, or sketch curves, open or closed, swept both ways along direction (the sketch’s normal when left out). Pieces are the faces cut apart and joined again where their edges meet away from the tool. The body keeps its id and its faces their names (#k for the pieces of one face). Refused: a solid (Split Body divides solids), the body as its own tool, no keep point; the kernel fails a tool that does not cut the surface apart.

untrim_surface 

{"type": "untrim_surface", "body": "F8.b0", "face": "F8:end(r{…})", "holes": true,
 "outer": false, "in_place": false}

A face restored towards its surface: holes (the default) takes its holes away, outer puts its outer boundary back at the surface’s own bounds (a surface without bounds, such as a plane or a cylinder, at the face’s span); at least one of them. The face may be of a solid or a surface body; the result is a new surface body of one face, <feature>:untrim(<face>). With in_place the face of a surface body is untrimmed where it is: the body and the face keep their names (a solid is refused).

unstitch 

{"type": "unstitch", "body": "F1.b0", "faces": ["F1:end(r{…})"]}

A body taken apart into surface bodies: each face in faces its own new body (<feature>.b0, .b1, … in the order named) and the faces left one surface body that keeps the body’s id. Without faces every face comes apart: the first stays the body, each other one a new body. A solid comes apart into surfaces; the faces keep their names.

reverse_normal 

{"type": "reverse_normal", "body": "F3.b0", "faces": []}

The surface body’s faces in faces (every face when left out) turned over: their normals point the other way, which decides the side thicken, offset_surface and the ruled surface’s normal mode go to. The body and the faces keep their names. A solid is refused (its normals point out of its material).

Chains of edges

Blend Surface, Boundary Surface and Match Surface take chains of a body’s edges: body, named edges and free edges of openings (Free edges) that join end to end into one chain (open or closed), and face (target_face for a match), the face beside the chain where an edge lies between two faces (else each edge’s one face; needed for G1 and G2 only). The body may be a surface body or a solid; it is not changed unless the feature says so.

blend_surface 

{"type": "blend_surface",
 "from": {"body": "F2.b0", "openings": [{"opening": {"faces": ["F2:side(c1)"]}, "at": [[10, 0, 5]]}],
          "continuity": "g1", "bulge": 0},
 "to": {"body": "F4.b0", "edges": ["E{F4:bottom|F4:side0}"], "face": "F4:side0", "continuity": "g2"},
 "stitch": false}

A new surface body of one face <feature>:blend bridging the chains from and to (both open or both closed; a closed pair starts the second where it is nearest the first’s start). Each end leaves its chain through the edges (g0: straight towards the other end), tangent to the face beside it (g1, the default) or also curved as it (g2), with a speed of the chord between the chains times 1 + bulge (bulge 0 the plain bridge, more fuller, down to -0.9 flatter). The chains are sampled by length (about a station a millimetre, 16 to 200) and the surface, cubic across (quintic with a g2 end), is fitted through the stations: its edges lie within a few micrometres of the chains. With stitch the blend is sewn onto both bodies within 0.01 mm, into from’s body, which keeps its id; to’s body (when another) is consumed and no new body is made.

boundary_surface 

{"type": "boundary_surface", "boundary": [
   {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1", "c2"], "continuity": "g1"},
   {"body": "F3.b0", "openings": [{"opening": {"faces": ["F3:side(c1)"]}}], "continuity": "g1"}]}
{"type": "boundary_surface", "u": [{"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1"]}, {"point": [5, 5, 10]}]}
{"type": "boundary_surface", "u": [{"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1"]}, {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c3"]}],
 "v": [{"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c2"]}, {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c4"]}]}

A new surface body of one face <feature>:boundary. Each curve is a chain of sketch curves (sketch, curves, chain), a chain of edges (Chains of edges) or a point, one of them.

  • boundary: a closed loop of curves in order (one closed chain, or chains end to end), filled (BRepOffsetAPI_MakeFilling). Each meets the face beside its edges, or along sketch curves the sketch’s plane, with its continuity (g0, the default, g1, g2). No points. See A loop through several sketches.
  • u (two or more) and v (none, or two or more): a network. Without v the surface is lofted through u in order, the first or the last of which may be a point (a cone-like patch); with v it runs through every curve each way (GeomFill_Gordon: a Coons patch of two each way), every u crossing every v. No continuity, no points.
  • Refused: both forms, a curve of none or several kinds, a point in a loop or among crossing curves, one crossing curve.

match_surface 

{"type": "match_surface", "body": "F5.b0", "face": "F5:side(c1)", "target": "F7.b0",
 "edges": ["E{F7:bottom|F7:side2}"], "target_face": "F7:side2", "continuity": "g2"}

A face of a surface body (face; left out: the body’s only face) rebuilt against a chain of target’s edges (another body): the side of the face nearest the chain moves onto it, meeting the face beside the chain through it (g0), tangent (g1) or also curved as it (g2, the default), while the opposite side stays where it was. The face is resampled with the changes fading across it (quintic blends, no change at the opposite side) and fitted again, its slopes across held at both sides. The face must be bounded by its surface’s parameter range alone (four sides, no holes; unsupported: … otherwise); a closed chain is not supported. The body keeps its id and the face its name; its faces are sewn again within 0.001 mm (neighbours along the moved sides come apart). A solid is refused.

fair_surface 

{"type": "fair_surface", "body": "F6.b0", "faces": ["F6:boundary"], "strength": 1, "iterations": 1,
 "keep_edges": true, "tolerance": 0.1}

The B-spline faces among faces (every face when left out) smoothed: each step moves the inner control points strength (more than 0, at most 1) of a damped bi-Laplacian step towards a net of less bending, for iterations steps (1 to 1000), none farther than tolerance (a parameter, mm, more than 0) from where it was. The boundary row of control points stays, so the faces keep meeting their neighbours; with keep_edges (the default) the row next to it stays too, so they keep their tangents there. Faces of other surface types are fair already and stay as they are; a faired face must be bounded by its surface’s parameter range alone. The body keeps its id and the faces their names. A solid is refused.

The .solidcraft import maps SolidCraft’s surface blend, boundary patch, network, match and fair to these (core/import-solidcraft/docs/solidcraft.md).

Tests (surface modelling): core/model-tests/features-solid/src/surface_modelling_tests.rs (mock kernel), geometry/tests/test_surface_modelling.cpp (geometry.surface_modelling, the input check on), the .solidcraft test designs surface-* (cli.import_solidcraft, areas and boxes through the OCCT kernel), core/import-solidcraft/src/tests.rs, tools/ui-surface-test.sh and tools/ui-surface-fill-test.sh (the SURFACE group on a hidden display).

Plastic part features

Molded plastic parts’ features (mitcad#459, core/model/src/features/plastic.rs): a Boss, a Lip, a Groove, a Snap Fit and a Rest, each on a face of one body which it joins (a groove cuts it), and the plastic rules they take their defaults from. The application’s Plastic Feature panel makes them all (app/COMMANDS.md).

A boss, a snap fit and a rest stand on point of face of body: put on the face’s plane for a planar face, else the face’s point nearest to it. They grow along direction ([x, y, z]; default: out of the face). The tools start a little inside the material (5 % of their height, 0.001 to 0.5 mm) so that they overlap the body; sizes are measured at the face, and a draft (draft_angle, radians or an angle expression) narrows the walls from there. Values left out take the defaults below.

plastic_rule 

{"type": "plastic_rule", "rule_name": "ABS (1.5mm)", "material": "ABS Plastic",
 "thickness": 1.5, "draft_angle": "2 deg", "clearance": 0.1, "min_thickness": 1.2,
 "max_thickness": 3.5}

A molded part’s design values; it changes no body. thickness is the nominal wall; nominal_radius (default half the thickness), clearance (0.1 mm), knife_edge (1 mm), reveal_height (0.5 mm), thickness_variation (0.15 times the thickness), draft_angle (2 degrees), min_draft_angle (0.5 degrees), min_thickness and max_thickness (no limit without). A boss, rest or groove names one by its uid in rule: a left-out draft_angle of a boss or rest and a left-out gap of a groove are the rule’s draft and clearance, and the feature warns when its draft is below the rule’s min_draft_angle, or a wall (a boss’s around its hole, a hollow rest’s) is outside the rule’s thicknesses. A suppressed rule is not used (a warning says so); a failed one fails the features that name it. Refused: a thickness not above 0, negative values, drafts of 85 degrees or more, a smallest thickness above the largest.

boss 

{"type": "boss", "body": "F1.b0", "face": "F1:top", "point": [30, 30, 3],
 "diameter": 10, "height": 12, "hole_diameter": 4, "hole_depth": 10,
 "draft_angle": "1 deg", "fillet": 1, "ribs": 4, "rib_thickness": 1.5,
 "rib_length": 6, "rib_offset": 2, "rule": "F2"}

A round post diameter across at the face, height high, narrowing by its draft (default the rule’s, else none). ribs (0 to 64, rounded; a count in a length slot, as pattern quantities) stand round it from half its radius out to rib_length past its wall (default its radius), rib_thickness thick (default 0.3 times its radius), their tops rib_offset below its top; the first along the direction × X (× Y for a direction near X: +Y on a face facing up). fillet rounds the root where the post meets the face (the post’s wall only). The hole of hole_diameter runs hole_depth down from the top (default: to the face), straight. Faces: the post side(c1) and its top end(r{c1}), rib k’s sides side(c<10+4k>…), the hole’s wall side(c2) and its bottom start(r{c2}), the root’s rounds fillet(<edge>). Refused: a draft that closes the post before its top, a hole not inside the top. A boss cannot be patterned or mirrored (its hole cuts after its post joins).

lip, groove 

{"type": "lip", "body": "F17.b0", "face": "F18:offset_cap(F17:top)", "width": 1, "height": 2}
{"type": "groove", "body": "F20.b0", "face": "F21:offset_cap(F20:top)", "width": 1,
 "depth": 2, "gap": 0.1, "outside": true, "rule": "F2"}

A band along a planar rim face: along its largest opening (an inner loop with no material over the face just inside it: the open end of a shelled body), or along its outer edge with outside. A lip raises the band width into the face and height up. A groove cuts it width + gap into the face and depth + gap down, gap defaulting to the rule’s clearance (else 0), the cutter reaching as far past the edge so that none of its walls lies on the body’s. Corners stay sharp; lines and arcs stay lines and arcs. Faces (Kernel::rim_band): band_side(<edge>) along the offset into the face and band_edge(<edge>) along the face’s edge they follow, band_top and band_bottom. Refused: a face that is not planar, one with no inner loop, one whose inner loops are the feet of features standing on it (“not an opening”), one with two openings alike in size (the second more than half the first’s area), a band that does not fit.

snap_fit 

{"type": "snap_fit", "body": "F15.b0", "face": "F15:top", "point": [20, 20, 4],
 "hook": [1, 0, 0], "length": 15, "thickness": 1.5, "width": 6,
 "catch_depth": 1, "catch_length": 3}

A cantilever arm thickness across (away from hook), width wide (centred on the point) and length up from the face, its face on the hook’s side on the point; the catch at its tip sticks out catch_depth towards hook (across the direction) over catch_length (shorter than the arm), a triangle from its foot out to the tip. Faces side(c1) … side(c6) round its side profile (c1 the arm’s foot, c2 its face on the hook’s side, c3 and c4 the catch, c5 the tip, c6 its back), its ends start(…) and end(…). It can be patterned and mirrored.

rest 

{"type": "rest", "body": "F10.b0", "face": "F10:top", "point": [430, 30, 3],
 "along": [1, 0, 0], "width": 10, "length": 20, "height": 4,
 "draft_angle": "2 deg", "thickness": 1, "rule": "F2"}

A pad centred on the point: round (width the diameter) or, with length, a rectangle length along along (default the direction × X, as a boss’s first rib) and width across; height high, narrowing by its draft (default the rule’s, else none), solid or with thickness a wall (thinner than half its width). Faces: its walls side(c1) … side(c4) (round: side(c1)), its hollow’s side(c5) … (side(c2)), its top end(…). Refused: a draft that closes it (or its wall) before its top. It can be patterned and mirrored.

Tests: core/model-tests/parts/src/plastic_tests.rs (mock kernel), cli.plastic (tools/cli/tests/plastic.json: analytic volumes, round rims, the rules’ defaults and warnings, refusals), the .solidcraft test design plastic (cli.import_solidcraft) and tools/ui-plastic-test.sh.

Body transfers

A body_transfer feature (mitcad#465, features/body_transfer.rs) moves bodies of another component into its own component, an existing one, at its point of the timeline. Moving features into components moves the features that made the bodies, as if they had been made in the destination; Create Components from Bodies makes a new component of each body. A body transfer moves only the bodies, from where it is on the timeline:

{"type": "body_transfer", "bodies": ["F2.b0"],
 "link": {"source": "", "target": "O1"}}
{"type": "body_transfer", "bodies": ["F5.b0"],
 "link": {"source": "O2", "target": ""},
 "transform": [[0, -1, 0, 0], [1, 0, 0, 30], [0, 0, 1, 0]]}
  • The feature belongs to the destination. bodies are all of one other component at that point (the source), each named by its id.
  • The bodies keep their ids, display names, attributes (appearance, material, visibility) and the topological names of their faces; their geometry is converted once from the source’s coordinates into the destination’s, so that they stay where they are in the design. From then on they are the destination’s: its later features work on them (in its coordinates), the source’s no longer see them (body F2.b0 (from Extrude1) belongs to Bracket; a feature works on the bodies of its own component), and a later Move of the destination’s occurrence takes them along. A sheet-metal body keeps its sheet state, moved with it.
  • link says where both components are seen, as the links of Geometry of other components: the occurrence path to the source (source) and to the destination (target, the first path to it when it does not lead there); empty paths are the root. The conversion is placement(target)⁻¹ · placement(source) at the feature’s point, so the bodies stay in place when placements before it change. transform (optional; rows of a rotation and a translation) is a fixed conversion used instead, as an import keeps the one its file records.
  • Fails (as features do, with the reason) when a body is not the source’s at that point, the source is the feature’s own component, or the conversion is not rigid. Moves of features, reparented components and copies follow the link like the other links; Paste New and Make Unique copy or refuse a component that takes bodies in as they do one made from bodies (its bodies, as a base feature, are copied).
CommandFieldsResult
transfer_bodiesbodies, source_occurrence (optional: where they are seen, the first path to their component by default), destination: {"component": "C2" or a name, "occurrence": "O2/O4"} (the occurrence path optional, as source_occurrence), name (optional)uid, name, component, component_name, bodies

transfer_bodies adds the feature at the marker in the destination, one undo step Move Body1 into Bracket (Move 2 bodies into Bracket). Refused, changing nothing, when the bodies are not of one component at the marker, the destination is their component, a linked component or a library part, the policy refuses it, or the transfer (or a feature that worked before) would fail. Features after the marker are not computed: one of the source that works on a moved body later fails when the marker passes it, with the reason above.

QueryFieldsResult
transfer_bodiesbodies, source_occurrencecomponent, name (the bodies’ component), source_occurrence, bodies (uid, name), destinations: every placed component by occurrence path, the root first, as move_to_component’s rows (component, name, occurrence, path, parent_occurrence, eligible, reason)

The .solidcraft import maps SolidCraft’s body transfers onto it (the file’s feature is in its destination already): the link from the components’ first placements, and the conversion the file records as transform only where the placements give another (.solidcraft import). The .f3d import translates a cut and paste of bodies into another component as this feature where Move to Component cannot take the features that made them (core/import/docs/f3d-undecoded.md, Copies and cut and paste of bodies). Tests: core/model-tests/assembly/src/body_transfer_tests.rs, cli.import_solidcraft (core/solidcraft/tests/designs/body-transfer.solidcraft.json), mitcad-import’s a_cut_and_paste_whose_features_cannot_go_transfers_the_body.

Drawings

export_drawing (mitcad#471, api/drawing.rs, crate::drawing) writes the bodies at the marker as a drawing on a sheet: orthographic views with hidden lines removed, the overall sizes of the views, the diameters of round holes, a hole table with their threads and a title block, as a PDF, SVG, DXF or DWG file. The views come from the kernel (Kernel::project_view: OCCT’s hidden line removal, geometry/include/mitcad/geometry/drawing.hpp), the holes from Kernel::round_holes, their threads from the threads query. A tangent edge is an edge between faces that meet smoothly (normals within 0.001 rad all along it, a fillet’s edges) however the body was made: the projection finds them on a copy of each body before it projects (mitcad#1438; OCCT’s hidden line removal goes by the continuity stored on an edge, which edges made by later fillets, booleans and imports lack, so such edges were drawn as visible edges with tangent_edges false). Seams and edges between faces of one surface are not drawn at all.

{"cmd":"export_drawing","path":"plate.pdf","bodies":["F2.b0"],
 "sheet":"A3","orientation":"landscape","scale":"fit","projection":"third_angle",
 "views":["front","top","right","iso"],"hidden_lines":true,
 "section":{"analysis":"Section1"},"title":"Plate","date":"2026-10-20"}
FieldDefaultWhat
paththe file; its extension (.pdf, .svg, .dxf, .dwg) gives the format
formatby the extensionpdf, svg, dxf or dwg
bodiesthe shown bodiesuids or names; each where the design shows it (every placement of a component’s body)
sheetA4A4 … A0 (ISO 216), ANSI_A … ANSI_E
orientationlandscapeor portrait
scalefitfit: the largest ISO 5455 scale (50:1 … 1:1000) at which the views fit; or "1:2", "2:1", a number (paper per model length)
projectionthird_angleor first_angle (ISO 5456-2)
views["front","top","right"]any of front (from -Y), top (from +Z), right (from +X), iso (from the front, right and above); Z is up
sectionnonea section view: {"analysis": "<Section Analysis>"} (where it cuts) or {"origin": [x,y,z], "normal": [x,y,z]}; what lies on the normal’s side goes, the view looks against the normal
hidden_linesfalsehidden edges dashed (not in the isometric and section views)
tangent_edgesfalseedges between faces that meet smoothly, thin
dimensionstruethe width and height of each orthographic view, and one callout per hole size (4x Ø6.6 THRU, CBORE Ø11 DEPTH 6.8, a tapped hole by its thread)
sketch_dimensionsfalsethe distances, lengths, radii and diameters of the sketches whose plane faces a view square on, in that view
hole_tabletruethe holes each view shows end on, tagged per view (A1, A2, … B1), with X and Y from the view’s lower left corner, size, depth and thread
unitsthe design’s length unitthe unit of the values (mm, in, …), and of a DXF file’s coordinates: the sheet in that unit of paper (mitcad#1408, DXF units); with drawing only the DXF file’s unit (each sheet’s own, else the design’s, when left out)
titleUntitledthe design’s name in the title block
datetoday (UTC)the date in the title block
per_bodyfalsea sheet per body: pages of one PDF, or SVG, DXF and DWG files <name>-2.svg, …
exacttrueexact edges; false: from a triangulation (quicker on large bodies; also the fallback when the exact projection fails, and for mesh bodies). Views of bodies with free-form faces (not planes, cylinders, cones, spheres or tori), or with many edges on B-splines against many faces (mitcad#1033), come from a triangulation either way, their edges as lines and arcs where they follow them, polylines elsewhere (mitcad#962: exact edges took half a minute a view on modelled threads): within 0.02 mm of the edges on the sheet at the view’s scale (0.1 mm in the model at 1:5), and never farther than 1.5 times a 2000th of the bodies’ size (mitcad#1671). Only those bodies, and the bodies whose outline in the view overlaps theirs, take the triangulation: the others keep the exact edges when they are not slow on their own
drawingnonea drawing kept in the design (D1 or its name, Drawings in the design), written as it is: its sheets, views and title blocks; the fields above are then its own and refused, except title (where its sheets have none) and units (a DXF file’s unit)
sheetallwith drawing: one sheet’s index (0 the first)

Without drawing the export lays out a temporary drawing from the fields above (api/drawing.rs, auto_drawing: each view a base view in the grid below, the section a section view without a parent) and draws it as a kept one is drawn, so the two give the same file; add_drawing with layout keeps such a drawing in the design (File › Export Drawing).

The sheet (ISO 5457): a frame 20 mm from the left edge and 10 mm from the others, the title block (ISO 7200) at the bottom right with the title, the bodies, the scale, the units, the date, the sheet, the projection method and its symbol; the hole table at the top right. Views go into a grid by the projection method (third angle: the top view above the front view, the right view on its right, the isometric view top right, the section right of the right view; first angle the other way), aligned with each other, each with room for its dimensions; the views are centred in what the title block and the table leave. Lines after ISO 128’s 0.35 series (mitcad#1112; one table, Pen::width in core/model-drawing/src/sheet.rs, for the PDF and SVG writers and the application’s sheet: visible 0.35 mm; dimensions, leaders, tangent edges and a thread’s roots 0.18 mm; hidden edges 0.18 mm dashed, as ISO 128 draws hidden outlines narrow; hatching 0.13 mm; the frame 0.5 mm; the cutting plane 0.18 mm long dash dotted with its arrows and letter); dimensions after ISO 129 (30° closed filled arrowheads, text 3.5 mm above the dimension line, reading from below or from the right); text in Helvetica (sans serif, as ISO 3098). A hole is coaxial cylindrical faces with the material all round outside them: the narrowest is its drilled wall, a wider cylinder or a cone that meets it on the side it opens to its counterbore or countersink; an end is closed when material lies on the axis within twice its diameter beyond it. A view shows a hole end on when it looks along the axis from the side it opens to (a hole open at both ends from either side).

Details smaller than the pen (mitcad#1112, core/model-drawing/src/convention.rs, simplified): lines closer than twice the visible line’s width (0.7 mm on the sheet, ISO 128-20’s least spacing) merge into a blot, so a view is drawn simplified at its scale. A fillet or chamfer whose size on the sheet is below 0.7 mm (an arc of a smaller radius, the polyline or short lines a triangulation made of it, a chamfer’s shorter line, between two other edges) is drawn as a sharp corner: it is left out with the tangent edges that end at it, and the edges on either side are extended to where they meet. A tangent edge that lies within 0.7 mm of other edges all along is left out, and so is any edge shorter than its pen is wide. This works on the projected lines, so the exact and the triangulated views alike; what a click picks on a view is still the view’s own edges.

Threads by ISO 6410 (convention::with_threads): every thread the threads query lists on a body a view shows, modelled or cosmetic (a hole or a shaft with a thread’s designation and no flanks), is drawn by convention instead of its geometry. In a view across its axis the crests (an external thread’s major diameter, an internal one’s minor) are drawn with the visible pen, the roots with the narrow one, and the thread’s end with a visible line across the major diameter where no face ends it; looking along its axis the crest circle is drawn whole and the root circle as a narrow three-quarter arc (open at the upper right). The thread’s own lines (crests, helices, flanks, the curves where its end chamfers cut them) are left out; the faces’ edges across the thread stay (its end faces, a groove’s), and in a pictorial view the circles about its axis. Only lines on the thread’s own surface are left out, not everything of the threaded body that its outline covers (mitcad#1145): across the axis, a straight line goes when both its ends lie on a crest’s or a root’s radius on one side of the axis, and a curve when it runs like a helix (it turns back across the axis only on the thread’s outline, between the root’s and the crest’s radius, and in a view square to the axis runs one way along it); curves that lie on one circle and together go a quarter of the way round or more (a cross hole’s edge, in pieces where the thread’s faces cut it) stay. In a triangulated view, which gives a helix as straight pieces and arcs, a straight piece goes when it starts on a crest’s or a root’s radius or continues the thread’s lines end to end. Looking along the axis, circles (and the spirals where an end chamfer cuts the flanks) from the root’s radius to the crest’s go, and an external thread’s end chamfer circle a thread’s depth inside the minor diameter; a narrower bore below a tapped hole and a flat’s chord stay. So a cross hole, a socket, a flat or a keyway on the threaded body is drawn as the kernel drew it. Only the threaded body’s own lines are left out and replaced: the kernel’s projection records each line’s body (ViewEdge::source, the index of the shape among those projected; OCCT’s hidden-line removal is asked for each shape’s lines on their own), so every other body’s lines (a nut’s bore and faces, a pin in front of the thread) stay as the kernel drew them. Hidden-line removal: each part of the convention’s lines takes, along the axis, the visibility the kernel’s hidden-line removal gave the lines it replaces, so where a nut, a wall or another body hides the thread its lines are hidden (dashed when the view shows hidden edges, else left out); end on, the crest and root circles each take that of the lines near them. A view at an angle to the axis (isometric; ISO 6410 has no pictorial representation, so the simplified one ISO 128 allows there) draws the thread on its cylinder the same way: the crests’ outlines wide, the roots’ narrow, and where no face ends it the thread’s end as the half of its crest circle the eye sees. A taper pipe thread (the query’s taper) is drawn with its crest and root lines following the taper from the diameters where it starts: an external one widens away from its narrow end, an internal one narrows away from its mouth (which end, from the lines it replaces, else from the face that ends it); end on, its circles are those where it starts.

Files: SVG in millimetres (width="420mm"), a <g class="…"> per group: view (id="view-front", view-top, view-right, view-iso, view-section), dimension, sketch-dimension, hole-tag, hole-table, hole-row (id the tag), hole-datum, section-line, view-label, frame, title-block. PDF 1.4, a page per sheet, the standard Helvetica font in WinAnsi encoding (Ø, °), uncompressed. DXF (R2000) in paper of the file’s length unit (units, else the sheet’s, else the design’s: an inch design’s sheet in inches of paper, its texts scaled with it, mitcad#1408), a layer per kind of line: VISIBLE, HIDDEN, THIN, HATCH, SECTION_LINE, FRAME, EXTRA_THICK (lines and arcs drawn with the extra_thick pen, mitcad#1402), lines and arcs drawn by hand with a width and a pattern no pen of before had (mitcad#1447) on HIDDEN_THICK (thick and dashed), HIDDEN_EXTRA_THICK (extra_thick and dashed), SECTION_LINE_THICK (thick and chain) and SECTION_LINE_EXTRA_THICK (extra_thick and chain; a thin dashed one stays on HIDDEN, a thin chain one on SECTION_LINE, a continuous one on THIN, VISIBLE or EXTRA_THICK), and TEXT (the writer has no dashed line types: hidden edges are told apart by their layer; arrowheads are outlines). DWG (R2000, AC1015, mitcad#728; core/model-drawing/src/dwg.rs) holds what the DXF file holds in paper millimetres, on the same layers, written by MitCad’s own writer (core/dwg/src/write.rs, README): lines, arcs, circles and single-line texts (a text of several lines as a text per line) in model space, the sheet as the layout’s paper and limits; texts in code page 1252, other characters as \U+XXXX.

The answer: path, format, files, sheets, pages (of a PDF; 1 otherwise), sheet, orientation, scale ("1:1", of the first sheet) and scales, views (per sheet), bodies and body_names (each body drawn once), placements (mitcad#2147: the placements drawn over the sheets written, each body once per occurrence path that places it: a component placed 100 times adds its bodies once to bodies and 100 times to placements; a laid-out drawing draws each body at every placement the 3D view shows, a hidden occurrence’s left out), dimensions, holes, hole_table_rows, units (of the values), file_units (DXF: the first file’s length unit), polygonal (a view came from a triangulation) and warnings (a view that shows nothing, views that do not fit at the given scale, rows the table had no room for, holes that could not be found). Refused: an unknown format, unit, view or sheet, no views, a listed body that is not at the marker, an unknown Section Analysis, no bodies to draw. File IO (classes.rs); MCP’s model_export writes one with format: "pdf" or "svg" (or "dxf" with drawing), the options in drawing (docs/mcp.md); mitcad-cli export-drawing runs it. Tests: geometry.drawing (the views, section and holes of a counterbored block), core/model-tests/drawing/src/drawing_tests.rs and core/model-tests/drawing/src/dwg_tests.rs, core/model-drawing/src/convention_tests.rs (the line set, details smaller than the pen, threads), core.dwg (the DWG writer), cli.export_drawing, app.ui-windows-drawing.

A laid-out view of an assembly’s top view on a reported design (mitcad#2174, GitHub #527): cli.drawing_placements_reported exports the top view of a design whose root holds only sketches and suppressed placeholders (items with no MitCad counterpart, which have no bodies and draw nothing) and whose one component, a cylinder, is placed six times; it checks the four corners of each placement’s outline at its place and the line 1 bodies in 6 placements, then hides one occurrence and checks it left out (1 bodies in 5 placements). The design is read from MITCAD_MITCAD_REPORTED (github-527/, by its content id); the test is skipped without it.

Gears

A gear feature (mitcad#472; core/model/src/features/gear.rs the definition and its placement, gear_profile.rs the teeth, the kernel’s gear_sweep and gear_cone (geometry/include/mitcad/geometry/gear.hpp) the solids, api/gears.rs the query and the command) makes a gear with involute teeth from parameters. The application’s Gear panel makes them (app/COMMANDS.md). Tests: features::gear_profile and features::gear_tests, features::seat_tests (seated on shafts), tools/cli/tests/gears.json, tools/cli/tests/gears_link.json, tools/ui-gear-test.sh, tools/ui-windows-gear-test.ps1.

{"type": "gear", "kind": "helical", "plane": "xy", "center": [0, 0], "module": 2, "teeth": 20,
 "face_width": 10, "helix_angle": "20 deg", "backlash": 0.1,
 "bore": {"type": "plain", "diameter": 8}, "keyway": true, "hub": {"diameter": 20, "length": 8},
 "operation": "new_component"}
FieldValue
kindspur, helical, herringbone, ring (internal), rack, bevel (straight)
plane, centerwhere the gear’s axis meets its plane (the plane’s normal), in the plane’s coordinates; a rack’s start. Not with mesh_with
angleturns the gear about its axis (tooth 1 centred on the plane’s x axis without it; a rack about its start). Not with mesh_with
module, teeththe normal module (mm) and the number of teeth (a whole number, at least 5; a rack’s at least 1)
pressure_anglethe normal pressure angle, 20 degrees without it (10 to 35)
face_widthalong the axis (a bevel gear’s along its pitch cone, less than half its cone distance)
helix_angle, left_handedhelical and herringbone gears (needed), helical rings and racks (optional): up to 45 degrees, right-handed unless left_handed
gapa herringbone gear’s gap between its halves, a groove a quarter module below the roots
rima ring gear’s rim outside its roots (needed)
height, lengtha rack’s height from its back to its tips (needed), its length (at least, and without it, teeth times the pitch)
shaft_angle, mate_teeth, paira bevel gear’s shaft angle (90 degrees), its mate’s teeth (its own) and whether it makes the mate too
backlashmm at the pitch circle: a tooth is thinner (a ring’s space wider) by half of it, so two gears with the same value mesh with it (at most a quarter of the pitch)
profile_shiftx in modules, away from the axis (-1 to 0.8; a ring’s teeth outwards)
bore{"type": "plain", "diameter": d} or {"type": "thread", "thread": {"designation": "M8x1.25"}} (the size’s minor diameter, its tap drill; standard as a thread’s): spur, helical, herringbone and bevel gears, through the gear and its hub
keywaya DIN 6885-1 (form A) keyway in a plain bore of 6 to 230 mm: the hub’s width and depth for the bore’s diameter, at the gear’s angle
hubdiameter (optional, mitcad#656: without it the bore plus a 2 mm wall all round, or half the root diameter without a bore, at least 4 mm), length: on the end face (a bevel gear’s back)
mesh_with{"gear": "F3", "angle": <angle>, "position": <length>}: in the plane of an earlier gear feature of the same component, at their mesh’s centre distance in the direction angle from its centre (from its plane’s x axis), or position along a rack from the middle of its teeth, turned so that the teeth engage
seaton a shaft instead of plane and center (Seats on shafts, mitcad#578): spur, helical, herringbone and single bevel gears, not with mesh_with; a gear meshing with a seated one lies in its plane. Without bore the bore is plain, the shaft’s diameter plus bore_clearance, and follows the shaft; a thread bore stays the thread’s; a plain bore of its own is refused
bore_clearancemm added to the shaft’s diameter for a seated gear’s plain bore (0 without it; a printed fit 0.2, say); only with seat and without bore
operation, participantsas an extrusion’s
  • Teeth: the ISO 53 basic rack (profile A): addendum 1 m, dedendum 1.25 m, root fillet 0.38 m (smaller where it does not fit). An external tooth is what that rack leaves rolling on the pitch circle: the flank is the involute of the base circle (a cubic B-spline within 1e-7 mm), the root the envelope of the rack’s tip fillet, which also cuts the undercut of small tooth counts (below 17 at 20 degrees) into the flank. Helical teeth have the transverse rack’s section (heights in the normal module) turned along the axis by the helix (a screw motion of the section’s curves within about 1e-7 mm; the volume is the section’s area times the width). An internal gear’s space is an external tooth’s shape with a circular root fillet, its tips at the base circle at least. A rack has straight flanks. A straight bevel gear follows Tredgold’s approximation (ISO 23509 nomenclature): the virtual spur gear of z / cos(delta) teeth on the back cone, wrapped onto it, the teeth ruled to the apex and trimmed by the back and front cones; its pitch angle delta from the teeth, the mate’s teeth and the shaft angle.
  • Faces: tooth k (from 1, counter-clockwise about the axis) has tip(k), flank_a(k) and fillet_a(k) on its clockwise side, flank_b(k) and fillet_b(k) on the other, root(k) after it (a rack’s root(0) before its first tooth); the caps start, end, a herringbone gear’s halves #k pieces; rim, back, end_a, end_b (a rack’s back and ends), back, front, back_cone, front_cone (a bevel gear’s), bore, keyway_a, keyway_top, keyway_b, hub, hub_end, groove.
  • Meshes: the gears must share the module, the pressure angle and the helix angle; external helical gears have opposite hands, a ring and its pinion or a rack and its pinion the same. The centre distance takes the profile shifts’ working pressure angle; a rack’s reference line lies r + x m from its pinion’s axis. A bevel gear meshes only through pair; two rings or two racks do not mesh. A gear’s result keeps its frame as the mount gear (x, y and the axis as columns).
  • Joints and links: gears made as components (new_component) turn on joints of their occurrences; link_gears couples two meshed gears' joints.
QueryFieldsResult
gear_valuesuid (a gear feature) or def (a definition as add_feature takes it, without type)kind, module, teeth, transverse_module, pressure_angle, circular_pitch; bore_diameter (given, or a seated gear’s from its shaft at the timeline marker, with shaft_diameter and the seat as seat_frame gives it); hub_diameter (given or worked out) and computed (["hub_diameter"] when worked out); pitch_diameter, base_diameter, outside_diameter, root_diameter, tooth_thickness (at the pitch circle), undercut, form_diameter (where the involute starts), helix_angle, lead (external gears); a ring’s inside_diameter, space_width; a rack’s pitch_line_length, length; a bevel gear’s pitch_angle, cone_distance, virtual_teeth, mate_teeth, mate_pitch_angle, shaft_angle; section_area (the transverse section’s, without bore and hub); with mesh_with centre_distance, mate, ratio, pitch_radii; error when the values make no gear
gear_linkgearcommand: the add_motion_link link_gears would run, or reason why it cannot
CommandFieldsResult
link_gearsgear (a gear with mesh_with), name (optional)as add_motion_link: a motion link between the joints the two gears’ components’ occurrences turn on (a rack’s slides on), the mate’s joint driving: gear (internal with a ring) by their pitch radii, or rack_pinion by the pinion’s; reverse when a joint’s axis runs against its gear’s. Refused when a gear has no such joint, a joint’s axis is not along its gear’s, or the two are linked already

The .f3d and .solidcraft imports can map their files’ gears onto the definition later; it is kept in the design file as it is.

Pulleys

A pulley feature (mitcad#562; core/model/src/features/pulley.rs the definition, its placement and the belt, pulley_profile.rs the grooves, the kernel’s gear_sweep the solids, api/pulleys.rs the query) makes a timing belt pulley, a smooth idler or a toothed idler from parameters. The application’s Pulley panel makes them (app/COMMANDS.md). Tests: features::pulley_profile and features::pulley_tests, features::seat_tests (seated on shafts), tools/cli/tests/pulleys.json, tools/ui-pulley-test.sh, tools/ui-windows-pulley-test.ps1.

{"type": "pulley", "kind": "toothed", "profile": "gt2_2mm", "plane": "xy", "center": [0, 0],
 "angle": 0, "teeth": 20, "belt_width": 6, "clearance": 1, "pitch_correction": 0,
 "flanges": {"sides": "both", "diameter": 18, "thickness": 1},
 "hub": {"diameter": 16, "length": 7},
 "bore": {"type": "plain", "diameter": 5}, "keyway": false,
 "set_screws": {"count": 2, "thread": {"designation": "M3x0.5"}, "position": 3.5},
 "operation": "new_component"}
FieldValue
kindtoothed (a pulley), idler (smooth, for the belt’s back or as a tensioner), toothed_idler (teeth on a bearing bore)
profilegt2_2mm, gt2_3mm, htd_3m, htd_5m, t5, xl: needed with teeth; optional for an idler (the belt’s pitch, and the check that two pulleys share a belt)
plane, centerwhere the axis meets its plane (the plane’s normal), in the plane’s coordinates. Not with belt_with
angleturns the pulley about its axis: tooth 1 is centred on the plane’s x axis without it; the keyway and the first set screw lie in this direction. Not with belt_with (refused: belt_with.angle places the pulley, its teeth then start on that plane’s x axis)
teeththe toothed kinds’ number of teeth: whole, from the profile’s minimum (12 for HTD 5M, 10 for the others) to 1000
diameteran idler’s running diameter (instead of teeth)
belt_width, clearancemm; the toothed (running) width is belt_width + clearance, the clearance 1 mm without it
pitch_correctionmm added to the outside diameter (a pitch-diameter correction, e.g. for backlash), at most a quarter of the pitch either way; 0 without it. The belt’s values keep the nominal pitch diameter
flangessides (none, one, both; both without it), diameter (more than the outside diameter; optional, mitcad#656: without it the outside diameter plus, all round, the profile’s groove depth and 1 mm, MitCad’s default; the outside diameter plus 2 mm without a profile), thickness. One flange lies on the plane’s side, away from the hub
hubdiameter (optional, mitcad#656: without it the bore (a seated pulley’s too) plus a wall all round of 2 mm, or of a set screw’s tap drill when that is more; half the root diameter without a bore, at least two walls), length: after the toothed part and the second flange, away from the plane
bore{"type": "plain", "diameter": d} or {"type": "thread", "thread": {"designation": "M8x1.25"}} (the size’s minor diameter, its tap drill), through the whole pulley; it stays 0.5 mm inside the groove bottoms (an idler’s running face) with its keyway
keywaya DIN 6885-1 (form A) keyway in a plain bore of 6 to 230 mm, at the pulley’s angle
set_screwscount (1 to 4, 90 degrees apart from angle), thread (a tap drill of that size, radial from the axis through the hub; listed as cosmetic threads by threads), position (mm from the hub’s outer end along the axis; the hub’s middle without it). Needs a hub
belt_with{"pulley": "F3", "center_distance": 80, "angle": <angle>}: in the plane of an earlier pulley feature of the same component, at center_distance from its centre in the direction angle (from its plane’s x axis; 0 without it), for one belt round both. The two share the belt profile (an idler without one takes the other’s); their pitch circles must not overlap
seaton a shaft instead of plane and center (Seats on shafts, mitcad#578): the pulley’s plane (where its first flange starts) at the seat’s offset along the shaft, running along the shaft from it; not with belt_with (a pulley running with a seated one lies in its plane). Without bore the bore is plain, the shaft’s diameter plus bore_clearance, and follows the shaft (a keyway in it too); a thread bore stays the thread’s; a plain bore of its own is refused
bore_clearancemm added to the shaft’s diameter for a seated pulley’s plain bore (0 without it; a printed fit 0.2, say); only with seat and without bore
operation, participantsas an extrusion’s

Values are parameters: numbers in mm (radians for angles; teeth and set_screws.count unitless) or names and expressions, as for gears.

  • Diameters: the pitch diameter is z p / pi (the belt’s pitch line); the outside diameter is the pitch diameter less twice the profile’s pitch line offset (PLD), plus pitch_correction; the root diameter is the outside diameter less twice the groove’s depth.
