    htd_3m3 mm0.381round: 1.289 deep, 2.27 wide, bottom radius 0.86, tip radius 0.3
    htd_5m5 mm0.5715round: 2.199 deep, 3.781 wide, bottom radius 1.49, tip radius 0.43
    t55 mm0.425straight-sided: 1.75 at the bottom, 1.25 deep, 50 degrees, bottom radius 0.4, tip radius 0.6
    xl5.08 mm0.254straight-sided: 1.32 at the bottom, 1.65 deep, 50 degrees, bottom radius 0.41, tip radius 0.64

  • Grooves: our own construction around the published belt dimensions (the sources per profile are in pulley_profile.rs); one fixed groove per profile, not generated by the belt’s motion. A round groove has a bottom arc centred on its axis and straight flanks tangent to it through the corners its width and depth give; a straight-sided groove a flat bottom with fillets and flanks at half its included angle; both have tip fillets tangent to the flanks and the outside circle. Too few teeth for a groove’s width leave no land and are refused.

  • Faces: tooth k (from 1, counter-clockwise about the axis) has tip(k) (its land on the outside circle), tip_fillet_a(k), flank_a(k) and root_fillet_a(k) (straight-sided grooves) on its clockwise side, tip_fillet_b(k), flank_b(k), root_fillet_b(k) on the other, root(k) the groove bottom after it; an idler’s running; the caps start, end; flange_a, flange_a_end, flange_a_inner, flange_b, flange_b_inner, flange_b_end; hub, hub_start, hub_end; bore, keyway_a, keyway_top, keyway_b; set_screw(k).

  • Mount frame: the result keeps its frame as the mount bore (x, y and the axis as columns, the origin on the axis on its plane), as a library pulley’s: joints and joint origins take it as {"mount": "F3:mount(bore)"} (a plane, the axis or its origin); a joint origin there with a mount (kind hole) is a mount frame of the design for Place Part (Mount frames).

  • Belts: the open belt round two pulleys of pitch radii R and r (an idler’s running radius), C apart: L = 2 C cos(t) + pi (R + r) + 2 t (R - r), sin(t) = (R - r) / C. It wraps pi - 2 t of the smaller pulley and pi + 2 t of the larger. A belt body is not made.

QueryFieldsResult
pulley_valuesuid (a pulley feature) or def (a definition as add_feature takes it, without type); belt_lengths (optional: catalogue belt lengths in mm)kind, tooth_width (the toothed width), length (along the axis); bore_diameter (given, or a seated pulley’s from its shaft at the timeline marker, with shaft_diameter and the seat as seat_frame gives it); flange_diameter and hub_diameter (given or worked out, with flanges and a hub) and computed (those worked out, so that a panel shows them as computed until one is typed); with a profile profile, pitch, pitch_line_offset, min_teeth; the toothed kinds’ teeth, pitch_diameter, outside_diameter, root_diameter; an idler’s diameter (and outside_diameter); section_area (the toothed or running section’s, without bore and flanges); with belt_with center_distance, mate (the other pulley’s uid), belt_length (the belt’s pitch length), wrap_angles (on the smaller and the larger pulley), belt_teeth (belt_length / pitch, with a profile), teeth_in_mesh (whole teeth on the smaller toothed pulley), catalogue_length (the nearest of belt_lengths, only when given); error when the values make no pulley or no belt

BUILD: timber frames

A wall, floor or roof frame of timber members made from a few values (mitcad#479), edited afterwards as one. Its members are ordinary BUILD parts (BUILD: timber construction): grounded members by two points of the library’s timber, in the cut list, junctions and lists like any other. The app’s Wall and Floor / Roof (mitcad#520) make them and Timber Frame lays them out again (app/COMMANDS.md, Timber). Code: core/model-build/src/frames.rs; tests core/model-tests/build-frames/src/frame_tests.rs.

{"cmd": "build_frame", "kind": "wall", "part": {"source": "S1", "config": "48x98"},
 "start": [0, 0, 0], "end": [3600, 0, 0], "height": "2400 mm", "spacing": 600,
 "openings": [{"offset": 600, "width": 900, "height": 1200, "sill": 900}],
 "fastener": {"library": "mitcad-parts", "url": "...", "rev": "...", "component": "wood-screw"}}

build_frame (class remote) takes kind (wall, floor or roof), part (the members’ timber: studs, joists, rafters; role: profile, kind: timber, cut to length, with its section) and, by kind, the fields below. Points are in the BUILD host’s coordinates, lengths values (mm or an expression), openings numbers in mm. name (optional) names the frame (Wall 1, Floor 1, Roof 1 by default; unique among the frames); the members’ components are named after it and their role (Wall 1 stud (3)). fastener (optional) is a wood fastener: two of them, sized from the members (Wood fasteners’ default), are driven at every junction of two of the frame’s members that has no connector; a junction they are refused at is left as it is.

  • A wall (kind: wall): start and end, its centre line at its base (made level with the start); height (default 2400 mm, the underside of the bottom plate to the top of the top plate); spacing (the studs’ centre distance, default 600); plates {bottom, top} (1 or 2 each, default 1); plate and header (parts, default part); openings [{offset, width, height, sill}] (offset from the start along the wall to the rough opening’s near side, sill its underside’s height above the base; 0 or left out: a door); joins {start, end, start_on}: the wall frames (any member of each) its ends butt against, start_on: end (mitcad#510) when instead that wall’s end face butts against this wall’s side at its start (left out: side); corner (mitcad#510): how they meet those walls, butt, lapped or straight (mitcad#524: a start on an end face continues in line, its ends otherwise butting) (left out: lapped, as walls saved before it keep their corners), kept in the definition and changed with build_edit.

    • The plates lie flat, the studs stand with the larger section size across the wall: the wall’s depth is the stud’s larger size. The end studs stand flush with its ends; the others at k × spacing from its start (centres), one that would touch the end stud left out.

    • Spliced plates (mitcad#536): a bottom or top plate longer than the plate’s timber’s longest (its length.max, else its longest stock length) is made of pieces butted end to end, from end A each as long as the longest stock length allows (at most its longest), the last one the remainder; each piece at least the timber’s least length (and two stud thicknesses). Each joint lies over the centre of a stud that bears on the plate (one reaching the top plates for a top plate, one standing on the bottom plates for a bottom plate: studs, king studs, junction studs, trimmer and cripple studs), the farthest that keeps the piece within the stock length; where no stud is in reach a backing stud goes in (full height, stud.splice.<n>, as far along as the piece may run, beside the openings’ framing and the other studs). The joints of a second plate (plates.top: 2 or plates.bottom: 2) are at least a stud spacing from the first’s (else a warning, Wall 1: the joints of its top plates are less than a stud spacing apart). A bottom plate is cut at its doors first, each run spliced alone. A plate’s first piece keeps its place (plate.top.0, so a top plate still leads the frame), the others plate.top.0.1, plate.top.0.2, …; a bottom plate’s pieces are plate.bottom.0.0, plate.bottom.0.1, … as at its doors. The pieces are ordinary members: the cut list lists each, cut from the stock. A frame’s fastener goes at the junction of each piece with the stud under the joint (each piece’s end over half the stud); the pieces’ own butt joint is an inline junction, which takes no wood fastener (an inline joint takes a plate), so it gets none. The wall is refused only when a piece cannot be made at all (no stud and no room for a backing stud within reach: Wall 1: its top plate from 0 to 7819 mm is longer than its timber's longest, 6000 mm, and no stud can take a joint between ...) or another member is longer than its timber (a stud taller than the stock: Wall 1: the stud stud.start: the length 6904 mm is longer than the part's longest, 6000 mm). Plates no longer than the timber’s longest stay one piece, as before. Tests: core/model-tests/build-timber/src/wall_splice_tests.rs.

    • An opening: king studs (full height) and trimmer studs (the bottom plate to the header) on each side; a header on edge between the king studs on the trimmers, of as many plies as the wall’s depth takes (floor(depth / thickness), two 48 mm plies in a 98 wall); a window’s sill flat between the trimmers; cripple studs at the stud places in the opening, above the header and below the sill. A door cuts the bottom plates. The studs at the opening’s place give way. Refused: an opening that does not fit between the end studs, openings whose studs overlap, a header above the top plate, a sill below the bottom plate.

    • Load-bearing or not (load_bearing, mitcad#519; kept in the definition and changed with build_edit): true or left out (as walls saved before keep) frames the openings as above; false (a partition, the app’s default for a new wall) leaves the trimmer studs out: the king studs stand at the opening’s sides (opening.<n>.king.a from offset - thickness, .king.b from offset + width), and one header lies flat between them, its wide face down as a plate (opening.<n>.header, role flat header, the header part, from offset to offset + width); the cripple studs above start at its top, the sill and the cripple studs below are as above. The opening’s framing is a stud narrower on each side, so an opening fits nearer the end studs. The preview’s roles and the cut list follow it.

    • Butting (corner: butt, mitcad#510): a wall’s end in joins stops at the face of the wall it names (on the side the wall is on), its end stud and plates square against it, neither lapped nor notched. That wall is neither run on, lapped nor notched; it gets a backing stud on each side of the joining wall (its keys as at a T, junction.<wall>.<end>.a and .b), one that would take its end stud’s place left out, so the sheathing of both walls has a stud behind its edges at the junction. With joins.start_on: end that wall’s end face butts against this wall’s side: that wall is not changed at all, this one runs from its own start and gets the backing studs on each side of that wall’s centre line where they fit (junction.<that wall>.0.a, .b). Either way the walls stay joined: editing one lays the other out again.

    • Corners and T-junctions (corner: lapped, left out): a wall’s end in joins stops at the face of the wall it names (on the side the wall is on); that wall gets a stud for each wall that joins it: where the joining wall’s centre line meets it within that wall’s depth of its end, a corner (it runs on to the joining wall’s outer face, the stud just inside the corner), else a T (a stud on each side of the joining wall). A wall that joins another one lays that one out again with it. At a corner the plates lap (mitcad#493): where each wall has one plate (at the top, and at the bottom), both run to the corner’s outer faces and are half-lapped over the other wall’s depth (a half_lap cut each, no junction, with the other wall’s lead), the joining wall’s half outside (the upper half of a top plate, the lower half of a bottom plate); with two, the joining wall’s outer plate (the upper top plate, the lower bottom plate) runs over the corner to the other wall’s outer face and the other wall’s stops at the joining wall’s inner face, the inner plates as at a butt. At a T the plates butt.

    • A wall started on another wall’s side (mitcad#493): with square: true and joins.start, start is a point on that wall’s side (a click; within its depth of its ends) and the wall starts square to it, at its base, towards the side the point is on (the end’s side when the point is on its centre line, else its left). With corner: butt (mitcad#510):

      • from the side (side): its centre line starts at the point’s place along the wall (snapped, or From and Offset, below), but at least half its own depth from the wall’s end faces (it never hangs past an end: its outer face at most flush with the end face); it butts against that wall’s side, which gets the backing studs;
      • from an end (end): a point on one of the wall’s end faces (within 0.5 mm of the face and inside its depth, or beyond the end; the faces where its plates end now) starts it beyond that end, its side against the end face: its centre line half its own depth past the face, its start flush with the wall’s side away from the side it runs to (the end’s side first here, then the point’s). It stays joined to the wall (joins.start_on: end): that wall is not changed, the new wall gets the backing studs where it meets it.

      With corner: lapped (or left out):

      • an L corner when the point is near one of its ends (within half its stud spacing, at least its depth, at most half its length): the new wall’s centre line starts at that end of the wall’s centre line;
      • a T elsewhere: its centre line starts at the point’s place along the wall.

      From and Offset (mitcad#514): on the side its place along the wall is measured as a side placement’s (mitcad#417), between the wall’s end faces (where its plates end now): from a (end A to the new wall’s near face), b (end B to its far face) or middle (the middle to its centre line, positive towards end B), offset that distance (a value; 0 is flush with that end, or centred). Without either, the point decides, snapped: flush with an end when the new wall’s face would be within its depth of that end (butting; lapped: within the L corner’s reach above), centred within a quarter of its depth of the middle, else the point’s place from the nearer end; snap (mm, optional) is the app’s least snap distance, as at.snap. With either given (end A and 0 when one is left out) they place it, the point only choosing the side (never an end face). It never hangs past an end: a typed offset that would is made flush with that end, with the warning <name>: flush with Wall 1's end A instead. Butting, flush with an end is a clean corner: its outer face in the plane of that end face, its end stud and plates against the side, the wall’s end stud outside it and a backing stud inside it; lapped, flush with an end is the L corner there, any other place a T.

      Its length runs from there: as far as end is along it (a second click, anywhere); else, unless auto_end is false (mitcad#515), to the first wall frame its run meets: one it crosses (not one parallel to it), its centre line between that wall’s end faces (not one it merely touches at a corner), beyond the side it starts from, their heights overlapping; the nearest along the run. It ends there butting against that wall’s side as a start on a side does (joins.end that wall: its end stud and plates square against the side, a backing stud each side of it in that wall; with corner: lapped that wall’s corner or T), its length to that wall’s face. Else (nothing met, or auto_end: false) length. Refused without end or length when nothing is met, and when it would not reach beyond the wall’s side (from an end, beyond its other side). The definition keeps the start, end and joins worked out (not square, from, offset, snap, auto_end). The answer, and build_preview’s with frame, add junction: {kind ("side", "end", "L" or "T"), corner ("butt" or "lapped"), wall (its name), frame (its lead), end ("a" or "b" for an end or an L, else null), at (mm along the wall from its start to the new centre line), length (mm), from ("a", "b" or "middle"; null at an end), offset (mm; null at an end), to ({wall, frame, auto}: the wall its end butts against, auto true when its run met it, false for an end clicked on it; else null), run (mm: the new wall between the faces it butts against, from the wall's side, at an end from its far side)}; null without square.

      Straight (corner: straight, mitcad#524): a start on one of that wall’s end faces continues it in line (kind: "straight", end the end clicked): its centre line that wall’s, its start on the end face, running away from it; the two walls are not joined (neither changes the other). On the side it starts as butt does.

    • A wall started on another body’s face (case B, mitcad#524): with square: true, no joins.start and face {body, face, occurrence} (the body’s uid, the face’s name and the occurrence that places it, its path from the root; left out: the body’s first placement), start the click on the face. A Timber wall frame’s member is case A above, recognised first (the app sends joins.start for it), so its behaviour does not change. The clicked body (an imported wall, a modelled solid, a loose Timber member, a floor frame’s member) is not changed and not linked; everything comes from the geometry:

      • side: the face’s outward side (its normal out of the body’s material, Kernel::face_plane), never into or behind it; direction: square from it, along its normal; a face that is not vertical (its normal more than 0.001 off the horizontal) is refused (<name> starts from a vertical face: the face of <body> clicked is not vertical);
      • base: the floor under the click: the first body a line down from a millimetre in front of the click enters (Kernel::segment_crossings, a slab’s top), else the face’s bottom edge (its box, Kernel::face_boxes, else the body’s), its bottom plate’s underside there, height from it;
      • along the face: at the click, or offset from from (a, the face’s end A: its left end seen from in front of it, b or middle), snapped as on a wall frame’s side with corner: butt (flush with an end within the new wall’s depth, centred within a quarter of it, else from the nearer end), never past an end;
      • an end face (narrower than the body is deep behind it: a solid wall’s thin end) makes a corner: with butt (or lapped, which has nothing to lap here) its side against the end face, running to the side of the face’s middle the end (else the click) is on, its start flush with the body’s far side, longer than the face is wide (kind: "face_end"); with straight in line beyond it, its centre line the face’s middle (kind: "face_straight"); a side face (kind: "face") is the same with any corner.
      • Its length as a start on a wall frame’s: end, else (unless auto_end is false) what its run meets first, else length. The auto end (mitcad#515, both cases) stops the run at a wall frame (as above) or at any other body’s face it meets nearer (the bodies shown other than timber frames’ members), butting it (no link: to.frame null, to.face true). The nearest face along the run is taken (mitcad#536): it looks along lines a quarter, half and three quarters of the wall’s height up and 10 mm under its top (the wall over a door in the wall ahead), each at its centre line and a millimetre inside each of its sides (a post or a wall’s end only its side meets); the body it starts on counts too, beyond its own face (a millimetre on), so a room modelled as one body ends it at its far wall.
      • The definition keeps the start and end worked out (the start at the base’s height), not face. The junction’s kind is face, face_end or face_straight, wall the body’s name, frame null, at along the face from its end A, and base {z, on ("floor", "face" or "origin"), body} names what it stands on. Tests: core/model-tests/build-frames/src/face_start_tests.rs.
  • A floor or ceiling (kind: floor): outline (a closed outline, three points at least, at its first point’s height: the joists' underside), spacing (default 400), direction (the joists’; default square to the outline’s first side, into it), rim (default part), blocking (rows of blocking, default 0), openings [{offset: [a, b], size: [w, l]}] (from the outline’s least corner across the joists and along them), trimmers (default 2).
    • Rim joists on edge along every side, inside the outline; at a corner the side across the joists runs through (exact at square corners). Joists on edge at k × spacing from the outline’s least point across them, from rim to rim (each place cut where the outline is open, as an L or a U), one that would touch a rim along the joists left out.
    • A row of blocking runs across the joists halfway (rows evenly along them), a block between each two neighbouring joists or rims.
    • An opening (a stair’s): trimmers trimmer joists each side, full span; as many header joists each side between the inner trimmers; tail joists from the rims to the headers at the joist places inside it. Refused when it does not fit inside the rims with its trimmers.
  • A roof (kind: roof): walls (two parallel wall frames, any member of each), roof (gable, the default, or mono), pitch (an angle, 5 to 75 degrees; a gable’s default 30; a mono-pitch roof’s default from the walls’ heights), spacing (the rafters’, default 600), overhang (the rafters’ horizontal run beyond the walls’ outer faces, default 300), ridge (default part).
    • The rafters stand on edge at the centre distance along the walls where both run (the first and last flush with those ends), each plumb cut at both ends (ends at the pitch: end A leaning up, its long point the bottom edge at the eave; end B leaning down, its long point the top edge) and notched by a birdsmouth over each wall’s top plate: a birdsmouth cut (Joinery) in its derived part, the box under the top of the plate over its width, with the wall’s lead. The seat is the plate’s width, or less so that the notch is at most a third of the rafter’s depth; a gable roof’s rafters bear on the outer edge of each wall.
    • Gable: the rafters of each side run from the eave to a ridge board on edge halfway between the walls’ outer faces, its top at the rafters' tops; the walls must be of one height. Mono-pitch: from the lower wall over the higher one, notched over both.
    • Warnings: a ridge board shallower than the rafters’ plumb cut, a birdsmouth deeper than a third of the rafter, rafters that do not bear on a wall.
    • Its fastener goes at the junctions of its own members (mitcad#521): through the ridge board into each rafter’s plumb cut end, square to the cut, from the board’s far side (Cut ends after How junctions are found); the two rafters of a pair are no junction, and a mono-pitch roof’s rafters have none among them. The rafters are not fastened to the walls’ plates (junctions of two frames).

The answer: component and frame (the lead), frame_component (the frame’s own component, below), name, kind, members ([{component, member}]), count, fasteners (the junctions given fasteners), relaid (other frames laid out again with it), warnings (the frame’s, the layout’s, and the first ten fasteners’ warnings), splices (a wall’s plates made of pieces, mitcad#536: [{plate, role, at, pieces, longest}], plate the first piece’s place, at the joints in mm along the wall from its start, longest the longest piece); undo step Place wall frame Wall 1, one step with the fasteners.

A frame is a component of its own (mitcad#522). build_frame makes a component named after the frame (Wall 1, Floor 1, Roof 1; Wall 1 (1) when a component has that name) in the BUILD host, placed at the host’s origin, and makes the frame’s members, their fasteners and the fasteners’ joints inside it: the host gets one component per frame, not its members, and a frame’s Joints are only its own. Joints between frames (a fastener connected by hand at a junction of two frames’ members) stay in the host, the common parent. Everything that works on a frame takes its component as well as any member: build_edit with frame (laid out again inside the same component, renamed with the frame), build_preview with frame and component, build_remove with set (the members, their fasteners and the component when nothing else is left in it; the answer’s components lists the parts as before, not the component), joins and a roof’s walls. The definition’s points (start, end, outline, direction) are in the component’s coordinates, the host’s until the component is moved: a frame moved as one (its occurrence moved) is laid out again where it is, and the frames around it read it there; a frame edit’s points are in the component’s coordinates too. build_parts gives each member frame_component; the lead’s record keeps it with the definition (framing.component). Frames saved before keep their members flat in their host and load and edit unchanged: laid out again (MODIFY Timber Frame, or as a frame another one depends on) they stay in the host, their fasteners there too; nothing is re-parented, so paths other parts’ joints and bound lengths name stay valid. Only a new frame is made as a component. The cut list goes by frame: a frame’s members are grouped only with members of the same frame, each row names its frame (frame, null for parts in no frame), the rows of parts in no frame first, then each frame’s by name; the stock is worked out over all of them as before. Tests: core/model-tests/build-frames/src/frame_component_tests.rs.

What is kept. The lead (a wall’s top plate, a floor’s first rim, a gable roof’s ridge board, a mono-pitch roof’s first rafter) keeps the frame’s definition in its record (framing: {frame, count}, its parts as {source, config}, joins and walls as the frames’ leads); every member’s record has frame (the lead) and member, its place in the frame: plate.top.0, plate.bottom.0 (.0, .1, … when a door cuts it or it is spliced; a spliced top plate’s further pieces plate.top.0.1, …, mitcad#536), stud.start, stud.end, stud.<k>, stud.splice.<n> (a backing stud under a plate’s joint), junction.<wall>.<end>, opening.<n>.king.a, .trimmer.b, .header.<ply>, .sill, .cripple.top.<k>, .cripple.bottom.<k>; rim.<side>, joist.<k>, joist.<k>.tail.a, opening.<n>.trimmer.a.<i>, .header.b.<i>, block.<row>.<k>; ridge, rafter.a.<k>, rafter.b.<k>, rafter.<k>. build_parts adds frame, member and the lead’s framing ({definition, count}).

Editing a frame. build_edit with frame (any of the fields above; {} lays it out again as it is) and optionally config (the members' row) through any member: the frame laid out again with these fields over its definition, in one undo step Edit Wall 1. A wall’s length moves its end along it. The members whose place stays keep their components (placed anew, their length, row and cuts; connectors on them stay), new places are made, the others removed as by build_remove; the frame’s fasteners are taken away and driven anew. The frames that depend on it are laid out again too: the walls it joins and those that join it (before and after the edit), and the roofs on any of these walls; one that can no longer be laid out stays as it was, with a warning. The answer as build_frame’s, with changed (frame, config). Members of a frame are otherwise ordinary parts: a member edited alone (its length, ends) keeps its change until the frame is laid out again.

Preview. build_preview with frame (build_frame’s fields, or a frame edit’s with component) answers place: "frame", kind, name, count, roles ({role: count}), members ([{member, role, start, end, length, x, section}] in the design: the axis, the section’s X and its [W, T]), warnings, problems, and for a wall length (as worked out: the auto end’s, mm) and splices (as build_frame’s, mitcad#536). A refused preview (mitcad#536) still answers which frame it is and what its start and auto end worked out: name (the default name given first, Wall 1), kind, junction, length, count: 0, no members, and the reason in problems (the same as build_frame’s refusal, which names the frame too).

Removing. build_remove with "set": true on a member removes the whole frame with its fasteners. A lead removed alone hands the frame to the next member. Walls that join a removed wall keep their layout until they are laid out again (their join is then left out, with a warning).

build_edit with frame is class remote (the fasteners are read from a library).

BUILD: choosing and swapping fasteners

The wood fastener of a timber frame and of a spacing set, its size and count, and fasteners of a design made from another fastener where they are (mitcad#497). The app’s Timber tool chooses them in its Frame and Spacing modes, Swap Fastener swaps them (app/COMMANDS.md, Timber and Swap Fastener). Code: core/model-build/src/frames.rs, spacing.rs, swap.rs; tests core/model-tests/build-timber/src/fastener_tests.rs.

A frame’s fastener. build_frame (and a frame’s build_edit) takes fastener (a wood screw or nail, Wood fasteners) and fastener_count (how many at each junction, default 2). With a row in fastener.config every junction gets that size (a nail 3.1x90); without one each junction’s are sized from its members, as build_connect sizes them. The definition keeps both: a frame laid out again drives the same fastener, size and count. The warnings are build_connect’s (the first ten).

The default fastener (mitcad#516). The model takes the fastener it is given; without fastener a frame has none. The app’s Timber tool sends, until the user chooses another, the library’s default wood fastener: the one marked wood.default (docs/libraries.md, Timber parts; library_build_candidates with kind: wood lists it first). MitCad’s library marks Wood screw, countersunk, seated by its head’s top (flush with the wood, Seating below), not the pan-head Connector screw (head_underside, for a metal connector’s plate), which by name came first and stood proud of every default frame. Without a mark the app takes the first screw seated by its head’s top. Tests: core/vcs/src/tests/library_build.rs (the mark, the picker’s order, the shipped group file’s one default) and tools/cli/build-timber-test.cmake (the generated library’s first wood fastener, a frame with it seated flush).

A spacing set’s fasteners. build_place with spacing takes spacing.fastener and spacing.fastener_count (as a frame’s; none: no fasteners, the default). Each member is then fastened to its hosts: at every junction of a member with a part outside the set that has no connector (a joist on the beams it stands on and reaches, a deck board on each joist it crosses), fastener_count of them as build_connect drives them, in the same undo step as the set. The answer adds fasteners, the junctions fastened, and its warnings the fasteners’. The set keeps them in its definition: build_edit with spacing (which may change fastener and fastener_count) takes the set’s fasteners away and drives them anew with the members, in its one undo step, and answers fasteners too; build_remove with "set": true removes them with the set. A set’s fasteners are the wood fasteners at junctions of exactly one of its members with another part; one connected there by hand is taken away with them when the set is laid out again. build_edit with spacing.fastener is class remote.

{"cmd": "build_swap_fasteners", "fasteners": ["C41", "C42"],
 "part": {"library": "mitcad-parts", "url": "...", "rev": "...", "component": "ring-nail",
          "config": "3.1x90"}}

Swapping fasteners. build_swap_fasteners (class remote; model with part.source) makes each fastener of fasteners (components of role fastener) from part, in place: the component, its occurrence, its derived part (another source and row), its joint (holding it by the new part’s frame of the same kind) and its junction stay, so it stays where it is and what removes or lists it finds it as before; its name becomes the new designation. One undo step, Swap 2 fasteners for Ring nail 3.1x90.

  • Which can replace which. A wood screw or nail (a wood block) only another wood fastener (... is no wood screw or nail: C41 is driven into timber); a connector’s nut, screw or washer only another fastener without wood, and when both name slot systems, one that fits (the systems do not fit: ...). Another part is refused (... is no fastener).
  • The size. part.config names the row. Left out, a wood fastener at a junction is sized from the junction’s members as build_connect sizes it (once per junction); one without a junction (a hanger’s screws) and a connector’s fastener take the source’s default row.
  • The warnings of each wood fastener at its junction for the new size, as build_connect gives them (embedment, edges, the member’s end, through), numbered by the fastener’s place at its junction.
  • The answer: swapped (the components), count, designation, sizes ([{component, config, diameter, length}], the diameter and length a wood fastener’s) and warnings.

Properties

Typed property sets (mitcad#496; core/model-base/src/properties.rs the types, values and the store, document/properties.rs the commands, what the document works out and the answers, api/properties.rs the JSON). A property is a key in a named set with a typed value and its source: Identity / Mark = W-12, Pset_WallCommon / FireRating = EI60, as IFC groups them, so that an export can map them directly. Properties are on three levels:

  • a component (C2, C0 the root): the definition’s, shared by its occurrences;
  • an occurrence (O3): its own values; it shows its component’s as inherited, and its own value of a set and key overrides the component’s for it only;
  • a body (F7.b0).

An owner is given by its id or by its name (a component’s, an occurrence’s Wall:2 or path from the root O1/O4, a body’s at the marker). Set names and keys compare without regard to case; a key has no / (it separates a set from a key in searches; an import writes one as ∕).

Types. The standard types are text, integer, number (a plain number, optionally with a unit label of its own that is shown and not converted, W/(m²·K)), length (kept in mm), area (mm²), volume (mm³), mass (kg), angle (radians), boolean (yes/no; yes/no and bool name it too) and date (YYYY-MM-DD). An own type is defined in the design: a name (not a standard type’s), a base standard type, optional allowed values (a property of the type is then edited as a choice and refuses any other value), an optional unit (a quantity’s shown unit, m, deg, g; a number’s label) and default, and a description.

Values in commands. A JSON number of a quantity is canonical (mm, mm², mm³, kg, radians); text is read in the type’s unit, else the design’s (set_units: a bare 1.2 in a metre design is 1.2 m), unless it names its own (1.2 m, 2 m^2, 500 g, 30 deg; a decimal comma works). yes/no, true/false, 1/0 for yes/no; integers and numbers as text too. A value of another dimension or kind is refused.

Sources. Every value records where it came from: user, rvt, ifc, ipt, f3d (the imports), 3mf (a slicer’s print settings, Print profiles), library (a library or BUILD part’s data) or computed. A user’s value set over an imported one keeps its source and the value the source gave (imported in the file), so the property shows that it differs (edited, source_value); set back to the source’s value it is no longer edited.

Worked out, never stored. computed values (the set Computed) and library values (the set Library) are worked out when asked for and never written to the design file, so a recompute leaves the file as it was:

LevelComputed (only with computed)Library
bodyVolume, Area, Mass (its material’s density), Material
componentVolume, Mass (its own bodies), Length (a BUILD member’s), Kind (mitcad#1980)Designation, Supplier, Part number, Library, Version; a BUILD part’s Material, Grade, Finish
occurrenceits component’s, inheritedits component’s, inherited

A stored value of the same set and key as a library value overrides it (and shows the library’s as its source value); the Computed set cannot hold stored values. A component’s Bill of Materials / BOM Structure is worked out and overridden likewise (mitcad#1985).

CommandFieldsResult
set_propertyowner, set, key, value (optional with a type that has a default, or for an existing property), type (a standard or own type; the property’s, else what the value is: text, integer, number, yes/no), unit (a quantity’s: the unit a number or bare text is in; a number’s label), source (default user; never computed)owner, set, key, type, value (as stored), edited. One undo step, nothing recomputed. An empty or blank text for a component’s (not the root’s) Part number or Description removes the stored property instead (its standing row shows again; no step when none is stored; mitcad#2138)
remove_propertyowner, set, key{}; an occurrence’s component value shows again. Refused when there is none
define_property_typename, base, values, unit, default, descriptionname. Refused for a standard type’s name, a name taken, a unit of another dimension, values not of the base, a default not among the values
edit_property_typename, and what changes: new_name (its properties follow), base (only while no property uses it), values (each property’s value must stay allowed), unit and default (null removes them), descriptionname
remove_property_typenameconverted: how many properties keep their values under its base type
QueryFieldsResult
property_setsbody, occurrence, component (at least one; the component follows from the occurrence or the body), computed (also the computed values)levels, the given ones most specific first: level (body, occurrence, component), owner, name, an occurrence’s component, sets: name, properties: set, key, type, base, value (as stored), text (in the shown unit, 1.2 m), unit, source, read_only (computed), inherited, overrides, edited, source_value (the source’s value as text, where it differs), choices (an own type’s values as text), standing (true on a component’s empty Identity/Part number and Identity/Description rows: listed while the component stores no property of that key in any set, never stored, not on the root, an occurrence or a body; mitcad#2138)
property_typesstandard (the standard types’ names), types: name, base, values (value, text), unit, default, description, uses
property_searchtext: Key or Set/Key, with a comparison =, !=, <, <=, >, >= (numbers and dates in order, quantities in units: Mass > 10 kg) or ~ (contains), or without one (the key is there)matches: every component, occurrence (with its inherited values) and body at the marker with a matching property, in that order: level, owner, name, component, set, key, text, inherited. Computed values only when the search names one

The properties query of this API is a different one: the bodies' physical properties (Analysis queries).

The design file keeps the own types as property_types and the stored properties as properties, one entry per owner (owner, sets: name, properties: key, type, value, source unless user, imported, unit), only for owners the design has (a deleted component’s are left out). Copies of components, and a design placed as a component, bring their components’, occurrences’ and bodies’ properties (another design’s root’s become the new component’s) with the own types they use.

Imports. Each import gives the values its file holds with its source; values MitCad does not otherwise use come in as well:

  • .rvt: each element’s bodies get Identity (ElementId, GlobalId, Category, Class, Family, Type, TypeId, Level), Instance Parameters (the record’s text, number and element id parameters) and Type Parameters (its family type’s; a wall’s type its Width, the total of its layers). Parameters are named and typed by their definitions (mitcad#501): a project, shared or family parameter by its definition in the file (name, and spec or class), a built-in one by the reader’s table of the common ones (Height, Width, Thickness, Base Offset, Mark, Type Mark, …), else Parameter <id>. Lengths, areas, volumes, angles and masses come in as length, area, volume, angle and mass in the model’s units (mm, mm², mm³, radians, kg, converted from the file’s feet, square and cubic feet, radians and kilograms), so they show in the design’s units; yes/no parameters as boolean, integer ones as integer, numbers, counts and currencies as number. A number of a kind not known or not converted (electrical, mechanical and structural quantities, built-in parameters not in the table, files before the 2021 release, which keep no spec) stays in the file’s internal units as a number with the unit label internal units. An element comes in as bodies of its level’s component, with no component of its type, so its type’s values are on its bodies too; were the import to make a component per element type, they would go on it.
  • IFC: an element’s Identity (GlobalId, Class, Name, ObjectType), its property sets (single and enumerated values) and element quantities (lengths, areas, volumes, counts, weights, times) in MitCad’s units, on its bodies and the occurrences of its type’s shape; its type object’s property sets (and Identity / Type) on the component its type’s shape became, and on its own bodies.
  • .ipt and .iam: the summary’s (Title, Subject, Author, Keywords, Comments, Last Saved By), the document summary’s (Category, Manager, Company), the design tracking set’s (Part Number, Material, Release) and the user’s own named properties (User Defined) on the root; an assembly’s parts’ on their components.
  • .f3d dumps that give them: a component’s Part Number and Description (set Component).

Tests: core/model-tests/appearance/src/properties_tests.rs, core/ifc/src/properties.rs, core/import-ifc/src/tests.rs (property_sets_land_on_their_levels), core/import-rvt/src/lib.rs (elements_bring_their_identity_and_parameters), core/import/src/tests/property_tests.rs, core/ipt/src/lib.rs, core/import-rvt/tests/corpus/rvt_corpus.rs and core/ifc/tests/corpus.rs (corpus files by content id), tools/ui-property-sets-test.sh, tools/ui-windows-property-sets-test.ps1.

The sketch’s axes and origin as entities

Constraints and dimensions refer to the sketch’s own x and y axes and its origin through entities that stand for them (mitcad#500), made on demand the first time something refers to them:

{"cmd": "sketch.axis", "sketch": "F1", "axis": "x"}
→ {"entity": "c4", "new": true, "entities": ["p5", "c4"], ...}
{"cmd": "sketch.axis", "sketch": "F1", "axis": "x"}
→ {"entity": "c4", "new": false, ...}
  • axis: "x", "y" or "origin" (anything else is refused: unknown axis “z” (x, y or origin)).
  • The origin is the sketch’s fixed point stored at [0, 0] (the one drawing makes when it snaps to the origin, mitcad#355): the first such point that is not projected. Without one, sketch.axis makes it.
  • An axis is a fixed construction line from the origin point (made first when there is none) to a fixed point 100 mm along the axis. The line and that far end carry "axis": "x" (or "y") in the sketch definition and the sketch query; the origin point does not. Only the line’s direction counts: constraints and dimensions take it as the infinite axis (coincident puts a point on it, point_line_distance is a point’s distance from it, angle a line’s angle to it, symmetric mirrors about it), and as construction geometry it bounds no profile. The app draws the axis across the view instead of the line and does not show its far end (app/COMMANDS.md, Sketch Dimension and the constraint tools).
  • One of each. An entity that is there is returned with "new": false, and nothing changes: no undo step. A new one is one undo step Axis in Sketch1, and the result has the editing commands’ fields (entities, status, …) besides entity and "new": true. The app runs it inside the action that needs it and merges the steps (merge_undo), so undo takes the axis back with the constraint or dimension.
  • Sketches saved before have no axis flags and read and save as they were. Copies (move, mirror, patterns) do not copy the flag. The DXF export (export_sketch) leaves the axes’ lines out, also with construction (mitcad#1445).
  • Mirror about an axis (mitcad#876): sketch.mirror takes "axis": "x" or "y" as well as a line; the axis is made (as sketch.axis makes it) in the mirror’s own undo step Mirror in Sketch1, and the copies are symmetric about it. Its made line’s c id works as any line.
  • Not redundant (mitcad#877): a fixed line whose both end points are fixed (an axis line, a projected line) is held in the solve by its points’ fixes alone, so the sketch’s redundant does not list it; the line stays "fixed": true in the definition and the sketch query. So is every fixed curve made only of fixed points (mitcad#1171): an arc with its centre and ends, a spline with its control or fit points (as a projection makes them). A circle or an ellipse keeps its own fix (its radius), and a set of fixes that only repeat each other (a projected arc’s three points, which its own equation ties; a projected circle’s centre) is not listed either.

Code: core/sketch/src/axes.rs. Tests: core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_axes_tests.rs, Mirror about an axis core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_mirror_876_tests.rs.

Reorient Design

The whole design turned by 90, 180 or 270 degrees about the origin’s X, Y or Z axis (mitcad#502), for a design started on the wrong origin plane. One undo step, Reorient Design:

{"cmd": "reorient_design", "axis": "x", "degrees": 90}
{"cmd": "reorient_design", "plane": "xz"}
→ {"turn": "90 degrees about X", "matrix": [[1, 0, 0], [0, 0, -1], [0, 1, 0]],
   "features": ["Sketch1", "Plane1", "Sketch3"], "moves": ["Move1"],
   "occurrences": [], "views": 1, "analyses": 0, "lights": 0}
  • axis (x, y, z) with degrees (90, 180, 270; -90 is 270), counter-clockwise looking against the axis; or plane (xz, yz): the turn that takes that origin plane’s frame onto XY’s (XZ: 90 about X, YZ: 270 about Y). xy and other turns of nothing are refused.
  • A rewrite, not a move. Every component that is not linked from another file turns in its own coordinates, so that its origin planes are where the turned design wants them:
    • references to the origin’s planes and axes become their turned counterparts: the origin datum the turn takes them onto, frame and sense included (XZ turned 90 about X is XY), else the fixed plane or axis there (XY turned 90 about X faces -Y: {"origin": [0, 0, 0], "normal": [0, -1, 0], "x_axis": [1, 0, 0]}; the Z axis runs along -Y). Fixed planes, axes, points and paths turn, and so do the positions and directions definitions keep (a hole’s points, a split’s direction, picks of surface features, a Move’s and a Move Face’s matrix (a Move Face’s since mitcad#1937), construction geometry given by coordinates, joint frame overrides);
    • a Move’s or a Move Component’s x, y and z go with their axes; a value of an axis the turn reverses is negated (its own dimension parameter; one that other values or features use refuses the command);
    • an Emboss’s Along Axis and Around count along its face’s axis made to point towards +Z of the component (else +Y, else +X): where the turn takes that direction to the other sense (a rod along +Z turned to lie along -Y counts along +Y), both are negated as a Move’s values are (mitcad#1315);
    • a sketch on an origin plane goes onto the origin plane the turn takes its plane onto, with its own frame (frame) set so that its geometry turns with the design, not mirrored. A sketch on a face or a construction plane keeps its plane; where the plane’s frame follows the model axes (a face’s x axis is the model’s X projected) its own frame is set from the turned design’s evaluation so that it stays turned with the design. A sketch that only solves in its turned frame (a projected line that a constraint keeps vertical lies horizontal while its plane’s frame is not yet corrected) gives no frame to correct by; its frame is then read from the turned design up to it with its constraints and dimensions left out (mitcad#1937);
    • an imported body (a base feature) gets a Move right after it that turns its bodies about the origin, named by their own ids (a body kept after Find Repeated Parts took copies out keeps its number, F1.b2 in the second place) (a base feature that joins, cuts or intersects is refused; one without bodies, which only removes the bodies it replaces, gets no Move, mitcad#1937); a body the kernel’s checker finds invalid (an imported shell that is not connected) turns as it is;
    • the pieces of split faces (F2:side(c1[c4,c2])#1) and the edges numbered between the same two faces (E{…}#1) are numbered by the kernel in a geometric order, which the turn changes: references to them (also inside other names, F5:fillet(E{…#1…})) are renamed after the turned design’s numbers, each piece to the one where the turn takes it (its box; an edge’s middle), feature by feature (mitcad#537);
    • occurrences’ placements turn in both coordinates they join (R · T · R⁻¹; an occurrence of a linked component R · T), so a component placed at the identity stays there; joints, constraints and links between components follow from them;
    • named views, section analyses’ planes and the lights placed in the design (not those that follow the camera) turn; what split features remember of their pieces turns with them;
    • image references’ planes turn as section analyses’ do, and comments' free points (at, in their components’ coordinates) and last known places turn with the design (mitcad#1315); comments on faces, edges and bodies follow their targets by name.
  • Faces, edges and bodies keep their names; nothing else is renamed.
  • Checked before it is taken: the command computes the turned design and refuses it, naming them, when a feature that built would fail (a Move it adds too), or a body (its bounding box and centre of mass) or an occurrence would not be where the turn takes it; the document is then as it was. Rules of the model axes that a definition cannot carry (a cylinder’s axis pointing along its largest component, a joint frame’s default x axis) can make a design refuse a turn so. The refusal says where (mitcad#537):
    • a feature with its component and error: Reorient Design cannot turn the design: Fillet3 (in Part) would fail: …, an added Move after the base feature it turns: Move1 (after Base1, in leg) would fail: …;
    • a body with its component, the first feature after which it is not its old self turned (a Move added after a base feature counts with it) and how far: Reorient Design cannot turn the design exactly: Body17 of leg (made by Base1) departs from the turn after Extrude2: its centre is 412.000 mm and its box up to 500.000 mm from where the turn takes it.
  • The application previews it on a command checkpoint (begin_command, restore_command for each choice, discard_command on OK) and logs the bodies’ boxes afterwards (app/COMMANDS.md, “Reorient Design”).

Code: core/model/src/reorient.rs (the turn and the rewrite of definitions), core/model/src/document/reorient.rs (the command and its checks). Tests: core/model-tests/files/src/reorient_tests.rs (mock kernel), cli.reorient_design (tools/cli/tests/reorient_design.json, OCCT), cli.reorient_pieces (a split face’s pieces renumbered by turns, also of a turned design) and iam.corpus_reorient (tools/cli/reorient-corpus.cmake: the test files’ assemblies c71542a1 and 1dc60c2a under MITCAD_IPT_CORPUS, skipped without them).

Mount frames

Any part may say where it mounts (mitcad#525; the library’s side in docs/libraries.md, the app’s Place Part in app/COMMANDS.md): a joint origin with a mount is a mount frame of its design.

{"type": "joint_origin", "geometry": {"body": "F1.b0", "face": "F1:top"},
 "mount": {"name": "head", "kind": "shaft", "joint": "cylindrical"}}
{"type": "joint_origin", "geometry": {"origin": [0, 0, 5], "normal": [0, 0, 1], "x_axis": [1, 0, 0]},
 "mount": {"name": "grid", "kind": "grid", "pitch": [42, 42], "cells": [3, 2]}}
{"type": "joint_origin", "geometry": {"origin": [21, 21, 0], "normal": [0, 0, -1], "x_axis": [1, 0, 0]},
 "mount": {"name": "foot", "kind": "foot", "footprint": [1, 1], "pitch": [42, 42]}}
  • name: 1 to 64 of letters, digits, _, -, + and ..
  • kind: face (the default), shaft, hole, grid or foot; what each frame is and what it goes on is the table of docs/libraries.md. Mated frames face each other: the placed frame’s z is opposite the target’s.
  • joint: how the placed part may move, the joint its placement makes: rigid (the default; the only one of grid and foot), planar and revolute on a face, revolute, cylindrical and slider (along the axis) in a hole or on a shaft.
  • pitch (two lengths, mm, along the frame’s x and y) of a grid and, optionally, of a foot; cells (two counts) of a grid, the cells along +x and +y from the frame’s origin; footprint (two counts) of a foot, the cells it covers along its x and y, the frame in their middle. A check of the feature refuses anything else (mount: a grid gives its cells).
  • A joint origin named mount:<name> without a mount (BUILD’s parts, BUILD) is a face frame of that name, fixed. A design’s frames are its joint origins before the marker, not suppressed, each name once (the first); a derived part’s frames (derived_part) are these too.

Inserted parts keep their frames. insert_component (a file or a library part):

  • linked: the design’s frames become joint origins of the new component on fixed planes where the design has them (in its row), each with its mount, named mount:<name> (mount:<name> (2) when the name is taken); update_links and update_library_parts move them with a new version or row (one the design no longer has stays where it was);
  • a copy: the copied joint origins are the frames (a mount:<name> one gets its mount and its name back).

So a part dropped in is joined later with add_joint by a frame as by any joint origin ("a": {"occurrence": "Lamp:1", "geometry": "F12"}). Paste New of a linked part copies its bodies only, not its frames.

Placing by a frame. insert_component with mount:

{"cmd": "insert_component", "library": {"id": "test-mounts", "url": "...", "rev": "v1.0.0", "component": "bin1x1"},
 "mount": {"frame": "foot",
           "at": {"occurrence": "Baseplate:1", "geometry": "F9", "point": [68, 21, 5], "toward": [0, 0, 1]},
           "rotate": "90 deg", "offset": 0, "flip": false}}
  • frame: the part’s frame (its name; the first frame when left out).
  • at: what was picked, as a joint’s origin from the active component: occurrence (a path, uids or names; empty: its own geometry), geometry, the click’s point and the way toward the viewer, both in the active component’s coordinates.
  • rotate (an angle about the frame’s z; a number is radians), offset (a length along it: a gap) and flip (the target turned over: a plane’s other side, a hole’s other end).

The part goes into the active component as without mount, placed where its frame meets the target face to face, and a joint of the frame’s joint is made in the active component: a the new occurrence’s frame, b the target, flip true, angle and offset the values given, its free motions driven at 0 (position) there. So the part moves with what it stands on (a planar joint does not slide when its face moves) and a drag still moves it as the joint lets it (drag_occurrence drives the new values). One undo step, Insert <name>.

The frameTakesSide b
face, grida planar face, an origin or construction plane, a joint originthe plane’s frame (a face’s: its middle), its shift the click’s place in the plane
shaft, holea cylindrical or conical face, a circular edge, an axisa cylindrical face’s frame at the end towards toward (the other with flip), z out of that end (frame_override z and shift); an edge’s or an axis’ frame with z towards the viewer
foota grid of the picked part: its joint origin, else the grid the click is on (any geometry of the part)the grid’s joint origin, its shift the middle of the footprint’s cells

On a grid the footprint is turned by rotate, which must be quarter turns (on a grid Bin 1x1 turns in quarter turns (0, 90, 180 or 270 deg)); its first cell is the one that centres the footprint nearest the click, kept within the grid ((0, 0) without a point). The cells another foot’s joint to the same grid covers (its shift, angle and footprint) are taken: a placement onto one is refused (the cell (0, 1) of Baseplate:1's grid is taken by Bin 2x1:1; several: the cells (0, 0) and (1, 0) ... are taken by A and B). A foot whose pitch is not the grid’s (Bin 1x1 stands on a grid of 40 × 40 mm; Baseplate:1's grid is 42 × 42 mm), a footprint larger than the grid, a pick the frame does not take (Lamp lies on a face: pick a flat face or a plane, not a round one, Screw goes into a hole or onto a shaft: pick its round face or its rim) and a frame the part has not (Lamp has no mount frame wall (its frames: ceiling)) are refused; the document is as it was.

QueryFieldsResult
mount_framesoccurrence (a path from the active component; empty: its own)component, frames: the mount frames at the marker of the component the path ends in and of those placed in it, each name, kind, joint, pitch, cells, footprint, feature, occurrence (its path name), path, frame ({origin, x_axis, y_axis, z_axis} in the design)
mount_previewinsert_component’s fields (link, name, transform taken, not used)the part’s name and frames (each frame in the part’s coordinates); with mount what the placement would do: frame, kind, joint, target (occurrence, path, geometry, frame_override and name: side b), at (where the frame goes, in the design), placement (rows, in the active component), world (4x4, in the design), grid (a foot’s: feature, occurrence, path, pitch, cells, cell, footprint, turns, covers: its cells), or problems with the refusal; nothing changes

analysis_shape with {"shape": "mount_preview", ...} and the same fields gives the part’s bodies where the placement puts them, in the design’s coordinates. mount_frames is class model, mount_preview file IO (it reads the part as insert_component does).
