Notices

What the model tells the user has a level (mitcad#1040, docs/ui-conventions.md “Messages and severity”): a notice is {"level": "error" | "warning" | "info", "message": …, "target": …, "places": […]} (mitcad_model::notice::Notice; target only when it is about something: a feature’s uid, an annotation’s name or id, a sketch item; places only when it has some). Error: the result is missing, the work stopped; warning: it ran, but something is wrong in the result or left out (never how it was built: a fillet built as rings, with the faces’ cut-outs cleared, or with the kernel’s own tangent chains warns only where its result is faulty, mitcad#1327); info: a neutral fact. Success, hints and progress are the application’s own; states (suppressed, rolled back, inactive, hidden, pending, driven) are no level.

Places (mitcad#1327). A notice’s message says what is wrong in the design’s terms and names no face, edge or vertex by its topological name (E{…}, F4:side(…), V{…}), which the user sees nowhere: “The fillet hangs 0.06 mm past the edge of the face beside it. Check the result.” The places it is about are its places, each one of

  • {"kind": "face" | "edge" | "vertex", "body": "F2.b0", "name": …}: a face, an edge or a vertex of a body by its topological name (body left out where it is not known);
  • {"kind": "point", "at": [x, y, z]}: a point (millimetres, in the body’s component);
  • {"kind": "box", "min": […], "max": […]}: a small box;
  • {"kind": "region", "sketch": "F1", "name": "r{…}"}: a region of a sketch by its key (mitcad#1334; sketch left out where it is not known), which the application paints as the profile.

Agents find and select them by those names; the application paints them in the view while the pointer is over the notice. A message the model builds with topological names or region keys in it has them taken out into its places, each named in the text by its kind instead (“the fillet of an edge”, “at a vertex”, “faces” for a list, “has no profile”; notice::plain_message). A reference a sketch change renamed reads “an edge found again after a change in Sketch1” (“a region found as 2 regions …” for a split region), its old and new names its places; a feature’s references of one kind a change in one sketch renamed are one notice, “2 edges found again after a change in Sketch1” (notice::merge_found_again). The places the geometry gives with its warnings (Kernel::note_places) come after them, and names without a body are of the body those give or the feature sets. The error of a feature and the warnings arrays keep the model’s own text (for one release, as below); the logs too.

  • Features. The timeline and feature queries, and the joints query’s joints, links, constraint sets and rigid groups, give a feature’s level (null when it has nothing to say) and its notices (when any), from one function (feature_level, feature_notices): failed an error (its error), built with warnings a warning (one notice per warning; one for the references of a kind a change in one sketch renamed, mitcad#1334), built with infos information (one notice per info, mitcad#1106), an import note information, then its remarks information (mitcad#1914; listed in its remarks too, and not counted in its level, so a feature with remarks alone has a null level). An import note or infos alone no longer make the status warning: the feature is ok with the info level. error carries only a failure; until mitcad#1040 it also carried the warnings and the import note, joined with ; .

    {"uid": "F4", "name": "Rim", "status": "warning", "error": null,
 "level": "warning",
 "notices": [{"level": "warning",
              "message": "The fillet runs onto a face beside it and leaves an edge there, 53 degrees between the faces. Check the result.",
              "target": "F4",
              "places": [{"kind": "face", "body": "F1.b0", "name": "F4:fillet(E{F1:top|F3:side0})"},
                         {"kind": "face", "body": "F1.b0", "name": "F2:fillet(E{F1:side0|F1:top})"},
                         {"kind": "edge", "body": "F1.b0", "name": "E{F2:fillet(E{F1:side0|F1:top})|F4:fillet(E{F1:top|F3:side0})}"},
                         {"kind": "point", "at": [30.0, 0.55, 19.7]}]}]}

    A preview’s result (preview) gives its warnings as such notices too, without target, and a failed preview’s error first; its remarks after them, as info notices with their places (mitcad#1914), their messages in its remarks.

  • Command and query results. A result with warnings lists them in notices as warnings too (notice::add_notices, in the command and query dispatch and for the bridge’s imports); notices a result gives itself come first. The warnings key stays beside them for one release, for readers of that key; new readers read notices.

  • Imports. The import_f3d, import_fcstd, import_ifc and import_solidcraft results have notices from their items’ outcomes (one per outcome that is a warning or an error, with a count, the worst first; notice::outcome_notices), then the report’s warnings:

    ImportInformationWarningError
    .f3d (replay)parametricpartial, fallback, skipped
    FreeCADbody, component, occurrence, included, parametricpartial, fallback, skipped
    IFCparametric, stored, mesh, mixed, occurrence, component, axes, cutpartial, not importedfailed
    SolidCraftparametric, skipped (nothing to bring in)partial, unmappedfailed

    Each outcome keeps its own word in the report’s rows (Outcome::level gives its level). The other imports’ warnings are warnings.

    The import_ipt, import_iam, import_rvt and import_dwg results (and their reports) have notices the same way (mitcad#1051), then the report’s warnings:

    ImportInformationWarningError
    .ipt bodies (BodyOutcome)importeda solid that is not validnot built
    .iam files (FileOutcome)part replayed, part as its stored bodies (asked, or no history), sub-assembly placeda part’s replay that fell back to its stored bodies, a file not found (its component empty), a sub-assembly that contains itselfa part not imported
    .rvt elements (mitcad_import_rvt::Outcome)features, parts, mesh, reference bodyboxnot built
    .dwg entities (EntityOutcome)taken, 2D entities left out by designa 3D entity left out, a body that is not valida body not built

    An .ipt part replayed with its history has the replay’s notices (as .f3d) with its bodies’; the watchdog’s notes are warnings. An .iam import’s placements that do not agree with the displayed ones and parts’ bodies outside their stored range boxes are warnings with their counts; an .rvt import’s elements of the kinds built as features that came in otherwise, its walls’ missing openings and its links whose models were not found are warnings too. The enums are in mitcad_import_base::outcomes (.ipt, .iam, .dwg, built in mitcad-ffi) and core/import-rvt/src/outcome.rs.

  • Annotations. A broken annotation is a warning: its entry in the annotations and drawing queries has level warning and a notices entry about it, its error the reason as before; one laid out with a caveat (warning) likewise.

  • Sheet metal. The sheet_state query’s notices: what invalidated the sheet an error, what blocks it a warning, each about its feature.

  • Sketches. The sketch query’s notices: a solve that did not converge or conflicting constraints (its error) an error, redundant constraints a warning per offset, pattern and the sketch’s own (mitcad#1171: An offset: 2 dimensions follow from the others, Redundant: 1 constraint follows from the others; also in its warnings, with their entities in warning_entities, and the ids in redundant), a redundant constraint that still takes freedom away information about it (mitcad#1992, its target the constraint: the Symmetry between two points about an axis partly repeats the others; it still removes one degree of freedom), unmet inactive constraints information (Inactive constraints the geometry does not meet: k5); the sketch’s warnings as warnings.

Tests: core/model-base/src/notice.rs (the type, the warnings read, add_notices, outcome_notices), a_feature_s_level_is_its_worst_notice (core/model/src/document/import_notes.rs), the importers' outcomes_map_onto_the_levels (with core/import-base/src/outcomes.rs and core/import-rvt/src/outcome.rs for the .ipt, .iam, .dwg and .rvt imports, and the .rvt house project’s box and missing openings in the_house_wall_attached_to_its_roof_names_it), a_solve_s_states_have_their_levels (core/model-api/src/sketch.rs), an_import_note_is_information_with_its_message (core/model-tests/files/src/import_notes_tests.rs), the broken annotations of core/model-tests/analysis/src/annotation_tests.rs and core/model-tests/drawing-views/src/drawing_annotation_tests.rs.

Material and process notes

mitcad#1049 (core/model-api/src/body_notes.rs, core/model-api/src/annotations.rs): two kinds of annotation whose text is written from the body they point at, for the application’s Make tab.

An annotation of the kind material (a material note, name Material1, …) or process_note (a process note, ProcessNote1, …) points at a body: its a is a body with an optional face, edge or vertex (with at where it was clicked, as a note’s). It is a leader as a note is (no value, format, tolerance or text of its own), stored and listed as the other annotations, edited and deleted by the same commands; no feature control frame stands under it. add_annotation needs its kind; a pick that is no body’s (a datum) is refused (a material note points at a body, a process note points at a body), and so is a text (a material has no text of its own).

Its label is {"text": …, "lines": […]}, worked out whenever the annotations are asked for, so that it follows the design:

  • A material note: the name of the material the body is made of, as body_material gives it (its own, else its component’s default along the pick’s occurrence, else the root’s): ["PLA"].
  • A process note: Printer: <profile> and Process: <profile>, the printer and process profiles the body prints with (the nearest level’s choice, Slicer default when none chose one), then each printer or process value set on the body, its occurrences or its components rather than taken from a profile, as print_settings gives it, in the key map’s order: ["Printer: Bench", "Process: Standard", "Walls: 5"].

A pick whose body is gone makes it broken (a pick is not there: …), as any annotation. Its drawing is a note’s; on a face its leader ends in a dot.

Tests: a_material_note_writes_the_body_s_material_and_follows_it, a_process_note_writes_the_profiles_and_the_values_set_on_the_body, a_material_or_process_note_points_at_a_body_and_breaks_when_it_goes (core/model-tests/analysis/src/body_note_tests.rs, mock kernel), a_material_or_process_note_points_at_a_body_and_has_no_text (core/model/src/document/annotations.rs) and a_process_note_lists_the_profiles_and_the_values_set_on_levels (core/model-api/src/body_notes.rs).

Export Face as DXF

mitcad#1049 (core/model-api/src/cut_sheets.rs): the Make tab’s Export Face as DXF writes one body’s outline for a laser, waterjet or plasma cutter, without a cut sheet:

{"cmd": "export_face_dxf", "body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:top",
 "occurrence": "O1", "path": "plate.dxf", "units": "in"}

The body is seen square on to its planar face face from outside, in the occurrence that places it (occurrence, uids or names; wherever it is shown when left out), and its outline is worked out as a cut sheet’s part has it: the silhouette of the projection along the face’s normal, outer loops on the layer CUT_OUTER, holes on CUT_INNER, at 1:1 with the lower left corner of its box at the origin, in units (the design’s length unit when left out, mitcad#1408, DXF units). Nothing is added to the design and nothing is an undo step (class file IO). The answer: path, body, name (the body’s), face, outer and inner (the loops written), width and height (the outline’s box, mm) and units (the unit written). A face that is not one of the body’s planar faces, or a body that is gone, is refused with the reason (F7:top is no planar face of Body1).

Test: a_face_s_outline_is_written_at_full_size_from_the_origin (core/model-tests/drawing/src/face_dxf_tests.rs, mock kernel); the unit: core/model-tests/drawing/src/dxf_units_tests.rs.

Bodies that differ from their component

mitcad#1049 (core/model-api/src/body_notes.rs): the Make tab marks the Browser rows of the bodies whose material or print settings differ from their component’s. The query {"query": "make_differences"} lists them:

[{"body": "F2.b0", "name": "Body1", "material": "ABS",
  "print": ["Walls", "Process profile", "gcode_comments (PrusaSlicer)"]}]
  • material: the name of the body’s own material when it is not the one its components give it in one of its placements (the nearest component’s default up the occurrence path, else the root’s, else the built-in default, as body_material takes it; mitcad#1150); null when it has none of its own or the same.
  • print: what the body itself sets of its print settings, in its property sets’ order: a printer or process value by its plain name (Walls), a profile choice as Printer profile or Process profile, a slicer’s own key with the slicer’s name. Print Filament is the material’s and is not listed.

A body with neither is left out; a design without such bodies gives []. Test: the_bodies_whose_material_or_print_settings_differ_are_listed (core/model-tests/analysis/src/body_note_tests.rs).

A filament’s colour is its appearance

A filament gets its colour from its appearance (mitcad#1055; core/model/src/material.rs, document/materials.rs, document/print_settings.rs, print_files/mod.rs): filaments are matte, glossy or translucent, so the appearance is the colour, and a colour alone does not exist. A material offers several appearances, and a body has a material and one of its appearances.

  • A material’s appearances. A material keeps its default appearance and appearances: the others it offers, in their order (PLA Basic: Bright Green, then Black, White, Translucent Blue). The materials query gives each material’s appearances: every one it offers, its default first (the default alone without a list, none without an appearance). create_material and edit_material take appearances, every appearance it offers in order, in the place of its list: the default stays when it is among them, else the first is the default (none for an empty list); each must exist. appearance alone makes one of the list the default (the old default staying in the list), or replaces the default with another one as before; with appearances too, it is the default and the list keeps the others. library_items gives a material row’s appearances too.
  • No colour of its own. A material keeps no filament_colour: the export writes the colour of the appearance a body prints with, and a colour the material sets is never written. One from before becomes an appearance of its list: when a design file loads, when a library’s item or an import comes into the design, and when create_material or edit_material sets it. An appearance of its list of that colour is used, else a new plastic appearance of the design (<name> color, as an import’s). Set by create_material or edit_material without an appearance, it becomes the default (the colour is what is to print; the old default stays in the list); with an appearance in the same command, and from a file, a library’s item or an import, it is the default only when the material has none, so that a design keeps the look it showed. The key is then gone. A slicer import makes every filament’s appearance itself (mitcad#1053).
  • A body’s appearance. A body has a material and one of its appearances: set_body_material takes appearance_id, the appearance for the body (Material ▸ PLA Basic ▸ Black), in the place of appearance (replace or keep, refused together). Without it, replace (and the default unless the body’s appearance was set by hand) keeps the body’s appearance when the new material offers it, else gives the material’s default. An appearance is set by hand when the material the body is made of does not offer it; material_conflicts lists the bodies whose appearance was set by hand and the new material does not offer.
  • A component’s appearance. set_component_material takes appearance_id too: the appearance of the component’s default material that its bodies without one of their own print with (left out: the material’s default; refused without a material). The design file keeps it in the component’s component_materials entry (appearance). A file whose entry names an appearance neither the design nor the library has (edited by hand) still opens: that appearance is dropped, the component keeps its material and shows the material’s appearance, and load_warnings says so (component_materials[0]: there is no appearance no_such_look; the component shows its material's; mitcad#1150). The materials query gives a material’s component_appearances ({"C2": "plastic_black"}, only the components that chose one).
  • Outside the list. An appearance a body gets outside the list of the design’s material it is made of joins that list for the design, in the same undo step: set_body_appearance (the Appearance command; not an expression), set_body_material and set_component_material with an appearance_id. A built-in material cannot change in a design: its list stays, and the body’s appearance counts as set by hand. The model’s own set_body_appearance (imports) adds nothing.
  • What prints. The appearance a body prints with is its own, else that of the component whose default material it is made of, else the material’s default; print_settings’ filament gives it as appearance, and its colour is the filament’s filament_colour. The export makes a filament slot per material and appearance in the order of first use: two bodies of one material in two colours are two slots with the same values (the material’s and its variant’s) and different colours, as the slicer’s colour map and an automatic material system take them. The purge_volumes query makes the same slots (each with its appearance, a material in two slots named PLA Basic (Black)); between two colours of one material the volume is their colours’, never one set by hand (the design’s volumes are by material). The warning for more filaments than the printer has slots counts these slots.
  • Deleting an appearance takes it out of the materials’ lists and the components’ choices too.
CommandFieldsResult
create_material, edit_materialas in Materials, and appearances (every appearance it offers, in order)as there
set_body_materialas in Visibility and display, and appearance_id{}; one undo step Set Material of Body1 (with the material’s list when it grows)
set_component_materialas in Materials, and appearance_id{}; one undo step Set Default Material of Arm
set_body_appearanceas in Appearances{}; one undo step Set Appearance of Body1, with the material’s list when the appearance joins it
  • A library’s material (mitcad#1067; print_library.rs, document/print_library.rs, document/library_items.rs) keeps its whole list: its file carries every appearance of the list that is not the library’s, the default’s in appearance as before and the others in appearances (in the list’s order; left out when there are none, so a material of one appearance is written as before). save_to_print_library, create_material and edit_material with a library carry them from the design (or from the item duplicated). Inserting the item into a design (copy_from_print_library, a library named by set_body_material or set_component_material, update_from_print_library, create_material based on it) brings the whole list: a carried appearance the design does not have is added; one the design has of the same id and look is used; one of the same id and another look comes under a free id (translucent_blue_1) in its place of the list, and counts as the same when a newer version is compared. Another of the list that is neither the library’s nor carried nor the design’s is left out. A default that is none of these (mitcad#1242: a slicer import or an older version wrote the item without it) refuses only a change that names it (appearance): edit_material and create_material with a library (a rename, a density, print settings, a Duplicate of the item) and merge_materials go on. When it is the material’s own color, <id>_colour of its id or of the one it was copied from (based_on), its - and / as _ (generic-tpu-bbl-a1m → generic_tpu_bbl_a1m_colour), it is made again as an import makes it (the library’s white plastic in the material’s filament color: its own filament_colour, else a slicer’s default_filament_colour it keeps, else the neutral gray #BFBFBF; named <name> color, an FDM plastic’s look) and the file carries it from then on (a design copy showing it gets it too); another id stays the default, carried by none, and the answer’s warnings names it (material generic-tpu: there is no appearance lost_look; kept as its default). library_items gives a library material row’s carried_appearances (id, name, base_color, display_color), so that its appearances are named and coloured before the design has them.
  • Replace Appearance (the application’s question when a material is assigned, app/COMMANDS.md) asks only about a body whose appearance was set by hand and is not one the new material offers, as replace keeps one it offers.

Designs and library files from before load unchanged: a material without appearances offers its default alone, and one with a filament_colour gets that colour as an appearance of its list; a library file without appearances carries its default appearance alone.

A library material without its own color (mitcad#1242): library_own_colour_tests (core/model-tests/print: renamed, its density and a print setting changed, each carrying the color made again; another missing default kept with a warning; a Duplicate; the design’s copy taking the edit) and the Materials window’s rename in tools/ui-library-material-own-colour-test.sh and app.ui-windows-library-material-own-colour.

Center of Mass

The Center of Mass marker (mitcad#1094; core/model/src/document/display.rs, core/model-api/src/center_of_mass.rs; the application’s Center of Mass in app/COMMANDS.md): the center of mass of the whole design, drawn as a marker, with a row under the root’s Origin folder.

CommandFieldsResult
add_center_of_massundo step Add Center of Mass; a hidden marker is shown (Show Center of Mass), a shown one stays as it is (no undo step)
set_center_of_mass_visiblevisibleundo step Show Center of Mass / Hide Center of Mass unless nothing changes; refused without a marker (the design has no Center of Mass marker)
delete_center_of_massundo step Delete Center of Mass; refused without a marker
QueryFieldsResult
center_of_masscenter_of_mass (mm, design coordinates; null without bodies of a material), mass (kg), volume (mm³), bodies (counted, one per placement), without_material (how many placements of bodies without a material were left out, mitcad#1817), marker: {"visible": bool}, or null without a marker
  • Display state, as the Origin folder is (Visibility and display): the commands recompute nothing, a project does not version them, and the design file keeps the marker in its display state, "display": {"center_of_mass": {"visible": false}} (left out without a marker). The document query’s display has center_of_mass ({"visible": bool}) while there is a marker.
  • Placed bodies. The query counts the bodies the properties query counts, each once per occurrence that places it, at the occurrence’s place in the design and with the material it has there: its own, else the nearest component default up the occurrence path, else the root’s; a body with none has no mass and is left out (mitcad#1817), never steel. Each body’s properties are computed once per density and their centers moved by the placements, so a component placed twice counts twice and moving a component moves the center. It is the properties query’s total over every body when every body has a material (mitcad#1110): both walk the bodies’ placements the same way and give each the same material (Physical Properties’ extent, placed bodies); only a body that no occurrence places counts in properties and not here. A body the kernel cannot measure fails the query with its name.

Tests: center_of_mass_tests (core/model-tests/api: the total of two bodies of different materials, one in a component, moved with its occurrence by its share of the mass, a material of its own counted; the marker added, shown, hidden, saved, read back, deleted, refused without a marker, undone).

Design properties

The design’s summary and statistics (mitcad#1088; File › Design Properties…, api/design_properties.rs, document/design_summary.rs, file/statistics.rs).

Summary. Title, Subject, Author, Keywords and Comments are the root component’s property set Summary (keys Title, Subject, Author, Keywords, Comments): the set and keys the .ipt import fills (Properties), so an imported summary shows in Design Properties… and a summary set there shows in Property Sets…, Find in Design and the title blocks like any property. A drawing’s title block falls back to them (Drawing templates and revisions): title to the root’s Title (a component’s drawing keeps its own Title or its name), author to Summary/Author, description to Summary/Comments, where the sheet and the component give none. A version’s description (Save with Description) is no part of it.

Statistics. When the design was created and last saved, by whom and with which MitCad, written by the application’s Save into the design file’s statistics (created, last_saved as UTC YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ; last_saved_by, the operating system’s user name; last_saved_with, MitCad 0.18.0); each left out while unknown. They are kept beside the design’s definition, not in it: undo leaves them, a design comparison does not see them, and the commands do not change them.

  • A save changes them only when the file changes: one that would write the bytes the file holds (nothing changed, or only the display state of a design in a project) leaves them and the file as they were, so it records no version.
  • created is set by a new design’s first save (also of a design an import made, recovered unsaved work, or a project’s new empty design). A design whose file was saved before MitCad kept statistics has it unknown, and keeps it unknown when saved again.
  • mitcad-cli and the MCP server’s document_save write the statistics as the design has them, without stamping them.
CommandFieldsResult
set_design_summarytitle, subject, author, keywords, comments (each optional: a field left out keeps its value; an empty or blank text removes the property)changed (how many changed), summary as below. One undo step, Design Properties; none when nothing changes. A user’s text over an imported one keeps the import’s value beside it (edited in property_sets)
QueryFieldsResult
design_propertiesset (Summary), summary: title, subject, author, keywords, comments (empty where not set), statistics: created, last_saved, last_saved_by, last_saved_with (null where not known)

Tests: core/model-tests/files/src/design_properties_tests.rs (the summary saved and read back, one undo step, an imported value kept; the statistics written by a stamped save, kept by a save that changes nothing, an old file read with created unknown, an empty design’s file created at its first save), template_tests::a_title_block_falls_back_to_the_design_summary (core/model-tests/drawing), file::statistics::tests; tools/ui-property-sets-test.sh and app.ui-windows-property-sets (Design Properties… sets Title and Author, Property Sets shows them on the root).

Comments

Notes pinned to the model that point an AI agent at the right place (mitcad#1119; core/model/src/document/comments.rs, api/comments.rs): the user marks a face, edge, feature or point with “make this hole an M6 thread”, the agent (MCP or the chat panel) reads the open comments, does the work and marks each addressed with what it did, and the user resolves them. They are not annotations, which are dimensions and notes of the design itself. Each change is an undo step of its own that recomputes nothing.

FieldMeaning
idC1, C2, …: the next one is one past the largest ever used, so an id is not given again within the design (a design whose comments were all deleted starts again at C1 when it is opened again).
textwhat is asked, trimmed; not empty.
targetwhat it is pinned to (below), stored as given: names trimmed, the root’s component and an empty occurrence left out.
statusopen, addressed (the work is done, with a resolution) or resolved (the user accepted it).
orphanedthe target is not found at the timeline marker (a feature removed the face, the feature was deleted or rolled back): the comment stays, at its last known place, until the target is found again or it is retargeted. A flag, not a status.
authoruser, or an MCP client’s name (claude-code): the MCP layer writes its client’s name on every comment command, so a client cannot pose as the user. Left out in a command: user.
resolution, addressed_bywhat was done and who wrote it, set by address_comment; kept when the comment is reopened, until the next address replaces them.
replies{"author", "text", "created"} each, in order, with attachments where it has images.
createdwhen it was written, UTC YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ.
attachmentsthe comment’s images (mitcad#2011), listed where it has any; see Images below.

Targets take the field names of the measure query’s picks:

targetPinned tolabelplace
{"feature": "F7"}a timeline feature, while it is in the timeline (also rolled back or suppressed)its name, Hole1its first body’s (F7.b0) box centre; null without one
{"body": "F2.b0", "occurrence": "O1/O4"}a bodyits name, Body1its box centre
{"body": …, "face": "F2:side(…)", "occurrence": …}a face by topological name, or its pieces after splitsBody1 › Extrude1 side face (the feature that made the face and its role)a planar face’s middle on its plane (as measure gives it), else its box’s middle
{"body": …, "edge": "E{…}", "occurrence": …}an edgeBody1 › edgeits middle, else a straight edge’s ends’ middle or a circle’s centre
{"body": …, "vertex": "V{…}", "occurrence": …}a vertexBody1 › vertexits point
{"sketch": "F1", "curve": "c4"}, "point": "p3", "constraint": "k2", "dimension": "k5"a sketch’s curve, point, constraint or dimension (constraints and dimensions share the k numbers)Sketch1 › line c4, Sketch1 › point p3, Sketch1 › horizontal k2, Sketch1 › dimension k5the middle of the points it uses as the sketch last solved
{"parameter": "width"}a parameter, by its name: a rename (rename_parameter, or a value slot’s name = expression) rewrites the target in its own undo step, so the comment follows it and is not orphaned (mitcad#1305)its namenull
{"at": [x, y, z], "component": "C3", "occurrence": "O1/O4"}a free point in its component’s coordinates (component empty or left out: the root), following the occurrence as an annotation’s at doesPointthe point placed
{"design": true}the whole design (mitcad#2010): a request about the design as a whole, also in an empty design before any geometry; alone (no other field, no occurrence); always found, so never orphaned; false is no targetDesignnull

occurrence is optional as in measure: left out, the root’s, or the owner’s only placement (a component placed more than once needs one). place is mm in the design’s (root’s) coordinates at the marker, where a pin goes. A target is refused when it is added or retargeted unless it is found at the marker (the comment's target: the face F2:end(…) is gone from Body1, the feature F9 is gone, c99 is gone from Sketch1, Extrude1 is no sketch, the parameter depth is gone, the component C5 is gone), or when its fields are no target (a target is {"feature"}, …, or {"design": true}).

CommandFieldsResult
add_commenttext, target, author (default user), optional attachments (images, below)id, and attachments (the images’ ids) when it has images; undo step Add Comment C1
edit_commentid, textchanged; undo step Edit Comment C1, none when the text stays
reply_commentid, text, author, optional attachmentsreply (its number from 1), and attachments when it has images; undo step Reply to C1; the status stays
retarget_commentid, targetchanged; clears orphaned and takes the new target’s place (none for a parameter or the whole design, never the old target’s, mitcad#1315); undo step Retarget C1, none when nothing changes
address_commentid, resolution (not empty), authorstatus addressed with its resolution and addressed_by; undo step Address C1, none when it is addressed so already. A resolved comment is refused (C1 is resolved: reopen it first)
resolve_commentidstatus resolved (from open or addressed); undo step Resolve C1, none when resolved already. An MCP client’s is refused unless Preferences › AI Assistants › Agents may resolve comments is on (the MCP layer’s check; the model does not know who calls)
reopen_commentid, optional text (a reply saying why) and authorstatus open; undo step Reopen C1. An open comment without a text changes nothing; with one it gets the reply
delete_commentidundo step Delete Comment C1; its id is not given again
remove_comment_attachmentcomment, id (A2)the image goes from the comment or the reply it is on; undo step Remove Image; its id is not given again

Several commands in one array are each their own step, as any array’s; MCP’s model_command merges an array’s steps into one (merge_undo), so an agent’s model change and its address_comment in one array undo and redo together.

Orphans. After every command (also undo and redo) the API finds every comment’s target at the marker and keeps what it found in the design without an undo step or a new revision: a target found keeps its place as the last known one and is no orphan; one gone is orphaned and keeps its place. Undo takes back a state as it was then (a face the undone feature removed is found again). The edits that change occurrence paths or body ids carry the targets along in their own undo step (mitcad#1318): Reparent Occurrence (a path through the occurrence goes its new way), Move Features into a Component and Move History into Component (a body that went, where a path placed it, goes on through the new occurrence) and Save Component as Design with replace (the component’s bodies, faces, edges and vertices by their new names).

QueryFieldsResult
commentsstatus (optional: "open", or a list ["open", "addressed"]), target (optional: only comments on that target, compared as stored)comments: each as above with label and place as its target is found now (for an orphan its last known place, label from what is left of the target, and error, why it is gone), orphaned, resolution (null until addressed) and addressed_by once addressed, and the images’ fields (attachments, no bytes); open: the number of open comments in the design, whatever the filters; revision: a number that grows whenever the comments as listed change (a command, an image attached or removed, undo, redo, a target found elsewhere or gone) and stays while they do not, for a client to tell whether to read them again
comment_attachmentcomment, idan image’s fields (below) with comment and data, the file’s bytes in base64, as they were attached. Through MCP’s model_query the bytes come as an image block with its mimeType instead of data

Images (mitcad#2011, GitHub mitcad/Mitcad#402). A comment and each reply may carry images: a picture of the place, marked up, or of the result (an agent’s too). add_comment and reply_comment take attachments, [{"data": "<base64>", "name": "capture.png"}]: each a PNG or JPEG file of at most 4 MB (the image is 5.2 MB, more than the 4 MB a comment's image may be; only PNG and JPEG images can be attached, and this one is BMP; image 2: … for the second of several), its name cut to the file’s name (image.png when none). The images come with their comment or reply in its one undo step. Each is listed as:

FieldMeaning
idA1, A2, …: one sequence for the design’s images, one past the largest ever used, so an id is not given again within the design and stays the image’s while it is there.
media_typeimage/png or image/jpeg.
width, heightin pixels, from the file’s header.
bytesthe file’s size.
sha256the file’s SHA-256, hex.
namethe file’s name, no folders.

A refused image refuses its command: nothing of it is added.

The file. comments (each with its stored fields and place, the last known one; "orphaned": true only for an orphan) and next_comment where it is not one past the largest id listed; a design without comments leaves both out, so older versions read it. Builds without comment support handle these as fields of a newer MitCad; builds before mitcad#1132 refuse unknown top-level fields. An id twice, an empty text, author, resolution or reply, or fields that are no target are refused on load, in words as the application shows it (a comment is damaged: its text is empty), with the field and the ids as the error’s detail for agents and the log (comments[1] (C2): the text is empty; mitcad#2011); a target that is not found loads as an orphan. A build before mitcad#2010 refuses a design with a comment on the whole design (design is an unknown field of a target), as it refuses a feature type it does not know; there is no compatibility layer.

The images (mitcad#2011) are kept apart from the comments, in comment_attachments, in the comments’ order: {"comment": "C1", "reply": 2, "id": "A3", "name": "capture.png", "image": {"format": "png", "width", "height", "data"}} (reply the reply’s number from 1, left out for the comment’s own image; data the file in base64), and next_comment_attachment where it is not one past the largest id listed. On load each must be on a comment and a reply of the file, its bytes a PNG or JPEG of the format and size its fields say and within the limit, each id once; the refusal says it in words (an image of a comment is damaged: the image is a 2 × 2 png file, not the 3 × 2 png it says), its detail names the field and the ids (comment_attachments[0]: image A1: …). A build without images handles both as fields of a newer MitCad: it opens the design with the comments and their text, and saving over it drops the images.

Tests: core/model-tests/analysis/src/comment_tests.rs (add, reply, address, resolve, reopen and delete with their undo steps and the filters; every kind of target with its label and place, and the refusals; undo, redo and revision; saved and read back; an orphan after a shell removes its face, and retargeting; a model change and its address_comment in one merged array undone as one step; a comment on the whole design in an empty design through every command, model changes, a save and a reload, mitcad#2010; images on a comment and a reply, removed, undone and redone, saved and read back, bytes that do not match refused on load, an image over the limit refused, and the query’s bytes equal to the stored ones, mitcad#2011), document::comments::tests (the targets’ forms, the ids).

Fields of a newer MitCad’s design

A design file’s top-level fields that this build does not know (mitcad#1132) are ignored when it is read: a newer MitCad wrote them (future_notes, say), and a field added later must not keep this build from opening the design. Builds before this rule refuse such a design (unknown field …). Unknown fields inside the known ones (a feature’s, a parameter’s) and a newer version are still errors (core/model/src/file/mod.rs).

  • Opening names them in the first of load_warnings (and the document query’s warnings): this design was written by a newer MitCad: the fields `future_notes`, `next_future_note` were not read (the field … was for one).
  • The document keeps them with the file it was read from (Document::unknown_fields; none for text read without a path: a version’s, recovered work). This build cannot write them back: a save over that file drops them, and then clears them; a save to another file keeps them, so a later save over the first file still drops them (Document::fields_dropped_by_saving(path)).
  • The application warns on opening (a warning in the status bar or the message band, “This design was written by a newer MitCad: future_notes, next_future_note not read. Saving over it drops them.”) and asks before it writes over the file: Save and Drop Them, Save As… (a new file; the old one stays as it is) or Cancel (nothing written). An MCP document_save that would write over it is refused, naming the fields, and asks nothing (docs/mcp.md). mitcad-cli (--save, convert) writes without asking and says on stderr warning: <path>: saving over this design drops the fields ….
QueryFieldsResult
unknown_fieldsoptional pathfields (names, sorted): the top-level fields of the design file read that this build did not read; with path, those a save to path drops (all of them when path is that file, by any spelling of its path; none for another file). file: the file they were read from (null for none). message, when fields has any: the open warning, or with path the save’s (saving over this design drops the fields `future_notes`, … that a newer MitCad wrote and this MitCad did not read). Class file IO: it is about the saved file

Tests: core/model-tests/files/src/unknown_fields_tests.rs (ignored and named, the saved file without them, unknown feature fields still refused; the save path’s flag kept by a save to another file and cleared by a save over the file read), tools/ui-unknown-fields-test.sh (mitcad-cli’s warnings; Floating: the warning, Cancel and Save As; Docked: Save and Drop Them) and app.ui-windows-unknown-fields (tools/ui-windows-unknown-fields-test.ps1).

Dimension spacing

A dimension placed on a drawing’s view, or dragged, snaps to the spacing of the dimension placed before it in the drawing and to multiples of it (mitcad#1173), so that dimensions stacked beside a view lie evenly apart; no grid and no setting. The drawing_snap query works it out; the commands still place exactly where they are told, so the application asks it with the command its click or drag would run and runs that command with the answer’s place.

What is spaced, in paper mm, by the kind of dimension (family):

  • line: a linear or ordinate dimension’s line, and a diameter’s or a radius’ line across a round face seen from the side: its distance beyond its view’s box on the side it lies. The multiples are counted from the box: one, two, three spacings out.
  • arc: an angle’s arc radius from the corner.
  • leader: a radius’ or diameter’s text on a leader: its reach beyond the circle.

The spacing comes from the dimension of the same family with the highest id in the drawing that was placed by hand (its line_offset, or a leader’s text_offset, set; a drag leaves out the one dragged). It is that dimension’s distance from the one stacked inside it on the same side of its view (a parallel line nearer the box, an arc or a leader about the same point), else its whole distance: three dimensions placed evenly give their step, not the outermost one’s distance. A place snaps when it lies within 4 mm of paper (and half a spacing) of a multiple, else it stays where it is. The first dimension of a drawing has nothing to snap to.

QueryFieldsResult
drawing_snapcommand: an add_drawing_annotation with its at, or an edit_drawing_annotation with its move; free (false): placed as given, only the result’s descriptionat (a new one) or move (a drag): the snapped place, or the one given; snapped; line_offset and text_offset that place gives; family and beyond (its distance as its family measures it, when it has one); when snapped spacing, multiple and from (the dimension the spacing came from). A note’s, a datum label’s or a frame’s drag (Leader angles, below): move, snapped, text_offset, and when snapped angle. What else is no dimension (a table, a line drawn outside the model; a note’s placing click) gets the place given and "snapped": false. Another command is refused

The logic is core/model-drawing/src/spacing.rs (gauge, spacing, snap_place, snap_move); the query model-api/src/drawing_spacing.rs. Class: the model’s.

Tests: core/model-drawing/src/spacing.rs (a line beyond its view’s box, multiples and the reach, a drag, stacked spacings, an angle’s radius and a leader’s reach), core/model-tests/drawing-views/src/spacing_tests.rs (the first dimension, the second at the first’s spacing, free, two and three spacings with the step of stacked ones, between multiples, a drag, a note, a wrong command, a note’s drag to 45 degrees), tools/ui-drawing-dimension-spacing-test.sh and app.ui-windows-drawing-spacing (tools/ui-windows-drawing-spacing-test.ps1).

Leader angles (mitcad#1294). A drag of a note’s text, a datum label’s square or a feature control frame (edit_drawing_annotation with move) snaps in drawing_snap so that its leader runs at a multiple of 45 degrees (0, 45, 90, … 315, counter-clockwise from the sheet’s x) when it would run within 4 degrees of one, its length kept: a note’s leader from its arrow to its shoulder, a frame’s from its arrow to the side of the frame it leaves, a datum’s from its triangle’s apex to the side of its square it meets (Annotations on drawing views). free: as dragged. The answer’s angle is the snapped one. A hole callout’s drag also returns preview when the callout can be drawn. Its group has the same items as in the drawing’s groups and its box gives the bounds in sheet millimetres. The group is laid out after applying the answer’s move, with or without a snap (mitcad#2253). The logic is core/model-drawing/src/annotate.rs (leader_line, snap_leader, datum_label); tests there (a datum on a horizontal edge with its square below left, above, left and right; a frame left, right, above and below its arrow; drags near 45, 90 and 180 degrees and ten degrees off) and in spacing_tests.rs.

Read-only BOM grouping (mitcad#1176)

{"query":"parts_list","group_identical":true} returns the Bill of Materials with equal measured parts combined; group_identical defaults to false. Single-body components have component rows; root bodies and the bodies of unstructured multi-body components have body rows instead of also being counted as a component row. Explicit feature-created, linked and library parts retain their component identity (including multi-body parts and their separate purchased-item rows). So does a component with a part number of its own (the row’s part_number: Identity › Part number, which Insert › Component from Web sets from the file’s name, or a library or BUILD part’s; mitcad#1663): it is one row with body null and its quantity by its placements, whatever its body count, so a downloaded bearing of nine bodies is one bearing. A multi-body component without a part number keeps a row per body. Bodyless component rows remain available, and purchased items remain separate. Each row has group_names for the source names and its summed quantity. Existing library, supplier and requested properties columns come from the first source. Grouping is a query only: it changes no saved state, body or undo item. The model’s internal component/library list and the BUILD cut list retain their existing contracts.

The key uses the kernel’s absolute volume, bounding-box dimensions along the component’s own axes, face count and effective material ids. Volume and each dimension must differ by at most 1e-6, face counts and material ids must be equal; names, placement translations and feature ids are not key fields. Mirrored equal geometry matches. Failed/nonfinite/unsupported measurements do not group, and the first member anchors tolerance comparisons without rounded bins. Different materials inherited along different placement paths are kept separate. This measured key is the report’s definition of equality; it is not a topological-identity or manufacturing-equivalence proof.

Requested Material and Computed/Material columns show the row’s effective physical material names, including materials inherited through its actual placement paths. They need no geometry-key measurements when grouping is off. Explicitly qualified user/library fields such as Identity/Material and Library/Material, and every other property column, keep their stored/library semantics. Bodyless component and purchased-item rows keep their legacy fields.

A drawing parts-list annotation’s table.group_identical boolean uses the same comparison, defaults to false, and can be supplied to add_drawing_annotation or edit_drawing_annotation. It is saved with the table as usual, with every source key and placement retaining the grouped item number for balloons. Row levels, sorting and shown property columns continue to apply.

A body’s own print values from the Make tab

mitcad#1178: the Make tab’s body card adds and clears a body’s own print values with the existing property commands; no command of its own.

  • Add Print Value… sets the chosen printer or process key on the body at the value the body prints with now: set_property with the body’s uid as owner, set Print Process (or Print Printer), the key and the value that print_settings gives for the body (its values[].value, as the profile or the nearer level holds it). One undo step, Set perimeters. A value typed on the card afterwards is another set_property (Set perimeters again).
  • Remove is remove_property with the same owner, set and key: one undo step, Remove perimeters; the body prints with the value it inherits again (an occurrence’s, a component’s or the profile’s).
  • These are the body-level properties of The Print property sets: print_settings gives them from: property, level: body, make_differences lists their plain names, and the 3MF exports write them as the body’s own (PrusaSlicer’s object perimeters, Bambu Studio’s part wall_loops, Cura’s wall_line_count).

Test: a_print_value_added_to_a_body_reaches_the_3mf_export (core/model-tests/print/src/print_files_tests.rs, mock kernel).

Print plates

mitcad#1050 (core/model/src/print_plates.rs, document/print_plates.rs, exchange/plates.rs, api/print_plates.rs): the design carries the plates it prints on, so that the 3MF goes to the slicer laid out and ready to print, with each plate’s own settings.

  • A plate has an id (plate1, the first free number; never another plate’s while the design has it), a name (Plate 1; unique ignoring case), its items and its own values. A design has at most 36 plates. The file keeps them as print_plates ([{"id", "name", "items": [{"body": "F1.b0", "count": 4}, {"occurrence": ["O1", "O4"]}], "values": {"spiral_vase": true}}], a count of 1 left out); an item whose body or occurrence is gone stays on its plate.
  • What goes on a plate: a body (the body itself, printed count times, each copy a piece of its own at its first shown placement) or an occurrence by its path (its printed bodies as assembled, count copies, each a piece). An item is on one plate at most: putting it on another moves it. What no item names goes on the first plate: each shown placement of a printed body without a body item that no occurrence item takes, each a piece of its own (a body that no occurrence places when its light bulb and its component’s Bodies folder show it). A body with no shown placement (hidden, or placed only in hidden occurrences) goes on no plate and is not exported (mitcad#2222): hiding a helper or reference body keeps it out of the plates’ 3MF, as hiding does for the other exports. A body item keeps its rule (its first shown placement, else its first), so a hidden body put on a plate on purpose still prints; an occurrence item prints its shown placements, all of them when none is shown. The print_plates query, plate_layout, the export and Send to Slicer’s plates follow.
  • Layout: automatic within each plate by the export’s arranger (Print bed faces): each piece on its print bed face, else the automatic orientation’s, dropped onto the bed, the pieces side by side along X, the row centred on the plate. With center: false the pieces keep their places in X and Y, but the copies of an item with a count are still set apart (mitcad#1311): each further copy beside the one before it along X, from the first copy’s place. Neighbours lie apart by the spacing beyond their brims, by the settings on their plate.
  • Plate settings: process values of the key map (the Print Process set, not the keys kept per slicer), in its JSON form, as a profile keeps them. The plate is a level of the settings order: profile < plate < component < occurrence < body. Its values come after the design’s own (the root’s values and its profiles) and before every component’s, occurrence’s and body’s, so a body’s own value still wins. A body prints on the plate of its own item, else of the outermost occurrence item of its placement, else the first plate (none without plates); print_settings gives a value from the plate as {"from": "plate", "plate": "plate2", "level": "plate", "owner_name": "Vase"} and names the plate ("plate": {"id", "name"}, null without one).

Commands, each one undo step that recomputes nothing (a plate by its id or name):

{"cmd": "add_print_plate", "name": "Vase"}          → {"id": "plate2", "name": "Vase"}   "Add Vase"
{"cmd": "edit_print_plate", "plate": "Vase", "name": "Vases",
 "values": {"spiral_vase": true, "layer_height": null}}        "Edit Vase"
{"cmd": "move_print_plate", "plate": "Vase", "index": 0}       "Move Vase"
{"cmd": "delete_print_plate", "plate": "Vase"}                 "Delete Vase"
{"cmd": "place_on_plate", "plate": "Vase",
 "items": [{"body": "Body1", "count": 4}, {"occurrence": "Arm:1"}]}   "Put 2 items on Vase"
{"cmd": "remove_from_plates", "items": [{"occurrence": "O1"}]} "Take Arm:1 off Vase"

name left out is Plate <n>. edit_print_plate renames (Rename …), sets values and takes them away (a key’s null); one value alone is Set Layer height of Vase or Clear Layer height of Vase. A body is given by uid or name (a printed body at the marker: a solid or a mesh body), an occurrence by its path of uids or names; count is 1 to 999, left out the count the item has (here or on the plate it leaves), else 1. What is on a deleted plate goes on no plate (the first one’s). Nothing changing is no undo step.

remove_from_plates takes items off: what it takes off goes back to the first plate in its shown placements. A body or occurrence that is no plate’s item refuses the whole call (also when it names items too), changing nothing and making no undo step, a line for each such target (mitcad#2222):

Body2 is not placed on a plate by itself: what no plate names prints on the first plate; hide it to leave it out.

Moves (mitcad#1595). An item is on one plate at most, so place_on_plate takes an item that is on another plate off it. Its result lists each such item, in the order of items, with the plate it left and the count it had there, and says so in warnings (one line each):

{"cmd": "place_on_plate", "plate": "two", "items": [{"body": "Body1"}]}
→ {"moved": [{"body": "F1.b0", "name": "Body1", "count": 2,
              "from": {"id": "plate1", "name": "one", "count": 2},
              "to": {"id": "plate2", "name": "two"}}],
   "warnings": ["Body1 moved from one to two (count 2)"]}      "Move Body1 from one to two"
  • An item is {"body": uid} or {"occurrence": "O1/O4"} (its path of uids), with name (the body’s, or the occurrence’s path of names Arm:1/Pin:2) as print_plates lists items. count is its count on the plate now: the one given, else the one it had (from.count). A count given that replaces another says so: Body1 moved from two to one (count 3, was 2).
  • A first placement, a change on the plate the item is on and a call that changes nothing move nothing: {"moved": [], "warnings": []}. In a batch only the items that left another plate are listed, each with its own from.
  • One moved item names the move in the undo text (Move Body1 from one to two, Move 3 of Body1 from two to one with a count above 1); several items keep Put 2 items on two. Undo puts the items back on the plates they left with their counts; redo moves them again.
  • Through MCP, model_command’s result is this result (the last command’s in an array). mitcad-cli run prints a line for each moved item before its report (to stderr with --json): Plates: Body1 moved from one to two (count 2).

Queries:

  • {"query": "print_plates"} → {"plates": [{"id", "name", "index", "items": [{"body" | "occurrence", "name", "count", "missing": true when gone}], "values": [{"key", "name", "value", "text"}], "pieces", "bodies": [{"body", "name", "occurrence", "occurrence_name"}]}], "unplaced": [{"body", "name", "occurrence", "occurrence_name"}]}: pieces the objects the plate prints (the first plate’s with the placements on no plate), bodies each placement it prints once, as the export makes them (a body item’s first shown placement, an occurrence item’s bodies by their paths, occurrence empty for a body not placed; mitcad#1807: print_settings of each gives the settings the export gives it), unplaced the placements on no plate.
  • {"query": "plate_layout", "plate": "Vase"} → {"plate", "name", "index", "bed": [[x, y], …], "shift": [x, y], "pieces", "bodies": [{"body", "name", "transforms": [[[a, b, c, t] × 3], …]}], "warnings"}: how the plate’s pieces lie, drawn beside the design (the bed’s left edge a fifth of its width right of the shown bodies, its middle level with theirs; without shown bodies centred on the origin): the bed’s outline and each body’s placements there from its component’s coordinates, the plate’s coordinates (the printer’s bed_shape, else 256 × 256 mm) moved by shift. Meshed coarsely.
  • print_settings takes "plate" (id or name): the settings on that plate; left out, a body’s or an occurrence’s own plate.

Export (export of a 3MF; on the print bed, on_bed implied; no bodies, occurrence, occurrences, whole or bed_face with it):

  • "plates": "one_file": every plate in the one file, for the slicers that keep several plates. The Bambu family (and no dialect) lays plates out on a grid of ceil(sqrt(n)) columns (one more when the square root rounds down), each a plate’s width and depth plus a fifth apart, rows towards −Y; each plate is a <plate> block of model_settings.config with plater_id (from 1), plater_name, locked, a model_instance per object on it (object_id, instance_id 0, identify_id) and the plate settings the family keeps per plate when the project does not set them for every part (spiral_mode true/false, print_sequence by its name), never as an object’s override. PrusaSlicer 2.9 and later reads its beds from where the objects lie: the beds on its grid growing in rings from the first ((0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1), (2, 0), …), a bed’s size plus a gap of 3/10 of its diagonal (at most 100 mm) apart; it keeps spiral_vase and complete_objects for the whole project, so a part’s own value of one is left out with a warning. Cura has one build plate: refused.
  • "plates": "file_per_plate": a file per plate beside the path, <name> - <plate name>.3mf (characters a file name cannot have become _; a name that gives the file of a plate before it, compared ignoring case, takes (2), (3), …: A/B and A:B write <name> - A_B.3mf and <name> - A_B (2).3mf, mitcad#1316), each plate a project of its own; an empty plate writes no file. For Cura and PrusaSlicer before 2.9.
  • "plate": "Vase": that plate alone, in the path.

Through MCP, model_export with "format": "3mf" takes these fields and the other 3MF and print bed fields of export (dialect, on_bed, center, drop, auto_orient, bed_face, spacing, occurrence, occurrences, whole) and answers with this result (mitcad#1490, docs/mcp.md): {"name": "model_export", "arguments": {"path": "kit.3mf", "format": "3mf", "plates": "one_file", "dialect": "bambu_studio"}}. Each file of file_per_plate must be a new file in the folders the agent may write to, or an existing one there with "overwrite": true (mitcad#1569), checked before any is written. The application’s File › Export of a 3MF file sends the same fields (plates or plate, dialect, on_bed, center, drop; mitcad#1679, app/COMMANDS.md Export and 3D Print).

The result adds "plates": [{"id", "name", "path" (null for an empty plate of a file per plate), "bodies", "pieces", "origin" (where its bed lies in a file of several plates), "bed" (as an export's bed), "warnings"}] and "files" (the paths written, each once); every body on a plate takes that plate’s settings. Items whose body or occurrence is gone are left out with a warning. Each placement prints on one plate, its body’s (mitcad#1310): an occurrence item leaves out the bodies under it that have an item of their own, or lie under an outer occurrence item, on another plate, with a warning when that leaves it nothing; the print_plates query’s pieces and plate_layout count alike.

Tests: core/model-tests/print/src/print_plates_tests.rs (mock kernel: items with counts, the settings order, the file, a Bambu-family project of two plates with the vase mode on its plate, PrusaSlicer’s beds, a Cura file per plate, a plate’s layout) and the unit tests of core/model/src/print_plates.rs (the slicers’ grids). The moves: core/model-tests/print/src/plate_moves_tests.rs (mock kernel), the ctest cli.plate_move (tools/cli/tests/plate_move.json) and test_place_on_plate_reports_the_plate_an_item_left in tools/cli/mcp-test.py.

How volumes and areas are computed (mitcad#1200)

Every volume, area, centre of mass, mass and inertia a query gives comes from one integration of the body’s faces in the geometry facade (the analysis library’s volume_properties and surface_properties, mitcad#140): the bodies and instances queries’ volume, area and center, properties (Physical Properties: volume, area, mass, center_of_mass, inertia), measure’s volume and area, section’s area, interference’s volume, the BOM’s and the reports’ masses and volumes, the print estimates (Print analysis and the Make tab’s), the design checks ("volume", "area") and the imports’ reports. So the same body gives the same value everywhere.

  • Each face is integrated span by span by the divergence theorem (a volume) or over its surface (an area): along its boundary curves and across the surface, split at the knots of the surface and the curves, where the curves cross the surface’s knot lines and at every eighth of a turn of an angle parameter, with Gauss rules exact for the polynomial pieces’ second moments and more points for rational and offset faces. Faces without a surface (mesh bodies) are integrated over their triangles; faces reaching to infinity keep the geometry kernel’s fixed rule.
  • Accuracy: within 1e-9 (relative) of the exact value for planes, cylinders, cones, spheres, tori, extrusions, revolutions and B-spline faces of the tests, and within 1e-8 of a reference integration for lofts and their shells and offsets (geometry.accurate_volumes: an adaptive Gauss-Kronrod rule for curved faces, a dense polygon through the boundary curves for plane ones). The geometry kernel’s own rules (OCCT’s BRepGProp, with or without an accuracy) integrate along a face’s boundary curves alone, so where an offset leaves gaps between the curves’ ends (within the edges’ tolerance) they leave out a strip at each gap, 3e-6 of a 1 mm shell of a loft; MitCad’s integration joins the gaps.
  • Cost: the number of points is fixed by the geometry, not by a tolerance, so a body measures the same every time: a piece per span (a rational span in four), at most 1024 steps of an angle parameter per stretch, at most 30 points per piece. Faces are integrated on all cores, and a body’s measures are kept with its shape, so it is measured once. There is no time limit with a coarser fallback.
  • The FreeCAD import’s reference check alone measures with the kernel’s default rule too (Kernel::fixed_point_properties), to compare with programs that measure so.

Material properties

A material’s mechanical and thermal properties, their units, the bundled material dataset and materials as JSON and CSV files (mitcad#1213; core/model/src/material.rs, material_units.rs, material_dataset.rs, material_exchange.rs, document/material_import.rs, api/materials.rs). The properties are data: no analysis uses them yet; they are shown on the material, in Physical Properties (properties) and in a parts list, and carried by the design file, the libraries and the files below.

  • Properties: a material’s properties holds the values given, in the model’s units: youngs_modulus (MPa, above 0), poissons_ratio (above -1, at most 0.5), yield_strength (MPa, above 0), max_service_temperature (°C, above absolute zero) and thermal_expansion (the coefficient, µm/(m·°C)); Mechanical the first three, Thermal the last two. A value not given is left out, never 0; designs and library files from before have none and read as before. create_material and edit_material take properties with the values that change (null takes one away; an unknown key is refused). The printing values are the print settings’ own (no second set): the extruder temperature is the filament’s temperature, the bed temperature its bed_temperature.
  • Reference: reference ({source, material, grade, revision}, the source required) says where the values came from: a dataset or a supplier’s sheet. A copy keeps it; null takes it away.
  • Units: the values are shown in the design’s unit system, its length unit’s: a metric design (mm, cm, m, km, µm) MPa, g/cm³ and µm/(m·°C), an inch design (in, ft, yd, mi, mil) psi, lb/in³ and µin/(in·°F) (the expansion coefficient’s degree follows the system); temperatures in °C or °F as the user prefers, everywhere (the material card, Physical Properties, parts lists and bills of materials): the application gives the model its setting at start and when it changes (the bridge’s set_temperature_unit, °C until then), and a query’s temperature left out is that unit. Commands always take the model’s units.
  • The dataset is the bundled material dataset (Apache-2.0, third_party/material-properties): typical values of 112 metals and 7 printing materials, offline; and beside it MitCad’s own woods and wood-based panels (mitcad#1552, MIT, core/model/data/wood_materials.json): 10 woods (wood/birch, wood/cedar, wood/cherry, wood/douglas_fir, wood/eucalyptus, wood/maple, wood/oak, wood/pine, wood/teak, wood/walnut) with their density and Young’s modulus at 12 % moisture, and 7 panels (panel/chipboard, panel/mdf_raw, panel/osb3, panel/plywood_birch, panel/plywood_eucalyptus, panel/plywood_pine, panel/plywood_spruce) with their density, all of the class wood, each with a look of its own from the appearance library (wood_oak, plywood_birch, panel_osb, …) and its reference naming the public source its values were checked against (material-files.md, “The woods and panels”); a value the source does not give is not given. Both are searched and listed as one, the third-party materials first. create_material with dataset (an entry’s id, aluminum/6061/t6) makes a material of the entry’s values, converted from the dataset’s units, its class, an appearance of its kind and the entry as its reference (the dataset, material, grade and the data’s revision); it is named as the entry (Aluminum 6061, T6, numbered when the name is taken) and is the user’s own: a newer dataset never changes it. With library it is made there. dataset and based_on together are refused; edit_material refuses dataset. create_dataset_materials (mitcad#1706, below) makes several at once, skipping a name that is there already. Five common woods and panels are built in with the dataset’s values (wood_oak, …, see Materials).
  • Files: material-files.md gives the JSON and CSV formats; both state their units.
CommandFieldsResult
import_materialstext (the file’s text: the application reads the file), format (json or csv), conflict (on a name that is there already: keep, the default, replace, keep_both, or ask), library (user or project: into that library; the design when left out), projectadded and replaced (ids), kept (names), conflicts (with ask: the names that are there already, and nothing imported; none: imported as with keep), errors ({row, name, message}: a material of the file that is not valid, its line in a CSV, its place from 1 in a JSON file, imported without it); one undo step Import Materials; a file that cannot be read at all is refused
create_dataset_materialsentries (the dataset entries’ ids, wood/walnut, panel/plywood_pine: one or more), library (user or project: into that library; the design when left out), project (mitcad#1706)added (the ids of the materials made, in the entries’ order: each as create_material with that dataset makes it, its values, class, look and reference), skipped (the names of the entries not made because a material of that name, any case, is there already: the design’s own or a built-in one it shows, or in a library its items or a built-in one; a second entry of the same name too); one undo step Create Materials (one made: Create Material <name>; none: no step), the library’s files written in it; an entry the dataset lacks, or none, is refused and nothing is made

A name is matched in any case: the design’s own materials and the built-in ones it shows, or the library’s items. replace gives the material the file’s values, the ones the file does not give kept (a built-in one gets a material of the design in its place, named as it); keep_both adds the file’s numbered (Steel (2)), past every name the design shows in any case (steel beside the built-in Steel is steel (2), mitcad#1315). A material the import adds needs a density.

QueryFieldsResult
material_unitsunits (metric or imperial: the design’s when left out), temperature (C or F, the preferred unit when left out)units, temperature, quantities (density, stress, temperature, expansion, ratio: each {symbol, scale, offset}, a value in the model’s unit shown as value * scale + offset: psi’s scale is 145.0377), properties ({key, name, group, group_title, quantity, unit} in their order), printing (the print settings’ temperature and bed_temperature: {key, name, quantity, unit})
material_datasetsearch (words each found material’s name, material, grade or id holds, any case; all when left out)name, license (the third-party dataset’s), caution (that the values are typical), sources ({name, license} of each part: material-properties dataset, Apache-2.0; MitCad wood and panel materials, MIT; mitcad#1552), count (all its materials), materials: {id, name, class, density, properties, filament, reference} in the model’s units
export_materialsformat (json or csv), ids (the design’s and built-in materials; the design’s own when left out and no materials are given), materials (materials given whole, as materials or library_items list them: a library’s items), units (the design’s when left out), temperature (the preferred unit when left out)text (the file), count, format, units, temperature

properties (Physical Properties) takes temperature too and gives each body with a material material_properties: {key, name, group, text} for each value given (group mechanical, thermal or printing for the print settings’ extruder and bed temperature), its text in the design’s units (29007500 psi, 212 °F). A parts list’s column named by a property’s name or key (Young's modulus, yield_strength) or Density shows the row’s material’s value, in the design’s units with temperatures in the preferred unit: a body’s material, a component’s when all its bodies share one (without bodies its default material); a stored property of the component of that name comes first.

Auto Fix

A feature whose stored reference is no longer found exactly is computed with what the model found instead and keeps a warning naming both: a region found as another region or the sum of several (Profile references after a sketch change), a face, edge or vertex a sketch change renamed (Faces, edges and vertices a sketch change renamed). The definition keeps the old reference, so the warning stays. Auto Fix (mitcad#1223; core/model/src/document/auto_fix.rs, api/auto_fix.rs) writes into the definitions what the model found and used, so that the bodies stay as they are and the warnings go:

CommandFieldsResult
auto_fixfeatures: uids (a selection, a timeline group’s members); all features when left out or empty; shared (parameter or own): what a thread’s fit does with a named parameter other places use (mitcad#1632)warnings (the reference problems and the thread fit warnings of those features before), fixed (those gone after), changed and followed (the features whose definitions changed; followed those not asked for), left (each problem left: feature, name, message, advice), fitted (each face fitted to its thread: thread, name, face, diameter, needed, internal, source, source_name, parameter, named, old and new expression, others, message), choices (the named parameters a fit left for a choice: feature, parameter, others), filament_faces (with every feature: the filament changes at faces an edit renamed, written with the names found, mitcad#1643), label (the undo step’s name, null when nothing changed) and message: Auto Fix: 2 of 3 warnings fixed; Hole1: the body has no edge E{…}, pick it again
  • What it writes is read from the warnings themselves, which name the stored reference and exactly what the computation used: face F2:side(c1[c4,c2]) found as F2:side(c1[c4,c9]) after a change in Sketch1 replaces the name wherever the definition holds it (a face, the faces of an edge or a vertex, a plane or a sketch on the face, a projection). region r{…} found as r{…} + r{…} after a change in Sketch1 gives a reference in a list of profiles every region it was found as, at its place and in that order, each once (a region the list has later moves up); a region reference elsewhere (a loft section, a sheet’s panel slot) takes the main region, the first one named, which is the one the computation used there. Only references of the sketch the warning names are changed.
  • The result stays. The fixed definition finds every reference exactly and builds the same bodies (the same regions, faces and edges). The faces made from a region now carry its new key (F2:end(r{…}) instead of the old one): a later feature that named them finds them again with a warning of its own, and Auto Fix fixes that too in the same step (followed; the message ends also updated: Shell1).
  • Checked before it is taken. Each feature’s fix is computed first, in timeline order. It is not taken, and its warnings stay with the reason in left, when it would make a feature that built fail (fixing it would make Fillet2 fail), when the warning would stay, when the definition does not hold the reference (the definition does not hold the reference) or when the feature’s component cannot be changed (a linked component).
  • Not fixable: a reference that is gone (the body has no edge E{…}, edge E{…} no longer exists after Chamfer1, Sketch1 has no profile r{…}) or ambiguous (F2:side(…) is ambiguous after a sketch change: …): the feature fails and nothing is changed; left names it with pick it again or pick one of them again. Other warnings (a fillet built as rings) are not references and are neither counted nor changed.
  • A thread whose face does not fit it (mitcad#1632, Fitting the face to the thread): after the references, the value or dimension that sets the face’s diameter is changed to the thread’s crest diameter, checked the same way; fitted names what was changed from what to what, and the message says it in words: Auto Fix: 1 of 1 warning fixed; Thread2: the hole fitted to the thread: Sketch2's dimension 72/2 is now 73.835/2. A face nothing Auto Fix can change sets is left with change the hole by hand (<why>); a fit that would change a named parameter other places use is left without shared (choices).
  • One undo step: Auto Fix Extrude8 for one feature, Auto Fix <group> when the features are a timeline group’s, else Auto Fix 3 Features. Nothing fixed: no step. A cancelled computation (P7) changes nothing.
  • The timeline query gives a feature whose warnings Auto Fix can write auto_fix: how many (left out when none); the application offers Auto Fix then. A thread whose fit would change a named parameter other places use also has auto_fix_choices (parameter, others): the application asks which way first.

Tests: core/model-tests/features-solid/src/auto_fix_tests.rs (a region found as another and as the sum of two, a renamed face, a face renamed by the fix followed in a later feature, an ambiguous reference left with its error; the definitions, the bodies, the warnings and undo), document::auto_fix::tests (the warnings read, the lists of profiles, names replaced).

Envelope

An envelope feature (mitcad#1271; features/envelope.rs, features/envelope/wrap.rs) makes a new body, a light outer skin of bodies, with add_feature and edit_feature, preview, Undo and persistence:

{"type": "envelope", "occurrence": "O1", "detail": 20}
{"type": "envelope", "bodies": ["F2.b0", "F4.b0"]}
{"type": "envelope"}
  • Source. occurrence (an occurrence path from the feature’s component, "O1/O4"; left out: the feature’s own component) names the component whose bodies it wraps, with the bodies of the occurrences placed in it (and in those), each where its occurrences put it, at the feature’s point of the timeline; a linked component’s too. bodies (of that component) wraps only those. Hidden bodies and occurrences count: the source is what the timeline holds.
  • detail (mm, more than 0; left out: 1 % of the diagonal of the source’s box, at least 5 mm): gaps, holes and features narrower than it are closed over; openings wider than it stay open; enclosed cavities fill.
  • How. The bodies are tessellated by the kernel within a quarter of the detail size (Kernel::triangle_mesh) and wrapped in plain Rust on a grid of cells half the detail size: the cells the triangles pass through are marked (a face on a cell boundary marks the cells inside it), grown by one cell, the outside flood-filled from the grid’s border, the rest made solid and shrunk back by one cell (a morphological closing), then made well-composed (cells that touch only at an edge or a corner joined), and the cells’ surface is taken in runs of flat faces. Convert Mesh’s faceted solid (faceted_solid) merges it into planar faces, and the kernel builds them as a solid (Kernel::boundary_body): faces <feature>:import(<n>), square to the component’s axes, outside the source by at most about one cell. No kernel method of its own. The body is <feature>.b0, a solid of each piece further apart than the detail size.
  • The new body is named after the feature (Envelope1) unless that name is taken, takes the appearance of the first source body that has one when the feature is added (the listed bodies in order, else the component’s own bodies before its occurrences’), and is marked "envelope": true in the bodies query. The feature’s information (infos) tells the detail size, the faces and the grid (detail size 20 mm: 10 faces wrapped on 27 × 27 × 27 cells of 10 mm).
  • Follows its source: built again on every recompute from the bodies and placements it read; the bodies are only read.
  • Refused: a body listed twice, a detail size of 0 or less. Fails: no bodies to wrap (there are no bodies to wrap), an occurrence path that does not exist, a detail size so small for the source that the grid would have more than 16 777 216 cells (the message names the smallest size that fits) or the surface more than 500 000 triangles.

Linked components shown by their envelopes

CommandFieldsResult
