The path is the result’s keys and list indexes joined by dots: sk.uid, l1.made.0 (the line), rect.entities.4, body.uid. The value takes the reference’s place as it is (a text, a number, a list or an object).
  • Points at the inputs. A drawing command’s result has inputs, the point at each point input as written (Sketch commands); a first key the result lacks is looked up there, so l1.end is l1.inputs.end, and outline.points.0 is a spline’s first point. They are the ends as the caller wrote them, whatever the stored orientation: arcs are stored counter-clockwise, so a clockwise arc’s definition (start, end) and the sketch query’s geometry run from the end written to the start written, but a1.start is still the point at the start written and a1.end the point at the end written. An input where the command makes no point of its own (an arc’s through) is null.

What is checked:

  • Before any entry runs: a reference that is not {"ref": "<name>.<path>"} alone with a path, a malformed name or one given twice, a reference to a name no entry has, to its own entry or to a later one, and a reference as cmd. The array is refused with nothing run: applied false, entry the entry, undone 0, the error naming the reference (commands[5]: {"ref": "a1.end"}: “a1” is entry 6, which runs after this one: …). A print import takes no references: it reads its sources before the array runs.
  • Right before its entry: a path the result lacks (the error lists the keys it has and its inputs), null, and a value of the wrong kind: not a point ("p<n>" or [x, y]) in a drawing command’s point input, not a text in a sketch command’s sketch. The entry is refused, and as for any refused entry the entries before it are undone and nothing of the array stays (applied false, entry, undone). The command a reference makes is checked again as MCP checks every command, so a reference cannot make one that MCP refuses (a file read).
  • Elsewhere the command checks the value as it checks any: a curve id where a constraint takes a point is refused by the constraint.

Refused and failed entries. A refused entry (a reference, a field, a sketch that would no longer solve) undoes the whole array. An entry whose added or edited feature fails is applied: the array stops after it (stopped_at), and the entries before it and the failed feature stay in the timeline (edit it, or undo); results has the result of each entry that ran, ran how many. Ordinary arrays are as before: entries without as and references run unchanged, and ids written out ("F1", "p3") are taken as they are.

When one array is enough, and when a query is needed. One array holds a sketch, its curves joined by references, the constraints and dimensions on them (by made, entities and inputs) and features whose references are made in the array or picked by geometry: a profile by a point inside it ({"sketch": {"ref": "sk.uid"}, "point": [u, v]}), a fillet’s edges by a filter. A query is still needed for topology the array cannot name ahead: the faces and edges of a body built in it (their names come from the modelling history; query faces or edges, or pick them by a filter), a profile no point picks alone, and to check the result. Region keys and edge names from an earlier run are no plan for a design made the first time: they hold only where the same steps made the same geometry.

A plate w × h (60 × 40) with its bottom left corner at the origin, a top side that sags 10 mm inwards (a clockwise arc of radius 50), fully constrained, extruded by t, in one array; changing w or h afterwards moves the corners they drive (Point coordinates as expressions):

[{"cmd": "add_parameter", "name": "w", "value": 60},
 {"cmd": "add_parameter", "name": "h", "value": 40},
 {"cmd": "add_parameter", "name": "t", "value": 5},
 {"cmd": "sketch.create", "as": "sk"},
 {"cmd": "sketch.add_line", "sketch": {"ref": "sk.uid"}, "as": "l1",
  "start": ["0", "0"], "end": ["w", 0]},
 {"cmd": "sketch.add_line", "sketch": {"ref": "sk.uid"}, "as": "l2",
  "start": {"ref": "l1.end"}, "end": ["w", "h"]},
 {"cmd": "sketch.arc", "sketch": {"ref": "sk.uid"}, "as": "a1", "mode": "three_point",
  "start": {"ref": "l2.end"}, "through": [30, 30], "end": [0, "h"]},
 {"cmd": "sketch.add_line", "sketch": {"ref": "sk.uid"}, "as": "l3",
  "start": {"ref": "a1.end"}, "end": {"ref": "l1.start"}},
 {"cmd": "sketch.add_constraint", "sketch": {"ref": "sk.uid"},
  "constraint": {"type": "horizontal", "line": {"ref": "l1.made.0"}}},
 {"cmd": "sketch.add_constraint", "sketch": {"ref": "sk.uid"},
  "constraint": {"type": "vertical", "line": {"ref": "l3.made.0"}}},
 {"cmd": "sketch.add_dimension", "sketch": {"ref": "sk.uid"},
  "dimension": {"type": "radius", "curve": {"ref": "a1.made.0"}}},
 {"cmd": "add_feature", "as": "body",
  "def": {"type": "extrude", "profiles": [{"sketch": {"ref": "sk.uid"}, "point": [30, 10]}],
          "extent": {"type": "distance", "distance": "t"}, "operation": "new_body"}}]

The arc’s end is written before l3 exists, so l3 starts at {"ref": "a1.end"}, the point at (0, h), although the arc is stored from there to (w, h); l3 closes the outline on {"ref": "l1.start"}. The dimension’s result has "status": {"dof": 0, …}.

Rules: core/mcp/src/array_refs.rs (check_refs, resolve_entry), used by both servers (core/ffi/src/mcp.rs run_commands, app/MainWindowMcp.cpp). Tests: core/mcp/src/array_refs.rs (the rules), core/model-tests/api/src/array_refs_1897_tests.rs (this array with the mock kernel, refusals, a failed extrusion), tools/cli/mcp-array-refs-test.cmake (through the headless server).

Point coordinates as expressions (mitcad#1897)

A coordinate of a new point of a drawing command is a number or a text: sketch.add_point’s at, and the point inputs of sketch.add_line, sketch.rectangle, sketch.circle, sketch.arc, sketch.polygon, sketch.slot, sketch.ellipse and sketch.spline.

  • A number is millimetres in sketch coordinates, a position as before: nothing holds the point there.
  • A text is an expression of the document’s parameters ("w", "w/2", "h + 3", "2 * pitch", also "20" or "0.5 in"), read as a dimension’s value is: bare numbers in the document’s length unit (Values). It is evaluated when the command runs and the point is drawn there. Then a driving signed horizontal_distance (x) or vertical_distance (y) from the sketch’s origin point to the new point holds it there, with the text as its value (Signed point dimensions): a parameter’s name makes the dimension use that parameter, another expression becomes a parameter of the dimension’s own (Sketch1 p5 x). Changing a parameter it uses moves the point at the next recompute, to either side of the origin.
  • Frame: x and y along the sketch’s axes from its origin. The origin point, a fixed point at [0, 0], is made in the same edit when the sketch has none (The sketch’s axes and origin as entities).
  • Mixed and shared points: ["w", 5] holds x and leaves y free; nothing else is fixed or dimensioned, so the sketch’s other degrees of freedom are the caller’s to constrain. A point given by its id ("p3", or a reference) is that existing point, with whatever holds it: only new points take expressions. To make an existing point follow a parameter, add the signed dimension (sketch.add_dimension).
  • Result: as other edits (the new dimensions in dimensions, new parameters in parameters, the origin point among entities when it was made), and coordinates, each coordinate’s dimension and the parameter it uses: [{"point": "p5", "axis": "x", "dimension": "k7", "expression": "w", "parameter": "w"}].
  • Refused, with the sketch and the parameters as they were: an expression that does not evaluate (end.x: parameter nope does not exist), one at an input where the command makes no point of its own (an arc’s through, a circumscribed polygon’s vertex: through: the command makes no point of its own there, …), a text in a field that is only a position or a direction (an arc’s centre mode end; a move’s and a scale’s fields say so in words, see Point coordinates as expressions in 3D sketches), and coordinates that over-constrain or contradict the sketch (on a fixed point: the coordinates written as expressions would over-constrain the sketch: …). A later constraint that the coordinates' dimensions already imply, or that contradicts them, is refused as any such constraint is.
  • Number coordinates and point ids are as before and add no dimension.
{"cmd": "sketch.add_line", "sketch": "F1", "start": [0, 0], "end": ["w", 5]}

in an empty sketch gives "made": ["c1"], "inputs": {"start": "p2", "end": "p3"} and "coordinates": [{"point": "p3", "axis": "x", "dimension": "k1", "expression": "w", "parameter": "w"}] (the origin point made for the dimension is p4); after set_parameter w 80 the end is at (80, 5).

Code: core/sketch/src/inputs.rs (DrawnInputs), read by the drawing commands in core/model-api/src/sketch.rs. Tests: core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_expression_points_1897_tests.rs.

Point coordinates as expressions in 3D sketches (mitcad#1912)

A 3D sketch’s drawing commands take coordinates written as expressions as the planar ones do (Point coordinates as expressions): a new point’s [x, y, z] coordinate is a number (millimetres in the sketch’s frame) or a text, an expression of the document’s parameters read as a dimension’s value is (["w", 0, "h / 2"]). The fields: sketch3d.add_point’s at, and the point inputs of sketch3d.add_line, sketch3d.add_arc (start, end, a centre arc’s center), sketch3d.add_circle, sketch3d.add_spline, sketch3d.add_ellipse, sketch3d.add_rectangle and sketch3d.add_polygon.

  • Held by Offset dimensions. The expression is evaluated when the command runs and the point is drawn there; a driving offset dimension (the signed b - a along the frame’s X, Y or Z) from the sketch’s origin point to the new point holds it there, with the text as its value, so that changing a parameter it uses moves the point at the next recompute. A number coordinate stays free, as before.
  • The origin point is a point attached to the sketch’s origin (an attach relation with the source "origin"): the first such point the sketch has (a line’s start given "start_source": "origin" is one), or a new one made in the same edit.
  • Which point: the point the command made at the input, also where the tool moved it (a line’s end put on its axis or offsets, a centre arc’s end on its circle).
  • Result: as other edits (the dimensions in dimensions, new parameters in parameters, the origin point among entities when it was made), and, when a coordinate was written as an expression, inputs (the point at each point input; null where none, a spline’s points as a list) and coordinates ([{"point": "p2", "axis": "x", "dimension": "k3", "expression": "w", "parameter": "w"}]). A command with numbers only answers as before.
  • Refused in words, the sketch as it was: an expression that does not evaluate (at.x: …); a text where the command makes no point of its own, a place only: a three-point arc’s through, a three-point rectangle’s c, a circumscribed polygon’s vertex, a text’s at and frame (through: the command makes no point of its own there, so its coordinates cannot follow parameters: give numbers, and dimension a point afterwards); sketch3d.add_point’s at given as a point id. On a point that is also fixed or attached the solve refuses a contradiction, or lists the redundant dimension in status’s redundant.

Planar position fields. A field that is only read once cannot follow parameters, and a text in it is refused in words: sketch.move’s by ("by" of a move is read once, so it cannot follow parameters: give numbers), from, to and rotate’s center (… give numbers or an existing point), and sketch.scale’s center. A circular pattern’s center (sketch.circular_pattern, sketch.edit_pattern) is a point of the sketch: written with an expression, the new centre point is held by signed horizontal_distance and vertical_distance dimensions from the origin in both coordinates (a number coordinate as a length of its own, "0 mm") instead of being fixed, so that the pattern follows the parameters:

{"cmd": "sketch.circular_pattern", "sketch": "F1", "entities": ["c1"], "center": ["w/2", 0], "count": 6}

Code: core/sketch/src/spatial_inputs.rs (SpatialDrawnInputs), read by core/model-api/src/sketch3d.rs; the planar fields in core/model-api/src/sketch.rs. Tests: core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_expression_points_1912_tests.rs.

Curved outlines and extreme points on drawing views; labels moved (mitcad#1909)

A view draws the outline of a curved face where it turns away from the eye (a pipe bend’s outer curve seen along its axis, a sphere, a cone seen from the side, a free-form face): a silhouette, no edge of the model. Dimension picks it as it picks edges, and the extreme points of curves are points a click picks, so that an overall size to the top of a curved outline can be placed (GitHub #363).

Silhouettes. drawing_pick (and a command’s picks given as sheet points) finds, beside each body’s edges and faces, the silhouettes of its curved faces other than cylinders (cones, spheres, tori, free-form faces) seen along the view’s direction, as the geometry kernel works them out (Kernel::face_silhouettes, kept per body version and direction). A torus seen from the side keeps its tube’s arcs either side of its axis (side, mitcad#1694); a silhouette on an edge’s line is that edge. A silhouette that is a line, or a circle or an arc seen end on (a torus’s outer and inner outlines seen along its axis and a sphere’s outline are their circles, taken from the surface), is picked whole: its pick is the face with outline, a point of it in its body’s coordinates, and the drawing_pick answer’s seen is line or circle. Alone it makes what an edge of its kind makes: an arc a radius, a circle a diameter, a line its length (between its extreme points along it). A silhouette of another curve is picked by its extreme points only. When the view is drawn again the outline is found again: of the face’s silhouettes seen along the view’s direction, the one nearest that point, so it follows the model; when the face has none there any more the annotation is broken, its error the outline of a curved face it was picked on is gone: the view no longer sees the face turn away there (no names).

Extreme points. A pick’s extreme (a direction in its body’s coordinates) makes it the point of what the rest of it names (an edge, a round face seen from the side or end on, a torus face’s side, an outline) that lies furthest that way as the view sees it: a circle’s point facing that way (an arc’s, or its end furthest that way), a line’s end (its middle when it runs square to the direction), a round face’s outline on that side. drawing_pick with want any, point, snap or neither (dimension) offers as points the extreme points of each silhouette along the view’s x and y, and takes from, a sheet point (the Dimension tool sends its first pick’s): then also those of circles seen end on and round faces seen from the side along the view’s x and y, and of each of these and the silhouettes along the line from from (its farthest and its nearest point), for an aligned dimension. One where a pick’s point already is (an edge’s end) is that pick. Its seen is point; alone it waits for a second pick ("alone": false). A linear dimension from an edge to an extreme point measures to that point, so a vertical one from a bend’s straight bottom edge to the top of its outline reads its overall height; the pick follows the model as the rest of it does. extreme takes no point, on_face, on_cut or drawn; outline is a pick of a curved face alone (with point center: a circle outline’s centre). A pick refused: an outline is a pick of a curved face alone, an extreme point is of an edge, a round face or an outline picked whole.

A view’s label moved. A section’s label (SECTION A-A), a detail’s (DETAIL B (2:1)) and any view’s own label is drawn under the middle of the view’s box, moved by the view’s label_offset (sheet mm), which edit_drawing_view sets: label_move (a drag: added to it) or label_offset (where it goes; [0, 0] puts it back under the view; undo step Move the label of view 2 of Drawing1 when nothing else changes). The offset is from the label’s own place, so it moves with the view. The drawing query lists each view’s label_offset (null when it was not moved) and, on the sheet asked for, its label_box (on the sheet, where the application starts a drag). Files: a view’s label_offset, left out when none.

Code: core/model-api/src/drawing_silhouettes.rs (silhouettes as a view sees them, their extreme points), core/model-api/src/drawing_annotations.rs (candidates_and_outlines, extreme_candidates, resolve_outline), core/model-drawing/src/annotate.rs (Seen::extreme), core/model-drawing/src/compose.rs (PlacedView::label_group), core/model-api/src/drawings.rs (label_move, label_offset), geometry::face_silhouettes through core/cpp/bridge/face_outline.cpp. Tests: core/model-tests/drawing-views/src/silhouette_tests.rs (a quarter torus seen along its axis: its outer outline a radius of 70, the vertical dimension from its bottom edge to the top of its outline 70, then 80 when the bend grows, broken in words when the outline is gone; a cylinder seen from the side: the top of its outline as a second pick, 30 then 32; a section’s and a detail’s labels dragged, moved with their views, put back and kept in the file), tools/ui-drawing-curved-outline-test.sh (the shared tools/ui-scripts/drawing-curved-outline.mitcad-ui, also app.ui-windows-drawing-curved-outline and app.ui-macos-drawing-curved-outline).

Bill of Materials kinds and the Sheet Metal list (mitcad#1980)

A Bill of Materials says what each component is, lists the sheet-metal parts with their developed blanks, and puts their Flat Patterns on a cut sheet (GitHub mitcad/Mitcad#414; code core/model/src/document/bom_kind.rs, document/properties.rs, api/libraries.rs, api/cut_sheets.rs, core/model-drawing/src/cut_sheet.rs).

Kind is a computed component property (Computed / Kind, read-only, never stored; Properties): the component’s form and origin, worked out from its own bodies at the timeline marker. Each body takes the first of these that holds:

KindWhen
Sheet metalthe body has a valid sheet state that belongs to its current shape (as the sheet_state query checks it)
Build profilethe component is a BUILD part that is a profile or cut to length
Library partthe component is a library part or a BUILD part
Importedthe body has no history: a base feature from an imported file (not the bodies of a design linked as a component)
Solidany other body

All bodies of one kind give the component that kind; bodies of different kinds give Mixed. A component without bodies of its own (a subassembly) is an Assembly; a library or BUILD part without them keeps its own kind. Convert to Sheet Metal makes an imported body sheet metal, so it is then Sheet metal.

Kind is usable wherever properties are: a parts_list query’s properties column (Kind), a drawing parts list’s column (Kind, sortable as any column), property_search (Kind = Sheet metal).

The parts_list query gives each row its kind (a row of one body of a component of several says that body’s kind) and takes a filter:

Field
kindkinds (["Sheet metal", "Imported"], any case): only rows of these; every kind when empty or left out. A kind that is none is refused (there is no kind Gadget; the kinds are Sheet metal, ...)

A filtered answer adds kinds, the filter as read. (A component’s BOM Structure, its filter and the structured and parts-only views: mitcad#1985.)

The sheet_metal_list query (no fields) lists every sheet-metal body at the marker whose component the design places (rows, in the order of the bodies’ ids): body, name (the body’s), component, component_name, quantity (how many times the design places its component), thickness (mm), material (its material’s name, or No material), width and height (the developed blank’s box, mm), area (mm²) and bends, from the body’s Flat Pattern with its own settings and side, or a new pattern’s settings when it has none (Document::developed_flat_pattern); a body whose Flat Pattern cannot be developed has no blank’s values and says why in problem, in words. It changes nothing.

Flat Pattern parts on cut sheets. add_cut_sheet and add_cut_sheet_parts take "flat": true: each body’s part is then its Flat Pattern instead of a face’s silhouette, a new kind of part (flat in the file’s part and in the queries): its developed blank from the body’s own Flat Pattern settings and side, its outline (each region’s exterior and holes, pieces of one line or circle joined again) as cut edges on CUT_OUTER and CUT_INNER, and its bends’ centre lines on BEND_UP and BEND_DOWN as the Flat Pattern’s DXF has them (in the SVG, layers of open paths). A body in bodies may give its own count ({"body": "F6.b0", "count": 2}). A flat part takes no face (refused in add_cut_sheet_parts and edit_cut_sheet_part). Adding a body whose pattern cannot be developed is refused with the reason; a flat part whose body is gone or whose pattern can no longer be developed stays on the sheet with a warning (part 2 (Body1): ...), as a missing part does. The cut_sheet query’s parts add flat and bends (their count), with geometry bend_lines ([{"line": [a, b], "up"}] on the sheet); export_cut_sheet answers bends too.

[{"query": "parts_list", "properties": ["Kind"], "kind": ["Sheet metal"]},
 {"query": "sheet_metal_list"},
 {"cmd": "add_cut_sheet", "flat": true,
  "bodies": [{"body": "F3.b0", "count": 1}, {"body": "F6.b0", "count": 2}]}]

The application’s Bill of Materials window has the filter and a Sheet Metal tab (app/COMMANDS.md, Cut List and Bill of Materials kinds). Tests: core/model-tests/sheet/src/bom_kind_tests.rs (the kinds of sheet-metal, imported, solid, mixed and subassembly components, as the property, the rows and a search; the BOM Structure’s default, an override, a value refused, the filters; the Sheet Metal list of a two-part assembly, one part placed twice; a cut sheet with two flat patterns, one seen from its back, writing their developed outlines to DXF and SVG, a solid refused and parts whose body is gone warned of), core/model-tests/build-frames/src/bom_kind_tests.rs (a BUILD profile Normal and a library cap Purchased, the user’s choice over the library’s), tools/ui-bom-kinds-test.sh and app.ui-windows-bom-kinds (the shared tools/ui-scripts/bom-kinds.mitcad-ui).

BOM Structure and the Bill of Materials’ views (mitcad#1985)

A component’s BOM Structure says how it enters a Bill of Materials (GitHub mitcad/Mitcad#414; code core/model/src/document/bom_structure.rs, document/properties.rs, api/libraries.rs, api/drawing_tables.rs, api/drawing_annotations.rs). It is the property Bill of Materials / BOM Structure (text) and works as a library’s values do: worked out when asked for and never written to the design file, Purchased for a library part that is not cut to length (a BUILD part with a length is made from its stock), Normal otherwise. A value the user sets with set_property in that set and key is stored and overrides it; the property then shows edited with the worked-out value as its source_value (its source_of_value computed). The property gives the five choices; another value is refused (BOM Structure is one of Normal, Purchased, Phantom, Reference, Inseparable, not Maybe), and the set and key are written as here whatever their case.

StructureStructured viewParts-only viewDrawing parts list
Normallisted, numbered, counted; its children below itlisted when it has bodies of its own or nothing below it; its children as partslisted and numbered
Purchasedone line item: its children are not listedone item, its children not listedat parts one item, its children not listed
Phantomnot listed: its children move up to its level, their quantities multiplied by its ownnot listed; its children as partsat top its children are rows at its level (numbered there); at parts its children are rows as any
Referencelisted without an item number, quantity 0, its children not listed; left out of the mass and volumelikewiselisted without a number, REF as its quantity; no balloon; at parts its children are not listed
Inseparablelisted with its children below itone item, its children not listedat parts one item, its children not listed

The parts_list query gives each row its bom_structure and takes:

Field
bom_structurestructures (["Purchased"], any case): only rows of these; every one when empty or left out. A structure that is none is refused (there is no BOM Structure Ghost; the structures are Normal, ...)
viewlist (default: every component, as before), structured (as the assembly nests them) or parts (the parts the design is made of). Another is refused (there is no view tree; ...)

A filtered answer adds bom_structures, the filter as read. A view’s rows are those of the list (the same fields and properties columns) for each component it lists, with level (1 right below the design; deeper in the structured view), item (2, 2.1; null for a Reference), quantity (how many its parent holds in the structured view, how many the whole design needs in the parts-only view; 0 for a Reference), placed (how many times it is placed there, a Reference’s too), bom_structure, and mass (kg; null while a body has no material) and volume (mm³) of one: its own bodies and those of what it holds, References left out. The design’s own bodies are rows of their own after its components. The answer adds view and totals: quantity (the rows’ quantities), mass and volume of the whole design, References left out. The parts-only view lists the hardware to buy for printable bearings (mitcad#577) too, each a numbered Purchased item. group_identical combines equal parts in the views too (mitcad#2215).

A drawing’s parts list (levels top or parts, Tables on drawing views) and its balloons apply the structures as the table above says: the row a body’s balloon takes is the one its structures give it (a Phantom’s child’s own row at top, its Purchased or Inseparable ancestor’s at parts); a balloon on a Reference is broken (Fixture is a reference: its parts list gives it no number) and "balloons": true places none on it.

[{"cmd": "set_property", "owner": "C2", "set": "Bill of Materials", "key": "BOM Structure", "value": "Phantom"},
 {"query": "parts_list", "view": "structured", "properties": ["BOM Structure"]},
 {"query": "parts_list", "view": "parts", "bom_structure": ["Purchased"]}]

The application’s Bill of Materials window has the view and the filter (app/COMMANDS.md, BOM Structure and the Bill of Materials’ views). Tests: core/model-tests/drawing/src/bom_structure_tests.rs (a small assembly with one component of each structure: the structured and parts-only views’ rows, quantities, numbers, masses and totals, a structure changed; a drawing’s parts list at both levels and its balloons), core/model-tests/sheet/src/bom_kind_tests.rs (the default, an override, a value refused, the filter), core/model-tests/build-frames/src/bom_kind_tests.rs (a BUILD profile Normal, a library cap Purchased), tools/ui-bom-structure-test.sh and app.ui-windows-bom-structure (the shared tools/ui-scripts/bom-structure.mitcad-ui: a subassembly set to Inseparable, Phantom and Reference and both views changing).

Print jobs: geometry only or a print project

A slicer’s 3MF (export with dialect, mitcad#2008) is delivered in one of two ways, decided by what is chosen, not by a switch:

  • Geometry only ("delivery": "geometry" in the result): nothing is chosen (every body’s material None, which a body has when neither it nor a component up its path has one; no printer or process profile; no print value set on the design, a component, an occurrence, a body or a plate; no slicer key of the design’s; no filament change at a print height). The file carries the geometry, the placements, the core 3MF colours and each part’s filament slot, slot 1 (MitCad keeps no slot number of a body’s own), in the Bambu family’s Metadata/model_settings.config (with the print plates and their objects when the plates are sent) or PrusaSlicer’s Metadata/Slic3r_PE_model.config, and no project settings: no project_settings.config or Slic3r_PE.config, no stand-in printer, process or filament, no machine G-code. The receiver keeps its own printer, process and filaments. Cura’s parts carry cura:extruder_nr 0 and nothing else.
  • Print project ("delivery": "project"): anything chosen sends the printer, process and materials chosen with their overrides, as the sections above describe. A project names every filament it uses: the slicer’s project format has one list of filaments for the whole project and a slot number per object, so it cannot leave one body to the slicer’s own filament while it sends materials for the others.

export’s print_materials is the print job’s material per body (uid or name): a material id, or null for “None (slicer’s own)”. A body not listed prints with the design’s material. A map with some bodies null and others not is refused in plain words (The slicer's project format cannot leave one body to the slicer's own filament while it sends materials for the others. …). The job’s choice changes nothing in the design.

The print_job query answers what a job sends, before Send:

queryfieldsanswer
print_jobbodies (uid or name, in the list’s order), dialect (the slicer), optional materials (the job’s choices so far per body: a material id or null; bodies not listed take the design’s material, their own or their component’s, else null; unless every body is listed, a mixed list is made sendable: the bodies without a material take the first body’s, so that the list shows what is sent), optional choose ({"body", "material"}: a choice in the list; without body it is Set to all)delivery, status, bodies, common, printer, process, notes, left_out, capabilities, and refused for a refused choice (below)

The rules of choose: Set to all gives every body the material (or null: the way back to geometry only). A material chosen for one body while every body is null goes to every body; with materials chosen, only that body changes. One body set to null while another carries a material is refused: the answer’s refused says why in words (no names or ids) and the materials stay as they were.

The answer: delivery (geometry or project), status (receiver: geometry only, the receiver’s own settings; complete: a printer, a process and every material chosen; partial: some parts come from the receiver’s defaults, or the destination leaves chosen settings out), bodies (body, name, material, material_name), common ({"material", "mixed"}: the job-level value, the material every body has or mixed), printer and process ({"chosen", "name"}), notes (in words, what comes from the receiver’s defaults: no printer, a printer with only MitCad’s own settings, no process), left_out (in words, the chosen settings the destination does not take) and capabilities (project, printer, materials, sends, note).

[{"query": "print_job", "bodies": ["Body1", "Body2"], "dialect": "bambu_studio"},
 {"query": "print_job", "bodies": ["Body1", "Body2"], "dialect": "bambu_studio",
  "choose": {"body": "Body1", "material": "pla"}}]

The export then takes the list as "print_materials": {"Body1": "pla", "Body2": "pla"}.

UltiMaker Cura gets no project stacks: capabilities are sends ["geometry", "extruder_slots", "process_values"] with printer and materials false and a note that Cura uses the printer and materials chosen in Cura. Each body’s slot is its object’s cura:extruder_nr (0-based) and its process values its per-model settings. A chosen printer, materials, or process values Cura has no per-model setting for are listed in left_out and in the export’s warnings.

Tests: core/model/src/print_files/delivery.rs (the list’s rules, the status, Cura’s capabilities), core/model-tests/print/src/print_send_tests.rs (geometry only for every slicer, a job’s material making a project with the stand-in printer’s warning, the mixed job refused, the print_job query’s rules, Cura’s subset, a plate sent as geometry).

New content under hidden parents is shown (mitcad#1995)

A component that only hidden occurrences place cannot be seen, whatever its own light bulb and its occurrence’s say. A command that adds content to such a component, add_feature (a new body), create_component, insert_component (Insert Component, Insert from Library), import_file and paste_new, shows those occurrences again as part of its own undo step, so that what it added can be seen (GitHub mitcad/Mitcad#430: a part inserted from the web into a component under a hidden parent stayed invisible with no word why).

  • What the command added is told from the bodies and occurrences it did not have before: a new occurrence’s component and a new body’s.
  • A component is in sight when it is the root or one of its placements has every occurrence on its path from the root shown; then nothing changes. Out of sight, the hidden occurrences on the path of its first placement are shown, the outermost first.
  • Left as they are: an occurrence that follows a Show When condition (setting its value would drop the condition) and an occurrence the command made itself (an import’s hidden part).
  • One undo step: the command’s, with its label; undo hides the occurrences again with what it added.
  • The reply’s shown_parents lists them: occurrence (uid), name (Fairlead:1) and path (the names from the root, Fairlead:1/Post:1). The application says it in the status bar (“Fairlead:1 was hidden; shown so the new component can be seen.”; a new body for add_feature) and logs Hidden parents shown: Fairlead:1 (by insert_component).

Code: core/model/src/document/hidden_parents.rs (Document::component_in_sight, hiding_occurrences, show_hiding_occurrences), core/model-api/src/hidden_parents.rs (the commands it applies to, run from run_checked_action). Tests: core/model-tests/assembly/src/hidden_parents_tests.rs, tools/ui-hidden-parent-insert-test.sh (the shared tools/ui-scripts/hidden-parent-insert.mitcad-ui, also app.ui-windows-hidden-parent-insert and app.ui-macos-hidden-parent-insert).

Sheet process profiles (mitcad#1939)

A sheet part’s process profile says what it is made of and how: its sheet rules hold it with the rules that go with it (the allowance method, the kerf, the flute). Process-specific logic lives in the profile (core/model/src/sheet/process.rs): the commands it offers, its output layers and its joint defaults.

  • metal (the default): folds with a bend allowance; hems and reliefs.
  • board (cardboard, corrugated board, folding carton, corrugated polypropylene): folds at creases, with a crease table or a measured allowance or deduction per fold; glue flaps, standard boxes, die lines.
  • laser_sheet (plywood, MDF, acrylic): plates are ordinary solids of the sheet’s thickness joined by finger joints, T-nut slots or mortises and tenons; the one bend it has is a kerf bend (a living hinge).
{"cmd":"add_feature","def":{"type":"sheet_rules","process":"board","flute":"C",
 "thickness":4,"bend_radius":0.5,
 "allowance":{"type":"crease_table","rows":[
   {"thickness":4,"flute":"C","direction":"across","deduction":3.2},
   {"thickness":4,"flute":"C","direction":"along","side":"inner","allowance":5.1}]},
 "kerf":0.1,"reference_side":"front",
 "bend_relief":{"type":"round","width":1,"depth":2},
 "corner_relief":{"type":"round","width":1,"depth":2}}}

process is metal, board or laser_sheet; left out, the rules' component’s material gives it: the material’s own sheet_process (create_material and edit_material take it, null takes it away), else its class’s (metal for Metal, laser sheet for Wood and General Plastic), else metal. Board is never guessed from a class: a board material says so by its sheet_process. kerf (mm, at least 0, default 0) is the width the cutting beam takes away: Cut sheets compensate for it, and a kerf bend’s slits take it as their width. flute names the board’s flute for the crease table.

Allowance methods

Every method gives a fold an effective K-factor, the neutral surface’s place in the thickness, so the fold engine, Unfold and the Flat Pattern develop each the same way. A measured value is of a 90 degree fold; other angles use the same neutral radius (allowance / (pi / 2)), so the K-factor is (allowance / (pi / 2) - r) / t.

  • {"type":"k_factor","k":0.44}: K in [0,1].
  • {"type":"bend_allowance","allowance":3.5}: the measured flat length of a 90 degree fold.
  • {"type":"bend_deduction","deduction":0.2}: the measured deduction of a 90 degree fold; the allowance is 2 (r + t) - deduction. A nearly sharp crease (a deduction close to 0) needs more than K = 1 gives: the neutral surface then lies outside the material, which the fold engine takes (the kernel maps the bend’s chart by any positive neutral radius). A deduction for which the fold develops to 0 mm or less is refused in words (“the measured fold gives no bend allowance: …”).
  • {"type":"crease_table","flute":"C","direction":"across","rows":[…]}: each row is thickness, optional flute, direction (along or across the flutes, any when left out), side (inner when the sheet’s front ends up inside the fold, outer, any) and exactly one of allowance and deduction (of a 90 degree fold). A fold takes, among the rows whose flute (the table’s, else the rules’ flute), direction and side match (a row’s missing flute and any match everything), the one of the nearest thickness, a more specific one first. A fold closing towards the front (a negative angle) is inner. A table needs rows; a row with both values or neither fails the rules. No row for a fold is refused in words (“the crease table has no row for a fold of 4 mm board of flute C across the flutes with the front outside the fold”).
  • {"type":"kerf_bend","slit_length":20,"gap":3,"pitch":1.5} (optional slit_width, else the rules’ kerf): a living hinge, below.

Rule slots are allowance.k, allowance.allowance, allowance.deduction, allowance.rows[i].thickness|allowance|deduction, allowance.slit_length|gap|pitch|slit_width and kerf: ordinary parameters (K is unitless, the rest lengths).

A fold’s own allowance

sheet_flange, sheet_bend and sheet_fold take allowance, any of the methods above, in place of the rules’ for that fold (a per-bend override, its slots under allowance.). A crease_table without rows picks the rules’ rows in its own direction (and flute, when it names one):

{"type":"sheet_fold","body":"F3.b0","panel":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},
 "line":{"sketch":"F4","curve":"c1"},"stationary_side":"left",
 "angle":1.5707963267948966,"allowance":{"type":"crease_table","direction":"along"}}

Commands by profile

{"query":"sheet_process"} (optional component, the active one when left out; MCP read-only) gives the profile of the component’s newest sheet rules at the marker, else of its material, and the commands the profiles filter:

{"component":"C0","rules":"F1","process":"board","label":"Board","source":"rules",
 "commands":[{"command":"sheet.corner_relief","available":false,
   "reason":"Corner reliefs are for metal sheet; this part's sheet rules are for board."},
  {"command":"sheet.glue_flap","available":true}, …]}

source is rules, material or default. Without sheet rules every command is available. The reason is in words, as the disabled command’s tooltip shows it. Filtered: Corner Relief and Hem (metal); Glue Flap, Standard Box and Export Die Line (board); Finger Joint, T-Nut Slot, Kerf Bend and Flat Pack (laser sheet). The other sheet commands are offered for every profile.

sheet_bodies adds allowance (the method’s type), process and kerf to each body; k_factor is null for another method than a K-factor.

Output layers

A profile writes each meaning on its preset’s layer (OutputPreset::of): metal CUT_OUTER, CUT_INNER, BEND_UP, BEND_DOWN; board’s die line CUT (outer and inner), CREASE and CREASE_REVERSE (a fold whose inside is on the other side: a reverse crease); laser sheet CUT_OUTER, CUT_INNER, SCORE, ENGRAVE.

Finger Joint 

{"cmd":"add_feature","def":{"type":"finger_joint","bodies":["F1.b0","F2.b0"],
 "finger_width":12,"clearance":0.1}}

Laser-sheet plates that meet at an edge get alternating fingers along it (core/model/src/features/finger_joint.rs). Plates whose faces lie along the component’s axes are planned exactly from their boxes, as below; plates at any other angle from their slabs (each plate’s largest planar face, its axes and its thickness behind it): where two plates’ solids overlap, the overlap is divided along the line their planes meet on (the cross product of their normals), each segment’s slab, wider by the clearance as below, kept to the overlap and cut from the plate that does not own it, a third plate’s overlap at a joint’s end kept by the first of the three. Plates at an angle that only touch, one’s end on the other’s face, are joined where the end meets the face: the end plate’s slab carried on past its end runs into the other plate there, and the end plate grows its fingers into it as for touching plates below. Plates that neither overlap nor touch are refused in words (“the plates do not meet: …”). Two plates meet where their boxes overlap (a corner prism: each plate drawn to the outside of the joint) or touch (one plate’s end against the other’s face). The joint’s region is the overlap, or for touching plates the end’s footprint taken through the other plate’s thickness, and runs along its longest side. Its length is divided into fingers of finger_width (default 2.5 times the joint’s thickness): the odd count nearest to the length over the width (the larger on a tie), or count when given. The first plate in bodies (the second with flip) takes the fingers at both ends of an odd count; end_margin (default 0) keeps that much at each end whole for it. Each plate’s fingers keep their size and the other plate’s slots are wider by clearance (default 0.1 mm) on each side along the joint, so every finger has the clearance on both sides. Touching plates: the end’s plate grows its fingers into the other plate, which loses them with the clearance. With more than two bodies every pair that meets is joined; where three plates meet (a box’s corner) the part of the joint inside the third stays with the plate listed first of the three. Both bodies keep their ids. Refused in words: fewer than two plates, “the two plates do not meet: …”, a count that is not a whole number from 1 to 1000, “the fingers (… mm) are too narrow for the clearance of … mm on each side”, a plate its slots cut apart. Slots are finger_width, count, clearance and end_margin (the count unitless). Volumes with OCCT: cli.sheet_laser_joints.

T-Nut Slot 

{"cmd":"add_feature","def":{"type":"t_nut_slot","body":"F7.b0","face":"F7:side1",
 "mating_body":"F8.b0","screw_diameter":3,"slot_length":12,"nut_width":5.5,
 "nut_thickness":2.4,"nut_distance":6}}

The screw-and-nut joint of laser sheet, beside Mortise and Tenon’s tab and slot (features/t_nut_slot.rs): a slot screw_diameter plus the clearance (default 0.1 mm) on each side wide and slot_length deep from the planar end face, a pocket nut_width plus the clearance on each side across it and nut_thickness plus the clearance on each side deep, its near side nut_distance from the face, both through the plate’s thickness; in mating_body (optional) the screw’s hole, a cylinder of the slot’s width along the face’s normal through that plate. The face’s axes are Mortise and Tenon’s (x along its longest straight edge). count slots (default 1) lie in the middles of equal shares of the face’s length. Refused in words: a face that is not planar, “the nut must be wider than the screw”, “the nut’s pocket reaches past the slot’s end: make the slot longer”, slots that do not fit along the face.

Cut sheets: kerf compensation and nesting

add_cut_sheet and edit_cut_sheet take kerf (mm, 0 to 10; 0 or left out: none); the drawing query of a cut sheet gives it. export_cut_sheet moves each loop’s path half the kerf away from the material, outer loops out and holes in (cut_sheet::kerf_compensated: each loop flattened, its edges moved along their normals, corners mitred, a mitre longer than four times the offset bevelled), so the beam leaves each part at its size.

{"cmd":"nest_cut_sheet","drawing":"CutSheet1","gap":5}

nest_cut_sheet (and add_cut_sheet with "nest": true) places every part by simple automatic nesting (cut_sheet::nest): each turned so that its longer side lies along the sheet’s width when it fits so, then in rows from the sheet’s lower left corner, the tallest first, gap (default 5 mm) apart and from the edges. Parts that do not fit on the sheet are warned about as before. One undo step, “Nest the parts of CutSheet1”.

Kerf bends (living hinges) 

{"type":"sheet_fold","body":"F3.b0","panel":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},
 "line":{"sketch":"F4","curve":"c3"},"stationary_side":"left",
 "angle":1.5707963267948966,"position":"bend_line",
 "allowance":{"type":"kerf_bend","slit_length":20,"gap":3,"pitch":1.5}}

A kerf bend is laser sheet’s one bend: a Fold (or Flange or Bend) whose allowance, its own or the rules’, is kerf_bend. Its neutral surface lies in the middle of the thickness (K 0.5), so the strip unfolds to its mid-thickness length. Its radius is at least the lattice’s least, t p / (2 w) - t / 2 (SlitLattice::min_radius: a row’s slit, w wide, closes at most by its width, so the inside surface may shorten by at most w / p); a fold without a radius of its own takes the larger of the rules’ radius and that least, and a smaller radius of its own is refused in words (“the kerf bend’s radius (5 mm) is smaller than its slit lattice bends to (6.5 mm): space the slits closer or widen them”). w is the lattice’s slit_width, else the rules’ kerf; without either the bend is refused. The bend’s record carries the lattice (lattice of the sheet_state’s bend), and its Flat Pattern bend (flat_pattern’s bends[].slits) has the slits in place of reliefs and its centre line: rows pitch apart across the developed strip (as many as fit, centred), each row’s slits slit_length long with gap between them and from the strip’s material ends (its chords: openings of the strip are kept), every other row shifted by half a period, pieces shorter than the gap left out. The Flat Pattern DXF writes the slits on the inner cut layer. OCCT: cli.sheet_kerf_bend.

Flat Pack 

{"cmd":"add_flat_pack","body":"F1.b0","thickness":6,"finger_width":15,"width":1000,"height":600}

add_flat_pack turns a box solid into the six plates of a laser-cut box: the flat_pack feature (features/flat_pack.rs) and a cut sheet with its plates nested (add_cut_sheet with nest), one undo step “Flat Pack”. The answer has the feature’s uid, its bodies, the cut sheet’s drawing and its warnings. width, height and kerf are the cut sheet’s.

{"type":"flat_pack","body":"F1.b0","thickness":6,"finger_width":15,"clearance":0.1}

The body must be a rectangular block along the component’s axes (its volume that of its box; else refused: “Flat Pack takes a box: …”). Its box is the outside of the flat pack, or with inside the room inside it. The plates are the bottom, the top, the front (smallest y), the back, the left (smallest x) and the right, the bodies F<feature>.b0 to .b5 in that order, each drawn to the outside of its edges, with Finger Joint’s plan at every edge (a corner of three plates kept by the first in that order); the block is removed. finger_width defaults to 2.5 times the thickness, clearance to 0.1 mm. A side not longer than twice the thickness is refused. OCCT: cli.sheet_flat_pack.

Standard boxes 

{"cmd":"add_standard_box","style":"fefco_0201","length":300,"width":200,"height":150,
 "board":"c_flute"}

A board box of a standard style from its options (sheet_process.rs): board rules (process board, a measured bend_deduction), the blank’s outline as a sketch, its creases as another, a Face of the blank and a Fold at every crease, and the Flat Pattern item; one undo step “Standard Box”. The answer names the rules, outline, creases, face, body and folds. length, width and height are inside sizes, mm. The board is board, one of sheet_process’s boards (folding carton 0.5 mm, E, B, C flute and BC double wall corrugated board, corrugated polypropylene 3, 4 and 5 mm), whose thickness, flute and crease deduction are taken unless thickness, flute or deduction are given (the deductions are starting values: calibrate them from a folded sample); without a board, thickness is needed and the deduction defaults to the thickness. radius (the creases’ inside radius) defaults to an eighth of the thickness, glue_flap to 30 mm, tuck to a third of the height, at most 20 mm. "folded": false leaves the blank flat with its creases.

Styles: fefco_0201, the regular slotted box (four flaps at each end, each half the width deep less the thickness); ecma_a20, the reverse tuck end carton (a closing panel with its tuck at the top of one long side and at the bottom of the other, dust flaps on the short sides: its tuck and lock flaps). The blank (blank): the four side panels along x (short, long, short, long) and the glue flap after the last; creases fold at their middle, so two creases are a wall’s straight plus one allowance apart; the long panels’ end creases lie a thickness further out than the short panels’, so their flaps fold over the short panels’; the glue flap folds under the first panel’s free edge and touches it inside; slots between the flaps are a thickness wider than the creases’ strips. The folds run: the short panels’ flaps, then the long panels’ (a stack outermost first, tucks before their closing panels), the glue flap, then the walls from the far end, so that each crease lies on the flat remainder of the blank’s panel when it folds and no earlier bend’s seam lies past a crease outside its ends (a fold refuses that). The slots reach half a crease strip into the band, and the walls’ creases run past the blank at both ends, through the slots, so the whole side past a wall’s crease folds with it. Sheets that lie against each other in the folded box keep a seam gap (a tenth of the thickness, at least 0.05 mm), since a sheet body holds no two walls touching over a face: the long panels’ flaps over the short panels’, the glue flap inside the first panel, a tuck inside its wall. The first panel’s flaps keep half a slot off its free edge, the glue flap and its crease a thickness clear of the flaps’ creases, and a tuck end’s dust flaps clear of the tucks. Flaps that touch each other or a panel (the glue flap, a tuck inside the opposite wall) build: cli.sheet_board_box and cli.sheet_board_polypropylene fold and unfold both styles. Its options are kept in its rules (standard_box: style, sizes, board and the rest but folded and component), so the box is a part with options:

{"cmd":"edit_standard_box","rules":"F1","height":200}

edit_standard_box makes the box’s rules, blank outline and creases again from its options with those given changed (null takes an option away), one undo step “Edit Standard Box”; its Face and Folds name the same curves and follow. Options that change the blank’s shape (another style) are refused: “these options change the shape of the box’s blank: make the box again”. With "component": true, add_standard_box makes the box in a new component of its own, activated (FEFCO 0201 Box, ECMA A20 Carton): a part to save into a library; the answer names it as component.

A Glue Flap is a Flange whose wall is tapered, as glue flaps are:

{"cmd":"add_glue_flap","taper":15,"inset":2,"def":{"type":"sheet_flange","body":"F3.b0",
 "boundary":{"panel":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},"curve":{"type":"sketch","sketch":"F2","segment":"c6[c5,c7]"}},
 "angle":1.5707963267948966,"length":{"mode":"tangent","value":30},"position":"inside"}}

add_glue_flap makes the flange’s profile sketch on its wall (sheet_flange_profile), turns its rectangle into a trapezoid (its root along the edge inset, default 0, in from each end, its sides slanting in by taper degrees, default 15, 0 to 60) and adds the flange with that profile, one undo step “Glue Flap”; the answer has the flange’s uid and its profile. A taper and inset that leave no flap are refused in words. OCCT: cli.sheet_glue_flap; a reverse crease is a fold whose inside is on the sheet’s back: its crease row is matched as inner/outer by its side, and the die line writes it on CREASE_REVERSE.

Die lines 

{"cmd":"export_die_line","body":"F4.b0","path":"box.pdf"}

Writes a sheet’s Flat Pattern as a die line: dxf with the layers of its profile’s output preset (board: CUT, CREASE, CREASE_REVERSE; for cutting tables), or pdf (a page at 1:1 with a 10 mm margin: cuts solid, creases dashed, reverse creases chain-dotted). The format is format or the path’s extension. The answer has path, format, body, process and the DXF layers with their entity counts. A sheet without a valid Flat Pattern is refused with its reasons. CF2 is not written yet.

Marks, profile layers and Flat Pack editing (mitcad#1939)

A cut sheet’s part takes marks (add_cut_sheet_parts with the parts, edit_cut_sheet_part in place of the part’s): [{"sketch":"F9","kind":"engrave"}], kind engrave or score. Each sketch’s curves and text outlines (construction curves left out) are laid on the part along the face it is seen along (on a Flat Pattern part, in its fixed panel’s plane, mirrored for a back view) and placed with it; export_cut_sheet writes them on the part’s profile’s engrave and score layers (ENGRAVE, SCORE for laser sheet and metal; PRINT, SCORE for board) and as SVG layers. A Flat Pattern part’s bend lines take its profile’s bend layers (BEND_UP and BEND_DOWN for metal, CREASE and CREASE_REVERSE for board, SCORE for laser sheet), and a kerf bend’s slits are cut on CUT_INNER in place of its line. A part’s profile is its body’s sheet rules’, else its component’s material’s, else metal. The Materials window’s Sheet Process (By Class, naming the class’s, or Metal, Board, Laser Sheet) sets a material’s sheet_process (edit_material). export_die_line takes marks too, laid on the Flat Pattern’s fixed panel.

A Flat Pack is edited as any feature (edit_feature), its plates made again; its cut sheet keeps its parts.

Panelize

A feature that splits planar faces of a body off as panels of one thickness (mitcad#2005, GitHub mitcad/Mitcad#423), for cabinetry, with add_feature and edit_feature, ordinary parameters, preview, Undo and persistence. The definition is core/model/src/features/panelize.rs, what the document adds (materials, components, names) core/model/src/document/panelize.rs. It has no kernel family of its own: each slab is the geometry kernel’s extrusion of a body face (Kernel::extrude_face) and booleans.

{"type": "panelize", "body": "F1.b0", "faces": ["F1:side3", "F1:side1"], "thickness": "18 mm"}
{"type": "panelize", "body": "F1.b0", "faces": ["F1:top", "F1:bottom"], "thickness": "t",
 "result": "components", "remove_remainder": true}
  • body, faces: planar faces of the body (a face that is not planar fails: a face to panelize is not planar: panels are made of planar faces, the face in its places), each listed once, at least one.
  • thickness (a slot, mm, > 0; the panel thickness must be greater than zero otherwise): each face’s slab is the face extruded this far into the body, intersected with it. Each slab is a body of its own, <feature>.b<i> for the i-th face; several solids of one slab are one body.
  • What is left of the body (the slabs cut off) stays the body, with its id, so the next Panelize works on it: panels made in an earlier step run through the corners, and the order of the steps decides the joints. Nothing left removes the body.
  • remove_remainder (default false): the body left after this step is removed (the block inside a cabinet, on the last step).
  • The slabs of one step must not overlap: faces that meet at an edge go in separate steps. Otherwise the feature fails: the panels of two faces overlap: faces that meet at an edge are panelized in separate steps, the first one running through the corner, both faces in its places, its detail naming them (Kernel::overlap_volumes of the slabs, 1e-6 mm³).
  • result: bodies (default) or components. With components the document adds a component_from_bodies feature right after the Panelize for each panel, in the same undo step: each panel moves into a component of its own, placed where it is. An edit keeps those in step (new faces get one, faces gone and a change to bodies remove them; a component that has features, occurrences or drawings of its own refuses that: Left has features, occurrences or drawings of its own; delete them first, or keep Result Components). They use the panels, so the Panelize is deleted with its dependents.
  • Names: after the recompute, a panel without a name is named by its face’s outward normal in the component’s axes, Left (−X), Right (+X), Front (−Y), Back (+Y), Bottom (−Z), Top (+Z), else Panel <n> (the face’s place in faces), unique among the bodies of its component (Left (2)); the component made for it takes the same name.
  • Materials: when the Panelize is added or edited, each panel without looks of its own takes the body’s material and appearance (with components also the default material of the body’s component, which its own component would not give it).

A cabinet of a box is three steps: the sides, the back, then the top and bottom with remove_remainder. A 600 × 400 × 300 box with 18 mm panels gives sides of 2 160 000 mm³, a back of 3 045 600 mm³ and a top and bottom of 3 878 064 mm³ each, and no remainder.

Tests: core/model-tests/features-solid/src/panelize_tests.rs (the mock kernel’s box booleans: that cabinet, two faces at an edge refused, Result Components and back to Bodies, a thickness parameter changed), tools/ui-panelize-test.sh, app.ui-windows-panelize and app.ui-macos-panelize (the shared tools/ui-scripts/panelize.mitcad-ui on tools/ui-scripts/panelize.json: the cabinet’s three steps on OCCT, each panel’s volume).

Auto Constrain of a sketch (mitcad#2019)

sketch.auto_constrain makes a sketch that exists (an imported DXF, a sketch drawn without inference, one whose constraints were deleted) fully constrained in one edit: first the relations its geometry already has, then driving dimensions for the degrees of freedom still free. One undo step, Auto Constrain <sketch>.

CommandFieldsNotes
sketch.auto_constrainsketch; entities (optional: the curves and points to constrain, c3, p4; the whole sketch when left out); relations (default true), dimensions (default true; not both false); length_tolerance (mm, default 0.01), angle_tolerance (degrees, greater than 0 and less than 45, default 0.5)the editing commands’ fields, and added (how many of each constraint and dimension type, {"coincident": 4, "horizontal": 2, "length": 2}), relations (constraints added plus ends joined), joined (curve ends that became one point), dof (the sketch’s degrees of freedom afterwards) and summary ("8 constraints, 4 dimensions; the sketch is fully constrained", or "…; 4 degrees of freedom left")
{"cmd": "sketch.auto_constrain", "sketch": "F1"}
{"cmd": "sketch.auto_constrain", "sketch": "F1", "entities": ["c3", "c4", "c5"], "dimensions": false, "length_tolerance": 0.05}

Phase 1, relations (relations), in this order, the stronger first:

  1. Curve ends (and lone points, a centre with an end) within the length tolerance of each other: two curve ends become one point, as sketch.add_constraint joins them (mitcad#260); the others get a point-to-point coincident.
  2. midpoint: a point at a line’s middle.
  3. coincident of a point on a curve (a line within its ends, a circle, an arc, an ellipse), away from the curve’s ends.
  4. tangent (with at) where a line and an arc, or two arcs, join with directions within the angle tolerance.
  5. equal radii of circles and arcs (before the lines’ directions: a slot’s lines held level would imply them).
  6. horizontal and vertical lines.
  7. collinear lines; where both directions are held already, an end of one on the other.
  8. perpendicular lines at a corner they share; parallel lines.
  9. equal lengths of lines (not construction lines).
  10. concentric circles and arcs.
  11. symmetric pairs of points about a construction line, a centre line or a sketch axis.
  12. A point at the origin (coincident with the origin point), on the x or y axis (coincident with the axis line).

Every candidate is tried on a copy of the sketch first and kept only when it takes a degree of freedom away, the redundant, conflicting and collapsed counts do not rise (nothing the others imply, not even in part), and the solve leaves every point and radius within the length tolerance of where it was when the command started. A refused candidate is skipped without a word. An angle relation found within the angle tolerance is thus kept only when it moves no point more than the length tolerance. Only what is not fully constrained is tried; with entities, a candidate may refer only to them (and their points), the origin and the axes.

Phase 2, dimensions (dimensions): driving dimensions with the values the geometry has (it does not move), each kept only when it takes a degree of freedom away:

  1. Sizes: length of lines (profile lines first), radius of arcs, diameter of circles, major_radius and minor_radius of ellipses.
  2. angle at a corner of two lines that are neither perpendicular nor parallel within the angle tolerance (its sides the corner’s rays).
  3. Positions, per connected part, the part nearest to the origin first: horizontal_distance and vertical_distance from the origin of the part’s point nearest to the origin (signed where it is on the axis), the angle of its longest line that is neither level nor upright to the x axis, then the distances of any point of it still free.

Each value is placed beside its curve (a length on the outer side of its line, a radius beyond its arc, the positions in rows below and left of the geometry), moved on where it would lie on one placed before. The origin point and the axes are made when a relation or a dimension needs them, and taken away again when nothing came to use them.

Code: core/sketch/src/auto_constrain.rs (SketchEdit::auto_constrain), core/model-api/src/sketch_auto_constrain.rs. Tests: core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_auto_constrain_2019_tests.rs; the application’s Auto Constrain command (app/commands/AutoConstrainCommands.cpp, app/COMMANDS.md) with tools/ui-sketch-auto-constrain-test.sh.

Mesh tools for reverse engineering

Tools that turn a scanned or exported mesh (a mesh body: an STL, OBJ or 3MF file’s triangles, Mesh bodies in surface operations) into geometry to build on (mitcad#1871; the algorithms in core/model/src/mesh_tools/, pure Rust on the mesh’s triangles; the features in core/model/src/features/mesh_tools.rs). Every tool first joins the corners its triangles share (an STL file stores each triangle’s own three corners): vertices within a billionth of the mesh’s size (at least 1e-9 mm) of each other are one, and triangles left without three corners are left out (mesh_tools::joined); Repair counts its own welding instead.

The mesh edits are features in the timeline, as Convert Mesh’s Faceted solid is: each makes new bodies of the mesh body and leaves it as it was, and add_feature (also at a timeline position) hides the mesh body in the same undo step and refuses a feature that fails with its reason, so that nothing changes (document/mesh_convert.rs; a Show When condition on the mesh body stays and is not followed while the edit is in the timeline, as for Convert Mesh). A body that is no mesh body is refused in words (“Decimate works on mesh bodies (triangles from an STL, OBJ or 3MF file); the body picked is not one”; the body’s uid only in the error’s detail for agents). What a feature did is its information (the infos of the feature query), in words. A new mesh body’s one face is <feature>:import(<n>).

Decimate 

{"type": "mesh_decimate", "body": "F2.b0", "triangles": 5000, "tolerance": 0.05, "sharp_angle": "30 deg"}

Fewer triangles, to triangles (a whole number, at least 4) or within tolerance (mm, more than 0 and at most 100), whichever comes first; one of them is needed. Edges are collapsed one at a time, the cheapest first: a vertex moves onto a neighbour (every vertex left is one of the mesh’s), the triangles on the edge go. The cost is the squared distance of the new place from the planes of the triangles the vertex has carried (the quadric error), so a collapse within the tolerance leaves every merged triangle’s plane within it.

  • Outline and sharp edges kept: edges of one triangle (the outline, the rims of holes), of more than two, and edges whose triangles meet at more than sharp_angle (radians; 30 degrees when left out, at most 180) are feature edges. A vertex on none moves freely, one on two only along them (an edge keeps its line with fewer points), one on one or on three or more (a corner) stays.
  • No collapse joins two sheets (the two vertices share a neighbour that is not across the edge), turns a triangle over or leaves one without area.
  • Information: Decimated from 1200 triangles to 600 triangles; the surface moved up to 0.012 mm. Default name Decimate<n>.

Repair 

{"type": "mesh_repair", "body": "F2.b0", "tolerance": 0.01, "max_hole": 10}

A new mesh body repaired, in this order:

  1. Weld: vertices within tolerance (mm, 0 to 1; 0 welds none) of a vertex kept before them are that vertex (the nearest).
  2. Triangles left with two corners the same go (without area), and of triangles on the same three vertices all but the first (lying on another).
  3. Manifold: at an edge of more than two triangles the two largest stay; a vertex where separate fans of triangles touch becomes one vertex per fan.
  4. Orient: the triangles are turned to agree with their neighbours across every edge, a closed shell outwards, an open surface the way most of its area already faced; a piece that cannot be oriented (a one-sided surface) is left as it was, with a warning.
  5. Holes up to max_hole across (mm; the diagonal of the box of the hole’s rim) are filled: ears clipped in the rim’s plane, or a fan to its centre where no ear is free (at most 4096 edges round). Without max_hole no hole is filled.

Information, in words: Welded 478 vertices, removed 1 triangle lying on another, turned 1 triangle to face the same way as their neighbors, filled 1 hole; 1 hole larger than the size to fill left open, or the mesh needed no repair. Default name Repair<n>.

Remove Region 

{"type": "mesh_remove", "body": "F2.b0",
 "lassos": [{"normal": [0, 0, 1], "points": [[0, 0, 20], [30, 0, 20], [30, 30, 20]]}],
 "brush": [[5, 5, 12]], "radius": "2 mm", "triangles": [17, 18], "through": false, "fill": true}

The triangles picked are removed; at least one of these picks them:

  • lassos: polygons of at least 3 points drawn on a plane square to the view (in the component’s coordinates), normal towards the viewer: the triangles whose centre, seen along the normal, lies inside (even-odd rule), of those facing the viewer (their normals within 85 degrees of normal), or all of them with through.
  • brush with radius (mm): the triangles whose centre lies within the radius of a point.
  • triangles: numbers in the mesh after its corners are joined (the stored order, triangles without three corners left out).

With fill the holes the removed triangles leave are filled (any size; a hole the mesh had before stays). Refused: nothing picked (the region picks no triangle of the mesh), everything picked (… nothing would be left), a brush without radius, a lasso of fewer than 3 points. Information: Removed 48 triangles; filled 1 hole. Default name RemoveRegion<n>.

Segment 

{"type": "mesh_segment", "body": "F2.b0", "angle": "20 deg", "tolerance": 0.05}

The mesh split into regions by curvature, one new mesh body per region (<feature>.b0, .b1, …, largest first; faces <feature>:import(<k>)):

  1. Smooth patches: triangles joined across edges where their normals differ by at most angle (radians, more than 0 and at most 90 degrees); edges of one or of more than two triangles end a patch.
  2. A patch within tolerance (mm) of the plane fitted to it is a plane, else within it of the cylinder fitted to it a cylinder.
  3. A patch that is neither is searched for planes inside it (grown from its largest triangles while each new triangle’s corners lie within the tolerance of the region’s plane, kept with at least a twentieth of the patch’s area); what is left, piece by connected piece, is fitted again, and free-form where nothing fits.

At most 500000 triangles and 1000 regions. Information: Found 3 regions: 1 plane, 1 cylinder and 0 free-form regions. Default name Segment<n>.

Fit Surface 

{"type": "mesh_fit_surface", "body": "F7.b0", "surface": "cylinder", "tolerance": 0.05}

A surface fitted to a mesh body (a region, typically one Segment made) as a new surface body built by Kernel::boundary_body and named <feature>:import(<n>). surface: auto (the default, written only otherwise), plane, cylinder, cone, sphere or bspline.

  • Plane: through the points’ mean, square to the direction they spread least along; the rectangle of their extent.
  • Cylinder: the axis first where the triangles’ normals are square to it, then the axis, its place and the radius refined by least squares on the vertices’ distances (Levenberg-Marquardt); a cone likewise with its half angle (its tip may not lie inside the region); a sphere by the algebraic fit, refined. Each is bounded by the vertices’ extent along its axis and around it; a gap round the axis of less than 45 degrees closes it all the way round. Faces of revolution are split into pieces of at most half a turn that share their edges; a sphere’s face reaches at most 89.4 degrees above and below its equator, which runs through the middle of the region.
  • B-spline: a bicubic surface (4 to 12 control points each way) over the vertices’ mean plane, fitted by least squares to their heights over it with a little smoothing, untrimmed; the region must face one side of that plane (the region folds over …).
  • The deviation is the largest distance of a vertex from the surface. auto takes the first of plane, cylinder, sphere, cone and B-spline within tolerance and is refused when none is (no surface lies within the tolerance 0.05 mm of the region; the closest, cylinder, lies up to 0.3 mm from it); a chosen kind is built anyway and warns when it lies farther than the tolerance.
  • Information: Fitted a cylinder of radius 10.002 mm; the mesh lies within 0.012 mm of it. Default name FitSurface<n>.

Mesh sections into sketches

mesh_section (core/model/src/document/mesh_sections.rs) cuts a mesh body by a sketch’s plane and puts the section into the sketch as its own lines, arcs and circles; with count it makes a series of parallel sections, a sketch each:

{"cmd": "mesh_section", "body": "F2.b0", "plane": "F4", "tolerance": 0.05, "count": 3, "spacing": 2}
{"cmd": "mesh_section", "body": "F2.b0", "sketch": "F5"}
  • sketch: the first section goes into it (its plane, in its frame); or plane (as sketch.create names one: xy, a construction plane "F4", {"face": …, "body": …}): a new sketch on it in the active component. One of the two.
  • tolerance (mm, more than 0 and at most 10; 0.05 by default): how far a curve may lie from the section’s points. count (1 to 200; 1 by default) sections in all; spacing (mm, not 0) between neighbours along the first sketch’s normal. The further sketches lie on XY of the first one’s component in a frame of their own moved along the normal (they do not follow the first one’s plane); a plane of the series that misses the mesh makes no sketch (missed).
  • The cut: each triangle the plane crosses gives a segment between the two edges it crosses; segments that share an edge join into polylines, closed ones counter-clockwise. A vertex lying in the plane counts as just above it.
  • The fit: a closed polyline of 8 or more points within the tolerance of one circle is that circle. Otherwise it is cut into runs from its sharpest corner on, each as long as a straight line between its ends or an arc through its ends (its centre on their bisector, fitted to the points between) stays within the tolerance of every point; an arc is taken where it runs half as far again as the line and bulges at least half the tolerance from its chord. A closed polyline’s last and first curves are one where they are the same line or arc.
  • The curves are the sketch’s own (not linked to the mesh; they stay when it changes, as an inserted drawing’s do), neighbouring curves sharing their end points. One undo step for all (Mesh Section, Mesh Sections); a failure takes back what was made. Refused: a body that is no mesh body (Mesh Section cuts mesh bodies …; a sketch’s Intersect cuts solids and surfaces), a mesh body after the sketch or in another component, a first plane that does not cut the mesh.
  • Result: sketches (uids, the first first), names, curves, lines, arcs, circles, missed.

The mesh_stats query 

{"query": "mesh_stats", "body": "F2.b0"}

A mesh body’s counts after its corners are joined: vertices, triangles, open_edges (edges of one triangle), non_manifold_edges (of more than two), holes (loops of open edges), area (mm²) and closed (no open and no non-manifold edge). Refused for a body that is no mesh body.

Tests: core/model/src/mesh_tools/tests.rs (core.model: a noisy cylinder and a noisy box written by the test, as a scanner gives them: sections a circle, four lines and a slot’s two lines and two arcs; decimation to a count keeping the rims and within a tolerance flattening a box; repair welding, orienting, filling and leaving a large hole open; lasso and brush removal; six planes of a box, a cylinder and two planes of a cylinder; cylinder, plane, sphere, cone and B-spline fits and their boundaries), core/model/src/features/mesh_tools_tests.rs (core.model: each feature on the mock kernel, the mesh body hidden in its undo step, the refusals, a series of sections), core/model-api/src/mesh_tools.rs (the command and the query), cli.mesh_tools (tools/cli/tests/mesh_tools.json: STL meshes through the OCCT kernel) and the UI test of every panel, tools/ui-mesh-tools-test.sh (the shared tools/ui-scripts/mesh-tools.mitcad-ui, also app.ui-windows-mesh-tools and app.ui-macos-mesh-tools).

CAM: turning on a lathe (mitcad#1869)

core/cam/src/turning/, core/model/src/document/cam/turning.rs; the design is docs/cam.md, “Turning”. A setup whose machine is a lathe turns its bodies about the spindle axis; the same commands and queries as milling (CAM: setups, operations and machines) carry it.

  • A lathe (cam_machine_put): a machine with "lathe": {"turret_stations", "chuck_diameter", "chuck_length", "axes"} and a turning dialect as its controller (fanuc_turning; a milling dialect is refused, as a turning dialect on a mill is, in words that name the kind the dialect writes for). Its travel and zones are in the lathe’s axes: X the controlled point’s distance from the spindle axis (a radius; Y unused), Z along the spindle. axes (c, live_tools, y, b) are kept for later work and unused. cam_dialects lists the turning dialects with "lathe": true.
  • Lathe tools (cam_tool_put, on a lathe only; milling tools on a mill only): shape {"kind": "turning", "nose_radius"}, {"kind": "boring", "nose_radius"}, {"kind": "grooving", "width", "nose_radius", "inside"}, {"kind": "parting", "width"}, {"kind": "threading", "angle" (60), "inside"}. The number is the turret station (1 to 99, written T0101 with the same offset), diameter the holder’s size (a boring bar’s diameter: it must fit the stock’s bore), flute_length the deepest the insert cuts (4 mm, a grooving insert’s 5, a parting blade’s 25 when left out), length the overhang.
  • A lathe setup: the work Z is the spindle axis, wcs.z an axis or a cylindrical face (the design’s Z through the middle of the bodies when left out), pointing away from the chuck; the work zero on the axis at the part’s face (or at the Z of wcs.origin’s point); stock around_bodies is a bar: side on the radius, top in front of the face, bottom behind the back; or a stock body. lathe {"stock_bore" (a diameter: a tube or a drilled hole), "change_diameter", "change_z" (the tool change position; 50 mm clear of the stock when left out), "program_number" (O1000), "chuck_gap" (how far the jaws are behind the stock's back, for the lathe check)}, cleared by null. cam_setups gives such a setup "turning": true and its work with turning {part, stock_back, change}: the turned profile (outside and bore as chains {x, z, bulge}, x a radius) and the stock.
  • Turning operations (on a lathe setup only; milling kinds refused there, turning kinds on a mill), each with the usual tool, heights (clearance from the stock, 2 mm; retract, 0.5 mm), stock_to_leave (radius), spindle (direction), coolant (flood only on Fanuc) and turning {surface_speed (m/min), max_rpm (the machine's when left out), constant_rpm (use cutting.spindle_rpm), feed_per_rev, depth_of_cut, peck, stock_to_leave_z}:
Kind (kind)FieldsWhat it does
{"type": "turn_face"}depth_of_cut (Z per pass), feed 0.2 mm/revThe front from the stock’s face to the part’s, from outside the stock to the centre (or into the stock’s bore)
{"type": "turn_rough", "side": "outside" | "inside"}depth_of_cut (2 mm or the insert’s), stock_to_leave 0.2 (stock_to_leave_z half of it), feed 0.25Passes along Z, backing off at 45 degrees, then once along the contour; grooves are bridged (left to grooving), a wall leaning back taken as a shoulder; the cycle G71
{"type": "turn_finish", "side"}feed 0.1Once along the contour; G70 over the blocks of an earlier roughing of the same contour
{"type": "turn_groove", "side", "z_from", "z_to"}the groove’s Z, or the groove’s bottom face as the input; peck, feed 0.05Plunges as wide as the insert between the Z, down to the profile there
{"type": "turn_part_off", "z"}z the part’s back when left out; peck, feed 0.05The blade’s side towards the face cuts at the back, down to the axis
{"type": "turn_thread", "side", "pitch", "diameter", "z_start", "z_end", "depth"}the diameter (major outside, minor inside) and the Z, or the threaded face as the input; depth 0.6134 of the pitch outside, 0.5413 inside; depth_of_cut the first pass (a third of the depth)Passes at a constant spindle speed, each the square root of its number deeper, then a finishing pass; the cycle G76
  • Spindle: a constant surface speed (G96) under the limit max_rpm (G50), 200 m/min (150 in a bore, 100 grooving and threading, 80 parting) when left out; threading, and any operation with constant_rpm, at a constant speed (G97): cutting.spindle_rpm, or the surface speed at the thread’s diameter.
  • cam_generate, cam_toolpaths: as for milling, "turning": true; a toolpath’s toolpath.moves lie in the section’s plane in work coordinates ([x, 0, z], x a radius, arcs as short lines, feeds per revolution) for the view, turn_path the moves as computed ([x, z], arcs about center with cw, threading moves with their lead, and the cycle a post may write). The lathe check (findings, when the setup has its placement: its Z is the work zero’s machine Z) finds the station not on the turret, a spindle speed or limit beyond the spindle, a feed (per revolution times the speed) beyond max_feed, the travel, the zones and the chuck.
  • cam_post: the program in the lathe’s dialect (Fanuc: %, the program number, X as a diameter, G99 feeds per revolution, G50/G96/G97, G71/G70 and the two-block G76 when post.canned_cycles, else G1, G2, G3 and G32), read back by the program check before it is given, with its cycles ([["G71", line], ...]).
