A program the check refuses is refused in words (“The written program does not read back as meant: …”).
  • cam_simulate: {"turning": true, work, stock {z, inner, outer}, left, left_at, gouges, rapid_cuts}: the stock’s section cut by the program (radii per Z, resolution apart, 0.05 mm), the most material left over the part, where tools cut into it and rapids that cut.

Refused in words: “The setup’s machine is a lathe: give it turning operations.”, “Turning operations need a lathe as the setup’s machine.”, “The lathe Lathe takes lathe tools only.”, “The stock has no hole for the boring bar: drill it first or give the stock a bore.”, “The part has no groove there.”, “Threading needs a threading tool.” and the like.

BUILD: a part’s automatic name (mitcad#2030)

A placed BUILD part is named after its designation (Profile 30x30 B8 L=1000, the library’s pattern with the part’s values; a second part of the same designation … L=1000 (1), as a free component name). The name follows the designation while it is automatic:

  • Automatic is a name equal to the designation it came from, or that with the (k) suffix a free name adds. The record keeps that designation (named_after, set at placement and at each automatic rename); in a design saved without it, a name equal to the part’s designation before the change (or with the suffix) counts as automatic. A name given at placement (build_place’s name), or set later (rename_component), is the user’s and never changes.
  • When: every command whose step changes what a part’s designation is made of: a typed length (build_edit’s length, Derived Component’s Length, Press Pull’s Edit Instead on its free end), a bound length that follows its face (the face’s part edited), an along-edge member’s edge or offsets (or the face it lies on moving), a length formula’s parameters (set_parameter), a row or the options (build_edit’s config, parameters). The part takes the new designation, made unique among the components (when two parts trade designations in one step, each takes the plain name the other leaves).
  • Where: inside the command’s own step, after its recompute (a bound length’s measured value counts) and before its undo step is kept: one Undo restores the length and the name, and the step keeps its label. A recompute without a command (opening a design) renames nothing; a part the step made, or renamed itself (Swap Fastener, which keeps its own rule), keeps the name the step gave it.
  • Only parts whose source, row or values changed in the step are checked, so an edit of a large frame configures no other source.
  • Renaming does not change the length: a value would detach a bound length, and a name that is not the library’s pattern says nothing. Length and Derived Component change it.
  • A library part (not BUILD) keeps its own rule (its options, row or version changed, set_component_parameters, update_links), with the same comparison: its old designation, or that with (k).

Press Pull on a part’s end. The face_run query (Press Pull continued) gives a cut-to-length BUILD part’s free end a feature_end: {"uid": <its derived_part>, "name": <the component's name>, "type": "derived_part", "input": "length"}. The free end is the one its length moves: not the end it is placed from (its joint’s own frame, end_b for a flipped part, else end_a), and neither end while its length is bound (to a face, or along an edge). Press Pull then offers Edit Instead, which opens Derived Component at its Length; OK sends build_edit with length, so the cut length, the cut list and the name follow.

Code: core/model/src/build/auto_name.rs (DocState::follow_build_designations, called from Document::apply; is_automatic_name), core/model-api/src/press_pull.rs (build_part_end). Tests: core/model-tests/build-frames/src/auto_name_tests.rs (a typed length and its undo, a suffixed name, a user’s name, a bound length, a formula, a row, a design saved before, the face_run ends), core/model-tests/build-timber/src/edge_tests.rs (an along-edge member’s offsets), and the UI test tools/ui-scripts/derived-part-edit.mitcad-ui (Press Pull on a profile’s free end, Linux, Windows and macOS).

Drawings: the dimensioning standard (mitcad#2047)

A drawing’s dimensions are written to ISO 129-1 (the default) or ASME Y14.5. It is the drawing’s, beside its decimals and letters’ height (Drawing defaults, sketches, patterns and turned views); the model’s 3D annotations keep ISO 129-1.

  • Commands. add_drawing takes standard (iso, asme); left out, the template’s (template), else iso. edit_drawing takes standard (undo step Edit Drawing1): every dimension of the drawing follows. The drawing query gives standard. File: the drawing’s defaults.standard, left out for iso, so drawings and files of before open as ISO and are written as they were.
  • Templates. A template’s optional standard is what a drawing made with it starts with, as its projection: the built-in ANSI template’s is asme, ISO’s iso. save_drawing_template keeps the drawing’s.
  • ASME layout. Linear, aligned, angular and ordinate values (their tolerances with them) are written horizontal, reading from the bottom of the sheet: a linear’s or an aligned one’s in a break of its dimension line, an angle’s in a break of its arc, centred there; an ordinate’s beyond its line’s end. A value that does not fit between the arrows (its box and the text gap on each side) goes beyond the line’s end, past an arrow, the line run on to it; an angle’s outside the arc. The text offset keeps its meaning: along the line (the way ISO’s text reads) and across it; the break follows the text while it sits on the line, and a text moved past an end has the line run on to it. Placing and dragging (placed_at, moved) are as under ISO. Radius, diameter of a circle seen end on and leader texts stay as they are (horizontal on a shoulder). The same layout serves the drawing editor and every export (PDF, SVG, DXF, DWG), and the retrieved sketch dimensions and the export’s automatic overall dimensions of a kept drawing.
  • ASME values in inches. When the sheet’s length unit is the inch, values have no unit after them (the title block’s units field names it) and no zero before the decimal point: .44, deviations +.005/-.005, ±.002. Both writers follow: the annotation words (value_text) and Units::length (automatic overall dimensions, retrieved sketch dimensions). Millimetre values under ASME keep their leading zero; ISO drawings keep their text exactly.

Code: core/model/src/drawing/mod.rs (Standard, Units::under, without_leading_zero), def.rs (DrawingDefaults::standard), template_def.rs, core/model-drawing/src/compose.rs (broken_line, unidirectional_middle), annotate.rs (Frame::standard, unidirectional_text, broken_arc), core/model-api/src/annotations.rs (dimension_label), drawings.rs. Tests: core/model-drawing/src/annotate_asme_tests.rs, core/model-api/src/annotations.rs (asme_inch_values_drop_the_unit_and_the_leading_zero), core/model-tests/drawing-views/src/standard_tests.rs, and the UI test tools/ui-scripts/drawing-standard.mitcad-ui (Linux, Windows, macOS).

A drawing’s own hole callouts (mitcad#2054)

A drawing annotation of the type hole_callout (add_drawing_annotation on a view, as the other leaders) writes a hole’s size information on a leader note, picked on the view instead of a hole table:

  • Its pick is one circle seen end on, or a round face seen from the side, of a hole, picked as a center mark’s is (drawing_pick with "type": "hole_callout" wants a circle or a round face). at is where its text goes; it is drawn as a note is, the text on a shoulder at the end of a leader with an arrow, in the drawing’s letters (height: its own).
  • Its arrow (mitcad#2212): on a circle seen end on its text is kept from the hole’s centre, as a diameter dimension’s is (text_offset: the shoulder from the centre, paper mm; stored with "text_from_center": true), and the arrow lands where the line from the shoulder to the centre crosses the circle, so the leader always points at the centre: placed left of the hole the arrow is on its left, and a drag of the text (shift) takes the arrow round the hole; the 45° snap of a leader’s drag (drawing_snap) turns it about the centre. Without at its text goes up and right of the circle’s right side. On a round face seen from the side the arrow stays at the pick’s point nearest where it was clicked, its text kept from it. A callout written before keeps its text where it was drawn: its text_offset (from where its arrow was) is read so when it is drawn, its arrow then pointing at the centre, and stored from the centre at its next move; edit_drawing_annotation’s text_offset is from the centre.
  • Its lines are the model’s hole callout’s (Hole callouts, api/hole_callouts.rs, the engine mitcad_model_drawing::compose::hole_callout), worked out whenever the sheet is drawn, so that they follow the hole’s size, depth and thread: the count of the feature’s holes (4x), the thread of a tapped hole or Ø and the drill, THRU or ↧ and the depth, then the counterbore (⌴ Ø11 ↧ 6.8) or countersink (⌵ Ø12 × 90°); a round face of a thread feature its thread; on a circle that is no hole feature’s, the circle’s Ø. In the sheet’s length unit.
  • Its own texts are format’s before, after and replace, as a dimension’s (edit_drawing_annotation’s format; no decimals, prefix or tolerance, no text: refused). before goes in front of the first line and after after the last, a space between; a line break in either makes a line of its own (the lines of before but its last stand above the first line, the lines of after but its first below the last). A line break at the end of before puts all its lines above the first line ("TYP\n": TYP on a line of its own), one at the start of after all its lines below the last ("\n2 PLACES"; mitcad#2212); edit_drawing_annotation keeps such a line break, the spaces around it and further empty lines trimmed, and the sheet trims each line’s spaces and drops empty lines. They are kept while the hole’s lines change. replace puts the drawing’s own text (its lines split at line breaks) in place of the hole’s lines, before and after kept, so that it no longer follows the hole while set; an empty one (null) is the hole’s lines again.
  • The drawing query gives its entry the hole’s lines as they are now, lines, and on one line each (split at \n) measured, what replace takes the place of (the panel’s placeholder and Measured row); label is what the sheet writes, its lines joined by /.
  • Refused when its pick gives no hole or circle, with the reason in words (a hole callout points at a hole: a circle seen end on, or a round face seen from the side); one whose hole is gone is broken as the other annotations are.
  • One undo step each: Add hole callout 3 to Drawing1, Edit hole callout 3 of Drawing1, Move hole callout 3 of Drawing1. Kept in the design file with its pick and format; drawn into the PDF, SVG, DXF and DWG exports and prints as the sheet draws it (its group hole-callout).
  • keep_drawing_model_items keeps a model hole callout as a drawing hole_callout on the same pick (The model’s items in drawing views).

The application (app/COMMANDS.md, Drawings): the Drawing tab’s Hole Callout (drawing.hole_callout) in the Text group after Note; its panel’s Text Before, Text After, Replace Value and Text Height.

Code: core/model/src/drawing/annotate_def.rs (AnnotationType::HoleCallout and its checks), core/model-drawing/src/annotate.rs (its layout and hole_callout_text), core/model-api/src/drawing_annotations.rs (hole_callout_lines_of, the drawing query’s entry, the keep). Tests: core/model-drawing/src/annotate.rs (hole_callout_tests: the exact lines of a simple, a counterbored, a countersunk and a tapped hole with texts before, after and in place of them, line breaks at their inner ends), core/model-drawing/src/annotate_callout_tests.rs (the arrow on the line to the centre placed left of, above and right of a hole, dragged round it, snapped, a callout written before, a round face seen from the side), core/model-api/src/annotations.rs (a format edit keeping the line break), core/model-tests/drawing-views/src/hole_callout_tests.rs (a counterbored hole’s lines following its diameter and depth, own texts kept, replace and back, a tapped hole, a round face of no hole, a refused pick, the file, undo, a kept model callout), core/model-tests/drawing/src/hole_callout_export_tests.rs (PDF, SVG, DXF and DWG), app/tests/drawing_tools.cpp and the UI test tools/ui-scripts/drawing-hole-callout.mitcad-ui (Linux, Windows, macOS).

In-app tutorials (mitcad#2012)

Tutorials are packages in git repositories, fetched with library_fetch as libraries are (docs/tutorials.md): a repository with mitcad-tutorials.json at its root is kind tutorials, its tutorials folders in tutorials/<id>/ with a tutorial.json each. library_list lists such a clone with name, description and the number of tutorials; library_show gives its tutorials (their manifests). The library pickers and the search leave them out.

CommandFieldsAnswer
tutorial_listurls (optional: only the clones of these sources, matched by repository_key)sources: for each fetched tutorials repository its url, rev (its default branch’s tip), dir, name, description, tutorials (the manifests: id, title, language, version, min_mitcad, license, description, start, designs, sorted by title) and problems (the tutorials left out and why)
tutorial_installurl (a fetched source), id, folder (where the installed tutorials are)id, folder (folder/id), start (the first page’s path), files, tutorial (its manifest), rev: the tutorial’s folder at the source’s tip written anew (an earlier one replaced once all is written), with .mitcad-tutorial-source.json (url, rev, version) beside it. Symbolic links and submodules are refused, and so is a tutorial over 2000 files or 100 MB

Make Driven and Make Driving on a sketch dimension (mitcad#2055)

sketch.set_driven (dimension, driven, default true) is one undo step named by the switch: Make Driven in Sketch1 when it makes a driving dimension driven, Make Driving in Sketch1 when it makes a driven one driving (before, both were “Change Dimension in Sketch1”), as sketch3d.set_driven names its steps. Driving again keeps the measured value; a driving dimension that would over-constrain the sketch is refused in words and the dimension stays driven. The sketch’s context menu on one selected dimension sends it (app/COMMANDS.md, Sketch Dimension).

BUILD: drags and travel limits (mitcad#2088)

A frame BUILD placed stays put when something is dragged, follows its parameters and Placement’s edits, and a carriage slides on its rail within limits (GitHub mitcad/Mitcad#411).

Drags leave placed parts at their Offset. The joint BUILD places a part with (on a side, an end, a plane or a face; a connector’s and its fasteners’) keeps its driven values under a drag: its Offset, From and Rotate change only through Placement (build_edit).

  • joint_drag and drag_occurrence solve those joints with each driven motion held at its value (its limits pinned there for the drag), so a drag of anything else moves no part of the frame, and a drag past a carriage’s limit does not push its rail along its slot.
  • A drag of a part BUILD joined (any but a carriage), or of a frame’s grounded first part, is refused in words that say to use Placement: Arm:1 stays where it was placed: move it with Placement. A part freed of a removed part (no joint, not grounded, mitcad#1811) drags as any other.
  • The joints query’s degrees-of-freedom units and joint_dof carry the refusal as held (the application’s drag hint shows it before a drag starts).
  • Nothing is grounded to hold a frame: a Placement edit of a lower profile moves it and every part placed on it, and a length change of a target keeps a part placed from its end B at its offset from there.

Travel limits for a carriage. A part placed by its linear.mate (a carriage on its rail, a slider in a slot) whose joint slides along a part cut to length gets limits on its slide (limits.tx):

  • by default from where it is flush with the target’s end A (its frame its reach behind the frame from end A, a number) to where it is flush with end B (an expression of the target’s length parameter, d12 - 20 for a carriage 40 long about its frame), so that they follow the target’s length;
  • build_place’s and build_edit’s limits ({"min", "max"}, lengths from end A to the part’s frame, each left out or null for its default) set them; limits for a part that does not slide on another is refused (… does not slide along another part: it has no travel limits), Min greater than Max too;
  • its slide stays draggable (the one exception to the rule above), within them: a drag past a limit stops it there;
  • a placement offset outside them is refused in words (the offset puts Carriage beyond its travel on Rail: it goes between Min and Max of its travel limits); a click past them puts the part at the nearer one; a build_edit of the limits that leaves the part outside them is refused;
  • a turn (build_edit’s rotate) takes the new reach’s default for each limit that was its default.

build_parts gives such a part slides and limits (min, max and the defaults, in mm); BUILD’s Placement shows them as Min and Max (empty while a limit is its default), and Linear Component offers them for a carriage.

Joint names. A joint BUILD makes is named <part> on <target>, after the components on its two sides (MGN12H on MGN12 L400; a connector’s after the connector and profile a; a part on the host’s own geometry after the host). It follows their names (the automatic ones of mitcad#2030 and a rename) in the step that changes them, while the joint has the name BUILD gave it; a joint renamed by the user keeps its name. Names need not be unique (feature names are not). A design saved before keeps its joints' Joint<n> names.

Code: core/model/src/build/held.rs (which joints a drag holds, the refusal), core/model/src/joints.rs (drag), core/model-build/src/travel.rs (the limits), core/model/src/build/auto_name.rs (DocState::follow_build_joint_names, called from Document::apply). Tests: core/model-tests/build-frames/src/drag_travel_tests.rs, and the UI test tools/ui-scripts/build-drag-travel.mitcad-ui (Linux, Windows and macOS).

Blend Curve in a sketch (mitcad#2107)

sketch.blend_curve (sketch/blend.rs) joins the ends of two curves with a smooth spline that stays attached to them. One undo step, Blend Curve in <sketch>; the work step’s kind is blend_curve.

commandfieldsresult
sketch.blend_curvesketch; curve1, at1 [x, y]; curve2, at2 [x, y] (the end of each curve nearest its pick is joined; curve2 may be curve1, its two ends then joined across the gap); continuity (tangent, the default, or curvature)the editing commands’ fields, made (the spline) and constraints (a tangent or smooth at each end, after a coincident for an end held at a projected point)
{"cmd": "sketch.blend_curve", "sketch": "F1", "curve1": "c3", "at1": [9, 0],
 "curve2": "c4", "at2": [20, 11], "continuity": "curvature"}
  • The spline: one Bézier span by control points, degree 3 for tangent and degree 5 for curvature, so that each end has free control points to meet its conditions. Its first and last control points are the curves’ end points themselves (the existing points, not new ones beside them). The inner ones leave each end along the curve’s direction outward from the end, a fifth (curvature) or a third (tangent) of the distance between the ends apart; for curvature the third control point from each end is set off to the side so that the blend’s curvature there is the curve’s. The blend so runs on from each curve smoothly, never in a cusp back over it.
  • Attached: a tangent (G1) or smooth (G2) constraint with at the end point holds each joint, so when a curve moves, is dimensioned again or the sketch is edited, the solve keeps the blend joined with its continuity. A curve deleted later takes its constraint with it, as any constraint.
  • Which ends: lines, arcs, elliptical arcs and open splines (by control points or fitted), sketch or projected. The solver holds a tangent or smooth between a spline’s end and an elliptical arc’s end (the spline’s leg along the arc’s tangent there, and for smooth the curvature |A| b / |E'(t)|^3 of the arc at that end; mitcad#2107). A projected end (or a pattern’s point) is held, not moved: the blend ends at a new point with a point-to-point coincident on it.
  • Refused in words: a circle, an ellipse or a closed spline (no end), a curve a derived offset computes (it takes no constraints), two picks at the same end of one curve, and ends that already meet. The message names no ids; its detail does for agents.

Sketch blocks

A sketch block (mitcad#2110) is sketch geometry saved as a named block of the design; instances of it go into any sketch of the design, each a rigid copy placed and turned by the sketch’s constraints and dimensions, and an edit of the block remakes every instance. Code: core/sketch/src/block.rs (the block, the instances’ solve, Create, Insert, Explode and Edit Block in a sketch), core/model/src/document/sketch_blocks.rs (the design’s blocks, each command one undo step) and core/model-api/src/sketch_blocks.rs.

{"sketch_blocks": [{"id": 1, "name": "Slot",
  "content": {"version": 1, "base": [0, 0], "entities": [], "constraints": [], "dimensions": []}}]}
{"blocks": [{"id": "k9", "block": 1, "base": "p20", "direction": "c22",
  "entities": {"p3": "p3", "c1": "c1"}, "shape": []}]}
  • The block (the design file’s sketch_blocks): its name (unique), and its content, a copied fragment (Copy and paste of sketch geometry) in the block’s own frame: the base point at the origin, the base direction along +x; its points and curves, the constraints and dimensions between them (a dimension keeps its value and, where it uses other parameters, its expression). Its instances are instances of other blocks inside it (nested blocks), in the content’s ids; a block holding itself, directly or through others, is refused. Projected and intersected geometry and texts cannot go into a block (refused in words); the sketch’s origin and axes are not taken.
  • An instance (a sketch’s blocks, k<n> with the constraints, dimensions, patterns and offsets): the block’s points and curves as ordinary sketch entities (entities maps the block’s ids to the sketch’s), a base point (base) and a base direction (direction, a construction line from the base point). It keeps the block’s entities as it was made from them (shape), so the sketch solves on its own: each solve holds every point of the block at its distance and direction from the base point (an arc’s end by its direction from its centre), circles and ellipses at their sizes, and the direction line at its length. The instance therefore has three degrees of freedom: where its base point is and its turn. The block’s own constraints and dimensions are not in the sketch.
  • Placing it: its points and curves (its base point and direction line among them) are picked for constraints and dimensions with the sketch’s own geometry: a coincident of its base point with a corner, a distance, an angle of its direction line. A constraint or dimension between its own points and curves is refused in words (it keeps its block’s shape: explode it first, or edit the block); horizontal and vertical constraints and distances, which turn or place it, are not its own. Trim, Extend, Fillet and Chamfer of its curves are refused the same way. Deleting any of its entities deletes the whole instance. sketch.remove with its id (k9) deletes it too. Its curves bound profiles and regions as any curves do.
  • Edits of a block remake every instance, in every sketch and in the blocks that hold it, where each is: the entities it keeps (by the block’s ids) keep their sketch ids and the constraints on them; new ones get new ids. A constraint or dimension of a sketch on what the edit removed goes, and the instance keeps it as lost (lost: its type and where its geometry was): the sketch warns “a constraint lost its geometry when its block was edited” with those places, and still solves.
  • Edit Block opens the block: in place (sketch and instance), its geometry free, the block’s constraints and dimensions in the sketch (a turned instance has the block’s horizontals and verticals parallel and perpendicular to its direction line; its horizontal and vertical alignments and distances are left out, said in a warning), or, without them, in a sketch made for the edit (“Block Slot”, on XY, the base point at the origin). Everything drawn while it is open joins the block; finish_sketch_block takes the open geometry, with the constraints and dimensions between it, as the block (instances of other blocks among it nest), and every instance follows; cancel leaves the block as it was. A sketch made for the edit goes when it ends. One block is open at a time.
  • Explode Block (sketch.explode_block) turns an instance into plain sketch geometry with its block’s constraints and dimensions; nested instances stay instances. Its base point and direction line go unless the sketch’s constraints use them.
  • Copy and paste: a copy of a whole instance (sketch_fragment) keeps it as an instance (the fragment’s instances) and brings the blocks it uses (blocks, with those they hold). A paste into the same design makes instances of the same block; into another design, a block of the same name and content is that block, another of the name takes the copy renamed Slot (2), and a missing block is added, in the paste’s undo step.
  • Steps: Create Block, Insert Block, Explode Block and Edit Block are steps of the sketch (create_block, insert_block, explode_block, edit_block).
CommandFieldsNotes
add_sketch_blocksketch, items (points and curves), name (default Block<n>), base [x, y] (default the first item’s first point), angle (radians, default 0)Create Block: the selection becomes block name and an instance of it in place, keeping its ids and the sketch’s constraints that place it (dropped when the sketch would not solve with them); undo step Create Block Slot; result as a sketch edit, with block, name, sketch, instance
rename_sketch_blockblock (a name or a number), namea name another block has is refused
remove_sketch_blockblockrefused in words while it has instances in sketches or blocks
sketch.insert_blocksketch, block, at ([x, y] or a point, default the origin), angle (radians)Insert Block: an instance, its base point at at; refused into the block being edited or a block that holds it; result with instance
sketch.explode_blocksketch, instance (k9)Explode Block
edit_sketch_blockblock, sketch and instance (in place)Edit Block: opens it; result with the sketch it is open in and the instance
finish_sketch_blockcancel (default false)Finish Block: the open block taken (every instance follows; warnings count lost constraints) or left as it was
QueryFieldsNotes
sketch_blocksblocks: id, name, instances (in sketches and blocks), holds (the blocks it holds), entities, outline (its curves as polylines in its frame, for a preview), bounds [x0, y0, x1, y1]; open: sketch, instance, block while a block is being edited

Tests: core/sketch/src/block_tests.rs (a block from a selection, exact geometry of an inserted instance, placing by a coincident and an angle, an edited block followed, a lost constraint, explode, refusals, nesting, an edit in place, copy and paste), core/model/src/sketch_block_tests.rs (two sketches, an edit in place and in a sketch of its own, the lost constraint’s warning, explode, removal, the cycle, the file, an instance’s region extruded), and the UI test tools/ui-scripts/sketch-blocks.mitcad-ui (Linux, Windows and macOS).

Folders of a component’s occurrences (mitcad#2103)

An occurrence can be listed in a folder of its parent component’s occurrences in the browser, as a body can in a folder of its component’s Bodies folder (Folders of the Bodies folder): organization only, like a name. It changes no geometry, timeline, bill of materials, joint, drawing or export; it is kept with the occurrence in the design file ("folder": "Frame" on its entry of occurrences, left out when in none; a file saved before has none) and restored by undo.

CommandFieldsEffect
set_occurrence_folderoccurrence (uid, name or path), folder (a name; null or left out: in no folder)undo step Move Rail:1 to Frame / Take Rail:1 out of its Folder unless nothing changes; nothing recomputed; result folder
rename_occurrence_foldercomponent (uid or name), folder, nameevery occurrence of the component in the folder takes the name; undo step Rename Frame to Profiles, none for the same name; nothing recomputed
rename_body_foldercomponent (uid or name), folder, namethe same for a folder of the component’s Bodies folder: every body of the component at the marker in it takes the name
  • A folder is a name: the occurrences of one parent with the same folder share it, and a folder no occurrence names any more is gone. Folders do not nest. Names are trimmed.
  • Refused: an empty name; an occurrence whose parent is linked from another file (its occurrences come from that file); a rename of a folder the component does not have, or to a name another of its folders of the same kind has.
  • Reparenting an occurrence (reparent_occurrence, Move to Component) leaves its folder: it comes into its new parent in none.
  • The components query lists "folder" on an occurrence in one (left out otherwise).
  • Several occurrences or bodies go into a folder by an array of these commands, one undo step (the application names it Move 3 Components to Frame; Ungroup on a folder’s row is such an array with no folder, Ungroup Frame).
  • The application’s browser lists a component’s folders among its occurrences, before the occurrences in no folder, in the order of their first occurrences, each with its occurrences under it in the model’s order; a folder’s eye shows whether an occurrence in it is shown and shows or hides them all (their light bulbs, one undo step: Hide Frame; occurrences that follow Show When stay as they are).

Code: core/model/src/document/occurrence_folders.rs (Document::set_occurrence_folder, rename_occurrence_folder, rename_body_folder), core/model/src/document/reparent.rs (take), the browser’s rows in app/browser/BrowserPanel.cpp and app/browser/BrowserOrder.cpp. Tests: core.model (core/model-tests/assembly/src/occurrence_folder_tests.rs), app.unit (browser_roles.cpp, browser_order.cpp), the UI test tools/ui-browser-folders-test.sh.

The order of occurrences among their siblings (mitcad#2104)

A parent component’s occurrences are kept in an order: the order the browser and the queries (components, instances) list them in, kept in the design file by the order of occurrences (a file saved before opens as it is). A new occurrence comes last.

CommandFieldsEffect
reorder_occurrenceoccurrence (uid, name or path), index (its new place among the occurrences of its parent, counted without those moved; 0: first), with (other occurrences of the same parent that follow it, in this order; default none)undo step Reorder Arm:2 (several: Reorder 3 Components) unless the order does not change; nothing recomputed; result index (its place now)
  • Placements, joints, rigid groups and the timeline stay as they are; only the order changes. The occurrences of other parents keep their places in occurrences.
  • Refused: an index past the end (more than the number of the parent’s other occurrences); occurrences of different parents; a parent linked from another file (its order is the file’s).
  • The browser’s folders (mitcad#2103) keep their places: the application moves a row within its folder by placing the folder’s occurrences together where its first one is (with), so that the folders stay in the order of their first occurrences.

Code: core/model/src/document/occurrence_order.rs (Document::reorder_occurrences, occurrence_index), the browser’s drag and Move Up / Move Down in app/browser/BrowserOrder.cpp (moveCommands) and app/browser/BrowserController.cpp (reorderOccurrences). Tests: core.model (core/model-tests/assembly/src/occurrence_order_tests.rs), app.unit (browser_order.cpp, browser_roles.cpp), the UI test tools/ui-browser-reorder-test.sh.

Assembly cuts (mitcad#2131)

A Cut made in an assembly may machine occurrences of components whose definition it may not change: a linked component (or one inside a linked component) and a component placed more than once. The cut changes each such occurrence it reaches, there only: a weldment drilled as a whole while each part’s own design keeps its undersized hole.

  • Which features: Extrude (Operation Cut), Revolve (Operation Cut) and Hole, with a cut_scope (Assembly scope for Extrude Cut above; revolve and hole take the same field, mitcad#2131). A hole with a scope cuts no modelled or taper thread (refused: holes with a cut_scope cut no modelled or taper thread; make the thread cosmetic); a surface revolution takes no scope.
  • Opt in, by name: an occurrence is machined when an explicit scope includes it. An automatic scope leaves such occurrences out, as before: their rows in cut_targets have eligible: false, a reason (Linked component, so it is left out; check it to machine this occurrence in this assembly only. Its design stays as it is. or Placed more than once, so it is left out; check it to machine this occurrence only. The other occurrences stay as they are.) and "assembly_cut": true; the Affected components list lets such a row be checked, which turns the scope explicit with it, as a row that moves through joints (mitcad#1789). So every saved cut keeps what it cut. An included occurrence to machine is a row with eligible: true and the note Machined in this assembly; its own design stays as it is.
  • Where the cut lies on the part is kept with the scope: cut_scope.frames, one {"component", "occurrence", "transform"} per included occurrence it machines, the transform from the cut’s coordinates (its component’s at the context occurrence) into the machined component’s. add_feature and edit_feature fill in the frames missing from where the occurrences are at the cut’s place in the timeline (an edit: where its last evaluation saw them) and drop those of occurrences no longer included. The removed material then stays where it is on the part whatever moves the part afterwards: joints and Drive Joint, drags, motion studies. A scope without frames (written by hand) machines where the occurrences are at the cut.
  • What the cut makes: for each body of an occurrence it machines, the pieces left, each a body of its own made by the cut (its uid is F<cut>.b<n> with n from 2^30 up, the same whatever else the cut reaches), in the machined component’s coordinates. The definition and the linked design’s file stay as they are, and so do the occurrences the cut does not reach: two occurrences of one part may differ in this assembly. A later cut that reaches the occurrence cuts its pieces and replaces them.
  • What shows them: the instances query lists, for a machined occurrence, its pieces in place of the bodies they stand for, each with machined_from (that body’s uid); its name, look and visibility are that body’s. Everything that goes by the instances uses them: the view, drawings of the assembly, STEP, mesh and 3MF exports, mass properties, interference and contact sets. The bodies query and a component’s bodies list the definition only; the Bill of Materials counts the occurrence as the part it machines (one row per part, as before). body_component of a piece is the component it machines; joints and references to a face the cut made name it on its piece.
  • Queries: the components query’s occurrence tree has, for a machined occurrence, machined: {"cuts": [feature uids, timeline order], "bodies": [the definition bodies machined], "note": "Machined in this assembly; its own design stays as it is."}.
  • Update Link reads the part’s new geometry and the timeline applies each cut again by its own definition. A cut that no longer reaches an occurrence it machines leaves it as it is with the warning The cut no longer reaches a component it machines in this assembly; that component is left as it is.; a cut that then machines nothing and includes no other target succeeds with that warning instead of failing.
  • Not followed (yet): features of a multiply placed component’s own definition later in the timeline than the cut do not reach the pieces of its machined occurrences (put them before the cut); copy and paste and Save Component as Design rewrite the scope of an Extrude cut only.

Code: core/model/src/assembly_cut.rs (Machined, MachinedChange, MACHINED_HOLDER, piece_uid), core/model/src/features/extrude_scope.rs (CutScope::discover, apply, keep_frames, machines), EvalContext::bodies_at, the recompute’s Recomputed::machined, Document::instances, machined_occurrences, body_component. Tests: core.model (core/model-tests/assembly/src/assembly_cut_tests.rs, core/model-tests/features-profile/src/extrude_scope_tests.rs), the real kernel’s core/tests/test_bridge.cpp (test_assembly_cut_through_two_linked_plates), the UI tests tools/ui-cut-linked-assembly-test.sh, app.ui-windows-cut-linked-assembly and app.ui-macos-cut-linked-assembly.

Linked parts of a design (mitcad#2130)

A linked insert takes the whole design (as before), or only chosen parts of it: occurrences of the design, each by its path from the design’s root (the form reparent_occurrence uses: O1/O4, or names: Arm:1/Pin:2), and bodies of the design’s root by their uids.

{"cmd": "insert_component", "path": "board.mitcad", "base": "/project/designs",
 "parts": {"occurrences": ["Bracket:1", "Frame:1/Chip:1"], "bodies": ["F3.b0"]}}
  • What comes in. Each chosen occurrence comes in as the design places it, in the design’s coordinates, with the components in it. A component the design places twice comes in once for each chosen occurrence: one of its two occurrences chosen brings that one only. An occurrence chosen inside a parent that is not chosen comes in alone, where the parent’s placement puts it. A body lies in the most particular chosen part it is in. Only visible bodies come in, as a whole-design link takes them; a chosen occurrence the design hides brings nothing while it is hidden.
  • The link records them (ExternalLink::parts, in the design file as the component link’s parts: each occurrence (uids from the design’s root) or body, its name there and the numbers of the bodies it gave, bodies). A design file without parts links the whole design, so designs saved before do not change.
  • With copy_into_project (mitcad#2137): the parts are resolved against the copy, which has the file’s occurrences and body uids, so the link_parts query of the file asked for (before anything is copied) gives the paths and uids to send; the link records them with the copy’s path. A part the file does not have is refused after the copy is made, as any refused insert is (the copy stays).
  • Reading the file again (update_links on opening, update_link: Update Link, Update All Links and the changed-file notice) takes only the chosen parts’ visible bodies; a change elsewhere in the design changes nothing in the link. Show as Envelope (set_link_envelope) makes the envelope of what the link holds; another component shown so is one that links the same parts of the same file.
  • A chosen part the design no longer has keeps its saved bodies, and the read’s messages say so in words, with no ids or paths: Bracket:1 is no longer in board.mitcad; its saved shape is kept.
  • Body ids stay. Each part’s bodies keep their numbers in the base feature (<feature>.b<number>) and their face names where they can, so that what uses one part keeps working when another part is taken out or added; a whole-design link switched to parts gives each part’s bodies the ids they had in the whole design (while the file is unchanged).
  • Refused: parts with "link": false (a copy takes the whole design), with parameters (a design linked with options) and with library; no part at all; an occurrence the design does not have; a body uid that is not a body of the design’s root.
CommandFieldsResult
insert_componentparts (occurrences: paths, bodies: uids) besides its other fieldsas without, plus parts (below)
set_link_partscomponent (a linked component: uid or name), parts (as insert_component’s; null or left out: the whole design), base (the folder of a relative link path; left out: the design file’s)component, changed (false: it linked those parts already, no undo step), parts, messages (a line per chosen part the design no longer has), bodies (the component’s bodies now)
QueryFieldsResult
link_partscomponent (a linked component), or path (a design file, against base), basefile (the file’s name), occurrences (the design’s tree from its root: uid, name, path (uids, O1/O4), visible, children), bodies (the root’s bodies at its marker: uid, name, visible), chosen (the component’s parts; null for the whole design or with path)

parts in a result: {"occurrences": ["O1", "O3/O4"], "bodies": ["F3.b0"], "names": ["Bracket:1", "Chip:1", "Body1"]} (names in the order of the parts: occurrences first, then bodies), or null for the whole design. The components query lists a linked component’s link_parts in the same form.

Choosing again (set_link_parts, Choose Linked Parts…) reads the file from the link’s path, as Show as Envelope does, and changes the choice in one undo step, Choose Linked Parts of <component>; nothing changes when the component links those parts already. A part chosen before keeps its bodies’ ids; one the design no longer has keeps its saved bodies with the message; a new one must be in the design. A design linked with options and a library part are refused.

What used a part no longer chosen. A joint whose origin is on a body of a part no longer chosen keeps the place it had there (its frame, ExternalLink::unlinked, kept with the link in the design file) and gets the warning “the geometry it joins to is in a part of the linked design that is no longer linked; it keeps the place it had there” (in words, no names, ids or paths; the place shows on hover); choosing the part again lets it follow the part again. Sketches and features that used its geometry behave as with any reference to geometry that is gone (a projection keeps its last curves).

Code: core/model/src/document/link_parts.rs (Document::chosen_parts, set_link_parts, link_parts_tree), components.rs (design_shapes_chosen), link_updates.rs, envelope.rs, joints.rs (EnvelopeSide::Unlinked); the dialogs in app/files/FileDialogs.cpp (askLinked, chooseLinkParts). Tests: core.model (core/model-tests/links/src/link_parts_tests.rs), the UI tests tools/ui-link-parts-test.sh, app.ui-windows-link-parts and app.ui-macos-link-parts.

A union holds every body it joins (mitcad#2053)

Every union a union of bodies would return (a Combine’s join, a pattern’s combine; the exact one and each fuzzy one of Unions of many bodies) is checked to hold each of its bodies, whether the geometry kernel warned or not: a point inside each solid of each body (halfway along the inward normal of one of its faces to where the line leaves it; the two deepest of a few such points) must lie in or on the union. A body of which both points lie outside is missing, and the union is wrong. The bodies it holds and the bodies it misses are then united each on their own (each union checked and mended the same way) and the two together, exactly; a union of two that still misses one tries the fuzzy values from 1e-4 mm up to 1e-3 mm (or the join tolerance), and where none holds both the union fails with the union lost material of the shapes it joins. Combine then fails as for any failing union, with that message in the panel and the timeline: the target keeps its shape and the tools stay. The check of the volume against the largest body stays as before.

Before that, a wrong union whose bodies include some that lie wholly inside another body is made again without them, exactly: they add nothing to the union. A body counts as inside another when its box lies in the other’s (1e-3 mm around) and the geometry kernel’s solid classifier puts its inside points, its vertices, points along its edges and points across its faces all in or on the other (within 1e-6 mm); not by a boolean’s volume, which the kernel got wrong for the reported bodies below. That union is taken only where it holds every body, those left out too.

Before, only a union that came out with no solid, or that held less volume than the largest of its bodies where the kernel warned, was wrong. Found on a reported design (GitHub mitcad/Mitcad#463): a STEP file of 31 bodies (a hub, blades, triangles, rods and a ring around them that the triangles and rods run into), joined with the hub as the target, kept the hub and the six blades on it and reported Done; the other 24 bodies were removed with the tools. The cause: six of the bodies are each a rod with three thin fins, two of which touch at their tips along one short edge (an edge on four faces), and five more are each the bare rod of one of them, lying wholly inside it. The kernel’s exact union of such a rod and its finned rod gives nothing of either, without a warning (its intersection of the two is empty, its cut the whole rod, its general fuse loses a piece of the rod); the union of all gave the hub and the six flat blades that touch none of them, and nothing of the 24 others. Left out, the rods add nothing, and the kernel’s exact union of the other 26 holds every body, but it was not valid: each finned rod’s side face (its cylinder) has an inner wire that touches its outer wire at a vertex (where the third fin’s knife edge grazes the rod), and the union of such a rod with a body that trims that face (the ring, a triangle) left a face the kernel could not orient, with an open wire. No fuzzy value and no shape healing (of the finned rods or of the union) mended it. This design’s Join therefore failed in words and kept its bodies, instead of removing 24 of them; the kernel’s split of such a face is mended by mitcad#2170 (below), and the Join gives one body.

Code: geometry/src/union_groups.cpp (points_inside, missing_inputs, lies_inside, contained_inputs), geometry/src/pattern.cpp (MaterialCheck::missing, united). Tests: geometry.join_holds_inputs (candidates that miss bodies and unions that hold them all; blocks inside and overlapping others, a bare rod inside a finned rod, a bare rod’s common with finned rods holding it; from MITCAD_MITCAD_REPORTED the reported join: the five rods found inside the finned rods, the union of the others holding every body, the union never returning a result without some of them, and each of the 31 bodies’ common with the union holding its volume, mitcad#2217).

Texts in a sketch’s DXF and Explode Text (mitcad#2163)

A sketch text (and a QR code, a text with code) is no sketch geometry: the sketch keeps it in texts and lays its outlines out at every solve. Its glyph contours bound profiles, but they are no entities that Trim, Offset and the other sketch tools take. The outline pieces are straight lines and quadratic or cubic Bézier curves; each is exactly a sketch line or a spline of degree 2 or 3 by its control points with the default clamped knots on [0, 1], so both of the following lose nothing. The mapping is one (core/sketch/src/text_explode.rs, piece).

The DXF export. export_sketch writes each text’s and QR code’s outlines with the sketch’s curves: every piece a LINE or a SPLINE (degree 2 or 3) on the layer 0, so a cutting file has the letters and Insert DXF (sketch.import_dxf) reads them back as curves. entities counts them. A sketch that holds only a text is no longer an empty drawing.

Explode Text. sketch.explode_text replaces a text by plain sketch curves where it is laid out now:

CommandFieldsResult
sketch.explode_textsketch, text (t5; a text or a QR code)the editing commands’ fields (entities: the new points and curves; removed: the text), made (the new curves in order: contour by contour, piece by piece), rewritten ({"uid", "name"} of each later feature whose names of the text’s pieces were rewritten), warnings
  • One line per straight piece and one spline per Bézier piece (its control points as points). The pieces of a contour share their end points, so each contour stays a closed chain and the same profile regions come out (the same areas). The curves are unconstrained and not construction. A text’s frame rectangle or path curve stays as it is. A contour whose pieces do not join (the sketch’s “not closed” warning, mitcad#1993) is left out, with a warning.
  • A text that follows a text parameter is exploded with its current string; the parameter stays in the design (only the text’s link to it goes).
  • One undo step Explode Text in Sketch1 and a work step explode_text (work steps). The app logs Exploded text t2 in Sketch1: 46 curves.
  • Later features keep working. The names later features use for the text’s pieces are rewritten to the new curves’ ids, as the 3D sketch conversion rewrites later features’ paths: a profile region whose key names the text’s contours (r{t5.g2.c0}, in a feature’s profile of this sketch) takes the key of the region with the same area and centre after the explode; the faces, edges and vertices of the features that sweep the sketch’s profiles take the new segments (F3:side(t5.g2.c0) becomes F3:side(c12[c11,c13]), F3:end(r{t5.g2.c0}) the new region’s cap; names in keys, a fillet’s edge, the same way). A side face numbered #k among the pieces of one contour (the pieces of a split face are numbered in geometric order) takes the piece whose middle it passes nearest to, on the bodies before the explode. A face without #k means every piece: in a list (a fillet’s edges) it becomes every piece’s, and an edge numbered #k between such faces is the k-th piece’s, in the order the old loop ran. The result’s rewritten lists the features changed; the rewrite is part of the one undo step.
  • A name that cannot be mapped stays as it was and is a warning, as for the other sketch edits that change the name of a region a later feature uses: Fillet2 uses the edge E{…}, whose name changes: check it; nothing is refused for it.
  • Refused in words for a text that does not exist or has no outlines (a text of spaces).

A stencil font needs no bridges; with another font, lines drawn across an exploded text and trimmed (or a text left whole with bridges drawn over it) split its letters into separate profiles.
